chapters.title_en: The Book's Opening Sermon (Khuṭbah) and the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence (Uṣūl al-Fiqh)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [خطبة الكتاب]

الحمد لله القوي القادر، الولي الناصر، اللطيف القاهر، المنتقم الغافر،
الباطن الظاهر، الأول الآخر الذي جعل العقل أرجح الكنوز والذخائر، والعلم
أربح المكاسب والمتاجر، وأشرف المعالي والمفاخر، وأكرم المحامد والمآثر
وأحمد الموارد والمصادر؛ فشرفت بإثباته الأقلام والمحابر، وتزينت بسماعه
المحاريب والمنابر، وتحلت برقومه الأوراق والدفاتر، وتقدم بشرفه الأصاغر
على الأكابر، واستضاءت ببهائه الأسرار والضمائر، وتنورت بأنواره القلوب
والبصائر، واستحقر في ضيائه ضياء الشمس الباهر على الفلك الدائر، واستصغر
في نوره الباطن ما ظهر من نور الأحداق والنواظر حتى تغلغل بضيائه في أعماق
المغمضات جنود الخواطر، وإن كلت عنها النواظر، وكثفت عليها الحجب والسواتر.
والصلاة على محمد رسوله ذي العنصر الطاهر، والمجد المتظاهر، والشرف
المتناصر، والكرم المتقاطر، المبعوث بشيرا للمؤمنين ونذيرا للكافرين،
وناسخا بشرعه كل شرع غابر ودين دائر، المؤيد بالقرآن المجيد الذي لا يمله
سامع ولا آثر، ولا يدرك كنه جزالته ناظم ولا ناثر، ولا يحيط بعجائبه وصف
واصف ولا ذكر ذاكر وكل بليغ دون ذوق فهم جليات أسراره قاصر، وعلى آله
وأصحابه وسلم كثيرا كثرة ينقطع دونها عمر العاد الحاصر. أما بعد فقد تناطق
قاضي العقل وهو الحاكم الذي لا يعزل ولا يبدل، وشاهد الشرع وهو الشاهد
المزكى المعدل، بأن الدنيا دار غرور لا دار سرور، ومطية عمل لا مطية كسل،
ومنزل عبور لا متنزه حبور، ومحل تجارة لا مسكن عمارة، ومتجر بضاعتها الطاعة
وربحها الفوز يوم تقوم الساعة.
والطاعة طاعتان عمل وعلم، والعلم أنجحها وأربحها، فإنه أيضا من العمل
ولكنه عمل القلب الذي هو أعز الأعضاء وسعي العقل الذي هو أشرف الأشياء لأنه
مركب الديانة وحامل الأمانة إذ عرضت على الأرض والجبال والسماء فأشفقن من
حملها وأبين أن يحملنها غاية الإباء.
ثم العلوم ثلاثة: عقلي محض لا يحث الشرع عليه ولا يندب إليه كالحساب
والهندسة والنجوم وأمثاله من العلوم فهي بين ظنون كاذبة لائقة، وإن بعض
الظن إثم؛ وبين علوم صادقة لا منفعة لها ونعوذ بالله من علم لا ينفع وليست
المنفعة في الشهوات الحاضرة والنعم  الفاخرة فإنها فانية دائرة، بل النفع
ثواب دار الآخرة.
ونقلي محض كالأحاديث والتفاسير، والخطب في أمثالها يسير؛ إذ يستوي في
الاستقلال بها الصغير والكبير؛ لأن قوة الحفظ كافية في النقل وليس فيها
مجال للعقل. وأشرف العلوم ما ازدوج فيه العقل والسمع واصطحب فيه الرأي
والشرع، وعلم الفقه وأصوله من هذا القبيل فإنه يأخذ من صفو الشرع والعقل
سواء السبيل، فلا هو تصرف بمحض العقول بحيث لا يتلقاه الشرع بالقبول ولا هو
مبني على محض التقليد الذي لا يشهد له العقل بالتأييد والتسديد.
ولأجل شرف علم الفقه وسببه وفر الله دواعي الخلق على طلبه وكان العلماء
به أرفع العلماء مكانا وأجلهم شأنا وأكثرهم أتباعا وأعوانا؛ فتقاضاني في
عنفوان شبابي اختصاص هذا العلم بفوائد الدين والدنيا وثواب الآخرة والأولى
أن أصرف إليه من مهلة العمر صدرا وأن أخص به من متنفس الحياة قدرا، فصنفت
كتبا كثيرة في فروع الفقه وأصوله، ثم أقبلت بعده على علم طريق الآخرة
ومعرفة أسرار الدين الباطنة فصنفت فيه كتبا بسيطة ككتاب " إحياء علوم الدين
" ووجيزة ككتاب جواهر القرآن ووسيطة ككتاب كيمياء السعادة.
ثم ساقني قدر الله تعالى إلى معاودة التدريس والإفادة، فاقترح علي طائفة
من محصلي علم الفقه تصنيفا في أصول الفقه أصرف العناية فيه إلى التلفيق بين
الترتيب والتحقيق وإلى التوسط بين الإخلال والإملال على وجه يقع في الفهم
دون كتاب " تهذيب الأصول " لميله إلى الاستقصاء والاستكثار، وفوق كتاب "
المنخول " لميله إلى الإيجاز والاختصار، فأجبتهم إلى ذلك مستعينا بالله،
وجمعت فيه بين الترتيب والتحقيق لفهم المعاني فلا مندوحة لأحدهما عن
الثاني، فصنفته وأتيت فيه بترتيب لطيف عجيب يطلع الناظر في أول وهلة على
جميع مقاصد هذا العلم ويفيده الاحتواء على جميع مسارح النظر فيه، فكل علم
لا يستولي الطالب في ابتداء نظره على مجامعه ولا مبانيه فلا مطمع له في
الظفر بأسراره ومباغيه؛ وقد سميته كتاب " المستصفى من علم الأصول والله
تعالى هو المسئول لينعم بالتوفيق ويهدي إلى سواء الطريق وهو بإجابة
السائلين حقيق.

### | [صدر الكتاب]

### | [بيان حد أصول الفقه]

صدر الكتاب اعلم أن هذا العلم الملقب بأصول الفقه قد رتبناه وجمعناه في
هذا الكتاب وبنيناه على مقدمة وأربعة أقطاب، المقدمة لها كالتوطئة
والتمهيد، والأقطاب هي المشتملة على لباب المقصود. ولنذكر في صدر الكتاب
معنى أصول الفقه وحده وحقيقته أولا، ثم مرتبته ونسبته إلى العلوم ثانيا، ثم
كيفية انشعابه به إلى هذه المقدمة والأقطاب الأربعة ثالثا، ثم كيفية اندراج
جميع أقسامه وتفاصيله تحت الأقطاب الأربعة رابعا، ثم وجه تعلقه بهذه
المقدمة خامسا. بيان حد أصول الفقه
اعلم أنك لا تفهم معنى أصول الفقه ما لم تعرف أولا معنى الفقه، والفقه
عبارة عن العلم والفهم في أصل الوضع، يقال فلان يفقه الخير والشر أي يعلمه
ويفهمه، ولكن صار بعرف العلماء عبارة عن العلم بالأحكام الشرعية الثابتة
لأفعال المكلفين خاصة، حتى لا يطلق بحكم العادة اسم الفقيه على متكلم
وفلسفي ونحوي ومحدث ومفسر بل يختص بالعلماء بالأحكام الشرعية الثابتة
للأفعال الإنسانية كالوجوب والحظر والإباحة والندب والكراهة وكون العقد
صحيحا وفاسدا وباطلا وكون العبادة قضاء وأداء وأمثاله. ولا يخفى عليك أن
للأفعال أحكاما عقلية أي مدركة بالعقل ككونها أعراضا وقائمة بالمحل ومخالفة
للجوهر وكونها أكوانا حركة وسكونا وأمثالها، والعارف بذلك يسمى متكلما لا
فقيها.
وأما أحكامها من حيث إنها واجبة ومحظورة ومباحة ومكروهة ومندوب إليها
فإنما يتولى الفقيه بيانها، فإذا فهمت هذا فافهم أن أصول الفقه عبارة عن
أدلة هذه الأحكام وعن معرفة وجوه دلالتها على الأحكام من حيث الجملة لا من
حيث التفصيل، فإن علم الخلاف من الفقه أيضا مشتمل على أدلة الأحكام ووجوه
دلالتها ولكن من حيث التفصيل، كدلالة حديث خاص في مسألة النكاح بلا ولي على
الخصوص ودلالة آية خاصة في مسألة متروك التسمية على الخصوص.
وأما الأصول فلا يتعرض فيها لإحدى المسائل ولا على طريق ضرب المثال، بل
يتعرض فيها لأصل الكتاب والسنة والإجماع ولشرائط صحتها وثبوتها ثم لوجوه
دلالتها الجملية إما من حيث صيغتها أو مفهوم لفظها أو مجرى لفظها أو معقول
لفظها وهو  القياس من غير أن يتعرض فيها لمسألة خاصة فبهذا تفارق أصول الفقه
فروعه وقد عرفت
من هذا أن أدلة الأحكام الكتاب والسنة والإجماع، فالعلم بطرق ثبوت هذه
الأصول الثلاثة وشروط صحتها ووجوه دلالتها على الأحكام هو العلم الذي يعبر
عنه بأصول الفقه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The intellect as a binding faculty—that which restrains, holds back, and comprehends; its core sense is "the rope that ties the camel" (al-ʿiqāl), signifying restraint from error.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellect as the divinely-given instrument of discernment (tamyīz) by which one grasps necessary, theoretical, and religious knowledge; it is the locus of taklīf (moral obligation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes the cognitive faculty; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the "heart" as its seat and to the "religion" (dīn) as its fruit.
- Root: ف-ق-ه (f-q-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core linguistic sense is "understanding" (al-fahm) and "comprehension" (al-ʿilm bi-al-shayʾ), applicable to both good and evil.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qurʾān, it signifies deep, penetrating understanding of religious matters; technically, it becomes restricted to knowledge of sharʿī rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) pertaining to the acts of the legally responsible (mukallafūn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The shift from literal (linguistic) to customary-technical (ʿurfī) meaning is a recognized transfer (naql) in the scholarly idiom, not a metaphor.
- Root: د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes guidance and indication; a dalīl is that which points the way (al-murshid).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl, the dalīl is the evidence (adillah) from which rulings are derived—its "indication" (dalālah) is the mode by which the ruling is extracted, whether by explicit wording (ʿibārah), implication (ishārah), or analogical extension (qiyās).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal indication is direct (dalālah ʿalā al-ʿayn); in uṣūl, it is extended metaphorically to the relation between textual evidence and the derived legal norm.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author lists paired attributes (e.g., "the Strong, the Mighty"), each adjective functions as an independent predicate of the implied subject (Allāh), with the conjunction (wāw) coordinating them without ellipsis, preserving the periodic cadence of the khuṭbah.
chapters.translation:
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Praise be to Allah, the Strong, the Powerful, the Protecting Helper, the Subtle, the Subduer, the Avenger, the Forgiving, the Hidden, the Manifest, the First, the Last—He who made the intellect the most preponderant of treasures and stores, and knowledge the most profitable of gains and trades, the noblest of excellences and glories, the most honorable of praises and legacies, and the most praiseworthy of sources and origins. Through its affirmation, pens and inkwells were ennobled; through its hearing, prayer niches and pulpits were adorned; through its inscription, pages and registers were beautified; through its honor, the lesser were advanced over the greater; through its radiance, consciences and innermost thoughts were illuminated; through its lights, hearts and inner visions were enlightened; and in its glow, the dazzling light of the sun upon the revolving sphere was deemed insignificant, and in its inner light, the apparent gleam of pupils and eyes was reckoned small—until its radiance penetrated the deepest depths of hidden thoughts, the troops of inner reflections, even though eyesight faltered before them and veils and screens thickened upon them.

And prayers be upon Muhammad, His Messenger, of pure lineage, manifest glory, mutually supporting honor, and overflowing generosity—sent forth as a bearer of glad tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers, abrogating by his Law every preceding law and every passing religion; supported by the Glorious Qurʾān, which no listener wearies of and no transmitter exhausts, whose profound eloquence no prose-writer or poet can grasp, whose wonders no describer can encompass and no rememberer can recount, and every eloquent speaker falls short of tasting the understanding of the clear aspects of its secrets. And upon his Family and Companions, grant abundant peace, whose abundance exceeds the count of the most encompassing enumerator.

To proceed: The judge of the intellect—the arbiter who is neither dismissed nor replaced—and the witness of the Law—the attested, upright witness—have both declared that this world is an abode of delusion, not an abode of joy; a mount for labor, not a mount for idleness; a place of passage, not a park of delight; a station of commerce, not a dwelling of settlement; a market whose merchandise is obedience and whose profit is success on the Day the Hour arises.

And obedience is of two kinds: action and knowledge. Knowledge is the more successful and profitable of the two, for it too is an act—but it is the act of the heart, which is the noblest of organs, and the striving of the intellect, which is the most honorable of things, for it is the mount of religion and the bearer of the Trust (amānah), since it was offered to the earth, the mountains, and the heavens, and they shrank from bearing it and refused it with utmost refusal. {إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا الْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالْجِبَالِ} [We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains] (Qurʾān 33:72).

Then the sciences are three: a purely rational science that the Law neither urges nor recommends, such as arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and their like—these fall between false conjectures that are blameworthy, for "some conjecture is sin" {إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ} (Qurʾān 49:12), and true sciences that yield no benefit; and we seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not profit. For benefit lies not in present appetites and splendid favors, for these are transient and passing; rather, benefit is the reward of the Hereafter.

And a purely transmitted science, such as hadiths and Qurʾānic commentaries, and sermons in their like are easy, for the young and the old are equal in mastering them, since the power of memorization suffices for transmission, and therein is no scope for the intellect.

And the noblest of sciences is that in which the intellect and revelation are wedded, and in which reasoned opinion and the Law are companions—and the science of jurisprudence (fiqh) and its principles (uṣūl) are of this kind. For it takes from the pure essence of the Law and the intellect the middle path: it is neither a mere exercise of pure reason that the Law does not accept, nor is it built on sheer emulation (taqlīd) that the intellect does not witness with support and right guidance.

And because of the nobility of the science of jurisprudence and its cause, Allah made the inclinations of creation eager for its pursuit, and its scholars are the highest of scholars in rank, the greatest in standing, and the most numerous in followers and helpers. Thus, in the prime of my youth, the distinction of this science with the benefits of religion and this world, and the reward of the Hereafter, summoned me—and it was most fitting that I devote to it the foremost portion of my life's leisure and single out for it a share of my breathing moments. So I authored many books on the branches (furūʿ) of jurisprudence and its principles. Then, after that, I turned to the science of the path of the Hereafter and the knowledge of the inner secrets of religion, and I authored in it comprehensive books like the "Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn" (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), concise ones like the "Jawāhir al-Qurʾān" (The Jewels of the Qurʾān), and intermediate ones like the "Kīmiyāʾ al-Saʿādah" (The Alchemy of Happiness).

Then the decree of Allah Most High led me to resume teaching and imparting knowledge, and a group of accomplished students of jurisprudence requested from me a work on the principles of jurisprudence in which I would direct my attention to reconciling systematic arrangement with rigorous verification, and to steering a middle course between deficiency and tediousness—in a manner that would fall in understanding below the book "Tahdhīb al-Uṣūl" (The Refinement of Principles) due to its inclination toward exhaustiveness and abundance, and above the book "al-Mankhūl" (The Sifted) due to its inclination toward brevity and concision. So I answered their request, seeking help from Allah, and I combined in it systematic arrangement and rigorous verification for the understanding of meanings, for neither can dispense with the other. I composed it and brought to it a subtle, wondrous arrangement that lets the viewer, at first glance, perceive all the aims of this science and enables him to encompass all the fields of inquiry within it. For any science whose student does not, at the outset of his study, gain mastery over its comprehensive principles and foundations has no hope of attaining its secrets and objectives. And I have named it the book "al-Mustaṣfā min ʿIlm al-Uṣūl" (The Distilled Principles from the Science of Jurisprudence). Allah Most High is the One beseeched to grant success and to guide to the straight path, and He is worthy of answering the supplicants.

---

### [The Opening of the Book]

### [Statement of the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence]

Know that this science, titled the Principles of Jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), we have arranged and compiled in this book, building it upon an introduction (muqaddimah) and four pillars (aqṭāb). The introduction serves as its preface and groundwork, and the pillars comprise the pith of the intended purpose. Let us mention, at the opening of the book, the meaning of uṣūl al-fiqh, its definition, and its reality first; then its rank and relation to the sciences second; then the manner of its branching into this introduction and the four pillars third; then the manner of the inclusion of all its divisions and details under the four pillars fourth; then the aspect of its connection to this introduction fifth.

### [Statement of the Definition of the Principles of Jurisprudence]

Know that you will not understand the meaning of uṣūl al-fiqh unless you first know the meaning of fiqh. Fiqh, in its original linguistic coinage (waḍʿ), denotes knowledge and understanding. It is said, "So-and-so understands (yafqahu) good and evil," i.e., he knows and comprehends them. But by the customary usage of the scholars, it has come to denote specifically knowledge of the sharʿī rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) established for the acts of the legally responsible (mukallafūn)—such that, by habitual convention, the title "jurist" (faqīh) is not applied to a theologian (mutakallim), a philosopher, a grammarian, a hadith transmitter, or a Qurʾān commentator. Rather, it is restricted to those who know the sharʿī rulings established for human acts, such as obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), permissibility (ibāḥah), recommendation (nadb), disapproval (karāhah), the validity (ṣiḥḥah) or invalidity (fasād) or nullity (buṭlān) of a contract, whether an act of worship is a make-up (qaḍāʾ) or a performance (adāʾ), and the like.

Nor is it hidden from you that acts have rational rulings—i.e., those perceived by the intellect—such as their being accidents (aʿrāḍ), subsisting in a locus (qāʾimah bi-al-maḥall), being contrary to substance (jawhar), being occurrences (akwān) of motion and rest, and their like. The one who knows these is called a theologian (mutakallim), not a jurist (faqīh).

As for their rulings insofar as they are obligatory, prohibited, permissible, disapproved, and recommended—it is the jurist who undertakes to explain these. So when you have understood this, then understand that uṣūl al-fiqh denotes the evidences (adillah) of these rulings and the knowledge of the aspects of their indication (wujūh dalālatihā) upon the rulings, in a general manner (min ḥayth al-jumlah), not in a detailed manner (min ḥayth al-tafṣīl). For the science of disagreement (ʿilm al-khilāf) is also part of jurisprudence, comprising the evidences of rulings and the aspects of their indication, but in a detailed manner—such as the indication of a specific hadith concerning the issue of marriage without a guardian (al-nikāḥ bi-lā walī) upon the specific ruling, and the indication of a specific verse concerning the issue of omitting the basmalah upon the specific ruling.

As for the principles (uṣūl), they do not address any specific issue, nor do they proceed by way of example. Rather, they address the foundational sources—the Book, the Sunnah, and the Consensus (ijmāʿ)—and the conditions of their validity and establishment; then the aspects of their general indication, whether in terms of their wording (ṣīghah), the import of their expression (mafhūm lafẓihā), the extension of their expression (majrā lafẓihā), or the rational meaning of their expression (maʿqūl lafẓihā)—which is analogical reasoning (qiyās)—without addressing any specific issue. By this, the principles of jurisprudence are distinguished from its branches (furūʿ).

And you have come to know from this that the evidences of the rulings are the Book, the Sunnah, and the Consensus. Thus, knowledge of the methods of establishing these three foundational sources, the conditions of their validity, and the aspects of their indication upon the rulings—this is the knowledge that is expressed as the Principles of Jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Rank of the Science of Jurisprudential Principles and Its Relation to the Sciences
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان مرتبة علم الأصول ونسبته إلى العلوم]

بيان مرتبة هذا العلم ونسبته إلى العلوم
اعلم أن العلوم تنقسم إلى عقلية كالطب والحساب والهندسة وليس ذلك من
غرضنا. وإلى دينية كالكلام والفقه وأصوله وعلم الحديث وعلم التفسير وعلم
الباطن، أعني علم القلب وتطهيره عن الأخلاق الذميمة وكل واحد من العقلية
والدينية ينقسم إلى كلية وجزئية.
فالعلم الكلي من العلوم الدينية هو الكلام وسائر العلوم من الفقه وأصوله
والحديث والتفسير علوم جزئية، لأن المفسر لا ينظر إلا في معنى الكتاب خاصة
والمحدث لا ينظر إلا في طريق ثبوت الحديث خاصة، والفقيه لا ينظر إلا في
أحكام أفعال المكلفين خاصة، والأصولي لا ينظر إلا في أدلة الأحكام الشرعية
خاصة والمتكلم هو الذي ينظر في أعم الأشياء وهو الموجود، فيقسم الموجود
أولا إلى قديم حادث، ثم يقسم المحدث إلى جوهر وعرض، ثم يقسم العرض إلى ما
تشترط فيه الحياة من العلم والإرادة والقدرة والكلام والسمع والبصر وإلى ما
يستغني عنها كاللون والريح والطعم، ويقسم الجوهر إلى الحيوان والنبات
والجماد ويبين أن اختلافها بالأنواع أو بالأعراض.
ثم ينظر في القديم فيبين أنه لا يتكثر ولا ينقسم انقسام الحوادث، بل لا
بد أن يكون واحدا وأن يكون متميزا عن الحوادث بأوصاف تجب له وبأمور تستحيل
عليه وأحكام تجوز في حقه ولا تجب ولا تستحيل، ويفرق بين الجائز والواجب
والمحال في حقه.
ثم يبين أن أصل الفعل جائز عليه، وأن العالم فعله الجائز، وأنه لجوازه
افتقر إلى محدث، وأن بعثة الرسل من أفعاله الجائزة، وأنه قادر عليه وعلى
تعريف صدقهم بالمعجزات، وأن هذا الجائز واقع. عند هذا ينقطع كلام المتكلم
وينتهي تصرف العقل، بل العقل يدل على صدق النبي. ثم يعزل نفسه ويعترف بأنه
يتلقى  من النبي بالقبول ما يقوله في الله واليوم الآخر مما يستقل العقل
بدركه ولا يقضي أيضا باستحالته فقد يرد الشرع بما يقصر العقل عن الاستقلال
بإدراكه إذ لا يستقل العقل بإدراك كون الطاعة سببا للسعادة في الآخرة وكون
المعاصي للشقاوة، لكنه لا يقضي باستحالته أيضا، ويقضي بوجوب صدق من دلت
المعجزة على صدقه، فإذا أخبر عنه صدق العقل به بهذه الطريق فهذا ما يحويه
علم الكلام فقد عرفت هذا أنه يبتدئ نظره في أعم الأشياء أولا وهو الموجود،
ثم ينزل بالتدريج إلى التفصيل الذي ذكرناه فيثبت فيه مبادئ سائر العلوم
الدينية من الكتاب والسنة وصدق الرسول، فيأخذ المفسر من جملة ما نظر فيه
المتكلم واحدا خاصا وهو الكتاب فينظر في تفسيره، ويأخذ المحدث واحدا خاصا
وهو السنة فينظر في طرق ثبوتها، والفقيه يأخذ واحدا خاصا وهو فعل المكلف
فينظر في نسبته إلى خطاب الشرع من حيث الوجوب والحظر والإباحة، ويأخذ
الأصولي واحدا خاصا وهو قول الرسول الذي دل المتكلم على صدقه فينظر في وجه
دلالته على الأحكام إما بملفوظه أو بمفهومه أو بمعقول معناه ومستنبطه، ولا
يجاوز نظر الأصولي قول الرسول - عليه السلام - وفعله.
فإن الكتاب
إنما يسمعه من قوله والإجماع يثبت بقوله والأدلة هي الكتاب والسنة
والإجماع فقط وقول الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم - إنما يثبت صدقه وكونه حجة
في علم الكلام.
فإذا الكلام هو المتكفل بإثبات مبادئ العلوم الدينية كلها، فهي جزئية
بالإضافة إلى الكلام، فالكلام هو العلم الأعلى في الرتبة إذ منه النزول إلى
هذه الجزئيات فإن قيل: فليكن من شرط الأصولي والفقيه والمفسر والمحدث أن
يكون قد حصل علم الكلام لأنه قبل الفراغ من الكلي الأعلى كيف يمكنه النزول
إلى الجزئي الأسفل؟ قلنا: ليس ذلك شرطا في كونه أصوليا وفقيها ومفسرا
ومحدثا وإن كان ذلك شرطا في كونه عالما مطلقا مليئا بالعلوم الدينية، وذلك
أنه ما من علم من العلوم الجزئية إلا وله مباد تؤخذ مسلمة بالتقليد في ذلك
العلم ويطلب برهان ثبوتها في علم آخر.
فالفقيه ينظر في نسبة فعل المكلف إلى خطاب الشرع في أمره ونهيه وليس عليه
إقامة البرهان على إثبات الأفعال الاختياريات للمكلفين فقد أنكرت الجبرية
فعل الإنسان وأنكرت طائفة وجود الأعراض والفعل عرض. ولا على الفقيه إقامة
البرهان على ثبوت خطاب الشرع وأن لله تعالى كلاما قائما بنفسه هو أمر ونهي،
ولكن يأخذ ثبوت الخطاب من الله تعالى وثبوت الفعل من المكلف على سبيل
التقليد وينظر في نسبة الفعل إلى الخطاب فيكون قد قام بمنتهى علمه. وكذلك
الأصولي يأخذ بالتقليد من المتكلم أن قول الرسول حجة ودليل واجب الصدق، ثم
ينظر في وجوه دلالته وشروط صحته.
فكل عالم بعلم من العلوم الجزئية فإنه مقلد لا محالة في مبادئ علمه إلى
أن يترقى إلى العلم الأعلى فيكون قد جاوز علمه إلى علم آخر.

### | [بيان كيفية دوران علم الأصول على الأقطاب الأربعة]

بيان كيفية دورانه على الأقطاب الأربعة اعلم أنك إذا فهمت أن نظر الأصولي
في وجوه دلالة الأدلة السمعية على الأحكام الشرعية لم يخف عليك أن المقصود
معرفة كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، فوجب النظر في الأحكام، ثم في
الأدلة وأقسامها، ثم في كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، ثم في صفات
المقتبس الذي له أن يقتبس الأحكام، فإن الأحكام ثمرات وكل ثمرة فلها صفة
وحقيقة في نفسها ولها مثمر ومستثمر وطريق في الاستثمار.
والثمرة هي الأحكام، أعني الوجوب والحظر والندب والكراهة والإباحة والحسن
والقبح والقضاء والأداء والصحة والفساد وغيرها والمثمر هي الأدلة، وهي
ثلاثة الكتاب والسنة والإجماع فقط. وطرق الاستثمار هي وجوه دلالة الأدلة
وهي أربعة، إذ الأقوال إما أن تدل على الشيء بصيغتها ومنظومها، أو بفحواها
ومفهومها وباقتضائها وضرورتها أو بمعقولها ومعناها المستنبط منها.
والمستثمر هو المجتهد، ولا بد من معرفة صفاته وشروطه وأحكامه. فإذا جملة
الأصول تدور على أربعة أقطاب:
القطب الأول: في الأحكام، والبداءة بها أولى لأنها الثمرة المطلوبة.
القطب الثاني: في الأدلة، وهي الكتاب والسنة والإجماع وبها التثنية إذ
بعد الفراغ من معرفة الثمرة لا أهم من معرفة  المثمر.
القطب الثالث: في طريق الاستثمار، وهو وجوه دلالة الأدلة، وهي أربعة:
دلالة بالمنظوم، ودلالة بالمفهوم، ودلالة بالضرورة والاقتضاء، ودلالة
بالمعنى المعقول.
القطب الرابع: في المستثمر وهو المجتهد الذي يحكم بظنه، ويقابله المقلد
الذي يلزمه اتباعه، فيجب ذكر شروط المقلد والمجتهد وصفاتهما.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ل-ل (k-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Totality, comprehensiveness; that which encompasses all its parts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The universal (al-kullī) as opposed to the particular (al-juzʾī); in theological method, the science that treats the most general subject matter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the whole; metaphorically for the science whose object encompasses all subordinate sciences.
- Root: ن-ز-ل (n-z-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Descent, gradual downward movement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellectual descent from the universal to the particular in demonstrative order.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial descent; metaphorical here for the logical progression from higher principles to derived particulars.
- Root: ق-ل-د (q-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To adorn with a necklace; to imitate blindly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acceptance of a doctrine without demonstrative proof; technical term for the lay follower (muqallid).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for placing a collar; metaphorical for binding oneself to another's authority without independent verification.
- Root: ث-م-ر (th-m-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Fruit; produce of a tree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The result or outcome; in uṣūl al-fiqh, the legal ruling (ḥukm) as the fruit of the evidence (dalīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for botanical fruit; metaphorical for the consequential product of a methodological process.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Gradation (al-Tadrīj fī al-Tartīb) — The text employs a structured descent from the most general (al-mawjūd) through successive divisions to the specific objects of each science, mirroring the syntactic principle of proceeding from the encompassing clause to its subordinate specifications.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the sciences are divided into rational ones — such as medicine, arithmetic, and geometry — and this is not our concern. And [they are divided] into religious ones, such as kalām (theology), fiqh (jurisprudence) and its principles, the science of ḥadīth, the science of Qurʾanic exegesis, and the esoteric science — I mean the science of the heart and its purification from blameworthy character traits. Each of the rational and religious [categories] is divided into the universal and the particular.

The universal science among the religious sciences is kalām, while the rest of the sciences — fiqh, its principles, ḥadīth, and exegesis — are particular sciences. For the exegete (mufassir) looks only at the meaning of the Book specifically; the traditionist (muḥaddith) looks only at the path of establishing the ḥadīth specifically; the jurist (faqīh) looks only at the rulings of the acts of the legally accountable (mukallafūn) specifically; and the uṣūlī (specialist in jurisprudential principles) looks only at the evidences of the Sharīʿa rulings specifically. But the mutakallim (theologian) is the one who looks at the most general of things, namely, the existent (al-mawjūd). He first divides the existent into the eternal (qadīm) and the originated (ḥādith). Then he divides the originated into substance (jawhar) and accident (ʿaraḍ). Then he divides the accident into that which requires life — such as knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight — and into that which is independent of these — such as color, odor, and taste. And he divides the substance into the animal, the plant, and the inanimate, and he explains whether their differences are by species or by accidents.

Then he turns his consideration to the eternal, and he explains that it neither multiplies nor divides as originated things divide; rather, it must necessarily be one, and it must be distinguished from originated things by attributes that are necessary for it (wājib lahu), by matters that are impossible for it (mustaḥīl ʿalayhi), and by rulings that are permissible in its regard (jāʾiz fī ḥaqqihi) — neither necessary nor impossible. And he distinguishes between the permissible, the necessary, and the impossible in its regard.

Then he explains that the origin of the act is permissible for Him, that the world is His permissible act, and that due to its permissibility it stood in need of an originator (muḥdith). And that the sending of messengers is among His permissible acts, and that He is powerful over it and over making known their truthfulness through miracles (muʿjizāt), and that this permissible [matter] has actually occurred. At this point the discourse of the mutakallim comes to an end, and the operation of the intellect reaches its limit. Rather, the intellect indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet. Then the intellect withdraws itself and acknowledges that it receives with acceptance from the Prophet whatever he says concerning God and the Last Day — matters which the intellect is not independently capable of grasping, nor does it judge their impossibility. For the Sharīʿa may bring what the intellect falls short of grasping independently, since the intellect is not independently capable of apprehending that obedience is a cause of felicity in the Hereafter and that disobedience [is a cause] of misery. Yet it does not judge this impossible either. Rather, it judges the obligation of veracity for one whom the miracle has indicated to be truthful. So when he reports concerning [these matters], the intellect affirms him through this path. This, then, is what the science of kalām encompasses.

You have thus come to know that the mutakallim begins his consideration with the most general of things first, namely, the existent, then descends gradually to the detail we have mentioned. Thereby he establishes the principles of all the religious sciences — the Book, the Sunnah, and the veracity of the Messenger. So the exegete takes from the totality of what the mutakallim considered one particular thing, namely, the Book, and considers its interpretation. The traditionist takes one particular thing, namely, the Sunnah, and considers the paths of its establishment. The jurist takes one particular thing, namely, the act of the legally accountable, and considers its relation to the address (khiṭāb) of the Sharīʿa in terms of obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), and permissibility (ibāḥa). And the uṣūlī takes one particular thing, namely, the statement of the Messenger — whose veracity the mutakallim has demonstrated — and considers the manner of its indication of the rulings, whether by its expressed wording (manẓūm), or by its implied meaning (mafhūm), or by its intelligible meaning and what is derived from it (maʿqūl maʿnāhu wa mustanbaṭuhu). The consideration of the uṣūlī does not go beyond the statement and act of the Messenger — peace be upon him. For the Book is only heard from his statement, and consensus (ijmāʿ) is established by his statement, and the evidences are only the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus. And the veracity of the statement of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and its being an authoritative proof (ḥujja) is established in the science of kalām.

Thus kalām is the science that undertakes the establishment of the principles of all the religious sciences. They are particular relative to kalām, and kalām is the highest science in rank, since from it one descends to these particulars. If it is said: "Then it should be a condition for the uṣūlī, the jurist, the exegete, and the traditionist that they have acquired the science of kalām, for before completing the highest universal, how can one descend to the lower particular?" — We say: That is not a condition for one's being an uṣūlī, a jurist, an exegete, or a traditionist, even if it is a condition for one's being an absolute scholar, complete in the religious sciences. For there is no particular science except that it has principles that are taken as accepted premises (musallamāt) by way of taqlīd (authoritative acceptance) within that science, while the proof of their establishment is sought in another science.

Thus the jurist considers the relation of the act of the legally accountable to the address of the Sharīʿa in its command and prohibition. It is not incumbent upon him to establish the proof of the existence of voluntary acts for the legally accountable — for the Jabriyya denied the human act, and a group denied the existence of accidents, and the act is an accident. Nor is it incumbent upon the jurist to establish the proof of the existence of the address of the Sharīʿa, and that God — exalted — has speech subsisting in His essence (kalām qāʾim bi-l-nafs) that is command and prohibition. Rather, he takes the existence of the address from God — exalted — and the existence of the act from the legally accountable on the basis of taqlīd, and he considers the relation of the act to the address. Thus he has fulfilled the limit of his science. Likewise, the uṣūlī takes on the basis of taqlīd from the mutakallim that the statement of the Messenger is an authoritative proof and an evidence whose veracity is obligatory, then he considers the manners of its indication and the conditions of its validity.

So every scholar of a particular science is necessarily a muqallid (authoritative follower) with respect to the principles of his science, until he ascends to the highest science, at which point he has passed beyond his science to another science.

---

EXPOSITION OF HOW THE SCIENCE OF PRINCIPLES REVOLVES UPON THE FOUR POLES

I say: Know that when you have understood that the consideration of the uṣūlī concerns the manners of indication of the scriptural evidences (al-adilla al-samʿiyya) upon the Sharīʿa rulings, it will not be hidden from you that the objective is the knowledge of how rulings are derived (iqṭibās) from the evidences. Therefore, consideration is required: first, of the rulings (al-aḥkām); second, of the evidences and their divisions; third, of the manner of deriving rulings from the evidences; and fourth, of the attributes of the one who derives (al-muqtabis) who is entitled to derive rulings. For the rulings are fruits (thamarāt), and every fruit has an attribute and a reality in itself, and it has a fruit-bearer (muthmir), a fruit-gatherer (mustathmir), and a path of gathering (ṭarīq fī al-istithmār).

The fruit is the rulings — I mean obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), recommendation (nadb), disapproval (karāha), permissibility (ibāḥa), the good (ḥusn) and the evil (qubḥ), qaḍāʾ (adjudication) and adāʾ (performance), validity (ṣiḥḥa) and invalidity (fasād), and others. The fruit-bearer is the evidences, and they are three: the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus only. The paths of gathering are the manners of indication of the evidences, and they are four: for statements either indicate the thing by their wording and composition (ṣīghatuhā wa manẓūmuhā), or by their implication and understood meaning (faḥwāhā wa mafhūmuhā), or by their requirement and necessity (iqtiḍāʾuhā wa ḍarūratuhā), or by their intelligible meaning and the sense derived from them (maʿqūluhā wa maʿnāhā al-mustanbaṭ minhā).

The fruit-gatherer is the mujtahid (one who exerts independent judgment), and knowledge of his attributes, conditions, and rulings is indispensable. Thus the totality of the principles revolves upon four poles:

**The First Pole:** Concerning the rulings — and beginning with them is more appropriate, for they are the sought-after fruit.

**The Second Pole:** Concerning the evidences — namely, the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus — and with them comes the second [pole], for after completing knowledge of the fruit, nothing is more important than knowledge of the fruit-bearer.

**The Third Pole:** Concerning the path of gathering — namely, the manners of indication of the evidences, which are four: indication by the composed wording (dalāla bi-l-manẓūm), indication by the understood meaning (dalāla bi-l-mafhūm), indication by necessity and requirement (dalāla bi-l-ḍarūra wa-l-iqtiḍāʾ), and indication by the intelligible meaning (dalāla bi-l-maʿnā al-maʿqūl).

**The Fourth Pole:** Concerning the fruit-gatherer — namely, the mujtahid who judges by his considered opinion (ẓann), and opposed to him is the muqallid who is obligated to follow him. Thus it is necessary to mention the conditions and attributes of both the muqallid and the mujtahid.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Rank of the Science of Jurisprudential Principles and Its Relation to the Other Sciences

المعاصي للشقاوة، لكنه لا يقضي باستحالته أيضا، ويقضي بوجوب صدق من دلت
المعجزة على صدقه، فإذا أخبر عنه صدق العقل به بهذه الطريق فهذا ما يحويه
علم الكلام فقد عرفت هذا أنه يبتدئ نظره في أعم الأشياء أولا وهو الموجود،
ثم ينزل بالتدريج إلى التفصيل الذي ذكرناه فيثبت فيه مبادئ سائر العلوم
الدينية من الكتاب والسنة وصدق الرسول، فيأخذ المفسر من جملة ما نظر فيه
المتكلم واحدا خاصا وهو الكتاب فينظر في تفسيره، ويأخذ المحدث واحدا خاصا
وهو السنة فينظر في طرق ثبوتها، والفقيه يأخذ واحدا خاصا وهو فعل المكلف
فينظر في نسبته إلى خطاب الشرع من حيث الوجوب والحظر والإباحة، ويأخذ
الأصولي واحدا خاصا وهو قول الرسول الذي دل المتكلم على صدقه فينظر في وجه
دلالته على الأحكام إما بملفوظه أو بمفهومه أو بمعقول معناه ومستنبطه، ولا
يجاوز نظر الأصولي قول الرسول - عليه السلام - وفعله.
فإن الكتاب
إنما يسمعه من قوله والإجماع يثبت بقوله والأدلة هي الكتاب والسنة
والإجماع فقط وقول الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم - إنما يثبت صدقه وكونه حجة
في علم الكلام.
فإذا الكلام هو المتكفل بإثبات مبادئ العلوم الدينية كلها، فهي جزئية
بالإضافة إلى الكلام، فالكلام هو العلم الأعلى في الرتبة إذ منه النزول إلى
هذه الجزئيات فإن قيل: فليكن من شرط الأصولي والفقيه والمفسر والمحدث أن
يكون قد حصل علم الكلام لأنه قبل الفراغ من الكلي الأعلى كيف يمكنه النزول
إلى الجزئي الأسفل؟ قلنا: ليس ذلك شرطا في كونه أصوليا وفقيها ومفسرا
ومحدثا وإن كان ذلك شرطا في كونه عالما مطلقا مليئا بالعلوم الدينية، وذلك
أنه ما من علم من العلوم الجزئية إلا وله مباد تؤخذ مسلمة بالتقليد في ذلك
العلم ويطلب برهان ثبوتها في علم آخر.
فالفقيه ينظر في نسبة فعل المكلف إلى خطاب الشرع في أمره ونهيه وليس عليه
إقامة البرهان على إثبات الأفعال الاختياريات للمكلفين فقد أنكرت الجبرية
فعل الإنسان وأنكرت طائفة وجود الأعراض والفعل عرض. ولا على الفقيه إقامة
البرهان على ثبوت خطاب الشرع وأن لله تعالى كلاما قائما بنفسه هو أمر ونهي،
ولكن يأخذ ثبوت الخطاب من الله تعالى وثبوت الفعل من المكلف على سبيل
التقليد وينظر في نسبة الفعل إلى الخطاب فيكون قد قام بمنتهى علمه. وكذلك
الأصولي يأخذ بالتقليد من المتكلم أن قول الرسول حجة ودليل واجب الصدق، ثم
ينظر في وجوه دلالته وشروط صحته.
فكل عالم بعلم من العلوم الجزئية فإنه مقلد لا محالة في مبادئ علمه إلى
أن يترقى إلى العلم الأعلى فيكون قد جاوز علمه إلى علم آخر.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ل م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, perception, and cognition; the faculty by which a thing is apprehended in its true reality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿIlm as certain cognition (yaqīn) of a thing as it is; in the religious sciences, it denotes the apprehension of divine matters and their derivatives.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes firm, settled knowledge; metaphorically extended to denote the sciences themselves as organized bodies of cognitions.
- Root: ك ل ل (k-l-l) / ك ل ي (k-l-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Totality, comprehensiveness; the whole encompassing all parts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Kullī is that which applies to all particulars under it, as the universal (al-ʿāmm) in contradistinction to the particular (al-juzʾī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): In rhetorical usage, kullī denotes comprehensive scope of inquiry, while juzʾī denotes restricted focus on a single object.
- Root: ج ز ء (j-z-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A part, portion, or constituent of a whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Juzʾī is that which is restricted to a specific subject-matter, as opposed to the universal science which investigates the most general object.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a part; here used technically to denote subordinate sciences whose objects are particularized aspects of the universal object.
- Root: ن ظ ر (n-ẓ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To look, consider, reflect; intellectual examination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Naẓar is the ordered intellectual reflection that leads to knowledge; it is the method of the mutakallimūn.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: visual looking; metaphorical: intellectual consideration and inference (istidlāl).
- Root: ق ل د (q-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To adorn with a necklace; to imitate blindly, to accept authority without proof.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taqlīd is accepting a statement without evidence; in the hierarchy of sciences, the lower sciences accept their principles from the higher science by taqlīd.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: placing a collar (qilādah) on the neck; metaphorical: binding oneself to another's authority in matters of knowledge.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq and Conditional Clauses (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The sentence "فإن قيل... قلنا" (If it is said... we reply) follows the standard pattern of hypothetical objection and response, where the protasis (sharṭ) introduces the opponent's objection and the apodosis (jawāb) delivers the author's rebuttal, governed by the rules of conditionality in Arabic syntax.
chapters.translation:
Know that the sciences are divided into rational ones, such as medicine, arithmetic, and geometry — and these are not our concern — and into religious ones, such as kalām (theology), jurisprudence (fiqh) and its principles (uṣūl), the science of ḥadīth, the science of Qurʾānic exegesis (tafsīr), and the esoteric science (ʿilm al-bāṭin), by which I mean the science of the heart and its purification from blameworthy character traits. Each of the rational and religious sciences is divided into the universal (kullī) and the particular (juzʾī).

The universal science among the religious sciences is kalām, while all other sciences — jurisprudence, its principles, ḥadīth, and exegesis — are particular sciences. For the exegete (mufassir) looks only at the meaning of the Book specifically; the ḥadīth scholar (muḥaddith) looks only at the path of establishing the ḥadīth specifically; the jurist (faqīh) looks only at the rulings of the acts of the legally responsible persons (mukallafūn) specifically; and the uṣūlī (specialist in jurisprudential principles) looks only at the evidences of the legal rulings specifically. But the mutakallim (theologian) is the one who looks at the most general of all things, namely, the existent (al-mawjūd). He first divides the existent into the eternal (qadīm) and the originated (ḥādith); then he divides the originated into substance (jawhar) and accident (ʿaraḍ); then he divides the accident into that which requires life — such as knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight — and that which is independent of these, such as color, odor, and taste; and he divides the substance into animal, plant, and inanimate, and explains whether their differences are by species or by accidents.

Then he examines the eternal and explains that it neither multiplies nor divides as originated things divide; rather, it must necessarily be one, and it must be distinguished from originated things by attributes that are necessary for it (wājibah lahu), by matters that are impossible for it (mustaḥīlah ʿalayhi), and by rulings that are permissible in its regard (jāʾizah fī ḥaqqihi) — neither necessary nor impossible. He distinguishes between the permissible, the necessary, and the impossible in His regard.

Then he explains that the origin of the act is permissible for Him, that the world is His permissible act, and that because of its permissibility it stood in need of an originator (muḥdith); that the sending of messengers is among His permissible acts; that He is powerful over it and over defining their truthfulness through miracles (muʿjizāt); and that this permissible thing has indeed occurred. At this point the discourse of the mutakallim comes to an end, and the operation of the intellect reaches its limit. Rather, the intellect indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet. Then the mutakallim sets himself aside and acknowledges that he receives with acceptance from the Prophet whatever he (the Prophet) says concerning God and the Last Day — matters which the intellect is not independently capable of apprehending, yet it does not judge them impossible either. For the Law (al-sharʿ) may bring what the intellect falls short of apprehending independently, since the intellect is not independently capable of apprehending that obedience is a cause of felicity in the Hereafter and that disobedience is a cause of misery — yet it does not judge this impossible either. Rather, it judges the truthfulness of one whom the miracle has indicated to be truthful as obligatory (wujūb al-taṣdīq). So when he (the Prophet) reports concerning Him, the intellect affirms him as truthful by this path. This, then, is what the science of kalām encompasses.

You have thus come to know that the mutakallim begins his inquiry first in the most general of things, namely, the existent; then he descends gradually to the detail we have mentioned, and therein he establishes the principles of all the religious sciences — namely, the Book, the Sunnah, and the truthfulness of the Messenger. So the exegete takes from the totality of what the mutakallim examined one particular thing, namely, the Book, and examines its interpretation. The ḥadīth scholar takes one particular thing, namely, the Sunnah, and examines the paths of its establishment. The jurist takes one particular thing, namely, the act of the legally responsible person, and examines its relation to the address (khiṭāb) of the Law in terms of obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), and permissibility (ibāḥah). And the uṣūlī takes one particular thing, namely, the statement of the Messenger — whose truthfulness the mutakallim has demonstrated — and examines the manner of its indication of the rulings, whether by its expressed wording (manṭūq), its implied meaning (mafhūm), or the intelligible sense of its meaning and what is derived from it (maʿqūl maʿnāhu wa mustanbaṭuhu). The inquiry of the uṣūlī does not go beyond the statement and act of the Messenger — peace be upon him.

For the Book is only heard from his statement; consensus (ijmāʿ) is established by his statement; and the evidences are only the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus. The truthfulness of the statement of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and its being an authoritative proof (ḥujjah) is established only in the science of kalām.

Thus kalām is the science that undertakes the establishment of the principles of all the religious sciences. They are particular relative to kalām, and kalām is the highest science in rank, for from it one descends to these particulars. If it is said: "Then it should be a condition of the uṣūlī, the jurist, the exegete, and the ḥadīth scholar that they have already acquired the science of kalām, for before completing the highest universal, how can one descend to the lower particular?" We reply: That is not a condition for one's being an uṣūlī, a jurist, an exegete, or a ḥadīth scholar — even if it is a condition for one's being an absolute scholar (ʿālim muṭlaq) filled with the religious sciences. For there is no particular science except that it has principles that are taken as accepted premises (musallamāt) by way of taqlīd within that science, while the proof of their establishment is sought in another science.

Thus the jurist examines the relation of the act of the legally responsible person to the address of the Law in its command and prohibition, and it is not incumbent upon him to establish the proof of the existence of voluntary acts for the legally responsible persons — for the Jabriyyah have denied the human act, and a group has denied the existence of accidents, and the act is an accident. Nor is it incumbent upon the jurist to establish the proof of the existence of the address of the Law and that God — exalted be He — has speech subsisting in His essence (kalām qāʾim bi-l-nafs) which is command and prohibition. Rather, he takes the existence of the address from God — exalted be He — and the existence of the act from the legally responsible person on the basis of taqlīd, and he examines the relation of the act to the address. Thus he has fulfilled the limit of his science. Likewise, the uṣūlī takes on the basis of taqlīd from the mutakallim that the statement of the Messenger is an authoritative proof and an evidence whose truthfulness is obligatory, and then he examines the manners of its indication and the conditions of its validity.

So every scholar of a particular science is necessarily a muqallid (one who accepts authority) in the principles of his science, until he ascends to the highest science, at which point he has passed beyond his science to another science.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of How the Science of Jurisprudence Revolves upon the Four Poles
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان كيفية دوران علم الأصول على الأقطاب الأربعة]

بيان كيفية دورانه على الأقطاب الأربعة اعلم أنك إذا فهمت أن نظر الأصولي
في وجوه دلالة الأدلة السمعية على الأحكام الشرعية لم يخف عليك أن المقصود
معرفة كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، فوجب النظر في الأحكام، ثم في
الأدلة وأقسامها، ثم في كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الأدلة، ثم في صفات
المقتبس الذي له أن يقتبس الأحكام، فإن الأحكام ثمرات وكل ثمرة فلها صفة
وحقيقة في نفسها ولها مثمر ومستثمر وطريق في الاستثمار.
والثمرة هي الأحكام، أعني الوجوب والحظر والندب والكراهة والإباحة والحسن
والقبح والقضاء والأداء والصحة والفساد وغيرها والمثمر هي الأدلة، وهي
ثلاثة الكتاب والسنة والإجماع فقط. وطرق الاستثمار هي وجوه دلالة الأدلة
وهي أربعة، إذ الأقوال إما أن تدل على الشيء بصيغتها ومنظومها، أو بفحواها
ومفهومها وباقتضائها وضرورتها أو بمعقولها ومعناها المستنبط منها.
والمستثمر هو المجتهد، ولا بد من معرفة صفاته وشروطه وأحكامه. فإذا جملة
الأصول تدور على أربعة أقطاب:
القطب الأول: في الأحكام، والبداءة بها أولى لأنها الثمرة المطلوبة.
القطب الثاني: في الأدلة، وهي الكتاب والسنة والإجماع وبها التثنية إذ
بعد الفراغ من معرفة الثمرة لا أهم من معرفة  المثمر.
القطب الثالث: في طريق الاستثمار، وهو وجوه دلالة الأدلة، وهي أربعة:
دلالة بالمنظوم، ودلالة بالمفهوم، ودلالة بالضرورة والاقتضاء، ودلالة
بالمعنى المعقول.
القطب الرابع: في المستثمر وهو المجتهد الذي يحكم بظنه، ويقابله المقلد
الذي يلزمه اتباعه، فيجب ذكر شروط المقلد والمجتهد وصفاتهما.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-و-ر (d-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Circular motion, revolving around a center; the turning of a thing upon its axis.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Cyclical dependence of a discipline upon its constitutive principles; the ordered rotation of inquiry through necessary stages.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical rotation; metaphorical (majāz) for the logical organization of a science around its foundational topics.
- Root: ث-م-ر (th-m-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Fruit, produce, yield of a tree; that which is harvested.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The resultant outcome of a process; in uṣūl, the legal ruling (ḥukm) as the fruit yielded by the evidence (dalīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for botanical fruit; metaphorical for the consequential product of an intellectual operation.
- Root: ق-ب-س (q-b-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taking fire from a source; kindling a flame from another flame.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Deriving a ruling from its evidence; the act of extracting legal norms from scriptural sources.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for igniting fire; metaphorical for intellectual derivation of rulings from proofs.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Maḥdhūf (Ellipsis Restoration) — The phrase "طرق الاستثمار" governs the enumeration of four modes of indication, requiring the reader to supply the implicit copula and distributive structure for the fourfold division.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that once you have understood that the jurisprudent's (uṣūlī) inquiry concerns the modes of indication (wujūh dalālah) of the scriptural evidences (al-adillah al-samʿiyyah) upon the legal rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah), it will not remain hidden from you that the objective is to know the manner of deriving rulings (ikhtibās al-aḥkām) from the evidences. Thus, it becomes necessary to examine: first, the rulings themselves; second, the evidences and their divisions; third, the manner of deriving rulings from the evidences; and fourth, the attributes of the one who derives (al-muqtabis) — the one who has the right to extract rulings. For rulings are fruits (thamarāt), and every fruit has an attribute and a reality in itself, and it has a fruit-bearer (muthmir), a fruit-gatherer (mustathmir), and a path of gathering (ṭarīq fī al-istithmār).

The fruit is the rulings — namely, obligation (wujūb), prohibition (ḥaẓr), recommendation (nadb), disapprobation (karāhah), permissibility (ibāḥah), goodness (ḥusn), evil (qubḥ), performance (qaḍāʾ), fulfillment (adāʾ), validity (ṣiḥḥah), invalidity (fasād), and others. The fruit-bearer is the evidences, which are only three: the Book, the Sunnah, and Consensus (ijmāʿ). The paths of gathering are the modes of indication of the evidences, and they are four: for utterances either indicate the thing by their wording and composition (bi-ṣīghatihā wa manẓūmihā), or by their implication and understood meaning (bi-faḥwāhā wa mafhūmihā), or by their requirement and necessity (bi-iqtiḍāʾihā wa ḍarūratihā), or by their intelligible meaning and the sense derived from them (bi-maʿqūlihā wa maʿnāhu al-mustanbaṭ minhā).

The fruit-gatherer is the mujtahid, and it is indispensable to know his attributes, conditions, and rulings. Thus, the entirety of uṣūl al-fiqh revolves upon four poles:

The First Pole: Concerning the rulings (al-aḥkām) — and beginning with them is more appropriate, for they are the sought-after fruit.

The Second Pole: Concerning the evidences (al-adillah) — namely, the Book, the Sunnah, and Consensus — and with them comes the second step, for after completing knowledge of the fruit, nothing is more important than knowledge of the fruit-bearer.

The Third Pole: Concerning the path of gathering (ṭarīq al-istithmār) — namely, the modes of indication of the evidences, which are four: indication by the composed wording (al-manẓūm), indication by the understood meaning (al-mafhūm), indication by necessity and requirement (al-ḍarūrah wa al-iqtiḍāʾ), and indication by the intelligible meaning (al-maʿnā al-maʿqūl).

The Fourth Pole: Concerning the fruit-gatherer (al-mustathmir) — namely, the mujtahid who judges by his considered opinion (ẓann), and opposed to him is the muqallid who is obligated to follow him. Thus, it is necessary to mention the conditions of the muqallid and the mujtahid and their attributes.

chapters.title_en: On the Manner in Which the Numerous Branches of Jurisprudence Are Subsumed Under These Four Poles
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان كيفية اندراج الشعب الكثيرة من أصول الفقه تحت هذه الأقطاب الأربعة]

لعلك تقول أصول الفقه تشتمل على أبواب كثيرة وفصول منتشرة فكيف يندرج
جملتها تحت هذه الأقطاب الأربعة؟ فنقول: القطب الأول: هو الحكم.
وللحكم حقيقة في نفسه وانقسام، وله تعلق بالحاكم وهو الشارع والمحكوم
عليه وهو المكلف وبالمحكوم فيه وهو فعل المكلف وبالمظهر له وهو السبب
والعلة، ففي البحث عن حقيقة الحكم في نفسه يتبين أنه عبارة عن خطاب الشرع
وليس وصفا للفعل ولا حسن ولا قبح ولا مدخل للعقل فيه ولا حكم قبل ورود
الشرع، وفي البحث عن أقسام الحكم يتبين حد الواجب والمحظور والمندوب
والمباح والمكروه والقضاء والأداء والصحة والفساد والعزيمة والرخصة وغير
ذلك من أقسام الأحكام. وفي البحث عن الحاكم يتبين أن لا حكم إلا لله وأنه
لا حكم للرسول ولا للسيد على العبد ولا لمخلوق على مخلوق، بل كل ذلك حكم
الله تعالى ووضعه لا حكم لغيره. وفي البحث عن المحكوم عليه يتبين خطاب
الناسي والمكره والصبي، وخطاب الكافر بفروع الشرع، وخطاب السكران ومن يجوز
تكليفه ومن لا يجوز. وفي البحث عن المحكوم فيه يتبين أن الخطاب يتعلق
بالأفعال لا بالأعيان وأنه ليس وصفا للأفعال في ذواتها. وفي البحث عن مظهر
الحكم يتبين حقيقة السبب والعلة والشرط والمحل والعلامة، فيتناول هذا القطب
جملة من تفاريق فصول الأصول أوردها الأصوليون مبددة في مواضع شتى لا تتناسب
ولا تجمعها رابطة، فلا يهتدي الطالب إلى مقاصدها ووجه الحاجة إلى معرفتها
وكيفية تعلقها بأصول الفقه. القطب الثاني: في المثمر، وهو الكتاب والسنة
والإجماع. وفي البحث عن أصل الكتاب يتبين حد الكتاب وما هو منه وما ليس
منه، وطريق إثبات الكتاب وإنه التواتر فقط وبيان ما يجوز أن  يشتمل عليه
الكتاب من حقيقة ومجاز وعربية وعجمية. وفي البحث عن السنة يتبين حكم
الأقوال والأفعال من الرسول وطرق ثبوتها من تواتر وآحاد وطرق روايتها من
مسند ومرسل وصفات رواتها من عدالة وتكذيب، إلى تمام كتاب الأخبار. ويتصل
بالكتاب والسنة كتاب النسخ فإنه لا يرد إلا عليهما، وأما الإجماع فلا يتطرق
النسخ إليه. وفي البحث عن أصل الإجماع تتبين حقيقته ودليله وأقسامه وإجماع
الصحابة وإجماع من بعدهم إلى جميع مسائل الإجماع القطب الثالث: في طرق
الاستثمار.
وهي أربعة الأولى: دلالة اللفظ من حيث صيغته، وبه يتعلق النظر في صيغة
الأمر والنهي والعموم والخصوص والظاهر والمؤول والنص. والنظر في كتاب
الأوامر والنواهي والعموم والخصوص نظر في مقتضى الصيغ اللغوية وأما الدلالة
من حيث الفحوى والمفهوم فيشتمل عليه كتاب المفهوم ودليل
الخطاب، وأما الدلالة من حيث ضرورة اللفظ واقتضاؤه فيتضمن جملة من إشارات
الألفاظ كقول القائل: أعتق عبدك عني، فتقول: أعتقت، فإنه يتضمن حصول الملك
للملتمس ولم يتلفظا به لكنه من ضرورة ملفوظهما ومقتضاه. وأما الدلالة من
حيث معقول اللفظ فهو كقوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: «لا يقضي القاضي وهو
غضبان» فإنه يدل على الجائع والمريض والحاقن بمعقول معناه، ومنه ينشأ
القياس وينجر إلى بيان جميع أحكام القياس وأقسامه. القطب الرابع: في
المستثمر، وهو المجتهد وفي مقابلته المقلد، وفيه يتبين صفات المجتهد وصفات
المقلد والموضع الذي يجري فيه الاجتهاد دون الذي لا مجال للاجتهاد فيه
والقول في تصويب المجتهدين وجملة أحكام الاجتهاد. فهذه جملة ما ذكر في علم
الأصول وقد عرفت كيفية انشعابها من هذه الأقطاب الأربعة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ط-ب (quṭb)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The pole (quṭb) of a tent or millstone—that around which everything revolves; hence, the central axis.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The governing principle or axis upon which a discipline turns; here, the foundational categories of uṣūl al-fiqh.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the physical pivot. Metaphorical (majāz): the organizing epistemic center from which all derivative rulings (furūʿ) radiate.
- Root: ث-م-ر (thamara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To bear fruit; the yield of a tree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The productive source (muṯmir) from which rulings are derived—i.e., the revealed evidences.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: fruit-bearing. Metaphorical: that which generates legal knowledge, as opposed to the mere receptacle (mustathmir).
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (naẓar)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gazing, reflection, examination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Systematic intellectual inquiry (naẓar) leading to knowledge—here, the methodological paths of derivation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: visual sight. Metaphorical: rational consideration of linguistic and analogical indicators.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿāmil (Ellipsis of the Governing Operator) — In complex periodic sentences, the governing verb (e.g., naqūlu) is implied and governs multiple subordinate clauses, requiring the translator to preserve the logical subordination without redundancy.
chapters.translation:
You might say: The principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) comprise many chapters and scattered sections—how then can their entirety be subsumed under these four poles? We say: The first pole is the ruling (al-ḥukm). The ruling has an essence in itself and a division [into kinds]; it has a relation to the ruler (al-ḥākim), namely the Lawgiver (al-shāriʿ); to the one ruled upon (al-maḥkūm ʿalayhi), namely the legally responsible person (al-mukallaf); to the subject matter ruled upon (al-maḥkūm fīhi), namely the act of the responsible person; and to that which manifests it (al-maẓhar lahu), namely the cause (al-sabab) and the ratio (al-ʿillah). Thus, in investigating the essence of the ruling in itself, it becomes clear that it is an expression of the address of the Law (khiṭāb al-sharʿ)—not a description of the act, nor [a matter of] good or evil (ḥusn wa qubḥ), nor does the intellect have any entry into it, nor is there any ruling prior to the advent of the Law. In investigating the divisions of the ruling, the definitions become clear of the obligatory (al-wājib), the prohibited (al-maḥẓūr), the recommended (al-mandūb), the permissible (al-mubāḥ), the disliked (al-makrūh), the compensatory (al-qaḍāʾ), the performative (al-adāʾ), validity (al-ṣiḥḥah), invalidity (al-fasād), resolve (al-ʿazīmah), concession (al-rukhṣah), and other such divisions of rulings. In investigating the ruler, it becomes clear that there is no ruling except for God—that there is no ruling for the Messenger, nor for a master over his slave, nor for any creature over another creature; rather, all of that is God’s ruling and His imposition (waḍʿ), with no ruling for anyone other than Him. In investigating the one ruled upon, it becomes clear [the status of] the address to the forgetful one, the coerced one, and the child; the address to the unbeliever concerning the subsidiary branches of the Law (furūʿ al-sharʿ); the address to the intoxicated one; and who is eligible for legal responsibility (taklīf) and who is not. In investigating the subject matter ruled upon, it becomes clear that the address attaches to acts, not to [static] entities (aʿyān), and that it is not a description of acts in their essences. In investigating the manifestation of the ruling, the reality becomes clear of the cause (al-sabab), the ratio (al-ʿillah), the condition (al-sharṭ), the locus (al-maḥall), and the marker (al-ʿalāmah). Thus this pole encompasses a host of scattered chapters of the principles that the uṣūliyyūn have presented dispersed in various places—disconnected and bound by no unifying thread—so that the student cannot discern their aims, the point of needing to know them, or how they attach to the principles of jurisprudence.

The second pole concerns the productive source (al-muthmir), namely the Book, the Sunnah, and Consensus (al-ijmāʿ). In investigating the principle of the Book, the definition of the Book becomes clear—what is of it and what is not of it; the method of establishing the Book, namely that it is only by mass transmission (al-tawātur); and the exposition of what the Book may contain of literal (ḥaqīqah) and metaphorical (majāz) [usage], and of Arabic and non-Arabic [terms]. In investigating the Sunnah, the ruling becomes clear concerning the sayings and acts of the Messenger, the methods of their establishment—whether by mass transmission or by solitary report (āḥād)—the methods of their narration—whether connected (musnad) or interrupted (mursal)—and the attributes of their transmitters—whether of probity (ʿadālah) or of falsification—up to the completion of the Book of Reports (Kitāb al-Akhbār). Connected to the Book and the Sunnah is the Book of Abrogation (al-naskh), for it applies only to them; as for Consensus, abrogation does not extend to it. In investigating the principle of Consensus, its reality, its proof, its divisions, the consensus of the Companions, and the consensus of those after them become clear—up to all the issues of Consensus.

The third pole concerns the methods of derivation (ṭuruq al-istithmār). They are four. The first: the indication of the utterance (dalālat al-lafẓ) by virtue of its form (ṣīghah)—and to this attaches the inquiry into the forms of the command (al-amr), the prohibition (al-nahy), the general (al-ʿumūm), the specific (al-khuṣūṣ), the apparent (al-ẓāhir), the interpreted (al-muʾawwal), and the explicit text (al-naṣṣ). For the inquiry in the Books of Commands, Prohibitions, Generality, and Specificity is an inquiry into what the linguistic forms require. As for indication by virtue of the gist (al-faḥwā) and the implied meaning (al-mafhūm), it is encompassed in the Book of the Implied Meaning and the Indicator of the Address (dalīl al-khiṭāb). As for indication by virtue of the necessity of the utterance (ḍarūrat al-lafẓ) and its requirement (iqtiḍāʾuh), it comprises a host of implications of expressions—such as one’s saying: “Free your slave on my behalf,” and your replying: “I have freed [him]”—for this entails the acquisition of ownership for the requester, though neither uttered it; yet it is from the necessity of their two utterances and their requirement. As for indication by virtue of the rational import of the utterance (maʿqūl al-lafẓ), it is like his saying—peace be upon him: «لا يقضي القاضي وهو غضبان» (“The judge shall not judge while angry”)—for it indicates [the same ruling for] the hungry, the ill, and the one in urgent need of relieving himself, by virtue of its rational import. From this arises analogy (al-qiyās), and it extends to the exposition of all the rulings of analogy and its divisions.

The fourth pole concerns the one who derives (al-mustathmir), namely the independent jurist (al-mujtahid); and in contrast to him, the follower (al-muqallid). In it become clear the attributes of the mujtahid, the attributes of the muqallid, the locus in which ijtihād operates—as opposed to that in which there is no scope for ijtihād—and the doctrine concerning the correctness of all mujtahids (taṣwīb al-mujtahidīn), along with the sum of the rulings of ijtihād. This, then, is the totality of what has been mentioned in the science of principles; and you have come to know how it branches forth from these four poles.

chapters.title_en: On the Introduction and Its Relation to the Principles of Jurisprudence
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان المقدمة ووجه تعلق الأصول بها]

اعلم أنه لما رجع حد أصول الفقه إلى معرفة أدلة الأحكام اشتمل الحد على
ثلاثة ألفاظ: المعرفة والدليل والحكم فقالوا: إذا لم يكن بد من معرفة الحكم
حتى كان معرفته أحد الأقطاب الأربعة فلا بد أيضا من معرفة الدليل ومعرفة
المعرفة، أعني العلم. ثم العلم المطلوب لا وصول إليه إلا بالنظر، فلا بد من
معرفة النظر فشرعوا في بيان  حد العلم والدليل والنظر ولم يقتصروا على تعريف
صور هذه الأمور، ولكن انجر بهم إلى إقامة الدليل على إثبات العلم على
منكريه من السوفسطائية وإقامة الدليل على النظر على منكري النظر وإلى جملة
من أقسام العلوم وأقسام الأدلة، وذلك مجاوزة لحد هذا العلم وخلط له
بالكلام، وإنما أكثر فيه المتكلمون من الأصوليين لغلبة الكلام على طبائعهم
فحملهم حب صناعتهم على خلطه بهذه الصنعة، كما حمل حب اللغة والنحو بعض
الأصوليين على مزج جملة من النحو بالأصول فذكروا فيه من معاني الحروف
ومعاني الإعراب جملا هي من علم النحو خاصة، وكما حمل حب الفقه جماعة من
فقهاء ما وراء النهر كأبي زيد - رحمه الله - وأتباعه على مزج مسائل كثيرة
من تفاريع الفقه بالأصول، فإنهم وإن أوردوها في معرض المثال وكيفية إجراء
الأصل في الفروع فقد أكثروا فيه وعذر المتكلمين في ذكر حد العلم والنظر
والدليل في أصول الفقه أظهر من عذرهم في إقامة البرهان على إثباتها مع
المنكرين، لأن الحد يثبت في النفس صور هذه الأمور ولا أقل من تصورها إذا
كان الكلام يتعلق بها، كما أنه لا أقل من تصور الإجماع والقياس لمن يخوض في
الفقه.
وأما معرفة حجية الإجماع وحجية القياس فذلك من خاصية أصول الفقه، فذكر
حجية العلم والنظر على منكريه استجرار الأصول إلى الفروع. وبعد أن عرفناك
إسرافهم في هذا الخلط فإنا لا نرى أن نخلي هذا المجموع عن شيء منه لأن
الفطام عن المألوف شديد والنفوس عن الغريب نافرة، لكنا نقتصر من ذلك على ما
تظهر فائدته على العموم في جملة العلوم من تعريف مدارك العقول وكيفية
تدرجها من الضروريات إلى النظريات على وجه يتبين فيه حقيقة العلم والنظر
والدليل وأقسامها وحججها تبيينا بليغا تخلو عنه مصنفات الكلام.

### | [مقدمة الكتاب]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿalima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Certain apprehension (idrāk) of a thing as it is; knowledge as settled conviction (yaqīn) in the soul.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿIlm is the apprehension of a thing's quiddity (māhiyyah) with certainty; its opposite is jahl (ignorance). In uṣūl, it is the epistemic foundation for ḥukm.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — firm cognition; metaphorical (majāz) — mere opinion (ẓann) when used loosely.
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (naẓara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gazing with the eye; then transferred to intellectual reflection (taʾammul) and deliberation (tafakkur).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ordered movement of thought from premises (muqaddimāt) to conclusions (natāʾij); the instrument of theoretical knowledge (naẓarī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical sight; metaphorical — rational inference (istidlāl), as in «{قُلِ انْظُرُوا مَاذَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ}» (Yūnus 10:101).
- Root: د-ل-ل (dalla)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Guidance and indication; the sign (dalīl) that points beyond itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which, when correctly considered, yields knowledge of the indicated (madlūl); in uṣūl, the evidence for a legal ruling.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — a guide on a path; metaphorical — any indicant (amārah) leading the mind to a conclusion.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-bayān (Appositional explicative) — the clause «أعني العلم» (i.e., knowledge) functions as an explicative appositive clarifying the preceding «معرفة المعرفة», ensuring precise referential identity without altering the syntactic frame.
chapters.translation:
Know that since the definition of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) reduces to the knowledge of the evidences (adillah) of legal rulings (aḥkām), the definition comprises three terms: knowledge (maʿrifah), evidence (dalīl), and ruling (ḥukm). They said: Since there is no avoiding the knowledge of the ruling — such that its knowledge is one of the four poles — there is likewise no avoiding the knowledge of the evidence and the knowledge of knowledge itself, namely, science (ʿilm). Then, the science sought is not attained except through reflection (naẓar), so there is no avoiding the knowledge of reflection. Thus they commenced with the exposition of the definition of science, evidence, and reflection — and they did not confine themselves to defining the forms of these matters, but were drawn onward to adducing proof for the establishment of science against its deniers among the Sophists (al-sūfisṭāʾiyyah), and to adducing proof for reflection against its deniers, and to a host of the divisions of the sciences and the divisions of the evidences. And that is an overstepping of the boundary of this discipline and a mixing of it with theology (kalām). The theologians among the uṣūliyyūn engaged in this excessively only because of the predominance of kalām over their natural dispositions; their love of their own craft impelled them to mix it with this craft — just as the love of language and grammar impelled some uṣūliyyūn to blend a portion of grammar into uṣūl, so they mentioned therein matters of the meanings of particles (ḥurūf) and the meanings of grammatical inflection (iʿrāb) that belong exclusively to the science of grammar — and just as the love of jurisprudence impelled a group of the jurists of Transoxiana, such as Abū Zayd — may God have mercy on him — and his followers, to blend many subsidiary questions (masāʾil) of furūʿ al-fiqh into uṣūl. For even though they adduced them by way of example and of showing how the principle is applied to the branches, they nonetheless overindulged therein.

The excuse of the theologians for mentioning the definition of science, reflection, and evidence in uṣūl al-fiqh is more apparent than their excuse for establishing the proof of their validity against the deniers — because the definition fixes in the soul the forms of these matters, and at the very least their conceptualization (taṣawwur) is necessary since the discourse is connected to them, just as there is no less than the conceptualization of consensus (ijmāʿ) and analogical reasoning (qiyās) for one who plunges into jurisprudence. As for knowing the authoritative force (ḥujjiyyah) of consensus and the authoritative force of analogical reasoning, that is a peculiarity of uṣūl al-fiqh. Thus, mentioning the authoritative force of science and reflection against their deniers is a dragging of the principles into the branches.

And after we have apprised you of their extravagance in this mixing, we nonetheless do not see fit to strip this compendium entirely of it — because weaning from the familiar is severe, and souls are averse to the strange. But we shall confine ourselves therein to what manifests its benefit generally across the whole of the sciences: namely, the definition of the avenues of the intellects (madārik al-ʿuqūl) and the manner of their ascent from the necessary (ḍarūriyyāt) to the theoretical (naẓariyyāt), in a way that makes evident the reality of science, reflection, and evidence, their divisions, and their proofs — with an eloquent exposition (tabyīn balīgh) that the systematic works of kalām lack.

### | [Introduction to the Book]

chapters.title_en: The Encompassment of Theoretical Sciences' Perceptual Means in Definition and Demonstration
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [بيان حصر مدارك العلوم النظرية في الحد والبرهان]

مقدمة الكتاب بيان حصر مدارك العلوم النظرية في الحد والبرهان نذكر في
هذه المقدمة مدارك العقول وانحصارها في الحد والبرهان، ونذكر شرط الحد
الحقيقي وشرط البرهان الحقيقي وأقسامهما  على منهاج أوجز مما ذكرناه في كتاب
محك النظر " وكتاب معيار العلم ". وليست هذه المقدمة من جملة علم الأصول
ولا من مقدماته الخاصة به، بل هي مقدمة العلوم كلها، ومن لا يحيط بها فلا
ثقة له بعلومه أصلا، فمن شاء أن لا يكتب هذه المقدمة فليبدأ بالكتاب من
القطب الأول فإن ذلك هو أول أصول الفقه وحاجة جميع العلوم النظرية إلى هذه
المقدمة لحاجة أصول الفقه.
بيان حصر مدارك العلوم النظرية في الحد والبرهان اعلم أن إدراك الأمور
على ضربين: إدراك الذوات المفردة كعلمك بمعنى الجسم والحركة والعالم
والحديث والقديم وسائر ما يدل عليه بالأسامي المفردة، الثاني: إدراك نسبة
هذه المفردات بعضها إلى بعض بالنفي أو الإثبات، وهو أن تعلم أولا معنى لفظ
العالم وهو أمر مفرد ومعنى لفظ الحادث ومعنى لفظ القديم وهما أيضا أمران
مفردان، ثم تنسب مفردا إلى مفرد بالنفي أو الإثبات كما تنسب القدم إلى
العالم بالنفي فتقول: ليس العالم قديما، وتنسب الحدوث إليه بالإثبات فتقول:
العالم حادث، والضرب الأخير هو الذي يتطرق إليه التصديق والتكذيب.
وأما الأول فيستحيل فيه التصديق والتكذيب إذ لا يتطرق التصديق، إلا إلى
خبر، وأقل ما يتركب منه جزءان مفردان وصف وموصوف، فإذا نسب الوصف إلى
الموصوف بنفي أو إثبات، صدق أو كذب. فأما قول القائل حادث أو جسم أو قديم
فأفراد ليس فيها صدق ولا كذب، ولا بأس أن يصطلح على التعبير عن هذين
الضربين بعبارتين مختلفتين فإن حق الأمور المختلفة أن تختلف ألفاظها الدالة
عليها، إذ الألفاظ مثل المعاني فحقها أن تحاذى بها المعاني.
وقد سمى المنطقيون معرفة المفردات تصورا ومعرفة النسبة الخبرية بينهما
تصديقا فقالوا: العلم إما تصور وإما تصديق، وسمى بعض علمائنا الأول معرفة
والثاني علما تأسيا بقول النحاة في قولهم المعرفة تتعدى إلى مفعول واحد، إذ
تقول: عرفت زيدا، والظن يتعدى إلى مفعولين، إذ تقول: ظننت زيدا عالما، ولا
تقول: ظننت زيدا، ولا: ظننت عالما، والعلم من باب الظن، فتقول: علمت زيدا
عدلا.
والعادة في هذه  الاصطلاحات مختلفة. وإذا فهمت افتراق الضربين فلا مشاحة
في الألقاب، فنقول الآن: إن
الإدراكات صارت محصورة في المعرفة والعلم أو في التصور والتصديق وكل علم
تطرق إليه تصديق فمن ضرورته أن يتقدم عليه معرفتان أي: تصوران فإن من لا
يعرف المفرد كيف يعلم المركب ومن لا يفهم معنى العالم ومعنى الحادث كيف
يعلم أن العالم حادث، ومعرفة المفردات قسمان: أولي، وهو الذي لا يطلب
بالبحث وهو الذي يرتسم معناه في النفس من غير بحث وطلب كلفظ الوجود والشيء
وككثير من المحسوسات، ومطلوب وهو الذي يدل اسمه منه على أمر جملي غير مفصل
ولا مفسر فيطلب تفسيره بالحد، وكذلك العلم ينقسم إلى أولي كالضروريات، وإلى
مطلوب كالنظريات.
والمطلوب من المعرفة لا يقتنص إلا بالحد، والمطلوب من العلم الذي يتطرق
إليه التصديق والتكذيب لا يقتنص إلا بالبرهان، فالبرهان والحد هو الآلة
التي بها يقتنص سائر العلوم المطلوبة. فلتكن هذه المقدمة المرسومة لبيان
مدارك العقول مشتملة على دعامتين دعامة في الحد ودعامة في البرهان.

### | [الدعامة الأولى في الحد]

### | [الفن الأول في القوانين]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ص-ر (ḥ-ṣ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To confine, restrict, encompass within boundaries; to surround so that nothing escapes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Epistemic restriction—delimiting the avenues of cognition to their exhaustive categories, leaving no third possibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of physical enclosure; here transferred (majāz) to logical exhaustiveness of cognitive methods.
- Root: ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Boundary, limit, definition; the demarcation separating a thing from what it is not.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The logical definition (ḥadd) that articulates the quiddity (māhiyyah) of a simple concept through genus and differentia.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal—physical border; metaphorical—the conceptual boundary that fixes meaning.
- Root: ب-ر-ه-ن (b-r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clear proof, decisive evidence; from "burhān" as a whiteness that stands out.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Syllogistic demonstration yielding certain knowledge (yaqīn) from necessary premises.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal—brightness; metaphorical—the argument whose conclusion is made manifest with luminous clarity.
- Root: ت-ص-و-ر (t-ṣ-w-r) / ت-ص-د-ي-ق (t-ṣ-d-y-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taṣawwur—forming an image/shape of a thing in the mind; taṣdīq—declaring true, affirming a relation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taṣawwur = conception of simple quiddities; taṣdīq = assent to a predicative proposition, the locus of truth and falsity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Taṣawwur literal—mental picturing; taṣdīq literal—judging a report as veracious; both used technically by the logicians.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Transitivity in Verbal Predication (taʿaddī al-fiʿl) — The grammarians' distinction between "ʿarafa" (taking one object) and "ẓanna" (taking two objects) is invoked to justify the terminological split between "maʿrifah" (conception) and "ʿilm" (assent), showing that linguistic usage mirrors conceptual structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the perception of things is of two kinds. The first is the perception of simple essences (al-dhawāt al-mufradah)—such as your knowledge of the meaning of body, motion, the world, the originated, the eternal, and all that is signified by simple names. The second is the perception of the relation of these simples to one another, whether by negation or affirmation. This is when you first know the meaning of the word "world"—which is a simple matter—and the meaning of the word "originated" and the meaning of the word "eternal"—these also being two simple matters—then you relate one simple to another by negation or affirmation, as when you relate eternity to the world by negation, saying: "The world is not eternal," and you relate origination to it by affirmation, saying: "The world is originated." It is this latter kind that is susceptible to affirmation (taṣdīq) and denial (takdhīb).

As for the first kind, affirmation and denial are impossible in it, for affirmation attaches only to a report (khabar), and the least of what a report is composed of is two simple parts: an attribute and a subject. When the attribute is related to the subject by negation or affirmation, then it is either true or false. As for one's saying "originated," or "body," or "eternal"—these are isolated terms in which there is neither truth nor falsehood. There is no harm in agreeing upon two distinct expressions for these two kinds, for it is fitting that different things have different words signifying them, since words are counterparts of meanings, and it is proper that meanings be matched by their corresponding words.

The logicians have named the knowledge of simples "conception" (taṣawwur) and the knowledge of the predicative relation between them "assent" (taṣdīq), saying: "Knowledge is either conception or assent." Some of our scholars named the first "maʿrifah" and the second "ʿilm," following the grammarians' usage in their statement that "maʿrifah" (knowing) extends to a single object—for you say, "I knew Zayd" (ʿaraftu Zaydan)—whereas "ẓann" (opining) extends to two objects—for you say, "I opined Zayd to be learned" (ẓanantu Zaydan ʿāliman), and you do not say "I opined Zayd" nor "I opined learned."
