الفن الأول في السوابق فيه ثلاثة فصول الفصل الأول: في دلالة الألفاظ على
المعاني ويتضح المقصود منه بتقسيمات:
التقسيم الأول: أن دلالة اللفظ على المعنى تنحصر في ثلاثة أوجه وهي
المطابقة والتضمن والالتزام، فإن لفظ البيت دل على معنى البيت بطريق
المطابقة ويدل على السقف وحده بطريق التضمن لأن البيت يتضمن السقف لأن
البيت عبارة من السقف والحيطان، وكما يدل لفظ الفرس على الجسم إذ لا فرس
إلا وهو جسم. وأما طريق الالتزام فهو كدلالة لفظ السقف على الحائط فإنه غير
موضوع للحائط وضع لفظ الحائط للحائط حتى يكون مطابقا ولا هو متضمن، إذ ليس
الحائط جزءا من السقف كما كان السقف جزءا من نفس البيت وكما كان الحائط
جزءا من نفس البيت، لكنه كالرفيق الملازم الخارج عن ذات السقف الذي لا ينفك
السقف عنه. وإياك أن تستعمل في نظر العقل من الألفاظ ما يدل بطريق
الالتزام، لكن اقتصر على ما يدل بطريق المطابقة والتضمن، لأن الدلالة بطريق
الالتزام لا تنحصر في حد إذ السقف يلزم الحائط والحائط الأس والأس الأرض
وذلك لا ينحصر.
التقسيم الثاني: أن الألفاظ بالإضافة إلى خصوص المعنى وشموله تنقسم إلى
لفظ يدل على عين واحدة ونسميه معينا، كقولك زيد وهذه الشجرة وهذا الفرس
وهذا السواد، وإلى ما يدل على أشياء كثيرة تتفق في معنى واحد ونسميه مطلقا.
والأول حده اللفظ الذي لا يمكن أن يكون مفهومه إلا ذلك الواحد بعينه فلو
قصدت اشتراك غيره فيه منع نفس مفهوم
اللفظ منه.
وأما المطلق فهو الذي لا يمنع نفس مفهومه من وقع الاشتراك في معناه،
كقولك السواد والحركة والفرس والإنسان. وبالجملة الاسم المفرد في لغة العرب
إذا أدخل عليه الألف واللام  للعموم. فإن قلت: وكيف يستقيم هذا وقولك الإله
والشمس والأرض لا يدل إلا على شيء واحد مفرد مع دخول الألف واللام؟ فاعلم
أن هذا غلط، فإن امتناع الشركة ههنا ليس لنفس مفهوم اللفظ بل الذي وضع
اللغة لو جوز في الإله عددا لكان وجود هذا اللفظ عاما في الآلهة كلها، فإن
امتنع الشمول لم يكن لوضع اللفظ بل لاستحالة وجود إله ثان، فلم يكن امتناع
الشركة لمفهوم اللفظ.
والمانع في الشمس أن الشمس في الوجود واحدة، فلو فرضنا عوالم في كل واحد
شمس وأرض كان قولنا الشمس والأرض شاملا للكل. فتأمل هذا فإنه مزلة قدم في
جملة من الأمور النظرية، فإن من لا يفرق بين قوله السواد وبين قوله هذا
السواد وبين قوله الشمس وبين قوله هذه الشمس عظم سهوه في النظريات من حيث
لا يدري.
التقسيم الثالث: إن الألفاظ المتعددة بالإضافة إلى المسميات المتعددة على
أربعة منازل، ولنخترع لها أربعة ألفاظ وهي: المترادفة والمتباينة
والمتواطئة والمشتركة. أما المترادفة فنعني بها الألفاظ المختلفة والصيغ
المتواردة على مسمى واحد كالخمر والعقار والليث والأسد والسهم والنشاب،
وبالجملة كل اسمين لمسمى واحد يتناوله أحدهما من حيث يتناوله الآخر من غير
فرق.
وأما المتباينة فنعني بها الأسامي المختلقة للمعاني المختلفة كالسواد
والقدرة والأسد والمفتاح والسماء والأرض وسائر الأسامي وهي الأكثر. وأما
المتواطئة فهي التي تنطلق على أشياء متغايرة بالعدد ولكنها متفقة بالمعنى
الذي وضع الاسم عليها، كاسم الرجل فإنه ينطلق على زيد وعمرو وبكر وخالد،
واسم الجسم ينطلق على السماء والأرض والإنسان، لاشتراك هذه الأعيان في معنى
الجسمية التي وضع الاسم بإزائها وكل اسم مطلق ليس بمعين كما سبق فإنه ينطلق
على آحاد مسمياته الكثيرة بطريق التواطؤ كاسم اللون للسواد والبياض والحمرة
فإنها متفقة في المعنى الذي به سمي اللون لونا وليس بطريق الاشتراك ألبتة.
وأما المشتركة فهي الأسامي التي تنطلق على مسميات مختلفة لا تشترك في
الحد والحقيقة ألبتة، كاسم العين للعضو الباصر وللميزان وللموضع الذي يتفجر
منه الماء وهي العين الفوارة وللذهب  والشمس وكاسم المشتري لقابل عقد البيع
وللكوكب المعروف. ولقد ثار من ارتباك المشتركة بالمتواطئة غلط كثير في
العقليات حتى ظن جماعة من ضعفاء العقول أن السواد لا يشارك البياض في
اللونية إلا من حيث الاسم وأن ذلك كمشاركة الذهب للحدقة الباصرة في اسم
العين وكمشاركة قابل عقد البيع للكوكب في المشتري، وبالجملة الاهتمام
بتمييز المشتركة عن المتواطئة مهم فلنزد له شرحا فنقول: الاسم المشترك قد
يدل على المختلفين كما ذكرناه، وقد يدل على المتضادين كالجلل للحقير
والخطير والناهل للعطشان والريان والجون للسواد والبياض والقرء للطهر
والحيض.
واعلم أن المشترك قد يكون مشكلا قريب الشبه من المتواطئ ويعسر على الذهن
وإن كان في غاية الصفاء الفرق ولنسم ذلك متشابها، وذلك مثل اسم النور
الواقع على الضوء المبصر
من الشمس والنار والواقع على العقل الذي به يهتدى في الغوامض، فلا مشاركة
بين حقيقة ذات العقل والضوء إلا كمشاركة السماء للإنسان في كونها جسما إذ
الجسمية فيهما لا تختلف البتة مع أنه ذاتي لهما.
ويقرب من لفظ النور لفظ الحي على النبات والحيوان، فإنه بالاشتراك المحض
إذ يراد به من النبات المعنى الذي به نماؤه ومن الحيوان المعنى الذي به يحس
ويتحرك بالإرادة، وإطلاقه على الباري تعالى إذا تأملت عرفت أنه لمعنى ثالث
يخالف الأمرين جميعا.
ومن أمثال هذه تتابع الأغاليط مغلطة أخرى قد تلتبس المترادفة بالمتباينة،
وذلك إذا أطلقت أسام مختلفة على شيء واحد باعتبارات مختلفة ربما ظن أنها
مترادفة كالسيف والمهند والصارم، فإن المهند يدل على السيف مع زيادة نسبة
إلى الهند فخالف إذا مفهومه مفهوم السيف، والصارم يدل على السيف مع صفة
الحدة والقطع لا كالأسد والليث.
وهذا كما أنا في اصطلاحاتنا النظرية نحتاج إلى تبديل الأسامي على شيء
واحد عند تبدل اعتباراته، كما أنا نسمي العلم التصديقي الذي هو نسبة بين
مفردين دعوى إذا تحدى به المتحدي ولم يكن عليه برهان إن كان في مقابلة خصم
وإن لم يكن في مقابلة خصم سميناه قضية كأنه قضي فيه على شيء  بشيء، فإن خاض
في ترتيب قياس الدليل عليه سميناه مطلوبا، فإن دل بقياسه على صحته سميناه
نتيجة فإن استعمله دليلا في طلب أمر آخر ورتبه في أجزاء القياس سميناه
مقدمة، وهذا ونظائره مما يكثر.
مثال الغلط في المشترك قول الشافعي - رحمه الله - تعالى في مسألة المكره
على القتل: " يلزمه القصاص لأنه مختار ويقول الحنفي " لا يلزمه القصاص لأنه
مكره وليس بمختار " ويكاد الذهن لا ينبو عن التصديق بالأمرين، وأنت تعلم أن
التصديق بالضدين محال، وترى الفقهاء يتعثرون فيه ولا يهتدون إلى حله. وإنما
ذلك؛ لأن اللفظ المختار مشترك، إذ قد يجعل لفظ المختار مرادا، فاللفظ
القادر ومساويا له إذ قوبل بالذي لا قدرة له على الحركة الموجودة كالمحمول،
فيقال: هذا عاجز محمول، وهذا قادر مختار، ويراد بالمختار الذي يقدر على
الفعل وتركه وهو صادق على المكره.
وقد يعبر بالمختار عمن تخلى في استعمال قدرته ودواعي ذاته بلا تحرك
دواعيه من خارج، وهذا يكذب على المكره ونقيضه، وهو أنه ليس بمختار يصدق
عليه، فإذا صدق عليه مختار وإنه ليس بمختار ولكن بشرط أن يكون مفهوم
المختار المنفي غير مفهوم المختار المثبت. ولهذا نظائر في النظريات لا تحصى
تاهت فيها عقول الضعفاء فليستدل بهذا القليل على الكثير.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ل-ل (dalālah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to guide, show, or indicate" — the path (dalīl) that leads one to a destination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, dalālah is the rational or linguistic signpost that necessitates a cognitive transition from the known (al-madlūl ʿalayh) to the unknown, forming the basis of inference (istidlāl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes a direct, intended guidance; metaphorical (majāz) usage would imply an indirect or allusive indication, which is here strictly demarcated.
- Root: ل-ز-م (luzūm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be inseparable, necessary, or concomitant; that which cleaves to a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, luzūm denotes a necessary entailment between concepts, distinct from mere part-whole relations (taḍammun).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical attachment (e.g., a companion who never parts); here extended metaphorically to conceptual inseparability.
- Root: و-ط-أ (waṭaʾa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tread, level, or make smooth; a path that is trodden by many.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl, muwāṭaʾah signifies a term applied to multiple particulars under a single, shared meaning (maʿnā ʿāmm), like a level ground shared by all.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical treading; metaphorical for conceptual agreement among diverse individuals.
- Root: ش-ر-ك (sharaka)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To share, associate, or participate; a partnership in a common thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ishtirāk in terminology is the pure sharing of a name without any shared essence or definition (ḥadd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for co-ownership; metaphorical for linguistic homonymy, where the "partnership" is only in the utterance, not in reality.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taḍāyuf (Correlativity) and Taqābul (Opposition) — The syntactic and semantic parsing of terms like "mutarādifah" (synonyms) and "mutabāyinah" (disparate) requires distinguishing between the lafẓ (utterance) and its maʿnā (meaning), and between the maʿnā's essential (dhātī) versus accidental (ʿaraḍī) attributes, as applied in the analysis of the term "mukhtār" (free/choosing).
chapters.translation:
I say: The first art concerns the preliminaries, and it contains three chapters. The first chapter is on the indication of utterances upon meanings. Its intended purpose is clarified through divisions:

**The First Division:** The indication of an utterance upon a meaning is confined to three aspects: correspondence (muṭābaqah), inclusion (taḍammun), and entailment (iltizām). For the word "house" (bayt) indicates the meaning of "house" by way of correspondence, and it indicates "roof" alone by way of inclusion, because the house includes the roof — for the house is an expression of the roof and the walls — just as the word "horse" indicates the body, since there is no horse except that it is a body. As for the way of entailment, it is like the indication of the word "roof" upon the wall. For the roof is not posited for the wall — the word "wall" was posited for the wall such that it would be by correspondence — nor is it inclusive, since the wall is not a part of the roof as the roof was a part of the house itself, and as the wall was a part of the house itself. Rather, it is like the inseparable companion that is external to the essence of the roof, from which the roof is never disjoined. And beware of using, in intellectual speculation, utterances that indicate by way of entailment; rather, restrict yourself to what indicates by way of correspondence and inclusion, because indication by way of entailment is not confined to a limit — since the roof entails the wall, the wall entails the foundation, and the foundation entails the ground, and that is not confined.

**The Second Division:** Utterances, in relation to the specificity and generality of meaning, are divided into: an utterance that indicates a single specific entity, which we call "particularized" (muʿayyan) — like your saying "Zayd," "this tree," "this horse," and "this blackness" — and into what indicates many things that agree in a single meaning, which we call "absolute" (muṭlaq). The first is defined as the utterance whose concept cannot be anything other than that single specific one; were you to intend another's sharing in it, the very concept of the utterance would prevent it. As for the absolute, it is that whose very concept does not prevent the occurrence of sharing in its meaning, like your saying "blackness," "movement," "horse," and "human." In sum, the single noun in the Arabic language, when the definite article "al-" (alif-lām) enters upon it, indicates generality. If you say: "How does this hold, given your saying 'the deity' (al-ilāh), 'the sun' (al-shams), and 'the earth' (al-arḍ) — these indicate only a single, individual thing despite the entry of the definite article?" Know that this is an error. For the prevention of sharing here is not due to the very concept of the utterance; rather, had the one who posited the language allowed a plurality for "deity," this utterance would have been general over all deities. If generality is prevented, it is not due to the positing of the utterance, but due to the impossibility of the existence of a second deity. Thus, the prevention of sharing was not due to the concept of the utterance. And the preventer in "sun" is that the sun in existence is one; were we to suppose worlds, each having a sun and an earth, our saying "the sun" and "the earth" would encompass all. So contemplate this, for it is a slippery slope in a host of theoretical matters. For whoever does not distinguish between his saying "blackness" and his saying "this blackness," and between "the sun" and "this sun," his error in theoretical matters is immense, without his being aware.

**The Third Division:** The multiple utterances, in relation to the multiple named entities, are on four levels. Let us coin four terms for them: synonymous (mutarādifah), disparate (mutabāyinah), univocal (mutawāṭiʾah), and homonymous (mushtarakah). By "synonymous," we mean the different utterances and varied forms that come upon a single named entity — like "wine" (khamr) and "liquor" (ʿuqār), "lion" (layth) and "lion" (asad), "arrow" (sahm) and "arrow" (nushshāb). In sum, every two names for a single named entity, where one of them applies to it precisely as the other applies, without any difference. By "disparate," we mean the different names for different meanings — like "blackness," "power," "lion," "key," "sky," "earth," and the rest of names; these are the most numerous. By "univocal," they are those that apply to things differing in number but agreeing in the meaning upon which the name was posited — like the name "man" (rajul), which applies to Zayd, ʿAmr, Bakr, and Khālid; and the name "body" (jism), which applies to the sky, the earth, and the human — due to these entities' sharing in the meaning of "bodiliness" (jismiyyah) for which the name was posited. And every absolute name that is not particularized, as previously mentioned, applies to the individuals of its many named entities by way of univocity — like the name "color" (lawn) for blackness, whiteness, and redness, for they agree in the meaning by which color is named "color." This is not by way of homonymy at all. By "homonymous," they are the names that apply to different named entities that share nothing in definition (ḥadd) or reality (ḥaqīqah) whatsoever — like the name "eye" (ʿayn) for the seeing organ, for the balance-scale, for the place from which water gushes forth (the flowing spring), for gold, and for the sun; and like the name "buyer" (mushtarī) for the one who accepts a sales contract and for the well-known planet. Indeed, from the confusion of the homonymous with the univocal, much error has arisen in the rational sciences, until a group of the weak-minded supposed that blackness does not share with whiteness in "color-ness" except in name — and that this is like the sharing of gold with the seeing pupil in the name "eye," and like the sharing of the contract-acceptor with the planet in "buyer." In sum, attention to distinguishing the homonymous from the univocal is important. Let us add further explanation, saying: The homonymous name may indicate two different things, as we mentioned; and it may indicate two opposites — like "jalal" for the insignificant and the momentous, "nāhil" for the thirsty and the satiated, "jawn" for blackness and whiteness, and "qarʾ" for purity and menstruation.

Know that the homonymous may be problematic, closely resembling the univocal, and the distinction is difficult for the mind even if it be of the utmost clarity. Let us call that "ambiguous" (mutashābih). This is like the name "light" (nūr) applied to the visible illumination from the sun and fire, and applied to the intellect by which one is guided in obscure matters. There is no sharing between the reality of the intellect's essence and light, except like the sharing of the sky with the human in being a body — for bodiliness in both does not differ at all, despite being essential to both. Close to the word "light" is the word "living" (ḥayy) applied to the plant and the animal — for it is by pure homonymy, since what is meant by it for the plant is the meaning by which it grows, and for the animal the meaning by which it senses and moves by will. And its application to the Exalted Creator — if you reflect — you will know that it is for a third meaning that differs from both of these entirely.

Among the likes of these successive errors is another error: the synonymous may be confused with the disparate. That occurs when different names are applied to a single thing according to different considerations, and one might suppose they are synonymous — like "sword" (sayf), "Indian" (muhannad), and "sharp-cutting" (ṣārim). For "muhannad" indicates the sword with an added relation to India, so its concept differs from the concept of "sword"; and "ṣārim" indicates the sword with the attribute of sharpness and cutting — not like "asad" and "layth." This is just as, in our theoretical terminologies, we need to exchange names for a single thing when its considerations change. Thus, we call the assent-based knowledge (al-ʿilm al-taṣdīqī) that is a relation between two singulars a "claim" (daʿwā) when the claimant challenges with it and has no proof for it, if it is in opposition to an adversary; and if it is not in opposition to an adversary, we call it a "proposition" (qaḍiyyah), as if a judgment were made in it about something by something. If one delves into arranging the syllogism of the proof upon it, we call it a "demand" (maṭlūb). If it demonstrates its correctness by its syllogism, we call it a "conclusion" (natījah). If one uses it as a proof in seeking another matter and arranges it among the parts of the syllogism, we call it a "premise" (muqaddimah). This and its likes are numerous.

An example of error in the homonymous is the saying of al-Shāfiʿī — may God Most High have mercy on him — in the case of the one coerced into killing: "Retaliation is incumbent upon him, because he is free/choosing (mukhtār)." And the Ḥanafī says: "Retaliation is not incumbent upon him, because he is coerced and not free/choosing." The mind almost does not recoil from affirming both matters. And you know that affirming two opposites is impossible. You see the jurists stumbling over it and not being guided to its solution. That is only because the word "mukhtār" is homonymous. For the word "mukhtār" may be used to mean the one who is capable (qādir) and equivalent to it, when contrasted with the one who has no power over the movement that exists — like the carried one. Thus it is said: "This one is incapable, carried; this one is capable, free/choosing." And what is meant by "free/choosing" is the one who has power over the act and its abandonment — and this is true of the coerced one. And it may be expressed by "free/choosing" for the one who, in exercising his power and the motives of his own essence, is not moved by external motives — and this is false of the coerced one, and its opposite — namely, that he is not free/choosing — is true of him. So when "free/choosing" is true of him and "not free/choosing" is also true of him, this is only on the condition that the concept of the negated "free/choosing" is not the concept of the affirmed "free/choosing." And this has parallels in the theoretical sciences that are innumerable, in which the minds of the weak have gone astray. Let this small amount serve as an indication of the much.

chapters.title_en: Section 13 — Examination of Singular Meanings (al-Naẓar fī al-Maʿānī al-Mufradah)
chapters.arabic_text: ### | [الفصل الثاني النظر في المعاني المفردة]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (na-ẓa-ra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "gazing" or "scrutiny" — the physical act of directing the eye toward an object, extended to intellectual reflection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, naẓar denotes systematic rational inquiry (istidlāl) — the disciplined movement of thought from premises to conclusions, often contrasted with taqlīd (blind adherence).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = ocular sight; metaphorical (majāz) = mental perception and deliberation, as in "naẓara fī al-amr" (he pondered the matter).
- Root: م-ع-ن-ى (ma-ʿ-nā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Signifies "meaning," "intention," or "signification" — that which is understood from an expression (lafẓ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, maʿnā is the conceptual content (mafhūm) that a word conveys, distinct from its phonetic form; it is the object of juristic analysis.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = the intended sense of a speaker; metaphorical = the underlying rationale (ʿillah) or semantic core extracted from a term.
- Root: ف-ر-د (fa-ra-da)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Denotes singularity, isolation, or uniqueness — that which stands alone without composition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In logic and jurisprudence, mufrad (singular) refers to a term considered independently, prior to its combination into propositions (qaḍāyā) or compound rulings.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = one individual; metaphorical = a lexical unit (kalimah) taken in isolation, as opposed to a complete sentence (jumlah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis/Supposition) — The heading "al-naẓar fī al-maʿānī al-mufradah" implies an elided verb or nominal predicate (e.g., "hādhā al-naẓar fī..."), requiring the reader to supply the omitted element for full syntactic closure.
chapters.translation: I say: This is the second chapter, concerning the examination of singular meanings — that is, the inquiry into the significations of individual words (alfāẓ) as they stand alone, before their composition into compound statements or their application to particular legal cases. For the science of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) begins with the analysis of these discrete semantic units, since the understanding of divine address (khiṭāb) and prophetic utterance depends upon grasping the precise import of each term in its isolated form.

chapters.title_en: The Second Chapter of the First Art: Examination of Simple Meanings — The Threefold Divisions and the Hierarchy of Perceptive Faculties
chapters.arabic_text:
الفصل الثاني من الفن الأول النظر في المعاني المفردة النظر في المعاني
المفردة. ويظهر الغرض من ذلك بتقسيمات ثلاثة: الأول: أن المعنى إذا وصف
بالمعنى ونسب إليه وجد إما ذاتيا وإما عرضيا وإما لازما وقد فصلناه.
والثاني أنه إذا نسب إليه وجد إما أعم كالوجود بالإضافة إلى الجسمية، وإما
أخفى كالجسمية بالإضافة إلى الوجود، وإما مساويا كالمتحيز بالإضافة إلى
الجوهر عند قوم وإلى الجسم عند قوم.
الثالث: أن المعاني باعتبار أسبابها المدركة لها ثلاثة: محسوسة ومتخيلة
ومعقولة؛ ولنصطلح على تسمية سبب الإدراك قوة، فنقول في حدقتك معنى به تميزت
الحدقة عن الجبهة حتى صرت تبصر بها، وإذا بطل ذلك المعنى
بطل الإبصار، والحالة التي تدركها عند الإبصار شرطها وجود  المبصر، فلو
انعدم المبصر انعدم الإبصار وتبقى صورته في دماغك كأنك تنظر إليها.
وهذه الصورة لا تفتقر إلى وجود المتخيل، بل عدمه وغيبته لا تنفي الحالة
المسماة تخيلا وتنفي الحالة التي تسمى إبصارا. ولما كنت تحس بالتخيل في
دماغك لا في فخذك وبطنك فاعلم أن في الدماغ غريزة وصفة بها يتهيأ للتخيل
وبها باين البطن والفخذ كما باين العين الجبهة والعقب في الإبصار بمعنى
اختص به لا محالة والصبي في أول نشئه تقوى فيه قوة الإبصار لا قوة التخيل؛
فلذلك إذا ولع بشيء فغيبته عنه وأشغلته بغيره اشتغل به ولها عنه.
وربما يحدث في الدماغ مرض يفسد القوة الحافظة للتخيل ولا يفسد الإبصار
فيرى الأشياء ولكنه كما تغيب عنه ينساها، وهذه القوة يشارك البهيمة فيها
الإنسان؛ ولذلك مهما رأى الفرس الشعير تذكر صورته التي كانت له في دماغه
فعرف أنه موافق له وأنه مستلذ لديه فبادر إليه، فلو كانت الصورة لا تثبت في
خياله لكانت رؤيته لها ثانيا كرؤيته لها أولا حتى لا يبادر إليه ما لم
يجربه بالذوق مرة أخرى.
ثم فيك قوة ثالثة شريفة يباين الإنسان بها البهيمة تسمى عقلا محلها إما
دماغك وإما قلبك، وعند من يرى النفس جوهرا قائما بذاته غير متحيز محلها
النفس. وقوة العقل تباين قوة التخيل مباينة أشد من مباينة التخيل للإبصار،
إذ ليس بين قوة الإبصار وقوة التخيل فرق، إلا أن وجود المبصر شرط لبقاء
الإبصار وليس شرطا لبقاء التخيل، وإلا فصورة الفرس تدخل في الإبصار مع قدر
مخصوص ولون مخصوص وبعد منك مخصوص، ويبقى في التخيل ذلك البعد وذلك القدر
واللون وذلك الوضع والشكل حتى كأنك تنظر إليه.
ولعمري فيك قوة رابعة تسمى المفكرة شأنها أن تقدر على تفصيل الصور التي
في الخيال وتقطيعها وتركيبها وليس لها إدراك شيء آخر، ولكن إذا حضر في
الخيال صورة إنسان قدر على أن يجعلها نصفين فيصور نصف إنسان، وربما ركب
شخصا نصفه من إنسان ونصفه من فرس، وربما تصور إنسانا يطير إذ ثبت في  الخيال
صورة الإنسان وحده وصورة الطير وحده؛ وهذه القوة تجمع بينهما كما تفرق بين
نصفي الإنسان.
وليس في وسعها ألبتة اختراع صورة لا مثال لها في الخيال بل كل تصوراتها
بالتفريق والتأليف في الصور الحاصلة في الخيال، والمقصود أن مباينة إدراك
العقل لإدراك التخيل أشد من مباينة التخيل للإبصار، إذ ليس للتخيل أن يدرك
المعاني المجردة العارية عن القرائن الغريبة التي ليست داخلة في ذاتها،
أعني التي ليست ذاتية كما سبق، فإنك لا تقدر على تخيل السواد إلا في مقدار
مخصوص من الجسم ومعه شكل مخصوص ووضع مخصوص منك بقرب أو بعد ومعلوم أن الشكل
غير اللون والقدر غير الشكل؛ فإن المثلث له شكل واحد صغيرا كان أو كبيرا.
وإنما إدراك هذه المفردات المجردة بقوة أخرى اصطلحنا على تسميتها عقلا
فيدرك السواد ويقضي بقضايا ويدرك اللونية مجردة ويدرك الحيوانية والجسمية
مجردة وحيث يدرك الحيوانية قد لا يحضره الالتفات إلى العاقل وغير العاقل
وإن كان الحيوان لا يخلو عن القسمين؛ وحيث يستمر في نظره قاضيا على الألوان
بقضية قد لا يحضر معنى السوادية والبياضية وغيرهما.
وهذه من عجيب خواصها وبديع أفعالها، فإذا رأى فرسا واحدا أدرك الفرس
المطلق الذي يشترك فيه الصغير
والكبير والأشهب والكميت والبعيد منه في المكان والقريب، بل يدرك الفرسية
المجردة المطلقة متنزهة عن كل قرينة ليست ذاتية لها، فإن القدر المخصوص
واللون المخصوص ليس للفرس ذاتيا بل عارضا أو لازما في الوجود، إذ مختلفات
اللون والقدر تشترك في حقيقة الفرسية وهذه المطلقات المجردة الشاملة لأمور
مختلفة هي التي يعبر عنها المتكلمون بالأحوال والوجوه والأحكام ويعبر عنها
المنطقيون بالقضايا الكلية المجردة ويزعمون أنها موجودة في الأذهان لا في
الأعيان، وتارة يعبرون عنها بأنها غير موجودة من خارج بل من داخل - يعنون
خارج الذهن وداخله - ويقول أرباب الأحوال: إنها أمور ثابتة، تارة يقولون
أنها موجودة معلومة وتارة يقولون لا موجودة ولا معلومة ولا مجهولة، وقد
دارت فيه رءوسهم وحارت عقولهم.
والعجب أنه منزل ينفصل فيه المعقول عن المحسوس، إذ  من ههنا يأخذ العقل
الإنساني في التصرف وما كان قبله كان يشارك التخيل البهيمي فيه التخيل
الإنساني. ومن تحير في أول منزل من منازل العقل كيف يرجى فلاحه في تصرفاته.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n) — though not in the text, the governing term "المعاني" (meanings) derives from ع-ن-ي (ʿ-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: عَنِيَ بِالأَمْرِ — to be concerned with, to intend; المعنى is that which is intended or signified by an expression
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, المعنى denotes the conceptual content (maʿnā) as opposed to the verbal form (lafẓ); it is the intelligible reality grasped by the mind
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage — المعنى as the actual referent; metaphorical extension — when meanings are "described" or "attributed," this is a conceptual operation, not a physical one
- Root: ق-و-ي (q-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: القُوَّة — strength, power, faculty; the capacity to perform an act
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In psychology, القوة is the faculty (quwwah) by which the soul performs its acts — sight, imagination, intellect
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical strength; metaphorical — the technical sense of "faculty" as a cause of perception, as al-Ghazali explicitly stipulates ("let us term the cause of perception a faculty")
- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: العَقْل — intellect, understanding; the faculty that restrains (يَعْقِلُ) from error, binding one to truth
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): العقل is that by which the rational soul apprehends universals (al-kulliyyāt) — the distinctively human faculty separating man from beasts
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the rope that binds a camel (عِقَال); metaphorical — the intellect as that which binds and restrains the soul from falsehood
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause with فاء التسبيب (fāʾ al-sababiyyah) — when a conditional is followed by a clause indicating a necessary consequence, the fāʾ is required before the apodosis, as in "فلو انعدم المبصر انعدم الإبصار" (if the visible object ceased, sight would cease), where the fāʾ marks the causal entailment
chapters.translation:
I say: The second chapter of the first art concerns the examination of simple meanings. The purpose of this is made manifest through three divisions. The first: when a meaning is described by a meaning and attributed to it, it is found to be either essential (dhātī), or accidental (ʿaraḍī), or inseparable (lāzim) — and we have already detailed this. The second: when it is attributed to it, it is found to be either more general (aʿamm), like existence (al-wujūd) in relation to corporeality (al-jismiyyah), or more specific (akhaff), like corporeality in relation to existence, or equal (musāwin), like being spatially occupied (al-taḥayyuz) in relation to substance (al-jawhar) according to some, and to body (al-jism) according to others. The third: meanings, in consideration of their perceptive causes, are three: sensible (maḥsūsah), imaginative (mutakhayyalah), and intelligible (maʿqūlah). Let us agree to term the cause of perception a "faculty" (quwwah). We say: in your eye there is a meaning by which the eye is distinguished from the forehead, such that you see by it; and when that meaning is corrupted, sight is corrupted. The state you perceive at the moment of sight has as its condition the existence of the visible object; so if the visible object ceased to exist, sight would cease, yet its image remains in your brain as though you were looking at it. This image does not require the existence of the imagined object; rather, its non-existence and absence do not negate the state called imagination, though they negate the state called sight. And since you sense imagination in your brain, not in your thigh or belly, know that in the brain there is an innate disposition (gharīzah) and attribute by which it is prepared for imagination, and by which it is distinguished from the belly and thigh, just as the eye is distinguished from the forehead and heel in sight, by a meaning peculiar to it, necessarily. The infant, in its earliest development, has the power of sight strengthened, not the power of imagination; therefore, if it becomes attached to something and you remove it from its sight and occupy it with something else, it becomes occupied with that other and forgets the first. Sometimes a disease occurs in the brain that corrupts the power preserving imagination but does not corrupt sight, so one sees things, yet as soon as they disappear from him, he forgets them. In this power, man shares with the beast; therefore, when a horse sees barley, it recalls the image that was in its brain, and knows that it is agreeable to it and that it is pleasurable to it, so it hastens toward it. Were the image not established in its imagination, its second sight of it would be like its first sight, such that it would not hasten toward it unless it had tasted it once again.

Then in you there is a third, noble power by which man is distinguished from the beast, called the intellect (ʿaql). Its locus is either your brain or your heart — and according to those who hold the soul to be a self-subsistent substance, non-spatially occupied, its locus is the soul. The power of intellect is distinguished from the power of imagination by a distinction greater than that of imagination from sight. For between the power of sight and the power of imagination there is no difference except that the existence of the visible object is a condition for the continuance of sight, but not a condition for the continuance of imagination. Otherwise, the image of a horse enters into sight with a specific magnitude, a specific color, and a specific distance from you; and in imagination there remains that distance, that magnitude, that color, that position, and that shape, as though you were looking at it.

By my life, in you there is a fourth power called the cogitative (al-mufakkirah), whose function is to be able to detail the images in the imagination, to divide them, and to combine them. It has no perception of anything else. But when the image of a man is present in the imagination, it can make it into two halves, thus forming a half-man; and perhaps it composes a creature half of which is a man and half a horse; and perhaps it imagines a flying man, since the image of a man alone and the image of a bird alone are established in the imagination. This power combines them just as it separates the two halves of a man. It is not within its capacity at all to invent an image that has no model in the imagination; rather, all its imaginings are by division and composition of the images present in the imagination. The point is that the distinction of intellectual perception from imaginative perception is greater than the distinction of imagination from sight. For imagination cannot perceive abstract meanings stripped of extraneous concomitants that are not included in their essence — I mean, those that are not essential, as previously stated. For you cannot imagine blackness except in a specific magnitude of body, with a specific shape and a specific position relative to you, whether near or far. And it is known that shape is other than color, and magnitude other than shape; for the triangle has one shape whether it is small or large. Rather, the perception of these simple, abstract things is by another power which we have agreed to term the intellect. It perceives blackness and passes judgments (yaqḍī bi-qaḍāyā); it perceives color-ness (al-lawmiyyah) abstractly; it perceives animality (al-ḥayawāniyyah) and corporeality (al-jismiyyah) abstractly. When it perceives animality, the attention to the rational and non-rational may not be present, even though the animal is never devoid of the two divisions. And when it continues in its consideration, passing judgment on colors by a judgment, the meaning of blackness-ness (al-sawādiyyah) and whiteness-ness (al-bayāḍiyyah) and others may not be present. These are among its wondrous properties and marvelous acts. When it sees a single horse, it perceives the absolute horse that is shared by the small and the large, the white (ashhab) and the chestnut (kumayt), the distant in place and the near — rather, it perceives pure, absolute horse-ness (al-fursiyyah), purified of every concomitant that is not essential to it. For specific magnitude and specific color are not essential to the horse, but rather accidental or inseparable in existence, since differing colors and magnitudes share in the reality of horse-ness. These absolute, abstract universals encompassing diverse things are what the theologians (al-mutakallimūn) express as "states" (aḥwāl), "aspects" (wujūh), and "judgments" (aḥkām); the logicians express them as "abstract universal propositions" (al-qaḍāyā al-kulliyyah al-mujarradah), claiming that they exist in the minds (al-adhhān), not in external entities (al-aʿyān). Sometimes they express them as "not existing from outside, but from inside" — meaning outside the mind and inside it. The proponents of states (aṣḥāb al-aḥwāl) say they are "established things" (umūr thābitah); sometimes they say they are "existing and known" (mawjūdah maʿlūmah), and sometimes they say "neither existing nor known nor unknown" (lā mawjūdah wa-lā maʿlūmah wa-lā majhūlah). Their heads have spun over this and their intellects have been confounded.

And the wonder is that this is the first station (manzil) at which the intelligible separates from the sensible; for from here the human intellect begins its operation, whereas before this, human imagination shared with bestial imagination. And whoever is confounded at the first station of the stations of the intellect — how can his success in its operations be hoped for?

chapters.title_en: Section 15 — Chapter Three on the Rulings of Composite Meanings
chapters.arabic_text: ### | [الفصل الثالث في أحكام المعاني المؤلفة]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ل-ف (ʾ-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of joining, uniting, or reconciling parts into a coherent whole; also denotes familiarity and harmony (ulfah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, refers to the composition of conceptual elements (maʿānī) into a unified proposition, where the whole acquires a ruling (ḥukm) distinct from its parts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes physical or conceptual binding; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the synthesis of linguistic or logical units into a meaningful statement.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Composition (Qāʿidat al-Tarkīb) — The syntactic and semantic integration of multiple elements (e.g., subject-predicate, condition-answer) yields a new composite meaning, whose ruling is derived from the totality, not the isolated components.
chapters.translation: I say: This chapter concerns the rulings that attach to composite meanings—that is, when individual significations are joined together to form a unified expression, the jurisprudential assessment (ḥukm) applies to the whole, not to each part in isolation. For the composition itself introduces a novel semantic structure, and its ruling follows from the intended synthesis, as established in the principles of legal theory.

chapters.title_en: Section 16 — Judgments of Composite Meanings: Propositions (Qaḍāyā) and the Conditions of Contradiction (Tanāquḍ)
chapters.arabic_text:
الفصل الثالث من السوابق في أحكام المعاني المؤلفة قد نظرنا في مجرد
اللفظ ثم في مجرد المعنى، فننظر الآن في تأليف المعنى على وجه يتطرق إليه
التصديق والتكذيب، كقولنا مثلا: العالم حادث والباري تعالى قديم، فإن هذا
يرجع إلى تأليف القوة المفكرة بين معرفتين لذاتين مفردتين بنسبة إحداهما
إلى الأخرى إما بالإثبات كقولك العالم حادث أو بالسلب كقولك العالم ليس
بقديم؛ وقد التأم هذا من جزأين يسمي النحويون أحدهما مبتدأ والآخر خبرا،
ويسمي المتكلمون أحدهما وصفا والآخر موصوفا، ويسمي المنطقيون أحدهما موضوعا
والآخر محمولا، ويسمي الفقهاء أحدهما حكما والآخر محكوما عليه، ويسمى
المجموع قضية.
وأحكام القضايا كثيرة، ونحن نذكر منها ما تكثر الحاجة إليه وتضر الغفلة
عنه؛ وهو حكمان: الأول: القضية تنقسم بالإضافة إلى المقضي عليه إلى التعيين
والإهمال والعموم والخصوص، فهي أربع
الأولى: قضية في عين، كقولنا زيد كاتب وهذا السواد عرض.
الثانية: قضية مطلقة خاصة، كقولنا بعض الناس عالم وبعض الأجسام ساكن
الثالثة: قضية مطلقة عامة، كقولنا كل جسم متحيز وكل سواد لون
الرابعة: قضية مهملة، كقولنا: الإنسان في خسر وعلة هذه القسمة أن المحكوم
عليه إما أن يكون عينا مشارا إليه أو لا يكون عينا، فإن لم يكن عينا فإما
أن يحصر بسور يبين مقداره بكليته فتكون مطلقة عامة أو بجزئيته فتكون خاصة
أو لا يحصر بسور فتكون مهملة؛ والسور هو قولك كل " وبعض وما يقوم مقامهما.
ومن طرق المغالطين في النظر استعمال المهملات بدل القضايا العامة، فإن
المهملات قد يرد بها الخصوص والعموم فيصدق طرفا النقيض، كقولك: الإنسان في
خسر، تعني الكافر. الإنسان ليس في خسر، تعني الأنبياء. ولا ينبغي أن يسامح
بهذا في النظريات، مثال أن يقول الشفعوي مثلا: معلوم أن المطعوم ربوي
والسفرجل مطعوم فهو إذا ربوي؛ فإن  قيل: لم قلت المطعوم ربوي؟ فتقول: دليله
البر والشعير والتمر بمعنى فإنها مطعومات وهي ربوية.
فينبغي أن يقال: فقولك المطعوم ربوي أردت به كل المطعومات أو بعضها؟ فإن
أردت البعض لم تلزم النتيجة إذ يمكن أن يكون السفرجل من
البعض الذي ليس ربويا ويكون هذا خللا في نظم القياس كما يأتي وجهه، وإن
أردت الكل فمن أين عرفت هذا وما عددته من البر والشعير ليس كل المطعومات؟
النظر الثاني: في شروط النقيض. وهو محتاج إليه إذ رب مطلوب لا يقوم
الدليل عليه ولكن على بطلان نقيضه فيستبان من إبطاله صحة نقيضه، والقضيتان
المتناقضتان يعني بهما كل قضيتين إذا صدقت إحداهما كذبت الأخرى بالضرورة،
كقولنا: العالم حادث العالم ليس بحادث. وإنما يلزم صدق إحداهما عند كذب
الأخرى بستة شروط:
الأول: أن يكون المحكوم عليه في القضيتين واحدا بالذات لا بمجرد اللفظ،
فإن اتحد اللفظ دون المعنى لم يتناقضا، كقولك: النور مدرك بالبصر غير مدرك
بالبصر، إذا أردت بأحدهما الضوء وبالآخر العقل؛ ولذلك لا يتناقض قول
الفقهاء: المضطر مختار المضطر ليس بمختار، وقولهم: المضطر آثم المضطر ليس
بآثم، إذ قد يعبر بالمضطر عن المرتعد والمحمول المطروح على غيره، وقد يعبر
به عن المدعو بالسيف إلى الفعل، فالاسم متحد والمعنى مختلف
الثاني: أن يكون الحكم واحدا والاسم مختلف، كقولك: العالم قديم العالم
ليس بقديم، أردت بأحد القديمين ما أراده الله تعالى بقوله: {كالعرجون
القديم} [يس: 39] .
ولذلك لم يتناقض قولهم: المكره مختار المكره ليس بمختار؛ لأن المختار
عبارة عن معنيين مختلفين
الثالث: أن تتحد الإضافة في الأمور الإضافية، فإنك لو قلت زيد أب زيد ليس
بأب، لم يتناقضا إذ يكون أبا لبكر ولا يكون أبا لخالد وكذلك تقول زيد أب
زيد ابن، فلا يتعدد بالإضافة إلى شخصين، والعشرة نصف والعشرة ليست بنصف أي
بالإضافة إلى العشرين والثلاثين؛ وكما يقال المرأة مولى عليها المرأة غير
مولى عليها، وهما صادقان بالإضافة إلى النكاح والبيع لا إلى شيء واحد وإلى
العصبة والأجنبي لا إلى شخص واحد.
الرابع:  أن يتساويا في القوة والفعل، فإنك تقول: الماء في الكوز مرو، أي
بالقوة؛ وليس الماء بمرو أي بالفعل؛ والسيف في الغمد قاطع وليس بقاطع. ومنه
ثار الخلاف في أن البارئ في الأزل خالق أو ليس بخالق.
الخامس: التساوي في الجزء والكل، فإنك تقول الزنجي أسود الزنجي ليس
بأسود، أي ليس بأسود الأسنان؛ وعنه نشأ الغلط، حيث قيل إن العالمية حال
لزيد بجملته لأن زيدا عبارة عن جملته ولم يعرف أنا إذا قلنا زيد في بغداد
لم نعن به أنه في جميع بغداد بل في جزء منها وهو مكان يساوي مساحته.
السادس: التساوي في المكان والزمان فإنك تقول: العالم حادث العالم ليس
بحادث، أي هو حادث عند أول وجوده وليس بحادث قبله ولا بعده بل قبله معدوم
وبعده باق والصبي تنبت له أسنان والصبي لا تنبت له أسنان، ونعني بأحدهما
السنة الأولى
وبالآخر التي بعدها. وبالجملة فالقضية المتناقضة هي التي تسلب ما أثبتته
الأولى بعينه عما أثبتته بعينه، وفي ذلك الوقت والمكان والحال وبتلك
الإضافة بعينها وبالقوة إن كان ذلك بالقوة وبالفعل إن كان ذلك بالفعل وكذلك
في الجزء والكل، وتحصيل ذلك بأن لا تخالف القضية النافية المثبتة إلا في
تبديل النفي بالإثبات فقط
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā-yā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes cutting, deciding, and settling a matter definitively; a proposition (qaḍiyyah) is a decisive judgment linking two concepts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, qaḍiyyah is the assertive composite (tarkīb khabarī) amenable to truth and falsity, distinct from mere conception (taṣawwur).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the judge's binding verdict; metaphorically extended to any definitive cognitive assertion.
- Root: ن-ق-ض (na-q-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To unravel, break apart, or invalidate; contradiction (tanāquḍ) is the mutual destruction of two propositions.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In logic-theology, it is the relation where one proposition's truth necessitates the other's falsity by necessity (ḍarūrah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: demolishing a building; metaphorical: logical refutation that collapses an opposing claim.
- Root: س-و-ر (sūr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A wall or enclosure; in logic, the quantifier (sūr) that encloses the subject's extension.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The determiner of universality (kulliyyah) or particularity (juzʾiyyah) in categorical propositions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: city wall; metaphorical: the linguistic boundary that circumscribes the scope of the subject term.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Naqīḍ (Coordination of Contradictories) — For genuine contradiction, the predicate must be affirmed and denied of exactly the same subject under identical conditions; any variation in time, place, relation, potentiality, or part-whole scope voids the contradiction, as in the grammatical principle that negation (nafy) and affirmation (ījāb) must share identical referential anchors.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third chapter of the preliminaries concerns the judgments of composite meanings. We have already examined the bare utterance (mujarrad al-lafẓ) and then the bare meaning (mujarrad al-maʿnā). Now we examine the composition of meaning in a manner susceptible to affirmation (taṣdīq) and denial (takdhīb) — as when we say, for example: "The world is originated (al-ʿālam ḥādith)" and "The Creator, exalted, is eternal (al-Bārī taʿālā qadīm)." For this reverts to the compositive act of the reflective faculty (al-quwwah al-mufakkirah) between two simple cognitions, relating one to the other either by affirmation (ithbāt) — as you say "The world is originated" — or by negation (salb) — as you say "The world is not eternal." This has coalesced from two parts: the grammarians (nuḥāh) call one the subject (mubtadaʾ) and the other the predicate (khabar); the theologians (mutakallimūn) call one the attribute (waṣf) and the other the attributed (mawṣūf); the logicians (manṭiqiyyūn) call one the subject (mawḍūʿ) and the other the predicate (maḥmūl); and the jurists (fuqahāʾ) call one the ruling (ḥukm) and the other the ruled-upon (maḥkūm ʿalayh). The totality is termed a proposition (qaḍiyyah).

The judgments of propositions are numerous, and we shall mention from them what is most frequently needed and whose neglect is harmful — namely two judgments:

**The First Judgment:** The proposition, in relation to the subject of predication (al-maqḍī ʿalayh), divides into the determinate (taʿyīn), the unqualified-particular (ihmāl), the universal (ʿumūm), and the particular (khuṣūṣ) — thus four types:

**First:** A proposition about a determinate individual (qāḍiyyah fī ʿayn), as when we say: "Zayd is a scribe" and "This blackness is an accident (ʿaraḍ)."

**Second:** A particular unqualified proposition (qāḍiyyah muṭlaqah khāṣṣah), as when we say: "Some people are learned" and "Some bodies are at rest."

**Third:** A universal unqualified proposition (qāḍiyyah muṭlaqah ʿāmmah), as when we say: "Every body is extended (mutḥayyiz)" and "Every blackness is a color."

**Fourth:** An indeterminate proposition (qāḍiyyah muhmalah), as when we say: "Man is in loss" {«الإنسان في خسر»}.

The reason for this division is that the subject of predication is either a determinate individual pointed to (ʿayn mushār ilayh) or not. If it is not a determinate individual, then either it is circumscribed by a quantifier (sūr) that clarifies its extent — in its totality (kulliyyah) making it universal-unqualified, or in its partiality (juzʾiyyah) making it particular — or it is not circumscribed by a quantifier, making it indeterminate. The quantifier is your saying "every" (kull) and "some" (baʿḍ) and whatever stands in their place.

Among the devices of sophists (al-mughāliṭīn) in theoretical inquiry is the use of indeterminate propositions in place of universal ones. For indeterminate propositions may be intended with particularity or universality, such that both sides of a contradiction come out true — as when you say "Man is in loss," meaning the disbeliever, and "Man is not in loss," meaning the prophets. This must not be tolerated in theoretical matters. An example: suppose a Shāfiʿite says: "It is known that the edible (al-maṭʿūm) is usurious (ribawī), and quince is edible, therefore it is usurious." If it is said: "Why did you say the edible is usurious?" he replies: "Its evidence is wheat, barley, and dates — for they are edible and they are usurious."

It should then be said to him: "In your statement 'the edible is usurious,' do you mean all edibles or some of them? If you mean some, the conclusion does not follow, for quince may belong to the portion that is not usurious — and this is a defect in the syllogism's structure (khalal fī naẓm al-qiyās), as its manner will come later. If you mean all, then from where have you known this? For what you enumerated — wheat, barley, and dates — is not all edibles."

**The Second Inquiry:** Concerning the conditions of contradiction (tanāquḍ). This is needed because many a sought conclusion (maṭlūb) has no direct proof established for it, but rather proof is established for the falsity of its contradictory — so from the invalidation of the latter, the validity of its contradictory becomes evident. By "two contradictory propositions" (al-qāḍiyyatān al-mutanāqiḍatān) is meant any two propositions such that if one is true, the other is necessarily false — as when we say: "The world is originated" and "The world is not originated." The truth of one upon the falsity of the other is entailed only under six conditions:

**First Condition:** That the subject of predication in both propositions be one in essence (bi-al-dhāt), not merely in wording. If the wording is unified but the meaning differs, they do not contradict — as when you say: "Light is perceived by sight" and "Light is not perceived by sight," if by one you mean the luminous ray (al-ḍawʾ) and by the other the intellect (al-ʿaql). For this reason, the jurists' statements do not contradict: "The compelled one (al-muḍṭarr) is free-acting (mukhtār)" and "The compelled one is not free-acting," nor their statements "The compelled one is sinful" and "The compelled one is not sinful" — for "the compelled one" may refer to one trembling (al-murtiʿid) or one cast upon another (al-maṭrūḥ ʿalā ghayrih), and it may refer to one summoned by the sword to an act (al-madʿūw bi-al-sayf ilā al-fiʿl). Thus the name is unified but the meaning differs.

**Second Condition:** That the judgment be one and the name differ — as when you say: "The world is ancient (qadīm)" and "The world is not ancient," if by one of the two "ancient" (qadīmayn) you mean what God, exalted, meant in His saying: {«كالعرجون القديم»} [Yā Sīn: 39] ("like an ancient date-stalk"). For this reason, their statements do not contradict: "The coerced one (al-mukrah) is free-acting" and "The coerced one is not free-acting" — because "free-acting" (mukhtār) expresses two different meanings.

**Third Condition:** That the relation (al-iḍāfah) be unified in relative matters (al-umūr al-iḍāfiyyah). For if you said: "Zayd is a father" and "Zayd is not a father," they would not contradict — for he may be a father to Bakr and not a father to Khālid. Likewise, you say "Zayd is a father" and "Zayd is a son" — these do not conflict when related to two different persons. And "Ten is half" and "Ten is not half" — that is, in relation to twenty and to thirty. Similarly, it is said: "The woman is under guardianship (mawlā ʿalayhā)" and "The woman is not under guardianship" — both are true in relation to marriage (nikāḥ) and sale (bayʿ), not to a single thing; and in relation to the agnate (ʿaṣabah) and the stranger (ajnabī), not to a single person.

**Fourth Condition:** That they be equal in potentiality (quwwah) and actuality (fiʿl). For you say: "The water in the jug is wine (māʾ)" — that is, potentially; and "The water is not wine" — that is, actually. And "The sword in the sheath is cutting" and "is not cutting." From this arose the dispute over whether the Creator, in eternity (al-azal), is "creator" (khāliq) or "not creator."

**Fifth Condition:** Equality in part and whole (al-juzʾ wa-al-kull). For you say: "The Negro is black" and "The Negro is not black" — that is, not black of teeth. From this arose an error, where it was said that "worldliness" (al-ʿālamiyyah) is a state of Zayd in his entirety, because "Zayd" denotes his totality — without recognizing that when we say "Zayd is in Baghdad," we do not mean he is in all of Baghdad, but in a part of it, namely a place equal to his own area.

**Sixth Condition:** Equality in place (makān) and time (zamān). For you say: "The world is originated" and "The world is not originated" — that is, it is originated at the beginning of its existence, and it is not originated before that nor after it; rather, before it, it was non-existent (maʿdūm), and after it, it is enduring (bāqī). And "The child grows teeth" and "The child does not grow teeth" — meaning by one the first year and by the other the one after it.

In sum: the contradictory proposition (al-qāḍiyyah al-mutanāqiḍah) is that which negates exactly what the first affirmed, of exactly what it affirmed it, at that very time, place, and state, with that very relation, in potentiality if it was potential, in actuality if it was actual, and likewise in part and whole. The upshot of this is that the negative proposition must not differ from the affirmative except in exchanging negation for affirmation alone.
