chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة إذا مات في أثناء وقت الصلاة فجأة بعد العزم على الامتثال]

إذا مات في أثناء وقت الصلاة فجأة بعد العزم على الامتثال لا يكون عاصيا
وقال بعض من أراد تحقيق معنى الوجوب: إنه يعصي. وهو خلاف إجماع السلف،
فإنا نعلم أنهم كانوا لا يؤثمون من مات فجأة بعد انقضاء مقدار أربع ركعات
من وقت الزوال أو بعد انقضاء مقدار ركعتين من أول الصبح، وكانوا لا ينسبونه
إلى تقصير لا سيما إذا اشتغل  بالوضوء أو نهض إلى المسجد فمات في الطريق، بل
محال أن يعصي وقد جوز له التأخير فمن فعل ما يجوز له كيف يمكن تعصيته.
فإن قيل: جاز له التأخير بشرط سلامة العاقبة.
قلنا: هذا محال، فإن العاقبة مستورة عنه، فإذا سألنا وقال العاقبة مستورة
عني وعلي صوم يوم وأنا أريد أن أؤخره إلى غد فهل يحل لي التأخير مع الجهل
بالعاقبة أم أعصي بالتأخير؟ فلا بد له من جواب؛ فإن قلنا: لا يعصي فلم أثم
بالموت الذي ليس إليه، وإن قلنا: يعصي، فهو خلاف الإجماع في الواجب الموسع،
وإن قلنا: إن كان في علم الله تعالى أنك تموت قبل الغد فأنت عاص وإن كان في
علمه أن تحيا فلك التأخير، فيقول وما يدريني ماذا في علم الله فما فتواكم
في حق الجاهل؟ فلا بد من الجزم بالتحليل أو التحريم.
فإن قيل: فإن جاز تأخيره أبدا ولا يعصي إذا مات فأي معنى لوجوبه؟ قلنا
تحقق الوجوب بأنه لم يجز التأخير إلا بشرط العزم ولا يجوز العزم على
التأخير إلا إلى مدة يغلب على ظنه البقاء إليها، كتأخيره الصلاة من ساعة
إلى ساعة وتأخيره الصوم من يوم إلى يوم مع العزم على التفرغ له في كل وقت
وتأخيره الحج من سنة إلى سنة، فلو عزم المريض المشرف على الهلاك على
التأخير شهرا أو الشيخ الضعيف على التأخير سنين وغالب ظنه أنه لا يعيش إلى
تلك المدة عصى بهذا التأخير وإن لم يمت ووفق للعمل لكنه مأخوذ بموجب ظنه،
كالمعزر إذا ضرب ضربا يهلك أو قاطع سلعة وغالب ظنه الهلاك أثم وإن سلم؛
ولهذا قال أبو حنيفة: لا يجوز تأخير الحج؛ لأن البقاء إلى سنة لا يغلب على
الظن، وأما تأخير الصوم والزكاة إلى شهر وشهرين فجائز؛ لأنه لا يغلب على
الظن الموت إلى تلك المدة والشافعي - رحمه الله - يرى البقاء إلى السنة
الثانية غالبا على الظن في حق الشاب الصحيح دون الشيخ والمريض.
ثم المعزر إذا فعل ما غالب ظنه السلامة فهلك  ضمن لا؛ لأنه آثم لكن؛ لأنه
أخطأ في ظنه والمخطئ ضامن غير آثم.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ز م (ʿazama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firm intention, decisive resolution of the heart binding one to an act
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The resolve (ʿazm) that renders an obligation (wujūb) presently binding upon the subject, distinguishing it from mere inclination
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — a settled determination; metaphorical (majāz) — not used here, as it denotes an actual psychological state
- Root: و س ع (wasiʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Capacity, breadth, expansion
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The expanded obligation (al-wājib al-muwaqqat al-mūsaʿ) — a duty whose time-window exceeds the act's minimal duration, permitting delay
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — spatial/ temporal amplitude; metaphorical — legal latitude (tawsiʿah) granted by the Lawgiver
- Root: ظ ن (ẓanna)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Doubtful belief, prevailing opinion short of certainty
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Preponderant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann) as a legal criterion for permissibility and culpability
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — cognitive state; metaphorical — the jurisprudential standard replacing certainty where the latter is unattainable
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Suppressed Protasis (al-sharṭ al-maḥdhūf) — In "if he dies... he is not disobedient," the conditional's apodosis is governed by the legal norm (ḥukm), not by temporal sequence, requiring parsing of the protasis as a stipulated cause (sabab) for the ruling's application.
chapters.translation:
### [Issue: If One Dies Suddenly During the Prayer Time After Resolving to Comply]

I say: If one dies suddenly during the prayer time after having resolved to comply [with the obligation], he is not disobedient. Yet some who sought to verify the meaning of obligation (wujūb) claimed that he is disobedient. This contradicts the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the predecessors (salaf), for we know with certainty that they did not declare sinful one who died suddenly after the lapse of the measure of four rakʿahs from the time of noon (zawāl), or after the lapse of the measure of two rakʿahs from the beginning of dawn, nor did they attribute to him negligence — especially if he had occupied himself with ablution (wuḍūʾ) or set out toward the mosque and died on the way. Rather, it is impossible that he be disobedient when delay was permitted to him; for whoever does what is permissible to him — how can he possibly be deemed disobedient?

If it is said: "Delay was permitted to him only on condition of a sound outcome [i.e., that he live to perform the act]," we reply: This is impossible, for the outcome is veiled from him. If he asks us, saying: "The outcome is veiled from me, and I owe a day of fasting, and I wish to postpone it to tomorrow — is delay lawful for me despite my ignorance of the outcome, or do I disobey by delaying?" — then we must give an answer. If we say: "He does not disobey," then why is he sinful for a death that is not within his power? And if we say: "He disobeys," that contradicts the consensus regarding the expanded obligation (al-wājib al-mūsaʿ). And if we say: "If it is in God's knowledge that you will die before tomorrow, you are disobedient; and if it is in His knowledge that you will live, then delay is yours," he would respond: "How am I to know what is in God's knowledge? So what is your legal ruling (fatwā) regarding the ignorant one?" Thus one must decisively affirm either permissibility (taḥlīl) or prohibition (taḥrīm).

If it is said: "If delay is permissible indefinitely and he does not disobey upon dying, then what meaning remains for its obligation?" We reply: The reality of obligation is established by the fact that delay is not permitted except on condition of resolve (ʿazm), and resolve upon delay is not permissible except for a duration which one's prevailing conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann) deems one likely to survive — such as postponing prayer from one hour to another, postponing fasting from one day to another with the resolve to devote oneself to it at every moment, and postponing the pilgrimage (ḥajj) from one year to another. Thus, if a sick person on the brink of destruction resolves to delay for a month, or a weak old man resolves to delay for years, while his prevailing conjecture is that he will not live until that term, he disobeys by that delay — even if he does not die and is granted success to perform the act, yet he is held accountable according to the dictate of his conjecture. This is like the one who administers a beating (muʿazzir) that is lethal, or one who cuts off a growth while his prevailing conjecture is death — he is sinful even if he survives. For this reason, Abū Ḥanīfah held that delaying the pilgrimage is not permissible, because survival until the following year is not predominant in conjecture; whereas delaying fasting and alms (zakāh) for a month or two is permissible, because death within that term is not predominant in conjecture. Al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — holds that survival until the second year is predominant in conjecture for the healthy young man, but not for the old man or the sick.

Then, if the one administering the beating does what his prevailing conjecture deems safe, yet the victim dies, he is liable for compensation (ḍamān) — not because he is sinful, but because he erred in his conjecture; and the one who errs is liable for compensation without being sinful.

chapters.title_en: On Whether That Without Which an Obligation Cannot Be Completed Is Itself Described as Obligatory
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة ما لا يتم الواجب إلا به هل يوصف بالوجوب]

مسألة اختلفوا في أن ما لا يتم الواجب إلا به هل يوصف بالوجوب اختلفوا في
أن ما لا يتم الواجب إلا به هل يوصف بالوجوب؟
والتحقيق في هذا أن هذا ينقسم إلى ما ليس إلى المكلف كالقدرة على الفعل
وكاليد في الكتابة وكالرجل في المشي، فهذا لا يوصف بالوجوب بل عدمه يمنع
الإيجاب إلا على مذهب من يجوز تكليف ما لا يطاق، وكذلك تكليف حضور الإمام
الجمعة وحضور تمام العدد فإنه ليس إليه فلا يوصف بالوجوب بل يسقط بتعذره
الواجب. وأما ما يتعلق باختيار العبد فينقسم إلى الشرط الشرعي وإلى الحسي،
فالشرعي كالطهارة في الصلاة يجب وصفها بالوجوب عند وجوب الصلاة، فإن إيجاب
الصلاة إيجاب لما يصير به الفعل صلاة.
وأما الحسي فكالسعي إلى الجمعة وكالمشي إلى الحج وإلى مواضع المناسك،
فينبغي أن يوصف أيضا بالوجوب إذ أمر البعيد عن البيت بالحج أمر بالمشي إليه
لا محالة، وكذلك إذا وجب غسل الوجه ولم يمكن إلا بغسل جزء من الرأس، وإذا
وجب الصوم ولم يمكن إلا بالإمساك جزءا من الليل قبل الصبح فيوصف ذلك
بالوجوب. ونقول: ما لا يتوصل إلى الواجب إلا به وهو فعل المكلف فهو واجب.
وهذا أولى من أن نقول يجب التوصل إلى الواجب بما ليس بواجب، إذ قولنا: "
يجب فعل ما ليس بواجب " متناقض، وقولنا: " ما ليس بواجب صار واجبا " غير
متناقض فإنه واجب؛ لكن الأصل وجب بالإيجاب قصدا إليه، والوسيلة وجبت بواسطة
وجوب المقصود وقد وجب كيفما كان وإن كان علة وجوبه غير علة وجوب المقصود
فإن قيل: لو كان واجبا
لكان مقدرا، فما المقدار الذي يجب غسله من الرأس وإمساكه من الليل؟ قلنا:
قد وجب التوصل به إلى الواجب وهو غير مقدر، بل يجب مسح الرأس ويكفي أقل ما
ينطلق عليه الاسم وهو غير مقدر، فكذلك الواجب أقل ما يمكن به غسل  الوجه.
وهذا التقدير كاف في الوجوب. فإن قيل لو كان واجبا لكان يثاب على فعله
ويعاقب على تركه، وتارك الوضوء لا يعاقب على ما تركه من غسل الرأس بل من
غسل الوجه، وتارك الصوم لا يعاقب على ترك الإمساك ليلا. قلنا: ومن أنبأكم
بذلك؟ ومن أين عرفتم أن ثواب البعيد عن البيت لا يزيد على ثواب القريب في
الحج، وأن من زاد عمله لا يزيد ثوابه وإن كان بطريق التوصل؟ وأما العقاب
فهو عقاب على ترك الصوم والوضوء وليس يتوزع على أجزاء الفعل، فلا معنى
لإضافته إلى التفاصيل.
فإن قيل: لو قدر على الاقتصار على غسل الوجه لم يعاقب، قلنا: هذا مسلم؛
لأنه إنما يجب على العاجز أما القادر فلا وجوب عليه.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ج-ب (w-j-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "falling" or "being fixed/necessary" — an obligation (wujūb) is that which is firmly established and cannot be avoided.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, wujūb denotes a divine command that entails reward for compliance and punishment for neglect; it is tied to capacity (istitāʿah) and choice (ikhtiyār).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage applies to acts within the servant's power; metaphorical (majāz) extension to necessary preconditions is contested — the dispute here hinges on this distinction.
- Root: ت-و-س-ل (t-w-s-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Means "seeking access" or "means of approach" — a wasīlah is a path or instrument toward a goal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, the "means" (wasīlah) to an obligation is distinguished from the "end" (maqṣūd); its ruling derives from the ruling of the end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The phrase "the means is obligatory by virtue of the end's obligation" is a metaphorical transfer (majāz) of the predicate "obligatory" from the intended act to its prerequisite.
- Root: ق-د-ر (q-d-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Denotes measure, capacity, or determination — taqdīr is the fixing of a specific quantity or limit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal discourse, taqdīr concerns whether an obligation requires a determinate extent (miqdār) or suffices with the minimal instantiation of the act's name.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage requires precise measurement; here, the response invokes the minimal semantic threshold (aqall mā yanṭaliq ʿalayhi al-ism) as sufficient — a recognized juristic convention.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs "if it is said... we say" (fa-in qīla... qulnā) as a structured dialectical exchange, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the argumentative flow.
chapters.translation:
I say: The scholars have differed concerning whether that without which an obligation cannot be completed is itself described as obligatory. They differed concerning whether that without which the obligatory act cannot be completed is described as obligatory.

The verification of this matter is that it divides into [two categories]. First, that which is not within the servant's power — such as the capacity for the act, the hand in writing, and the leg in walking. This is not described as obligatory; rather, its absence prevents the imposition of obligation (ījāb), except on the doctrine of one who permits the imposition of what cannot be borne (taklīf mā lā yuṭāq). Likewise, the obligation of the imam's presence for Friday [prayer] and the completion of the requisite number [for the congregation] — for this is not within [the individual's] power, so it is not described as obligatory; rather, the obligation falls away with its impossibility.

As for that which pertains to the servant's choice, it divides into the legal condition (al-sharṭ al-sharʿī) and the sensory [condition] (al-ḥissī). The legal [condition] is like purification (ṭahārah) for prayer: it must be described as obligatory when prayer becomes obligatory, for the obligation of prayer is the obligation of that by which the act becomes prayer.

As for the sensory [condition], it is like striving (saʿy) to Friday [prayer], and walking to the Pilgrimage (ḥajj) and to the sites of the rituals. This too should be described as obligatory, for commanding the one who is distant from the House to perform the Pilgrimage is necessarily a command to walk to it. Likewise, when washing the face is obligatory and cannot be accomplished except by washing part of the head, and when fasting is obligatory and cannot be accomplished except by refraining for part of the night before dawn — then that [part] is described as obligatory.

And we say: That by which one cannot reach the obligatory act, when it is an act of the servant, is obligatory. This is more fitting than saying "one must reach the obligatory act by means of what is not obligatory," for our statement "one must do what is not obligatory" is self-contradictory, whereas our statement "what was not obligatory has become obligatory" is not contradictory — for it is obligatory. Rather, the original [end] became obligatory by an obligation directed toward it, and the means became obligatory by virtue of the obligation of the intended end. It has become obligatory in any case, even if the cause of its obligation is not the cause of the obligation of the intended end.

If it is said: "If it were obligatory, it would be determinate in measure (muqaddar). So what is the measure of what must be washed from the head and refrained from during the night?" — We say: The means to the obligatory act has become obligatory, and it is not determinate in measure. Rather, wiping the head is obligatory, and the least amount to which the name applies suffices, and it is not determinate in measure. Likewise, the obligatory [amount] is the least by which washing the face can be accomplished. And this determination (taqdīr) suffices for obligation.

If it is said: "If it were obligatory, one would be rewarded for doing it and punished for omitting it. Yet the one who omits ablution (wuḍūʾ) is not punished for omitting the washing of the head, but for omitting the washing of the face; and the one who omits fasting is not punished for omitting the nighttime refrainment." — We say: Who informed you of this? And from where have you known that the reward of the one distant from the House does not exceed the reward of the one near it in the Pilgrimage, and that the one whose deed is greater does not have his reward increased, even if it be by way of means? As for punishment, it is punishment for omitting the fast and the ablution, and it is not distributed over the parts of the act. So there is no meaning to attributing it to the details.

If it is said: "If he were able to suffice with washing the face alone, he would not be punished" — We say: This is conceded, for it is obligatory only upon the incapable one. As for the capable one, there is no obligation upon him.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة إذا اختلطت منكوحة بأجنبية]

مسألة قال قائلون إذا اختلطت منكوحة بأجنبية قال قائلون: إذا اختلطت
منكوحة بأجنبية وجب الكف عنهما.
لكن الحرام هي الأجنبية والمنكوحة حلال ويجب الكف عنها. وهذا متناقض، بل
ليس الحرمة والحل وصفا ذاتيا لهما بل هو متعلق بالفعل، فإذا حرم فعل الوطء
فيهما فأي معنى لقولنا وطء المنكوحة حلال ووطء الأجنبية حرام؟ بل هما
حرامان إحداهما بعلة الأجنبية والأخرى بعلة الاختلاط بالأجنبية، فالاختلاف
في العلة لا في الحكم.
وإنما وقع هذا في الأوهام من حيث ضاهى الوصف بالحل والحرمة الوصف بالعجز
والقدرة والسواد والبياض والصفات الحسية، وذلك وهم نبهنا عليه إذ ليست
الأحكام صفات للأعيان أصلا؛ بل نقول: إذا اشتبهت رضيعة بنساء بلدة فنكح
واحدة حلت واحتمل أن تكون هي الرضيعة في علم الله تعالى؛ ولا نقول إنها
ليست في علم الله تعالى زوجة له، إذ لا معنى للزوجة إلا من حل وطؤها بنكاح،
وهذه قد حل وطؤها فهي حلال عنده وعند الله تعالى.
ولا نقول هي حرام عند الله تعالى وحلال عنده في ظنه، بل إذا ظن الحل فهي
حلال عند الله تعالى وسيأتي تحقيق هذا في مسألة تصويب المجتهد. أما إذا قال
لزوجتيه: " إحداكما طالق " فيحتمل أن يقال يحل وطؤهما والطلاق  غير واقع؛
لأنه لم يعين له محلا فصار كما إذا باع أحد عبديه، ويحتمل أن يقال حرمتا
جميعا فإنه لا يشترط تعيين محل الطلاق ثم عليه التعيين وإليه ذهب أكثر
الفقهاء، والمتبع في ذلك موجب ظن المجتهد أما المصير إلى أن إحداهما محرمة
والأخرى منكوحة كما توهموه في اختلاط المنكوحة بالأجنبية فلا ينقدح ههنا؛
لأن ذلك جهل من الآدمي عرض بعد التعيين، وأما هنا فليس متعينا في نفسه بل
يعلمه الله تعالى مطلقا لإحداهما لا بعينها.
فإن قيل: إذا وجب عليه التعيين فالله تعالى يعلم ما سيعينه فتكون هي
المحرمة المطلقة بعينها في علم الله تعالى، وإنما هو مشكل علينا. قلنا:
الله تعالى يعلم الأشياء على ما هي عليه، فلا يعلم الطلاق الذي لم يعين
محله متعينا بل يعلمه قابلا للتعيين إذا عينه المطلق، ويعلم أنه سيعين زينب
مثلا، فيتعين الطلاق بتعيينه إذا عين لا قبله.
وكذلك نقول في الواجب المخير: الله تعالى يعلم ما سيفعله العبد من خلال
الكفارة ولا يعلمه واجبا بعينه بل واجبا غير معين في الحال، ثم يعلم
صيرورته متعينا بالتعيين بدليل أنه لم يعلم أنه يموت
قبل التكفير وقبل التعيين فيعلم الوجوب والطلاق على ما هو عليه من عدم
التعيين.

### | [مسألة الواجب الذي لا يتقدر بحد محدود]

مسألة اختلفوا في الواجب الذي لا يتقدر بحد محدود اختلفوا في الواجب الذي
لا يتقدر بحد محدود
كمسح الرأس والطمأنينة في الركوع والسجود ومدة القيام أنه إذا زاد على
أقل الواجب هل توصف الزيادة بالوجوب؟ فلو مسح جميع الرأس هل يقع فعله
بجملته واجبا أو الواجب الأقل والباقي ندب؟ فذهب قوم إلى أن الكل يوصف
بالوجوب؛ لأن نسبة الكل إلى الأمر واحد والأمر في نفسه أمر واحد وهو أمر
إيجاب ولا يتميز البعض من البعض فالكل امتثال. والأولى أن يقال: الزيادة
على الأقل ندب، فإنه لم يجب إلا أقل ما ينطلق عليه الاسم، وهذا في
الطمأنينة والقيام وما وقع متعاقبا أظهر، وكذلك المسح إذا وقع متعاقبا وما
وقع  من جملته معا وإن كان لا يتميز بعضه من بعض بالإشارة والتعيين، فيحتمل
أن يقال قدر الأقل منه واجب والباقي ندب وإن لم يتميز بالإشارة المندوب عن
الواجب؛ لأن الزيادة على الأقل لا عقاب على تركها مطلقا من غير شرط بدل فلا
يتحقق فيه حد الوجوب.

### | [مسألة الوجوب يباين الجواز والإباحة بحدة]

الوجوب يباين الجواز والإباحة بحده.
فلذلك قلنا: يقضى بخطإ من ظن أن الوجوب إذا نسخ بقي الجواز، بل الحق أنه
إذا نسخ رجع الأمر إلى ما كان قبل الوجوب من تحريم أو إباحة وصار الوجوب
بالنسخ كأن لم يكن. فإن قيل كل واجب فهو جائز وزيادة، إذ الجائز ما لا عقاب
على فعله والواجب أيضا لا عقاب على فعله وهو معنى الجواز، فإذا نسخ الوجوب
فكأنه أسقط العقاب على تركه فيبقى سقوط العقاب على فعله وهو معنى الجواز.
قلنا: هذا كقول القائل كل واجب فهو ندب وزيادة، فإذا نسخ الوجوب بقي الندب
ولا قائل به. ولا فرق بين الكلامين وكلاهما وهم، بل الواجب لا يتضمن معنى
الجواز فإن حقيقة الجواز التخيير بين الفعل والترك والتساوي بينهما بتسوية
الشرع وذلك منفي عن الواجب. وذكر هذه المسألة ههنا أولى من ذكرها في كتاب
النسخ، فإنه نظر في حقيقة الوجوب والجواز لا في حقيقة النسخ.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ ل ط (khalata)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intermingling, blending of distinct entities such that separation becomes impossible.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Connotes epistemic confusion (ishtibāh) where the legal subject (maḥall) is indeterminate, not a change in the essence of the objects.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal mixing of physical bodies; metaphorically, the confusion of legal predicates due to loss of specification (taʿyīn).
- Root: ع ي ن (ʿayna)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To specify, to fix upon a particular individual; the eye as the organ of discernment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for legal determination (taʿyīn) — the act of assigning a ruling to a concrete particular.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal visual pointing; metaphorical for judicial specification in contracts and oaths.
- Root: ج و ز (jawaza)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pass through, to be permissible; crossing a boundary without hindrance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal permissibility (jawāz) as the absence of prohibition, but not necessarily entailing equal license for act and omission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal passage through a gate; metaphorical for the Lawgiver's lifting of restriction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taḍāyuf (Correlativity) — Legal predicates like "forbidden" and "permissible" are relational (mutāʿalliqah bi al-fiʿl), not inherent attributes (ṣifāt dhātiyyah) of substances; hence their grammatical attachment to the act, not the object, governs parsing of the ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: Some have said: When a married woman is mixed with a foreign woman, it becomes obligatory to abstain from both. But the forbidden one is the foreign woman, while the married woman is lawful — yet abstention from her is obligatory. This is contradictory. Rather, lawfulness and unlawfulness are not essential attributes of the two women themselves; they are attached to the act. So when the act of intercourse is rendered forbidden with respect to both, what meaning remains in our saying "intercourse with the married woman is lawful" and "intercourse with the foreign woman is forbidden"? Rather, both are forbidden — one by reason of being foreign, the other by reason of being mixed with the foreign one. The difference lies in the cause (ʿillah), not in the ruling (ḥukm).

This confusion arose in minds only because describing something as lawful or forbidden was analogized to describing it as powerless or powerful, black or white, and other sensory attributes. That is a fallacy we have already exposed, for legal rulings are not attributes of concrete entities at all. Rather, we say: If a suckling infant is confused with the women of a town, and a man marries one of them, she becomes lawful for him, though it is possible that she is the suckling infant in God's knowledge. We do not say that in God's knowledge she is not a wife to him, for "wife" has no meaning except one whose intercourse is lawful by marriage — and this one's intercourse has become lawful, so she is lawful for him and before God.

Nor do we say she is forbidden before God but lawful in his estimation. Rather, if he deems her lawful, she is lawful before God. The verification of this will come in the question of validating the mujtahid (taṣwīb al-mujtahid). As for a man who says to his two wives: "One of you is divorced" — it is possible to say that intercourse with both is lawful and the divorce is not effected, because he did not specify a subject (maḥall) for it, making it like one who sells one of his two slaves. And it is possible to say both are forbidden, for specification of the divorce's subject is not a condition; rather, he must then specify — and this is the view of most jurists. What is followed therein is the preponderant conjecture (ẓann) of the mujtahid. As for holding that one of them is forbidden and the other married — as they imagined in the case of the mixed married and foreign woman — that does not arise here, because that case involved human ignorance occurring after specification, whereas here nothing is specified in itself; rather, God knows it as absolutely attached to one of them, not to a particular one.

If it is said: When specification is obligatory upon him, God knows what he will specify, so that one is the absolutely divorced woman in God's knowledge, and the difficulty is only for us — we reply: God knows things as they are. He does not know the divorce whose subject is unspecified as specified; rather, He knows it as susceptible to specification when the divorcer specifies it, and He knows that he will specify Zaynab, for example. Thus the divorce becomes specified by his specification when he specifies, not before.

Likewise we say regarding the obligatory choice (al-wājib al-mukhayyar): God knows what the servant will do among the options of expiation (kaffārah), but He does not know it as a specified obligation, rather as an unspecified obligation at present. Then He knows its becoming specified by the specification — evidenced by the fact that He does not know that the servant will die before expiating and before specifying. Thus He knows the obligation and the divorce as they are, namely, in their state of non-specification.

---

On the Obligation That Is Not Bounded by a Fixed Limit:

They differed concerning the obligation that is not bounded by a fixed limit — such as wiping the head (masḥ al-raʾs), tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah) in bowing and prostration, and the duration of standing — as to whether, when one exceeds the minimum obligatory amount, the excess is described as obligatory. If one wipes the entire head, is the whole act obligatory, or is the minimum obligatory and the rest supererogatory (nadb)? A group held that the whole is described as obligatory, because the relation of the whole to the command is one, and the command in itself is one — a command of obligation — and no part is distinguished from another, so the whole is compliance. The more correct view is to say: The excess over the minimum is supererogatory, for nothing is obligatory except the least to which the name applies. This is more evident in tranquility, standing, and whatever occurs successively. Likewise in wiping, when it occurs successively. As for what occurs simultaneously as a whole — even if no part is distinguished from another by indication or specification — it is possible to say that the minimum amount of it is obligatory and the rest supererogatory, even if the supererogatory is not distinguished from the obligatory by indication, because the excess over the minimum incurs no punishment for its omission absolutely, without any condition of substitution; hence the definition of obligation is not realized in it.

---

On Obligation Being Distinct from Permissibility and Licitness by Its Definition:

Obligation is distinct from permissibility (jawāz) and licitness (ibāḥah) by its very definition. Therefore we rule that one errs who thinks that when obligation is abrogated (naskh), permissibility remains. Rather, the truth is that when it is abrogated, the matter reverts to what it was before obligation — either prohibition or licitness — and the obligation becomes, by abrogation, as if it had never been. If it is said: Every obligatory act is permissible and more, for the permissible is that whose commission incurs no punishment, and the obligatory also incurs no punishment for its commission — which is the meaning of permissibility — so when obligation is abrogated, it is as if the punishment for omission is dropped, leaving the absence of punishment for commission, which is the meaning of permissibility — we reply: This is like one who says every obligatory act is supererogatory and more, so when obligation is abrogated, supererogation remains — and no one holds this. There is no difference between the two statements; both are fallacious. Rather, the obligatory does not entail the meaning of permissibility, for the reality of permissibility is the option between act and omission, and their equivalence by the Lawgiver's equalization — and that is negated for the obligatory. Mentioning this question here is more fitting than in the book on abrogation, for it concerns the reality of obligation and permissibility, not the reality of abrogation.
