صلى الله عليه وسلم - بوحي ليس بقرآن وكلام الله تعالى واحد هو الناسخ
باعتبار، والمنسوخ باعتبار، وليس له كلامان أحدهما قرآن والآخر ليس بقرآن،
وإنما الاختلاف في العبارات فربما دل كلامه بلفظ منظوم يأمرنا بتلاوته
فيسمى قرآنا وربما دل بغير لفظ متلو فيسمى سنة، والكل مسموع من الرسول -
عليه السلام - والناسخ هو الله تعالى في كل حال على أنهم طالبوه بقرآن مثل
هذا القرآن فقال لا أقدر عليه من تلقاء نفسي وما طالبوه بحكم غير ذلك، فأين
هذا من نسخ القرآن بالسنة وامتناعه؟ احتجوا بقوله تعالى: {ما ننسخ من آية
أو ننسها نأت بخير منها أو مثلها} [البقرة: 106] وبين أن الآية لا تنسخ إلا
بمثلها أو بخير منها فالسنة لا تكون مثلها.
ثم تمدح وقال: {ألم تعلم أن الله على كل شيء قدير} [البقرة: 106] بين أنه
لا يقدر عليه غيره. قلنا: قد حققنا أن الناسخ هو
الله تعالى وأنه المظهر له على لسان رسوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - المفهم
إيانا بواسطته نسخ كتابه، ولا يقدر عليه غيره.
ثم لو نسخ الله تعالى آية  على لسان رسوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - ثم أتى
بآية أخرى مثلها كان قد حقق وعده، فلم يشترط أن تكون الآية الأخرى هي
الناسخة للأولى. ثم نقول: ليس المراد الإتيان بقرآن آخر خير منها؛ لأن
القرآن لا يوصف بكون بعضه خيرا من البعض، كيفما قدر قديما أو مخلوقا، بل
معناه أن يأتي بعمل خير من ذلك العمل لكونه أخف منه أو لكونه أجزل ثوابا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-س-خ (n-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To erase, remove, replace, or transfer; in legal terms, the lifting of a previously established ruling by a later divine address.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Abrogation (naskh) as the divine act of superseding a temporal ruling with another, reflecting God's absolute will and wisdom, not a defect in His speech.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes removal; metaphorical (majāz) usage in jurisprudence denotes the indication of a ruling's expiry by a later evidence.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if it is said...") and exceptions to structure dialectical objections and responses, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: It is permissible for the Qur'an to be abrogated by the Sunnah, and for the Sunnah to be abrogated by the Qur'an, because all of it is from God, Mighty and Majestic. So what could prevent this? And homogeneity (tajānus) is not a condition, even though the intellect does not deem it impossible—how could it, when the transmitted evidence (al-samʿ) has already indicated its occurrence? For the orientation toward the Sacred House in Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) is not in the Qur'an but is in the Sunnah, while its abrogator is in the Qur'an. Likewise, His saying, the Exalted: {«فَالآنَ بَاشِرُوهُنَّ»} [Al-Baqarah: 187] abrogated the prohibition of intimate contact, and that prohibition was not in the Qur'an. Similarly, the fasting of ʿĀshūrāʾ was abrogated by the fasting of Ramaḍān, while ʿĀshūrāʾ was established by the Sunnah. And the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf) came in the Qur'an as an abrogator of what was established in the Sunnah regarding the permissibility of delaying it until the cessation of fighting—so much so that he, peace be upon him, said on the Day of the Trench (al-Khandaq), having delayed the prayer: «حَشَا اللهُ قُبُورَهُمْ نَارًا» ("May God fill their graves with fire") because they had detained him from the prayer. Likewise, His saying, the Exalted: {«فَلَا تَرْجِعُوهُنَّ إِلَى الْكُفَّارِ»} [Al-Mumtaḥanah: 10] abrogated what he, peace be upon him, had established of the covenant and truce.

As for the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah, there is the abrogation of the bequest (waṣiyyah) to parents and near relatives by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «أَلَا لَا وَصِيَّةَ لِوَارِثٍ» ("Indeed, no bequest to an heir"), because the verse of inheritance does not preclude the bequest to parents and near relatives, since combining both is possible. Likewise, he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «قَدْ جَعَلَ اللهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلًا، الْبِكْرُ بِالْبِكْرِ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَتَغْرِيبُ عَامٍ، وَالثَّيِّبُ بِالثَّيِّبِ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَالرَّجْمُ» ("God has indeed made a way for them: the virgin with the virgin—one hundred lashes and exile for a year; the married with the married—one hundred lashes and stoning"). This abrogates the detention of women in their homes [prescribed in the Qur'an]. Yet there is consideration here (wa fī hādhā naẓar), for he, peace and blessings be upon him, clarified that the verse of inheritance abrogated the verse of bequest—he did not abrogate it himself, peace and blessings be upon him—and he clarified that God, the Exalted, made a way for them, having already promised this, when He said: {«أَوْ يَجْعَلَ اللهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلًا»} [Al-Nisāʾ: 15].

If it is said: Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, held that the Sunnah cannot be abrogated by the Qur'an, just as the Qur'an cannot be abrogated by the Sunnah—and he is too eminent to be unaware of these instances of abrogation—so it is as if he says: The Sunnah is only annulled by the Sunnah, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, lifts his own Sunnah by his Sunnah, and he is the one who clarifies his own speech and the Qur'an; the Qur'an does not clarify the Sunnah. And where this is not found [in transmission], it is because it was not transmitted; otherwise, abrogation never occurred except in this manner.

We say: If this concerns its permissibility by reason, then it is not hidden that the obligation of turning toward the Kaʿbah is understood from the Qur'an, even if the orientation toward Jerusalem was established by the Sunnah. Likewise, its converse is possible. And if he says this never occurred, we have transmitted its occurrence, and there is no need to posit a hidden, extinct Sunnah, for there is no necessity in such a supposition. And the judgment that it never occurred at all is pure arbitrary assertion (taḥakkum).

And if he says: The majority of cases were like that—perhaps there is no dispute over this.

They argued with His saying, the Exalted: {«قَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَرْجُونَ لِقَاءَنَا ائْتِ بِقُرْآنٍ غَيْرِ هَذَا أَوْ بَدِّلْهُ قُلْ مَا يَكُونُ لِي أَنْ أُبَدِّلَهُ مِنْ تِلْقَاءِ نَفْسِي إِنْ أَتَّبِعُ إِلَّا مَا يُوحَى إِلَيَّ»} [Yūnus: 15]. This indicates that the Qur'an is not abrogated by the Sunnah. We say: There is no disagreement that he does not abrogate it from his own accord, but rather by revelation revealed to him—yet that revelation is not in the wording (naẓm) of the Qur'an. And if we permit abrogation by independent reasoning (ijtihād), then the permission for ijtihād is from God, Mighty and Majestic. The reality is that the abrogator is God, Mighty and Majestic, upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him.

The point is that it is not a condition that a ruling of the Qur'an be abrogated by a Qur'an; rather, it may be abrogated upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him, by a revelation that is not Qur'an. And the speech of God, the Exalted, is one—it is the abrogator in one respect and the abrogated in another. He does not have two speeches, one being Qur'an and the other not Qur'an. The difference is only in the expressions: sometimes His speech is conveyed in a composed wording (lafẓ manẓūm) that He commands us to recite, and it is called Qur'an; sometimes it is conveyed in a non-recited wording, and it is called Sunnah. All of it is heard from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the abrogator is God, the Exalted, in every case. For they demanded of him a Qur'an like this Qur'an, and he said: "I am not able to produce it from my own accord"—but they did not demand of him a ruling other than that. So where is this [argument] in relation to the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah and its impossibility?

They argued with His saying, the Exalted: {«مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنْسِهَا نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنْهَا أَوْ مِثْلِهَا»} [Al-Baqarah: 106], and they held that a verse is only abrogated by its like or by something better than it—and the Sunnah is not like it. Then He praised Himself and said: {«أَلَمْ تَعْلَمْ أَنَّ اللهَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ»} [Al-Baqarah: 106], indicating that none other than Him is capable of this.

We say: We have already established that the abrogator is God, the Exalted, and that He is the one who manifests it upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him, making us understand through his mediation the abrogation of His Book—and none other than Him is capable of this. Then, if God, the Exalted, abrogated a verse upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace be upon him, and then brought another verse like it, He would have fulfilled His promise. So it is not a condition that the other verse itself be the abrogator of the first. Then we say: The meaning is not the bringing of another Qur'an better than it, for the Qur'an is not described as some parts being better than others—however one conceives it, whether eternal or created. Rather, its meaning is that He brings a deed better than that deed, either because it is lighter or because it carries greater reward.

chapters.title_en: The Question of Consensus Not Abrogating
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة الإجماع لا ينسخ به]

الإجماع لا ينسخ به إذ لا نسخ بعد انقطاع الوحي وما نسخ بالإجماع
فالإجماع يدل على ناسخ قد سبق في زمان نزول الوحي من كتاب أو سنة. أما
السنة فينسخ المتواتر منها بالمتواتر والآحاد بالآحاد، أما نسخ المتواتر
منها بالآحاد فاختلفوا في وقوعه سمعا وجوازه عقلا، فقال قوم: وقع ذلك سمعا،
فإن أهل مسجد قباء تحولوا إلى الكعبة بقول واحد أخبرهم وكان ذلك ثابتا
بطريق قاطع فقبلوا نسخه عن الواحد والمختار جواز ذلك عقلا لو تعبد به
ووقوعه سمعا في زمان رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - بدليل قصة قباء،
وبدليل أنه كان ينفذ آحاد الولاة إلى الأطراف وكانوا يبلغون الناسخ
والمنسوخ جميعا، ولكن ذلك ممتنع بعد وفاته بدليل الإجماع من الصحابة على أن
القرآن والمتواتر المعلوم لا يرفع بخبر الواحد، فلا ذاهب إلى تجويزه من
السلف والخلف، والعمل بخبر الواحد تلقي من الصحابة وذلك فيما لا يرفع
قاطعا، بل ذهب الخوارج إلى منع نسخ القرآن بالخبر المتواتر حتى إنهم قالوا
رجم ماعز وإن كان متواترا لا يصلح لنسخ القرآن وقال الشافعي - رحمه الله -:
لا يجوز نسخ القرآن بالسنة وإن تواترت، وليس ذلك بمحال؛ لأنه يصح أن يقال:
تعبدناكم بالنسخ بخبر الواحد في زمان نزول الوحي وحرمنا ذلك بعده.
فإن قيل: كيف يجوز ذلك عقلا وهو رفع القاطع بالظن؟ وأما حديث قباء فلعله
انضم إليه من القرائن ما أورث العلم. قلنا تقدير قرائن معرفة توجب إبطال
أخبار الآحاد وحمل عمل الصحابة على المعرفة بالقرائن ولا سبيل إلى وضع ما
لم ينقل،  وأما قولهم: إنه رفع للقاطع بالظن فباطل؛ إذ لو كان كذلك لقطعنا
بكذب الناقل، ولسنا نقطع به بل نجوز صدقه، وإنما هو مقطوع به بشرط أن لا
يرد خبر نسخه، كما أن البراءة الأصلية مقطوع بها وترتفع بخبر الواحد لأنها
تفيد القطع بشرط عدم خبر الواحد.
فإن قيل: بم تنكرون على من يقطع بكونه كاذبا لأن الرسول - عليه السلام -
أشاع الحكم فلو ثبت نسخه للزمه الإشاعة؟ قلنا ولم يستحيل أن يشيع الحكم
ويكل النسخ إلى الآحاد كما يشيع العموم ويكل التخصيص إلى المخصص؟
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-س-خ (n-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Removal, obliteration, transcription; in legal theory, the lifting of a prior ruling by a later divine address.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Abrogation (naskh) as the temporal supersession of one revealed ruling by another, tied to the cessation of revelation (inqiṭāʿ al-waḥy).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for textual replacement; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to consensus, which merely indicates a prior abrogator.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the protasis "if it is said" (fa-in qīla) governs the apodosis, requiring precise counter-argumentation.
chapters.translation:
I say: Consensus is not abrogated by [anything], for there is no abrogation after the cessation of revelation. Whatever is abrogated by consensus, the consensus indicates an abrogator that preceded during the time of revelation's descent, whether from the Book or the Sunnah. As for the Sunnah, the mutawātir (mass-transmitted) is abrogated by the mutawātir, and the āḥād (solitary reports) by the āḥād. As for the abrogation of the mutawātir by the āḥād, they differed over its occurrence according to revelation (samʿan) and its permissibility according to reason (ʿaqlan). A group said: It occurred according to revelation, for the people of the Qubāʾ Mosque turned toward the Kaʿbah upon a single report (qawl wāḥid) conveyed to them, and that [earlier direction] was established by a decisive path (ṭarīq qāṭiʿ), yet they accepted its abrogation by the single reporter. The chosen position is its permissibility by reason if one were obligated to it, and its occurrence by revelation in the time of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — evidenced by the story of Qubāʾ, and by the evidence that he would dispatch solitary governors to the regions, and they would convey both the abrogating and the abrogated [rulings]. However, that is impossible after his death, by the evidence of the Companions' consensus that the Qurʾān and the known mutawātir cannot be lifted by a solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid). Thus, no one from the predecessors (salaf) or successors (khalaf) holds its permissibility. Acting upon the solitary report is received from the Companions, and that is [only] in what does not lift a decisive [proof]. Rather, the Khārijites went so far as to prohibit the abrogation of the Qurʾān by a mutawātir report, such that they said: The stoning of Māʿiz, though mutawātir, is not fit to abrogate the Qurʾān. And al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — said: It is not permissible to abrogate the Qurʾān by the Sunnah, even if it is mutawātir. And that is not impossible, for it is valid to say: We obligated you to abrogate by the solitary report during the time of revelation's descent, and We forbade that after it.

If it is said: How is that permissible by reason, given it is the lifting of a decisive [proof] by conjecture (ẓann)? And as for the ḥadīth of Qubāʾ, perhaps there were attendant indications (qarāʾin) that engendered knowledge. We say: The supposition of indications that necessitate nullifying solitary reports, and the interpretation of the Companions' practice as [based on] knowledge through indications, is a path to positing what has not been transmitted — and there is no way to that. As for their statement that it is the lifting of a decisive [proof] by conjecture, it is false; for if that were so, we would be certain of the transmitter's falsehood, yet we are not certain of that, but rather deem his truthfulness possible. It is merely decisive on the condition that no report of its abrogation arrives, just as the original presumption of innocence (al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah) is decisive and is lifted by a solitary report, because it yields certainty only on the condition of the absence of a solitary report.

If it is said: How do you reject one who is certain of his falsehood, because the Messenger — peace be upon him — publicized the ruling, so had its abrogation been established, he would have been obliged to publicize it? We say: Why is it impossible that he publicized the ruling and delegated the abrogation to solitary [reports], just as he publicized the general [text] and delegated specification (takhṣīṣ) to the specifying [evidence]?

chapters.title_en: On the Abrogation of a Definitive, Mass-Transmitted Text by Analogical Reasoning
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة نسخ النص القاطع المتواتر بالقياس]

لا يجوز نسخ النص القاطع المتواتر بالقياس المعلوم بالظن والاجتهاد على
اختلاف مراتبه جليا كان أو خفيا، هذا ما قطع به الجمهور إلا شذوذا منهم
قالوا: ما جاز التخصيص به جاز النسخ به. وهو منقوض بدليل العقل وبالإجماع
وبخبر الواحد، فالتخصيص بجميع ذلك جائز دون النسخ.
ثم كيف يتساويان والتخصيص بيان والنسخ والبيان تقرير والرفع إبطال؟ وقال
بعض أصحاب الشافعي: يجوز النسخ بالقياس الجلي ونحن نقول لفظ الجلي مبهم،
فإن أرادوا المقطوع به فهو صحيح وأما المظنون فلا. وما
يتوهم القطع به على ثلاث مراتب:
الأولى: ما يجري مجرى النص وأوضح منه، كقوله تعالى: {فلا تقل لهما أف}
[الإسراء: 23] فإن تحريم الضرب مدرك منه قطعا، فلو كان ورد نص بإباحة الضرب
لكان هذا ناسخا لأنه أظهر من المنطوق به.
وفي درجته قوله تعالى: {فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره} [الزلزلة: 7] الآية
في أن ما هو فوق الذرة كذلك. وكذلك قوله تعالى: {وورثه أبواه فلأمه الثلث}
[النساء: 11] في أن للأب الثلثين.
الرتبة الثانية: لو ورد نص بأن العتق لا يسري في الأمة ثم ورد قوله - صلى
الله عليه وسلم - «من أعتق شركا له في عبد قوم عليه الباقي» لقضينا بسراية
عتق الأمة قياسا على العبد لأنه مقطوع به، إذ علم قطعا قصد الشارع إلى
المملوك لكونه مملوكا.
الرتبة الثالثة: أن يرد النص مثلا بإباحة النبيذ، ثم يقول الشارع: حرمت
الخمر لشدتها، فينسخ  إباحة النبيذ بقياسه على الخمر إن تعبدنا بالقياس وقال
قوم: وإن لم نتعبد بالقياس نسخنا أيضا إذ لا فرق بين قوله " حرمت كل منتبذ
" وبين قوله " حرمت الخمر لشدتها "، ولذلك أقر النظام بالعلة المنصوصة وإن
كان منكرا لأصل القياس.
ولنتبين أنه إن لم نتعبد بالقياس، فقوله: حرمت الخمر عليكم لشدتها، ليس
قاطعا في تحريم النبيذ، بل يجوز أن تكون العلة شدة الخمر خاصة كما تكون
العلة في الرجم زنا المحصن، خاصة والمقصود أن القاطع لا يرفع بالظن بل
بالقاطع. فإن قيل استحالة رفعه بالمظنون عقلي أو سمعي؟ قلنا الصحيح أنه
سمعي، ولا يستحيل عقلا أن يقال: تعبدناكم بنسخ النص بالقياس على نص آخر،
نعم يستحيل أن نتعبد بنسخ النص بقياس مستنبط من عين ذلك النص لأن ذلك يؤدي
إلى أن يصير هو مناقضا لنفسه فيكون واجب العمل به وساقط العمل به.
فإن قيل: فما الدليل على امتناعه سمعا؟ قلنا: يدل عليه الإجماع على بطلان
كل قياس مخالف للنص، وقول معاذ - رضي الله عنه -: " أجتهد رأيي " بعد فقد
النص وتزكية رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - له، وإجماع الصحابة على ترك
القياس بأخبار الآحاد، فكيف بالنص القاطع المتواتر؟ واشتهار قولهم عند سماع
خبر الواحد: " لولا هذا لقضينا برأينا " ولأن دلالة النص قاطع في المنصوص
ودلالة الأصل على الفرع مظنون فكيف يترك الأقوى بالأضعف؟ وهذا مستند
الصحابة في إجماعهم على ترك القياس بالنص.
فإن قيل: إذا تناقض قاطعان وأشكل المتأخر فهل يثبت تأخر أحدهما بقول
الواحد حتى يكون هو الناسخ؟ قلنا: يحتمل أن يقال ذلك لأنه إذا ثبت الإحصان
بقول اثنين مع أن الزنا لا يثبت إلا بأربعة دل على أنه لا يحتاط للشرط بما
يحتاط به للمشروط. ويحتمل أن يقال: النسخ إذا كان بالتأخر والمنسوخ قاطع
فلا يكفي فيه قول الواحد فهذا في محل الاجتهاد، والأظهر قبوله لأن أحد
النصين منسوخ قطعا، وإنما هذا مطلوب قبوله للتعين.

### | [مسألة لا ينسخ حكم بقول الصحابي]

لا ينسخ حكم بقول الصحابي: نسخ حكم كذا،  ما لم يقل: سمعت رسول الله - صلى
الله عليه وسلم - يقول نسخت حكم كذا، فإذا قال ذلك نظر في الحكم إن كان
ثابتا بخبر الواحد صار منسوخا بقوله، وإن كان قاطعا فلا. أما قوله: نسخ حكم
كذا، فلا يقبل قطعا، فلعله ظن ما ليس بنسخ نسخا فقد ظن قوم أن الزيادة على
النص نسخ، وكذلك في
مسائل وقال قوم: إن ذكر لنا ما هو الناسخ عنده لم نقلده لكن نظرنا فيه،
وإن أطلق فنحمله على أنه لم يطلق إلا عن معرفة قطعية. وهذا فاسد، بل الصحيح
أنه إن ذكر الناسخ تأملنا فيه وقضينا برأينا، وإن لم يذكر لم نقلده وجوزنا
أن يقول ذلك عن اجتهاد ينفرد به، هذا ما ذكره القاضي - رحمه الله -. والأصح
عندنا أن نقبل كقول الصحابي أمر بكذا ونهى عن كذا، فإن ذلك يقبل كما سنذكره
في كتاب الأخبار ولا فرق بين اللفظين. فإن قيل: قالت عائشة - رضي الله عنها
-: ما مات رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - إلا وقد أحلت له النساء اللاتي
حظرن عليه بقوله تعالى {إنا أحللنا لك أزواجك} [الأحزاب: 50] فقبل ذلك
منها. قلنا: ليس ذلك مرضيا عندنا، ومن قبل فإنما قبل ذلك للدليل الناسخ
ورآه صالحا للنسخ ولم يقلد مذهبها.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-س-خ (n-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To efface, transfer, or supersede; in legal usage, the removal of a previously established ruling by a later divine address.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Abrogation (naskh) as the divine act of terminating a temporal ruling while preserving the eternal wisdom; distinct from mere specification (takhṣīṣ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — the lifting of a ruling; metaphorical (majāz) — the clarification of a limited scope, hence naskh is stronger than takhṣīṣ.
- Root: ق-ي-س (q-y-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To measure, compare, or estimate; the root of qiyās (analogical reasoning).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Extension of a ruling from an original case (aṣl) to a branch case (farʿ) based on a shared effective cause (ʿillah); yields probable knowledge (ẓann), not certainty (qaṭʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical measurement; metaphorical — intellectual estimation, hence inherently conjectural.
- Root: ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cut off, sever; hence decisive and definitive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Certainty (qaṭʿ) as the epistemic grade of necessary assent, opposed to ẓann (conjecture).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — cutting; metaphorical — decisive proof that admits no doubt.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The particle "law" (if) introduces a hypothetical protasis whose apodosis is governed by the speaker's stipulation; the negation "lā" preceding "yajūz" (it is not permissible) establishes a categorical prohibition, while the exception "illā" restricts the scope of the preceding general statement.
chapters.translation:
### | [Issue: The Abrogation of a Definitive, Mass-Transmitted Text by Analogical Reasoning]

It is not permissible to abrogate a definitive, mass-transmitted text (al-naṣṣ al-qāṭiʿ al-mutawātir) by analogical reasoning (qiyās) that is known only through conjecture (ẓann) and independent judgment (ijtihād), regardless of its varying degrees — whether it be evident (jalī) or subtle (khafī). This is what the majority (al-jumhūr) have definitively affirmed, except for a deviant few among them who said: "Whatever may be used for specification (takhṣīṣ) may also be used for abrogation (naskh)." This position is refuted by the proof of reason, by consensus (ijmāʿ), and by the solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid) — for specification by all of these is permissible, but not abrogation.

Then how could the two be equivalent, when specification is a clarification (bayān), while abrogation — and clarification is a confirmation (taqrīr) — is a lifting and an annulment (ibṭāl)? Some of al-Shāfiʿī's companions said: "Abrogation by evident analogy (al-qiyās al-jalī) is permissible." But we say: the term "evident" (al-jalī) is ambiguous. If they mean that which is definitively established (al-maqṭūʿ bih), then it is correct; but as for the conjectural (al-maẓnūn), then no.

What is imagined to be definitive falls into three ranks:

**The First Rank:** That which runs in the course of the explicit text (al-naṣṣ) or is even clearer than it — such as His saying, the Exalted: {«فلا تقل لهما أف»} [Al-Isrāʾ 17:23] ("So do not say to them 'Uff!'"). For the prohibition of striking (al-ḍarb) is derived from it with certainty. So if an explicit text had come permitting striking, this [verse] would abrogate it, because it is more manifest than the articulated text (al-manṭūq bih).

In the same degree is His saying, the Exalted: {«فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره»} [Al-Zalzalah 99:7] ("So whoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it") — regarding that which is above an atom being likewise. And similarly His saying, the Exalted: {«وورثه أبواه فلأمه الثلث»} [Al-Nisāʾ 4:11] ("And if his parents inherit him, then for his mother a third") — regarding the father having two-thirds.

**The Second Rank:** If an explicit text came stating that manumission (al-ʿitq) does not carry over (lā yasrī) to a slave-girl (al-amah), then came his saying — peace and blessings be upon him: «من أعتق شركا له في عبد قوم عليه الباقي» ("Whoever manumits a share he has in a male slave, the remainder is assessed against him") — we would judge the carrying over of manumission of the slave-girl by analogy to the male slave, because it is definitive. For it is known with certainty that the Lawgiver's intent was directed at the owned person (al-mamlūk) by virtue of his being owned.

**The Third Rank:** That an explicit text comes, for example, permitting nabīdh (date-wine), then the Lawgiver says: "I have prohibited wine (al-khamr) for its intoxicating strength (shiddah)" — thereby abrogating the permissibility of nabīdh by analogy to wine, if we are bound by analogical reasoning. And some people said: "Even if we are not bound by analogical reasoning, we would still abrogate, for there is no difference between His saying 'I have prohibited every infused drink' and His saying 'I have prohibited wine for its intoxicating strength.'" For this reason, al-Naẓẓām affirmed the explicitly stated cause (al-ʿillah al-manṣūṣah), even though he denied the very foundation of analogical reasoning.

Let us clarify: If we are not bound by analogical reasoning, then His saying: "I have prohibited wine upon you for its intoxicating strength" is not definitive regarding the prohibition of nabīdh. Rather, it is possible that the cause is the intoxicating strength of wine specifically — just as the cause in stoning (al-rajm) is the adultery of the muhṣan (married person) specifically. The point is that the definitive (al-qāṭiʿ) is not lifted by conjecture (al-ẓann), but only by the definitive.

If it is said: "Is the impossibility of lifting it by the conjectural a rational or a scriptural (samʿī) matter?" We say: The correct view is that it is scriptural. It is not rationally impossible that it be said: "We have bound you to abrogate the text by analogy to another text." Indeed, it is impossible that we be bound to abrogate the text by an analogy derived from that very same text itself — because that would lead to it becoming self-contradictory, such that it would be both obligatory to act upon it and void of action upon it.

If it is said: "Then what is the scriptural proof of its impossibility?" We say: What indicates it is the consensus (ijmāʿ) upon the invalidity of every analogy that contradicts the text, and the saying of Muʿādh — may God be pleased with him: "I will exercise my own judgment (ajtahid raʾyī)" — after the absence of the text, and the commendation of the Messenger of God — peace and blessings be upon him — for him. And the consensus of the Companions upon abandoning analogy in favor of solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād) — so how [would they act] with a definitive, mass-transmitted text? And the notoriety of their saying upon hearing a solitary report: "Were it not for this, we would have judged by our own opinion." And because the indication of the text is definitive regarding the articulated matter (al-manṣūṣ), while the indication of the original case (al-aṣl) upon the branch case (al-farʿ) is conjectural — so how could the stronger be abandoned for the weaker? This is the basis of the Companions' consensus upon abandoning analogy in favor of the text.

If it is said: "When two definitive proofs contradict and the later one is problematic, is the lateness of one of them established by the statement of a single person (qawl al-wāḥid), such that it becomes the abrogating one?" We say: It is possible to say that — because when the status of iḥṣān (being married) is established by the testimony of two persons, while adultery (al-zinā) is not established except by four, this indicates that one does not exercise caution for the condition (al-sharṭ) to the degree one exercises caution for the conditioned (al-mashrūṭ). And it is possible to say: If abrogation is by lateness, and the abrogated is definitive, then the statement of a single person does not suffice for it. This is a matter of ijtihād, and the more apparent view is its acceptance — because one of the two texts is definitively abrogated, and this [acceptance] is only sought for the sake of determination (al-taʿayyun).

### | [Issue: A Ruling Is Not Abrogated by the Statement of a Companion]

A ruling is not abrogated by the statement of a Companion: "Such-and-such a ruling is abrogated" — unless he says: "I heard the Messenger of God — peace and blessings be upon him — say: 'Such-and-such a ruling is abrogated.'" If he says that, then the ruling is examined: if it was established by a solitary report, it becomes abrogated by his statement; but if it was definitive, then no.

As for his saying: "Such-and-such a ruling is abrogated" — it is not accepted categorically. For perhaps he conjectured that which is not abrogation to be abrogation. Indeed, some people conjectured that an addition (al-ziyādah) upon the text is abrogation, and likewise in other issues.

And some people said: "If he mentions to us that which is the abrogator in his view, we do not follow him (taqlīd), but rather we examine it ourselves. And if he speaks absolutely, we interpret it as his not speaking absolutely except from definitive knowledge." This is corrupt. Rather, the correct view is: if he mentions the abrogator, we reflect upon it and judge by our own opinion; and if he does not mention it, we do not follow him, and we deem it possible that he said that on the basis of an independent judgment (ijtihād) unique to him. This is what al-Qāḍī — may God have mercy on him — mentioned. But the more correct view in our estimation is that we accept it — just as we accept the Companion's saying "He commanded such-and-such" and "He forbade such-and-such" — for that is accepted, as we shall mention in the Book of Reports (Kitāb al-Akhbār), and there is no difference between the two expressions.

If it is said: "ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — said: 'The Messenger of God — peace and blessings be upon him — did not die until the women who had been forbidden to him were made lawful for him by His saying, the Exalted: {«إنا أحللنا لك أزواجك»} [Al-Aḥzāb 33:50] ("Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives")' — and this was accepted from her." We say: That is not satisfactory in our view. And whoever accepted it only accepted it because of the abrogating proof (al-dalīl al-nāsikh), seeing it as fit for abrogation — not by way of following her opinion (taqlīd).
