chapters.arabic_text:
### | [خاتمة الكتاب فيما يعرف به تاريخ الناسخ]

فيما يعرف به تاريخ الناسخ
اعلم أنه إذا تناقض نصان فالناسخ هو المتأخر، ولا يعرف تأخره بدليل العقل
ولا بقياس الشرع بل بمجرد النقل، ذلك بطرق:
الأول: أن يكون في اللفظ ما يدل عليه كقوله - عليه السلام -: «كنت نهيتكم
عن ادخار لحوم الأضاحي فالآن ادخروها» ، وكقوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -:
«كنت نهيتكم عن زيارة القبور فزوروها» .
الثاني: أن تجمع الأمة في حكم على أنه المنسوخ وأن ناسخه الآخر.
الثالث: أن يذكر الراوي التاريخ مثل أن يقول: سمعت عام الخندق أو عام
الفتح وكان المنسوخ معلوما قبله، ولا فرق بين أن يروي الناسخ والمنسوخ راو
واحد أو راويان. ولا يثبت التاريخ بطرق:
الأول: أن يقول الصحابي كان  الحكم علينا كذا ثم نسخ لأنه ربما قاله عن
اجتهاد.
الثاني: أن يكون أحدهما مثبتا في المصحف بعد الآخر؛ لأن السور والآيات
ليس إثباتها على ترتيب النزول بل ربما قدم المتأخر.
الثالث: أن يكون راويه من أحداث الصحابة فقد ينقل الصبي عمن تقدمت صحبته
وقد ينقل الأكابر عن الأصاغر وبعكسه.
الرابع: أن يكون الراوي أسلم عام الفتح ولم يقل إني سمعت عام الفتح؛ إذ
لعله سمع في حالة كفره ثم روى بعد الإسلام أو سمع ممن سبق بالإسلام.
الخامس: أن يكون الراوي قد انقطعت صحبته، فربما يظن أن حديثه مقدم على
حديث من بقيت صحبته وليس من ضرورة من تأخرت صحبته أن يكون حديثه متأخرا عن
وقت انقطاع صحبة غيره.
السادس: أن يكون أحد الخبرين على وفق قضية العقل والبراءة الأصلية، فربما
يظن تقدمه ولا يلزم ذلك، كقوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: «لا وضوء مما مسته
النار» ، ولا يلزم أن يكون متقدما على إيجاب الوضوء مما مست النار؛ إذ
يحتمل أنه أوجب ثم نسخ والله أعلم. وقد فرغنا من الأصل الأول من الأصول
الأربعة وهو الكتاب، ويتلوه القول في سنة رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

### | [الأصل الثاني من أصول الأدلة سنة رسول الله]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-س-خ (n-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To efface, remove, replace, or transfer; in legal usage, the abrogation of one ruling by a later one.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Abrogation (naskh) as the divine lifting of a previously established ḥukm, known only through revelation, not reason.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of textual supersession; metaphorical (majāz) if applied to mere chronological priority without legal effect.
- Root: ت-ا-ر-ي-خ (t-ā-r-y-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The time or date of an event; from the root denoting "to date" or "to mark time."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Chronological determination as a purely transmitted (naqlī) matter, not a rational (ʿaqlī) inference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the stated time of narration; metaphorical if inferred from circumstantial assumptions.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses "if two texts contradict" (idhā tanāqaḍa naṣṣān) as a conditional clause governing the apodosis, and "only by transmission" (bi-mujarrad al-naql) as a restrictive exception excluding rational or analogical proofs.
chapters.translation:
Know that when two texts contradict each other, the abrogating one is the later in time. Its being later is not known by rational proof, nor by legal analogy, but solely by transmission (naql). This is established through [several] ways:

First: That the wording itself indicates it, such as his saying — peace be upon him: «I had forbidden you from storing the meat of sacrificial animals, so now store it», and his saying — may God bless him and grant him peace: «I had forbidden you from visiting graves, so visit them».

Second: That the community (ummah) agrees in a ruling that one [text] is the abrogated and the other is its abrogator.

Third: That the narrator mentions the date, such as saying: "I heard [it] in the year of the Trench" or "the year of the Conquest," while the abrogated [text] was known to precede it. There is no difference between one narrator transmitting both the abrogating and the abrogated [texts] or two narrators.

And the date is not established by [the following] ways:

First: That a Companion says, "The ruling upon us was such-and-such, then it was abrogated," for perhaps he said it based on his own juristic reasoning (ijtihād).

Second: That one of them is fixed in the muṣḥaf after the other; for the sūrahs and verses are not fixed in the order of revelation — indeed, the later may be placed first.

Third: That its narrator is among the younger Companions; for a youth may transmit from one whose companionship [with the Prophet] preceded [his own], and the elder may transmit from the younger, and vice versa.

Fourth: That the narrator embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest but did not say, "I heard [it] in the year of the Conquest"; for perhaps he heard [it] while in a state of unbelief and then narrated [it] after Islam, or he heard [it] from one who preceded [him] in Islam.

Fifth: That the narrator's companionship [with the Prophet] was interrupted; for one might suppose that his ḥadīth takes precedence over the ḥadīth of one whose companionship continued, yet it is not necessary that the one whose companionship was later have his ḥadīth later than the time of the other's interrupted companionship.

Sixth: That one of the two reports accords with the dictate of reason and the original presumption (barāʾah aṣliyyah); for one might suppose its precedence, but that is not entailed — such as his saying — may God bless him and grant him peace: «No ablution [is required] for what fire has touched», and it is not necessary that it precede the obligation of ablution for what fire has touched; for it is possible that he obligated it, then abrogated [it]. And God knows best.

We have completed the first of the four principles (uṣūl), which is the Book [the Qurʾān]. It is followed by the discourse on the Sunnah of the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace.

### | [The Second Principle of the Sources of Evidence: The Sunnah of the Messenger of God]

chapters.title_en: The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (Peace Be Upon Him) and the Gradations of Companion Reports
chapters.arabic_text:
سنة رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وقول رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - حجة؛ لدلالة المعجزة على صدقه
ولأمر الله تعالى إيانا باتباعه؛ ولأنه لا ينطق عن الهوى إن هو إلا وحي
يوحى. لكن بعض الوحي يتلى فيسمى كتابا وبعضه لا يتلى وهو السنة. وقول رسول
الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - حجة على من
سمعه شفاها. فأما نحن فلا يبلغنا قوله إلا على لسان المخبرين إما على
سبيل التواتر وإما بطريق الآحاد، فلذلك اشتمل الكلام في هذا الأصل على
مقدمة وقسمين: قسم في أخبار التواتر، وقسم في أخبار الآحاد. ويشتمل كل قسم
على أبواب.
أما المقدمة ففي بيان ألفاظ الصحابة - رضي الله عنهم - في نقل الأخبار عن
رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وهو على  خمس مراتب:
الأولى:، وهي أقواها: أن يقول الصحابي: " سمعت رسول الله - صلى الله عليه
وسلم - يقول كذا " أو " أخبرني " أو " حدثني " أو " شافهني " فهذا لا يتطرق
إليه الاحتمال، وهو الأصل في الرواية والتبليغ قال - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
«نضر الله امرأ سمع مقالتي فوعاها فأداها كما سمعها» الحديث.
الثانية: أن يقول قال رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - كذا أو " أخبر "
أو حدث " فهذا ظاهره النقل إذا صدر من الصحابي وليس نصا صريحا؛ إذ قد يقول
الواحد منا قال رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - اعتمادا على ما نقل إليه
وإن لم يسمعه منه، فلا يستحيل أن يقول الصحابي ذلك اعتمادا على ما بلغه
تواترا أو بلغه على لسان من يثق به ودليل الاحتمال ما روى أبو هريرة عن
رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال «من أصبح جنبا فلا صوم له» فلما
استكشف قال: حدثني به الفضل بن عباس، فأرسل الخبر أولا ولم يصرح.
وروي عن ابن عباس - رضي الله عنهما - قوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: «إنما
الربا في النسيئة» فلما روجع فيه أخبر أنه سمعه من أسامة بن زيد. إلا أن
هذا وإن كان محتملا فهو بعيد، بل الظاهر أن الصحابي إذا قال: قال رسول الله
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - " فما يقول إلا وقد سمع رسول الله بخلاف من لم
يعاصر إذا قال: قال رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - " فإن قرينة حاله
تعرف أنه لم يسمع، ولا يوهم إطلاقه السماع بخلاف الصحابي فإنه إذا قال قال
رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أوهم السماع فلا يقدم عليه إلا عن سماع
هذا هو الظاهر وجميع الأخبار " إنما نقلت إلينا كذلك، إذ يقال قال أبو بكر
قال رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، قال عمر قال رسول الله - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -، فلا نفهم من ذلك إلا السماع.
الثالثة: أن يقول الصحابي: " أمر رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - بكذا
أو نهى عن كذا " فهذا يتطرق إليه احتمالان:
أحدهما: في سماعه كما في قوله " قال ".
والثاني: في الأمر، إذ ربما يرى ما ليس بأمر أمرا فقد اختلف الناس في أن
قوله " افعل " هو للأمر، فلأجل هذا قال بعض أهل الظاهر: لا حجة فيه ما لم
ينقل اللفظ. والصحيح أنه لا يظن بالصحابي إطلاق ذلك إلا إذا علم تحقيقا أنه
أمر بذلك، وأن يسمعه يقول أمرتكم بكذا، أو يقول افعلوا، وينضم إليه من
القرائن ما يعرفه كونه أمرا ويدرك ضرورة قصده إلى الأمر.
أما احتمال بنائه الأمر على الغلط والوهم فلا نطرقه إلى الصحابة بغير
ضرورة، بل يحمل ظاهر قولهم وفعلهم على السلامة ما أمكن، ولهذا لو قال قال
رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - كذا " ولكن شرط شرطا ووقت وقتا فيلزمنا
اتباعه، ولا يجوز أن نقول لعله غلط في فهم الشرط والتأقيت ورأى ما ليس بشرط
شرطا، ولهذا يجب أن يقبل قول الصحابي " نسخ حكم كذا " وإلا فلا فرق بين
قوله " نسخ " وقوله " أمر "، ولذلك قال علي - رضي الله عنه - وأطلق: " أمرت
أن أقاتل الناكثين والمارقين
والقاسطين " ولا يظن بمثله أن يقول أمرت إلا عن مستند يقتضي الأمر.
ويتطرق إليه احتمال ثالث في عمومه وخصوصه، حتى ظن قوم أن مطلق هذا يقتضي
أمر جميع الأمة. والصحيح أن من يقول بصيغة العموم أيضا ينبغي أن يتوقف في
هذا؛ إذ يحتمل أن يكون ما سمعه أمرا للأمة أو لطائفة أو لشخص بعينه وكل ذلك
يتيح له أن يقول " أمر " فيتوقف فيه على الدليل، لكن يدل عليه أن أمره
للواحد أمر للجماعة إلا إذا كان لوصف يخصه من سفر أو حضر، ولو كان كذلك
لصرح به الصحابي كقوله: «أمرنا إذا كنا مسافرين أن لا ننزع خفافنا ثلاثة
أيام ولياليهن» نعم لو قال: " أمرنا بكذا " وعلم من عادة الصحابي أنه لا
يطلقه إلا في أمر الأمة حمل عليه وإلا احتمل أن يكون أمرا للأمة أو له أو
لطائفة.
الرابعة: أن يقول: " أمرنا بكذا ونهينا عن كذا " فيتطرق إليه ما سبق من
الاحتمالات  الثلاثة واحتمال رابع، وهو الآمر، فإنه لا يدري أنه رسول الله -
صلى الله عليه وسلم - أو غيره من الأئمة والعلماء، فقال قوم: لا حجة فيه،
فإنه محتمل. وذهب الأكثرون إلى أنه لا يحمل إلا على أمر الله تعالى وأمر
رسوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - لأنه يريد به إثبات شرع وإقامة حجة، فلا يحمل
على قول من لا حجة في قوله.
وفي معناه قوله: " من السنة كذا والسنة جارية بكذا ". فالظاهر أنه لا
يريد إلا سنة رسول الله وما يجب اتباعه دون سنة غيره ممن لا تجب طاعته. ولا
فرق بين أن يقول الصحابي ذلك في حياة رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أو
بعد وفاته. أما التابعي إذا قال " أمرنا " احتمل أمر رسول الله - صلى الله
عليه وسلم - وأمر الأمة بأجمعها والحجة حاصلة به، ويحتمل أمر الصحابة، لكن
لا يليق بالعالم أن يطلق ذلك إلا وهو يريد من تجب طاعته، ولكن الاحتمال في
قول التابعي أظهر منه في قول الصحابي.
الخامسة: أن يقول: " كانوا يفعلون كذا " فإن أضاف ذلك إلى زمن الرسول -
عليه السلام - فهو دليل على جواز الفعل؛ لأن ذكره في معرض الحجة يدل على
أنه أراد ما علمه رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وسكت عليه دون ما لم
يبلغه. وذلك يدل على الجواز، وذلك مثل قول ابن عمر - رضي الله عنه -: «كنا
نفاضل على عهد رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - فنقول خير الناس بعد رسول
الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أبو بكر ثم عمر ثم عثمان فيبلغ ذلك رسول الله
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - فلا ينكره» وقال: «كنا نخابر على عهد رسول الله -
صلى الله عليه وسلم - وبعده أربعين سنة حتى روى لنا رافع بن خديج» الحديث
وقال أبو سعيد: «كنا نخرج على عهد رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - صاعا
من بر في زكاة الفطرة» وقالت عائشة - رضي الله عنها -: «كانوا لا يقطعون في
الشيء التافه» .
وأما قول التابعي: " كانوا يفعلون " لا يدل على فعل  جميع الأمة بل على
البعض فلا حجة فيه، إلا أن يصرح بنقله عن أهل الإجماع فيكون نقلا للإجماع
وفي ثبوته بخبر الواحد كلام سيأتي فقد ظهر من هذه المقدمة ما هو خبر عن
رسول الله وما ليس خبرا عنه. والآن فلا بد من بيان طرق انتهاء الخبر إلينا،
وذلك إما بنقل التواتر أو الآحاد.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ج-ج (ḥ-j-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes "proof," "argument," or "that which establishes a case" — a decisive evidence that compels acceptance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ḥujjah is the authoritative proof that renders a claim binding upon the believer, whether from revelation or reason.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to a concrete argument presented in disputation; metaphorically, it extends to any evidence that silences doubt and establishes obligation.
- Root: ن-ب-أ (n-b-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To inform" or "to convey news" — the act of transmitting a report from one party to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Nabāʾ is distinguished from khabar as a report of great import, often carrying legal or theological consequence; here it denotes prophetic transmission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for direct verbal communication; metaphorical when used for written or intermediary conveyance, as in the graded levels of ḥadīth transmission.
- Root: ت-و-ر (t-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To recur successively" or "to follow in sequence" — the root of tawātur, meaning continuous, unbroken transmission.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tawātur signifies a report conveyed by such a multitude that collusion on falsehood is inconceivable, yielding certain knowledge (ʿilm yaqīnī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for sequential recurrence; metaphorical for epistemic certainty achieved through mass transmission, as opposed to isolated reports (āḥād).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ẓāhir vs. Naṣṣ (Apparent vs. Explicit Meaning) — When a Companion's wording admits multiple interpretations, the apparent sense (ẓāhir) governs unless a textual or contextual indicator (qarīnah) necessitates a shift to the explicit (naṣṣ) or to metaphorical construal (majāz).
chapters.translation:
I say: The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and the statement of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — constitute a decisive proof (ḥujjah); this is due to the miracle (muʿjizah) indicating his veracity, and due to Allah Most High commanding us to follow him, and because he does not speak from whim — it is but revelation revealed (waḥy yūḥā). However, some revelation is recited (yutlā) and is termed "the Book," while some is not recited and is the Sunnah.

The statement of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — is a proof upon whoever hears it directly (shifāhan). As for us, his statement reaches us only through the tongues of reporters — either by way of mass transmission (tawātur) or by the path of isolated reports (āḥād). For this reason, the discourse on this principle comprises an introduction (muqaddimah) and two sections: a section on reports of tawātur, and a section on reports of āḥād. Each section contains chapters.

As for the introduction, it concerns the clarification of the expressions of the Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — in transmitting reports from the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and this is upon five gradations (marātib):

**The First Gradation** — and it is the strongest of them: that the Companion says: "I heard the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — say such-and-such," or "he informed me (akhbaranī)," or "he narrated to me (ḥaddathanī)," or "he addressed me directly (shāfahanī)." No possibility (iḥtimāl) attaches to this; it is the foundation of narration and conveyance. He — peace be upon him — said: {«May Allah brighten a person who heard my statement, comprehended it, and conveyed it as he heard it»} — the ḥadīth.

**The Second Gradation**: that he says: "The Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — said such-and-such," or "he informed (akhbara)," or "he narrated (ḥaddatha)." This is, in its apparent sense (ẓāhir), a transmission when it issues from a Companion, but it is not an explicit text (naṣṣ ṣarīḥ); for one of us might say "The Messenger of Allah said," relying upon what was conveyed to him even if he did not hear it from him directly. Thus it is not impossible that a Companion says this relying upon what reached him by tawātur or upon the tongue of one he trusts. The evidence for this possibility is what Abū Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — that he said: {«Whoever wakes up in a state of janābah, there is no fasting for him»} — then when he was investigated, he said: "Al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās narrated it to me," so he first sent the report without specification. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās — may Allah be pleased with them both — his saying — peace be upon him —: {«Indeed, ribā is only in delayed payment (al-nasīʾah)»} — then when he was pressed on it, he informed that he heard it from Usāmah ibn Zayd.

However, although this is possible, it is remote (baʿīd). Rather, the apparent sense is that when a Companion says "The Messenger of Allah said," he does not say it except having heard from the Messenger of Allah — unlike one who was not a contemporary, for when he says "The Messenger of Allah said," the contextual indication (qarīnah) of his state makes known that he did not hear, and his unqualified utterance does not suggest hearing. This differs from the Companion, for when he says "The Messenger of Allah said," it suggests hearing, so he would not venture upon it except from hearing. This is the apparent sense, and all reports have only been conveyed to us in this manner — for it is said: "Abū Bakr said: The Messenger of Allah said," "ʿUmar said: The Messenger of Allah said" — and we understand from that nothing but hearing.

**The Third Gradation**: that the Companion says: "The Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — commanded such-and-such" or "prohibited such-and-such." Two possibilities attach to this:

The first: regarding his hearing, as in his saying "he said."

The second: regarding the command itself, for perhaps he saw what is not a command as a command. People have differed over whether his saying "Do (ifʿal)" is for command. For this reason, some of the Ẓāhirīs said: there is no proof in it unless the wording is transmitted. The correct view is that it is not presumed of the Companion that he utters this unqualifiedly except when he knows with certainty that it was a command — that he heard him say "I command you with such-and-such," or he says "Do (ifʿalū)," and there attaches to it contextual indicators (qarāʾin) by which he recognizes it as a command and perceives by necessity his intent toward commanding.

As for the possibility of his basing the command upon error or delusion (ghalaṭ wa wahm), we do not extend that to the Companions without necessity. Rather, we carry the apparent sense of their statements and actions upon soundness (salāmah) as much as possible. For this reason, if he said "The Messenger of Allah said such-and-such, but he stipulated a condition and specified a time," then following him is incumbent upon us, and it is not permissible to say: "Perhaps he erred in understanding the condition and the time specification, and saw what is not a condition as a condition." For this reason, the statement of the Companion "such-and-such a ruling was abrogated (naskh)" must be accepted; otherwise there would be no difference between his saying "abrogated" and his saying "commanded." Therefore ʿAlī — may Allah be pleased with him — said, unqualifiedly: "I was commanded to fight the breakers of oaths (al-nākithīn), the renegades (al-māriqīn), and the deviators (al-qāsiṭīn)" — and it is not presumed of the like of him to say "I was commanded" except upon a basis that necessitates the command.

A third possibility attaches to it regarding its generality (ʿumūm) and specificity (khuṣūṣ), such that some people presumed that the unqualified utterance of this necessitates a command to the entire ummah. The correct view is that even one who affirms the general form (ṣīghat al-ʿumūm) should pause regarding this; for it is possible that what he heard was a command to the ummah, or to a group, or to a specific person — and all of that permits him to say "he commanded." Thus one pauses regarding it pending evidence. However, what indicates [generality] is that his command to one is a command to the group, except when it is for a specific attribute particular to him, whether of travel or presence; and were it so, the Companion would have specified it, as in his saying: {«He commanded us, when we were travelers, not to remove our leather socks (khuffāyn) for three days and their nights»}. Yes — if he said "He commanded us with such-and-such," and it is known from the Companion's habit that he does not utter it unqualifiedly except regarding a command to the ummah, then it is carried upon that; otherwise, it is possible that it is a command to the ummah, to him, or to a group.

**The Fourth Gradation**: that he says: "We were commanded with such-and-such and prohibited from such-and-such." The three aforementioned possibilities attach to it, plus a fourth: the commander himself — for one does not know whether it is the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — or other than him from the imams and scholars. Some people said: there is no proof in it, for it is ambiguous. The majority (al-aktharūn) held that it is not carried except upon the command of Allah Most High and the command of His Messenger — peace be upon him — because he intends by it to establish a sacred law (sharʿ) and to mount a proof (ḥujjah); thus it is not carried upon the statement of one whose statement carries no authority.

In its meaning is his saying: "From the Sunnah is such-and-such," and "The Sunnah is operative with such-and-such." The apparent sense is that he intends nothing but the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and what must be followed, not the sunnah of other than him from those whose obedience is not obligatory. There is no difference between the Companion saying this during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — or after his death. As for the Successor (tābiʿī), when he says "We were commanded," it is possible [that it means] the command of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and the command of the ummah in its entirety, and the proof is established by it; and it is possible [that it means] the command of the Companions. However, it is not fitting for a scholar to utter this unqualifiedly except intending one whose obedience is obligatory. But the possibility in the statement of the Successor is more apparent than in the statement of the Companion.

**The Fifth Gradation**: that he says: "They used to do such-and-such." If he attributes that to the era of the Messenger — peace be upon him — it is evidence for the permissibility (jawāz) of the act; because his mentioning it in the context of mounting a proof indicates that he intended what the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — knew of and remained silent upon, not what did not reach him. And that indicates permissibility. An example is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar — may Allah be pleased with him —: {«We used to rank (fāḍil) during the era of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and say: The best of people after the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — is Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān; and that reached the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and he did not disapprove of it»}. And he said: {«We used to practice sharecropping (mukhābarah) during the era of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — and after it for forty years, until Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj narrated to us»} — the ḥadīth. And Abū Saʿīd said: {«We used to give, during the era of the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — a ṣāʿ of wheat for the alms of breaking the fast (zakāt al-fiṭr)»}. And ʿĀʾishah — may Allah be pleased with her — said: {«They did not cut off [the hand] for a trifling thing»}.

As for the saying of the Successor: "They used to do," it does not indicate the action of the entire ummah but rather of some, so there is no proof in it — except if he explicitly states his transmission from the people of consensus (ahl al-ijmāʿ), in which case it is a transmission of consensus; and regarding its establishment through an isolated report (khabar al-wāḥid), there is discussion to come. Thus it has become clear from this introduction what is a report from the Messenger of Allah and what is not a report from him. Now it remains to clarify the paths by which the report reaches us — and that is either through transmission of tawātur or of āḥād.

chapters.title_en: The First Part of This Principle: Discourse on Tawātur (Consecutive Transmission) and Its Chapters — Chapter One: Establishing That Tawātur Yields Certain Knowledge
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [القسم الأول من هذا الأصل الكلام في التواتر وفيه أبواب]

### | [الباب الأول في إثبات أن التواتر يفيد العلم]

القسم الأول من هذا الأصل الكلام في التواتر وفيه أبواب الباب الأول: في
إثبات أن التواتر يفيد العلم ولنقدم عليه حد الخبر، وحده أنه
القول الذي يتطرق إليه التصديق أو التكذيب، أو هو القول الذي يدخله الصدق
أو الكذب، وهو أولى من قولهم: يدخله الصدق والكذب؛ إذ الخبر الواحد لا
يدخله كلاهما بل كلام الله تعالى لا يدخله الكذب أصلا، والخبر عن المحالات
لا يدخله الصدق أصلا. والخبر قسم من أقسام الكلام القائم بالنفس، وأما
العبارة فهي الأصوات المقطعة التي صيغتها مثل قول القائل زيد قائم وضارب،
وهو ليس خبرا لذاته بل يصير خبرا بقصد القاصد إلى التعبير به عما في النفس،
ولهذا إذا صدر من نائم أو مغلوب لم يكن خبرا.
وأما كلام النفس فهو خبر لذاته وجنسه إذا وجد لا يتغير بقصد القاصد. أما
إثبات كون التواتر مفيدا للعلم فهو ظاهر، خلافا للسمنية حيث حصروا العلوم
في الحواس وأنكروا هذا. وحصرهم باطل، فإنا بالضرورة نعلم كون الألف أكثر من
الواحد، واستحالة كون الواحد قديما محدثا وأمورا أخر ذكرناها في مدارك
اليقين سوى الحواس. بل نقول: حصرهم العلوم في الحواس معلوم لهم، وليس ذلك
مدركا بالحواس الخمس.
ثم لا يستريب عاقل في أن في الدنيا بلدة تسمى بغداد وإن لم يدخلها، ولا
يشك في وجود الأنبياء بل في وجود الشافعي وأبي حنيفة رحمهما الله، بل في
الدول والوقائع الكبيرة. فإن قيل لو كان هذا معلوما ضرورة لما خالفناكم.
قلنا من يخالف في هذا فإنما يخالف بلسانه أو  عن خبط في عقله أو عن عناد،
ولا يصدر إنكار هذا من عدد كثير يستحيل إنكارهم في العادة لما علموه
وعنادهم، ولو تركنا ما علمناه ضرورة لقولكم للزمكم ترك المحسوسات بسبب خلاف
السوفسطائية أما بطلان مذهب الكعبي حيث ذهب إلى أن هذا العلم نظري، فإنا
نقول: النظري هو الذي يجوز أن يعرض فيه الشك وتختلف فيه الأحوال فيعلمه بعض
الناس دون بعض ولا يعلمه النساء والصبيان ومن ليس من أهل النظر ولا يعلمه
من ترك النظر قصدا، وكل علم نظري فالعالم به قد يجد نفسه فيه شاكا ثم طالبا
ونحن لا نجد أنفسنا شاكين في وجود مكة ووجود الشافعي - رحمه الله - طالبين،
لذلك فإن عنيتم بكونه نظريا شيئا من ذلك فنحن ننكره، وإن عنيتم به أن مجرد
قول المخبر لا يفيد العلم ما لم ينتظم في النفس مقدمتان إحداهما: أن هؤلاء
مع اختلاف أحوالهم وتباين أغراضهم ومع كثرتهم على حال لا يجمعهم على الكذب
جامع ولا يتفقون إلا على الصدق والثانية: أنهم قد اتفقوا على الإخبار عن
الواقعة فيبتنى العلم بالصدق على مجموع المقدمتين، فهذا مسلم.
ولا بد أن تشعر النفس بهاتين المقدمتين حتى يحصل له العلم والتصديق وإن
لم تتشكل في النفس هذه المقدمات بلفظ منظوم فقد شعرت به حتى حصل التصديق
وإن لم يشعر بشعورها. وتحقيق القول فيه أن الضروري إن كان عبارة عما يحصل
بغير واسطة كقولنا: القديم لا يكون محدثا والموجود لا يكون معدوما، فهذا
ليس بضروري، فإنه حصل بواسطة المقدمتين المذكورتين.
وإن كان عبارة عما يحصل بدون تشكل الواسطة في الذهن فهذا ضروري، ورب
واسطة حاضرة في الذهن لا يشعر الإنسان بوجه توسطها وحصول العلم بواسطتها
فيسمى أوليا وليس بأولي كقولنا: الاثنان نصف الأربعة، فإنه لا يعلم ذلك إلا
بواسطة، وهو أن النصف أحد جزئي الجملة المساوي للآخر والاثنان أحد الجزأين
المساوي للثاني من جملة الأربعة، فهو إذن نصف
فقد حصل هذا العلم بواسطة لكنها جلية في الذهن حاضرة، ولهذا لو قيل ستة
وثلاثون هل  هو نصف اثنين وسبعين؟ يفتقر فيه إلى تأمل ونظر حتى يعلم أن هذه
الجملة تنقسم بجزأين متساويين أحدهما ستة وثلاثون؛ فإذا العلم بصدق خبر
التواتر يحصل بواسطة هذه المقدمات وما هو كذلك فهو ليس بأولى.
وهل يسمى ضروريا هذا ربما يختلف فيه الاصطلاح. والضروري عند الأكثرين
عبارة عن الأولى لا عما نجد أنفسنا مضطرين إليه، فإن العلوم الحسابية كلها
ضرورية وهي نظرية. ومعنى كونها نظرية أنها ليست بأولية، وكذلك العلم بصدق
خبر التواتر ويقرب منه العلم المستفاد من التجربة التي يعبر عنها باطراد
العادات، كقولنا: الماء مرو، والخمر مسكر، كما نبهنا عليه في مقدمة الكتاب.
فإن قيل لو استدل مستدل على كونه غير ضروري بأنه كان ضروريا لعلمنا
بالضرورة كونه ضروريا ولما تصور الخلاف فيه فهذا الاستدلال صحيح أم لا؟
قلنا: إن كان الضروري عبارة عما نجد أنفسنا مضطرين إليه فبالضرورة نعلم من
أنفسنا أنا مضطرون إليه، وإن كان عبارة عما يحصل بغير واسطة فيجوز أن يحتاج
في معرفة ذلك إلى تأمل ويقع الشك فيه، كما يتصور أن نعتقد شيئا على القطع
ونتردد في أن اعتقادنا علم محقق أم لا.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ب-ر (khabara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes information, report, or news conveyed from one to another; its core sense is the communication of an occurrence (ḥadath) to one unaware of it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, khabar is a statement (qawl) susceptible to verification (taṣdīq) or falsification (takdhīb), distinct from the divine speech (kalām nafsī) which is true in itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, khabar is what enters into truth or falsehood; metaphorically, it may denote the inward speech (kalām al-nafs) when expressed, though the expression itself is not khabar by essence.
- Root: ت-و-ت-ر (tawātara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes succession and continuity, one following another without interruption; tawātur is the arrival of reports in succession from multiple sources.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technically, tawātur is the aggregate transmission by a multitude whose agreement upon falsehood is inconceivable (muḥāl ʿādan), yielding necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal succession of reports; metaphorically, the epistemic force of the multitude, where quantity and diversity preclude collusion.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍarra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root signifies harm or necessity; ḍarūrī is that which imposes itself upon the mind without choice or acquisition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī) is that which the self finds itself compelled toward, without volitional seeking or deliberation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, that which is compelled by force; technically, the self-evident (badīhī) as opposed to the acquired (naẓarī).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditioned Predication (al-ḥaml al-mashrūṭ) — The definition of khabar is given as a disjunctive predicate (al-ṣidq aw al-kidhb), where the particle "aw" indicates permissive division (taqsīm), not simultaneous conjunction, as the author clarifies by rejecting "al-ṣidq wa al-kidhb."
chapters.translation:
I say: The first part of this principle is the discourse on tawātur (consecutive transmission), and it comprises chapters. The first chapter concerns establishing that tawātur yields knowledge (ʿilm). Let us preface it with the definition of the report (khabar). Its definition is that it is the statement (qawl) which is susceptible to verification (taṣdīq) or falsification (takdhīb) — or it is the statement into which truth or falsehood enters. This definition is more appropriate than their saying: "into which truth and falsehood enter," for a single report does not admit both simultaneously. Rather, the speech of God — exalted be He — does not admit falsehood at all, and the report of impossibilities does not admit truth at all. The report is a species of the speech subsisting in the self (kalām al-nafs). As for the expression (ʿibārah), it is the articulated sounds whose form is like the saying of one who says: "Zayd is standing" or "Zayd is striking." It is not a report in itself, but rather becomes a report by the intent of the one intending to express thereby what is in the self. For this reason, when it issues from a sleeper or one overcome [by unconsciousness], it is not a report.

As for the speech of the self, it is a report in itself and in its genus; when it exists, it does not change by the intent of the one intending. As for establishing that tawātur is productive of knowledge, this is evident — contrary to the Sumaniyyah, who confined the sciences to the senses and denied this. Their confinement is false, for we know by necessity that the many is more than the one, and the impossibility of the one being both eternal and originated, and other matters which we have mentioned in the "Perceptions of Certainty" (Madārik al-Yaqīn) besides the senses. Rather, we say: their confinement of the sciences to the senses is itself known to them, and that is not perceived by the five senses.

Then no rational person doubts that in the world there is a city called Baghdad, even if he has not entered it; nor does he doubt the existence of the prophets — rather, the existence of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on them both — nor the great dynasties and events. If it is said: "Were this known by necessity, we would not have opposed you," we say: whoever opposes this only opposes with his tongue, or from confusion in his intellect, or from obstinacy. The denial of this does not issue from a multitude whose denial is inconceivable in custom, given what they know and their obstinacy. And if we were to abandon what we know by necessity because of your saying, then it would be incumbent upon you to abandon the perceived things because of the opposition of the Sophists.

As for the falsity of the doctrine of al-Kaʿbī, who held that this knowledge is theoretical (naẓarī), we say: the theoretical is that in which doubt may occur and states differ, such that some people know it and others do not — women, children, and those not of the people of reflection do not know it, nor does one who deliberately abandons reflection know it. And every theoretical knowledge is such that its knower may find himself in doubt concerning it, then seeking [its resolution]. But we do not find ourselves doubting the existence of Mecca or the existence of al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — nor seeking [proof of it]. Therefore, if you mean by its being theoretical something of this sort, we deny it. But if you mean by it that the mere statement of the reporter does not yield knowledge unless two premises are organized in the self — the first being that these [reporters], despite their differing conditions and divergent aims, and despite their multitude, are in a state such that no unifier gathers them upon falsehood, nor do they agree except upon truth; and the second being that they have agreed upon reporting the occurrence — so that the knowledge of truth is built upon the conjunction of the two premises — then this is conceded.

It is necessary that the self be aware of these two premises until knowledge and verification are obtained for it. Even if these premises are not formed in the self in ordered wording, it has been aware of them until verification was obtained, even if it is not aware of its own awareness. The verification of the statement concerning this is that if "the necessary" (al-ḍarūrī) is an expression for what is obtained without mediation — like our saying: "the eternal is not originated" and "the existent is not non-existent" — then this is not necessary, for it is obtained by means of the two aforementioned premises. But if it is an expression for what is obtained without the formation of the mediation in the mind, then this is necessary. And there may be a mediation present in the mind of which one is not aware of the manner of its intermediation, nor of the obtaining of knowledge by its means; this is called "primordial" (awwalī) — and it is not primordial — like our saying: "two is half of four." For this is not known except by a mediation, namely that the half is one of the two parts of the whole equal to the other, and two is one of the two parts equal to the second of the whole of four; it is therefore half. Thus this knowledge is obtained by a mediation, but it is evident in the mind and present. For this reason, if one said: "Is thirty-six half of seventy-two?" one would need reflection and consideration until one knows that this whole divides into two equal parts, one of which is thirty-six. So the knowledge of the truthfulness of the tawātur report is obtained by means of these premises, and whatever is so is not primordial.

Whether this is called "necessary" — perhaps terminology differs therein. The necessary according to the majority is an expression for the primordial, not for that which we find ourselves compelled toward. For all the arithmetic sciences are necessary, yet they are theoretical. The meaning of their being theoretical is that they are not primordial. Likewise is the knowledge of the truthfulness of the tawātur report. Near to it is the knowledge derived from experience (tajribah), which is expressed as the constancy of customs (iṭṭirād al-ʿādāt) — like our saying: "water quenches thirst" and "wine intoxicates" — as we have alerted to in the introduction of this book.

If it is said: "Let one who argues adduce, for its being non-necessary, that were it necessary, we would know by necessity that it is necessary, and disagreement concerning it would not be conceivable" — is this argument sound or not? We say: if "the necessary" is an expression for that which we find ourselves compelled toward, then by necessity we know of ourselves that we are compelled toward it. But if it is an expression for what is obtained without mediation, then it is possible that knowing that requires reflection and that doubt occurs concerning it — just as it is conceivable that we believe something with certainty and yet hesitate whether our belief is verified knowledge or not.

chapters.title_en: The Conditions of Tawātur (Mass Transmission)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الباب الثاني في شروط التواتر]

. شروط التواتر. وهي أربعة:
الأول: أن يخبروا عن علم لا عن ظن، فإن أهل بغداد لو أخبرونا عن طائر
أنهم ظنوه حماما أو عن شخص أنهم ظنوه زيدا لم يحصل لنا العلم بكونه حماما
وبكونه زيدا، وليس هذا معللا، بل حال المخبر لا تزيد على حال المخبر؛ لأنه
كان في قدرة الله تعالى أن يخلق لنا العلم بخبرهم وإن كان عن ظن ولكن
العادة غير مطردة بذلك.
الشرط الثاني: أن يكون علمهم ضروريا مستندا إلى محسوس؛ إذ لو أخبرنا أهل
بغداد عن حدوث العالم وعن صدق بعض الأنبياء لم يحصل لنا العلم، وهذا أيضا
معلوم بالعادة، وإلا فقد كان في قدرة الله تعالى أن يجعل ذلك سببا للعلم في
حقنا.
الشرط الثالث: أن يستوي طرفاه وواسطته في هذه الصفات وفي كمال العدد،
فإذا نقل الخلف  عن السلف وتوالت الأعصار ولم تكن الشروط قائمة في كل عصر لم
يحصل العلم بصدقهم؛ لأن خبر أهل كل عصر خبر مستقل بنفسه فلا بد فيه من
الشروط، ولأجل ذلك لم يحصل لنا العلم بصدق اليهود مع كثرتهم في نقلهم عن
موسى - عليه الصلاة والسلام - تكذيب كل ناسخ لشريعته، ولا بصدق الشيعة
والعباسية والبكرية في نقل النص على إمامة علي أو العباس أو أبي بكر - رضي
الله عنهم - وإن كثر عدد الناقلين في هذه الأعصار القريبة، لأن بعض هذا
وضعه الآحاد أولا ثم أفشوه ثم كثر الناقلون في عصره وبعده، والشرط إنما حصل
في بعض الإعصار فلم تستو فيه الأعصار، ولذلك لم يحصل التصديق بخلاف وجود
عيسى - عليه السلام - وتحديه بالنبوة ووجود أبي بكر وعلي - رضي الله عنهما
- وانتصابهما للإمامة، فإن كل ذلك لما تساوت فيه الأطراف والواسطة حصل لنا
علم ضروري لا نقدر على تشكيك أنفسنا فيه، ونقدر على التشكيك فيما نقلوه عن
موسى وعيسى - عليهما السلام - وفي نص الإمامة.

### | [مسألة عدد المخبرين]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ت-و-ر (t-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Succession, consecutive recurrence; a thing following another without interruption.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for a report whose transmitters at every level are so numerous that collusion on falsehood is impossible, yielding necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of sequential continuity; metaphorical extension to epistemic certainty through mass testimony.
- Root: ظ-ن (ẓ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Unverified opinion, doubt, suspicion; the opposite of certainty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Conjecture lacking demonstrative or sensory grounding; epistemically deficient in legal-theological proof.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: doubt; metaphorical: any probabilistic judgment not rising to ʿilm.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Necessity, compulsion; that which cannot be avoided.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿIlm ḍarūrī — knowledge arising in the mind without acquisition (kasb) or deliberation, like sensory perception.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical harm; metaphorical: epistemic necessity that overwhelms the knower.
- Sībawayh Rule: Ḥāl Clause (Jumla Ḥāliyya) — circumstantial clauses (e.g., "while they were numerous") provide the condition under which the main assertion holds, requiring grammatical agreement in case and tense.
chapters.translation:
I say: The conditions of tawātur are four.

The first: that the transmitters report from knowledge (ʿilm), not from conjecture (ẓann). For if the people of Baghdad informed us about a bird that they conjectured to be a pigeon, or about a person that they conjectured to be Zayd, no knowledge would arise for us of its being a pigeon or his being Zayd. This is not rationally necessitated (muʿallal); rather, the state of the transmitter adds nothing beyond the state of the one informed — for it was within the power of God most high to create knowledge for us through their report even if it were based on conjecture, but the customary course (al-ʿādah) does not run consistently in that manner.

The second condition: that their knowledge be necessary (ḍarūrī), grounded in sense-perception (maḥsūs). For if the people of Baghdad informed us of the temporal origination of the world (ḥudūth al-ʿālam) or of the veracity of certain prophets, no knowledge would arise for us. This too is known by custom (al-ʿādah) — otherwise, it was within God's power to make that a cause of knowledge for us.

The third condition: that its two ends and its middle be equal in these attributes and in the completeness of number. Thus, when the successors (al-khalaf) transmitted from the predecessors (al-salaf) across successive ages, but the conditions were not fulfilled in every age, no knowledge of their veracity arises. For the report of the people of each age is an independent report in itself, requiring the conditions [in that age]. For this reason, no knowledge arises for us of the veracity of the Jews — despite their multitude in transmitting from Moses (peace and prayer be upon him) the denial of every abrogator (nāsikh) of his law — nor of the veracity of the Shīʿa, the ʿAbbāsiyya, or the Bakriyya in transmitting the explicit designation (naṣṣ) of the imamate of ʿAlī, al-ʿAbbās, or Abū Bakr (may God be pleased with them all), even though the number of transmitters multiplied in these recent ages. For some of this was first fabricated by individuals (āḥād), then they publicized it, then the transmitters multiplied in their own time and after it. The condition was fulfilled only in some ages, so the ages were not equal in it. Therefore, no assent (taṣdīq) arises — unlike the existence of Jesus (peace be upon him), his challenge with prophethood, the existence of Abū Bakr and ʿAlī (may God be pleased with them both), and their appointment to the imamate. For in all of that, since the ends and the middle were equal, necessary knowledge arose for us, such that we are unable to cast doubt into ourselves concerning it — whereas we are able to cast doubt concerning what they transmitted from Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both) and concerning the text of the imamate.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Condition: Concerning the Number (of Reporters), and the Refinement of Its Purpose Through the Formulation of Questions
chapters.arabic_text:
الشرط الرابع: في العدد، وتهذب الغرض منه برسم مسائل:
مسألة: عدد المخبرين
ينقسم إلى ما هو ناقص فلا يفيد العلم، وإلى ما هو كامل وهو
الذي يفيد العلم وإلى زائد وهو الذي يحصل العلم ببعضه وتقع الزيادة فضلا
عن الكفاية. والكامل وهو أقل عدد يورث العلم ليس معلوما لنا، لكنا بحصول
العلم الضروري نتبين كمال العدد لا أنا بكمال العدد نستدل على حصول العلم.
فإذا عرفت هذا فالعدد الكامل الذي يحصل التصديق به في واقعة هل يتصور أن
لا يفيد العلم في بعض الوقائع قال القاضي - رحمه الله -: ذلك محال، بل كل
ما يفيد العلم في واقعة يفيد في كل واقعة، وإذا حصل العلم لشخص فلا بد وأن
يحصل لكل شخص يشاركه في السماع ولا يتصور أن يختلف. وهذا صحيح إن تجرد
الخبر عن القرائن، فإن العلم لا يستند إلى مجرد العدد ونسبة كثرة العدد إلى
سائر الوقائع وسائر الأشخاص واحدة.
أما إذا اقترنت به قرائن  تدل على التصديق فهذا يجوز أن تختلف فيه الوقائع
والأشخاص. وأنكر القاضي ذلك ولم يلتفت إلى القرائن ولم يجعل لها أثرا وهذا
غير مرضي؛ لأن مجرد الإخبار يجوز أن يورث العلم عند كثرة المخبرين وإن لم
تكن قرينة ومجرد القرائن أيضا قد يورث العلم، وإن لم يكن فيه إخبار؛ فلا
يبعد أن تنضم القرائن إلى الأخبار فيقوم بعض القرائن مقام بعض العدد من
المخبرين، ولا ينكشف هذا إلا بمعرفة معنى القرائن وكيفية دلالتها، فنقول:
لا شك في أنا نعرف أمورا ليست محسوسة، إذ نعرف من غيرنا حبه لإنسان وبغضه
له وخوفه منه وغضبه وخجله، وهذه أحوال في نفس المحب والمبغض لا يتعلق الحس
بها قد تدل عليها دلالات آحادها ليست قطعية، بل يتطرق إليها الاحتمال، ولكن
تميل النفس بها إلى اعتقاد ضعيف.
ثم الثاني والثالث يؤكد ذلك، ولو أفردت آحادها لتطرق إليها الاحتمال،
ولكن يحصل القطع باجتماعها، كما أن قول كل واحد من عدد التواتر يتطرق إليه
الاحتمال لو قدر مفردا ويحصل القطع بسبب الاجتماع. ومثاله أنا نعرف عشق
العاشق لا بقوله بل بأفعال هي أفعال المحبين من القيام بخدمته وبذل ماله
وحضور مجالسه لمشاهدته وملازمته في تردداته وأمور من هذا الجنس، فإن كل
واحد يدل دلالة لو انفرد لاحتمل أن يكون ذلك لغرض آخر يضمره لا لحبه إياه،
لكن تنتهي كثرة هذه الدلالات إلى حد يحصل لنا علم قطعي بحبه، وكذلك ببغضه
إذا رئيت منه أفعال ينتجها البغض، وكذلك نعرف غضبه وخجله لا بمجرد حمرة
وجهه لكن الحمرة إحدى الدلالات، وكذلك نشهد الصبي يرتضع مرة بعد أخرى فيحصل
لنا علم قطعي بوصول اللبن إلى جوفه وإن لم نشاهد اللبن في الضرع لأنه
مستور، ولا عند خروجه فإنه مستور بالفم، ولكن حركة الصبي في الامتصاص وحركة
حلقه تدل عليه دلالة ما مع أن ذلك قد يحصل من غير وصول اللبن، لكن ينضم
إليه أن المرأة الشابة لا يخلو ثديها عن لبن ولا تخلو حلمته عن ثقب، ولا
يخلو الصبي عن  طبع باعث على الامتصاص مستخرج للبن وكل ذلك يحتمل خلافه
نادرا وإن لم يكن غالبا، لكن إذا انضم إليه سكوت الصبي عن بكائه مع أنه لم
يتناول طعاما آخر صار قرينة.
ويحتمل أن يكون بكاؤه عن وجع وسكوته عن زواله، ويحتمل أن يكون تناول شيئا
آخر لم نشاهده وإن كنا نلازمه في أكثر الأوقات، ومع هذا فاقتران هذه
الدلائل كاقتران الأخبار وتواترها وكل دلالة شاهدة يتطرق إليها الاحتمال
كقول كل مخبر على حياله، وينشأ من الاجتماع العلم، وكأن هذا مدرك سادس من
مدارك العلم سوى ما
ذكرناه في المقدمة من الأوليات والمحسوسات والمشاهدات الباطنة والتجريبات
والمتواترات فيلحق هذا بها.
وإذا كان هذا غير منكر فلا يبعد أن يحصل التصديق بقول عدد ناقص عند
انضمام قرائن إليه لو تجرد عن القرائن لم يفد العلم، فإنه إذا أخبر خمسة أو
ستة عن موت إنسان لا يحصل العلم بصدقهم، لكن إذا انضم إليه خروج والد الميت
من الدار حاسر الرأس حافي الرجل ممزق الثياب مضطرب الحال يصفق وجهه ورأسه
وهو رجل كبير ذو منصب ومروءة لا يخالف عادته ومروءته والتجربة تدل عليه.
وكذلك العدد الكثير ربما يخبرون عن أمر يقتضي إيالة الملك وسياسة إظهاره،
والمخبرون من رؤساء جنود الملك، فيتصور اجتماعهم تحت ضبط الإيالة بالاتفاق
على الكذب، ولو كانوا متفرقين خارجين عن ضبط الملك لم يتطرق إليهم هذا
الوهم فهذا يؤثر في النفس تأثيرا لا ينكر.
ولا أدري لم أنكر القاضي ذلك وما برهانه على استحالته فقد بان بهذا أن
العدد يجوز أن يختلف بالوقائع وبالأشخاص، فرب شخص انغرس في نفسه أخلاق تميل
به إلى سرعة التصديق ببعض الأشياء، فيقوم ذلك مقام القرائن وتقوم تلك
القرائن مقام خبر بعض المخبرين فينشأ من ذلك أن لا برهان على استحالته. فإن
قيل: فهل يجوز أن يحصل العلم بقول واحد؟ قلنا: حكي عن الكعبي جوازه.
ولا يظن بمعتوه تجويزه مع انتفاء القرائن. أما إذا اجتمعت قرائن فلا يبعد
أن تبلغ القرائن مبلغا لا يبقى بينها وبين  إثارة العلم إلا قرينة واحدة،
ويقوم إخبار الواحد مقام تلك القرينة، فهذا مما لا يعرف استحالته ولا يقطع
بوقوعه، فإن وقوعه إنما يعلم بالتجربة ونحن لم نجربه، ولكن قد جربنا كثيرا
مما اعتقدناه جزما بقول الواحد مع قرائن أحواله ثم انكشف أنه كان تلبيسا.
وعن هذا أحال القاضي ذلك وهذا كلام في الوقائع مع بقاء العادات على المعهود
من استمرارها، فأما لو قدرنا خرق هذه العادة فالله تعالى قادر على أن يحصل
لنا العلم بقول واحد من غير قرينة فضلا عن أن تنضم إليه القرائن.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-د-د (ʿAdad)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Enumeration, counting, numerical quantity; the act of reckoning discrete units.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The determinate quantity of transmitters (nāqilūn) requisite for generating necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī) in the transmission of reports (khabar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) numerical count versus metaphorical (majāz) sufficiency—where "completeness" (kamāl) is a functional, not arithmetic, threshold.
- Root: ق-ر-ن (Qarīn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Conjunction, coupling, association; that which is joined to another thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Circumstantial indicators (qarāʾin) that augment or substitute for numerical multiplicity in producing certainty (yaqīn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical conjunction versus metaphorical cognitive coupling—where indicators coalesce like strands of a rope to yield firm belief.
- Root: خ-ب-ر (Khabar)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Information, report, news; the conveyance of a statement about a matter.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The transmitted report as a vehicle for knowledge, distinguished from direct sensory apprehension (ḥiss).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal utterance (qawl) versus metaphorical indication (dalālah)—where non-verbal signs function as implicit reports.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditionality (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb)—The conditional structure "if...then..." (idhā...fa...) governs the logical dependence of knowledge upon the conjunction of number and indicators, mirroring Arabic syntax where the protasis establishes the condition and the apodosis the result.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth condition concerns the number (of reporters), and the refinement of its purpose is achieved through the formulation of questions.

**Question: The Number of Reporters**

It divides into that which is deficient—yielding no knowledge—and that which is complete—yielding knowledge—and that which is excessive, where knowledge is attained through a portion of it and the excess is superfluous beyond sufficiency. The complete (number), being the least count that engenders knowledge, is not known to us; rather, through the occurrence of necessary knowledge we discern the completeness of the number, not that we infer the occurrence of knowledge from the completeness of the number.

Now that you have understood this, the question arises: Can the complete number that produces assent (taṣdīq) in one particular event be conceived to fail in yielding knowledge in some other events? Al-Qāḍī—may God have mercy on him—said: That is impossible; rather, everything that yields knowledge in one event yields it in every event, and if knowledge occurs for one person, it must occur for every person who shares in the hearing, and it cannot be conceived to differ. This is sound if the report is stripped of circumstantial indicators (qarāʾin), for knowledge does not rest upon mere number, and the ratio of numerical multiplicity to other events and other persons is uniform.

However, if indicators conjoin with it that point toward assent, then it is permissible for events and persons to differ therein. Al-Qāḍī denied this, paid no heed to the indicators, and assigned them no effect—and this is unsatisfactory. For mere reporting may engender knowledge when the reporters are numerous even if no indicator exists, and mere indicators may also engender knowledge even if no report is present. Thus it is not far-fetched that indicators join with reports, such that some indicators stand in the place of some of the number of reporters. This is not disclosed except by understanding the meaning of indicators and the manner of their signification. So we say:

There is no doubt that we know matters that are not sensible. For we know of another person his love for someone, his hatred of him, his fear of him, his anger, and his shame—and these are states within the soul of the lover and the hater that the senses do not apprehend. Individual indicators may point to them that are not decisive, but rather probability intrudes upon them; yet the soul inclines through them to a weak conviction.

Then the second and third (indicator) reinforce that. Were their individual instances isolated, probability would intrude upon them, but certainty (qaṭʿ) is attained through their conjunction—just as the statement of each individual in a mass-transmission (tawātur) count is subject to probability if supposed in isolation, yet certainty is attained through the conjunction. An example: we know the lover's passion not by his words but by his acts—the acts of lovers: standing in service, expending his wealth, attending gatherings to behold (the beloved), accompanying him in his comings and goings, and matters of this sort. For each one indicates in a manner that, were it isolated, could be (explained) as serving some other hidden purpose rather than love—but the multiplicity of these indications reaches a limit where we attain decisive knowledge of his love. Likewise with his hatred, when acts that hatred produces are observed from him. And likewise we know his anger and his shame not merely by the redness of his face, but the redness is one of the indications.

Similarly, we witness an infant suckling repeatedly, and we attain decisive knowledge that milk has reached his belly—though we do not observe the milk in the breast, for it is concealed, nor at its exit, for it is concealed by the mouth. But the infant's movement in sucking and the movement of his throat indicate it with a certain indication—even though this could occur without milk reaching (him). Yet there joins to this that a young woman's breast is not devoid of milk, nor is her nipple devoid of a pore, nor is the infant devoid of a natural instinct impelling him to suck and extract the milk. All of this admits of its contrary rarely, even if not predominantly. But when there joins to it the infant's silence from his crying—given that he has not partaken of other food—it becomes an indicator.

It is possible that his crying was from pain and his silence from its cessation, and it is possible that he partook of something else we did not observe, even if we accompany him most of the time. Yet despite this, the conjunction of these indications is like the conjunction of reports and their mass-transmission. Every witnessing indication is subject to probability, like the statement of each reporter taken singly, and from the conjunction knowledge arises. It is as though this is a sixth avenue of the avenues of knowledge, besides what we mentioned in the Introduction—namely, primary intelligibles (awwaliyyāt), sensibles (maḥsūsāt), inner perceptions (mushāhadāt bāṭinah), experiential matters (tajrībāt), and mass-transmitted reports (mutawātirāt)—so this is annexed to them.

And since this is not deniable, it is not far-fetched that assent be attained through the statement of a deficient number when indicators join to it—whereas were it stripped of indicators, it would not yield knowledge. For if five or six report the death of a man, we do not attain knowledge of their truthfulness. But if there joins to it the deceased's father emerging from the house bare-headed, bare-footed, garments torn, in a state of agitation, slapping his face and head—he being a man of rank and honor (murūʾah) who does not depart from his custom and his honor—and experience points to this, (then knowledge is attained).

Likewise, a great number might report a matter pertaining to the king's administration (iyālah) and the policy of its public disclosure, the reporters being from among the king's military commanders. It is then conceivable that they conspire under the control of the administration to agree upon falsehood. Were they scattered, outside the king's control, this suspicion would not intrude upon them. So this affects the soul with an effect that cannot be denied.

I do not know why al-Qāḍī denied this, nor what his proof is for its impossibility. For it has become clear through this that the number may differ according to events and according to persons. For a person may have ingrained in his soul dispositions that incline him to swift assent to certain things, and that stands in the place of indicators; and those indicators stand in the place of the report of some of the reporters. From this it arises that there is no proof of its impossibility.

If it is said: Is it permissible that knowledge be attained through the statement of a single person? We say: It has been related of al-Kaʿbī that he deemed it permissible. And no one of sound mind would deem it permissible with the absence of indicators. But if indicators accumulate, it is not far-fetched that they reach a degree where nothing remains between them and the arousal of knowledge except a single indicator, and the report of the one stands in the place of that indicator. This is something whose impossibility is not known, nor is its occurrence affirmed with certainty. For its occurrence is known only through experience, and we have not experienced it. But we have experienced much that we believed with certainty through the statement of a single person with the indicators of his circumstances, and then it was disclosed that it was deception (talbīs). And it is on account of this that al-Qāḍī deemed it impossible.

This discourse concerns actual events while customs (ʿādāt) remain upon their accustomed continuity. But were we to suppose the breaking of this custom, then God—exalted is He—is capable of producing knowledge in us through the statement of a single person without any indicator—let alone that indicators should join to it.

chapters.title_en: The Judge's Assertion that the Testimony of Four is Deficient of the Complete Number
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة قطع القاضي بأن قول الأربعة قاصر عن العدد الكامل]

مسألة قطع القاضي - رحمه الله - بأن قول الأربعة قاصر عن العدد الكامل
لأنها بينة شرعية يجوز بالإجماع للقاضي وقفها على المزكين لتحصل غلبة
الظن، ولا يطلب الظن فيما علم ضرورة وما ذكره صحيح إذا لم تكن قرينة، فإنا
لا نصادف أنفسنا مضطرين إلى خبر الأربعة، أما إذا فرضت قرائن مع ذلك فلا
يستحيل حصول التصديق لكن لا يكون ذلك حاصلا عن مجرد الخبر بل القرائن مع
الخبر، والقاضي - رحمه الله - يحيل ذلك مع القرائن أيضا.
مسألة: قال القاضي علمت بالإجماع أن الأربعة ناقص
، أما الخمسة فأتوقف فيها لأنه لم يقم فيها دليل الإجماع وهذا ضعيف، لأنا
نعلم بالتجربة ذلك، فكم من أخبار نسمعها من خمسة أو ستة ولا يحصل لنا العلم
بها فهو أيضا ناقص لا نشك فيه.

### | [مسألة أقل عدد يحصل به العلم الضروري]

مسألة: إذا قدرنا انتفاء القرائن فأقل عدد يحصل به العلم الضروري معلوم
لله تعالى وليس معلوما لنا ولا سبيل لنا إلى معرفته، فإنا لا ندري متى حصل
علمنا بوجود مكة ووجود الشافعي ووجود الأنبياء - عليهم السلام - عند تواتر
الخبر إلينا وأنه كان بعد خبر المائة والمائتين ويعسر علينا تجربة ذلك وإن
تكلفناها.
وسبيل التكلف أن نراقب أنفسنا إذا قتل
رجل في السوق مثلا وانصرف جماعة عن موضع القتل ودخلوا علينا يخبروننا عن
قتله، فإن قول الأول يحرك الظن وقول الثاني  والثالث يؤكده، ولا يزال يتزايد
تأكيده إلى أن يصير ضروريا لا يمكننا أن نشكك فيه أنفسنا.
فلو تصور الوقوف على اللحظة التي يحصل العلم فيها ضرورة وحفظ حساب
المخبرين وعددهم لأمكن الوقوف، ولكن درك تلك اللحظة عسير، فإنه تتزايد قوة
الاعتقاد تزايدا خفي التدريج نحو تزايد عقل الصبي المميز إلى أن يبلغ حد
التكليف ونحو تزايد ضوء الصبح إلى أن ينتهي إلى حد الكمال، فلذلك بقي هذا
في غطاء من الإشكال وتعذر على القوة البشرية إدراكه.
فأما ما ذهب إليه قوم من التخصيص بالأربعين أخذا من الجمعة وقوم إلى
التخصيص بالسبعين أخذا من قوله تعالى: {واختار موسى قومه سبعين رجلا
لميقاتنا} [الأعراف: 155] وقوم إلى التخصيص بعدد أهل بدر فكل ذلك تحكمات
فاسدة باردة لا تناسب الغرض ولا تدل عليه، ويكفي تعارض أقوالهم دليلا على
فسادها. فإذا لا سبيل لنا إلى حصر عدده، لكنا بالعلم الضروري نستدل على أن
العدد الذي هو الكامل عند الله تعالى قد توافقوا على الإخبار. فإن قيل:
فكيف علمتم حصول العلم بالتواتر وأنتم لا تعلمون أقل عدده؟ قلنا: كما نعلم
أن الخبز يشبع والماء يروي والخمر يسكر، وإن كنا لا نعلم أقل مقدار منه،
ونعلم أن القرائن تفيد العلم وإن لم نقدر على حصر أجناسها وضبط أقل
درجاتها.

### | [مسألة العدد الكامل إذا أخبروا ولم يحصل العلم بصدقهم]

فيجب القطع بكذبهم
لأنه لا يشترط في حصول العلم إلا شرطان أحدهما كمال العدد، والثاني: أن
يخبروا عن يقين ومشاهدة. فإذا كان العدد كاملا كان امتناع العلم لفوات
الشرط الثاني فنعلم أنهم بجملتهم كذبوا أو كذب بعضهم في قوله إني شاهدت
ذلك، بل بناه على توهم وظن أو كذب متعمدا، لأنهم لو صدقوا وقد كمل عددهم
حصل العلم ضرورة وهذا أيضا أحد الأدلة على أن الأربعة ليسوا عدد التواتر؛
إذ القاضي لم يحصل له العلم بصدقهم وجاز له القضاء بغلبة الظن بالإجماع،
ولو تم عددهم لكان انتفاء العلم بصدقهم دليلا قاطعا على كذب جميعهم أو كذب
واحد منهم، ولقطعنا  بأن فيهم كاذبا أو متوهما، ولا يقبل شهادة أربعة يعلم
أن فيهم كاذبا أو متوهما.
فإن قيل: فإن لم يحصل العلم بقولهم وقد كثروا كثرة يستحيل بحكم العادة
توافقهم على الكذب على اتفاق ويستحيل دخولهم تحت ضابط وتساعدهم على الكذب
بحيث ينكتم ذلك على جميعهم ولا يتحدث به واحد منهم، فعلى ماذا يجمل كذبهم
وكيف يتصور ذلك؟ قلنا: إنما يمكن ذلك بأن يكونوا منقسمين إلى صادقين
وكاذبين، أما الصادقون فعددهم ناقص عن المبلغ الذي يستقل بإفادة العلم،
وأما الكاذبون فيحتمل أن يقع منهم التواطؤ لنقصان عددهم عن مبلغ يستحيل
عليهم التواطؤ مع الانكتام، فإن كانوا مبلغا لا يستحيل التواطؤ عليهم مع
الانكتام فلا يستحيل الانكتام في الحال إلى أن يتحدث به في ثاني الحال.
ونقل الشيعة نص الإمامة مع كثرتها إنما لم يفد العلم لأنهم لم يخبروا عن
المشاهدة والسماع، بل لو سمعوا عن سلف فهم صادقون، لكن السلف الواضعون لهذا
الكذب يكون عددهم ناقصا عن مبلغ يستحيل منهم التواطؤ مع
الانكتام، وربما ظن الخلف أن عددهم كامل لا يستحيل عليهم التواطؤ فيخطئون
في الظن فيقطعون بالحكم ويكون هذا منشأ غلطهم.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ص-ر (qa-ṣād-rā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deficiency, falling short of a limit or completion; to be insufficient in measure or degree.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In epistemic contexts, denotes the failure of a cause to produce its full effect—here, the failure of four reporters to generate necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in quantitative deficiency; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to epistemic force—i.e., the report's power is "short" of certainty.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Protasis (al-sharṭ al-muḍmar) — the phrase "if no contextual indicator (qarīnah) exists" governs the entire argument, requiring the reader to supply the unstated condition for the judge's claim to hold.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Judge (Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī) — may God have mercy on him — asserted that the statement of four [witnesses] falls short of the complete number [required for necessary knowledge], because it is a legal evidence (bayyinah sharʿiyyah) which, by consensus (ijmāʿ), the judge may suspend upon the character-verifiers (muzakkīn) so that preponderant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann) is obtained; and conjecture is not sought in matters known by necessity. What he mentioned is sound when no contextual indicator (qarīnah) exists, for we do not find ourselves compelled by necessity toward the report of four. However, if contextual indicators are supposed alongside that, the attainment of assent (taṣdīq) is not impossible—but that [assent] would not arise from the bare report alone, rather from the indicators together with the report. And the Judge — may God have mercy on him — deems that impossible even with contextual indicators.

Another question: The Judge said: "I know by consensus that four is deficient; as for five, I suspend judgment therein, because no consensus-based proof has been established for it." This is weak, for we know by experience that this is so. How many reports do we hear from five or six [transmitters] and yet no knowledge of them is obtained for us? So it too is deficient—of that we have no doubt.

Another question: If we suppose the absence of contextual indicators, then the minimal number by which necessary knowledge is obtained is known to God — exalted be He — but is not known to us, nor do we have any path to knowing it. For we do not know at what moment our knowledge of the existence of Mecca, the existence of al-Shāfiʿī, and the existence of the Prophets — peace be upon them — was obtained when the report reached us by mass transmission (tawātur), and that it was after the report of the hundredth and two-hundredth [transmitter]. And it is difficult for us to experiment with that, even if we undertake it.

The method of undertaking it is that we observe ourselves: when, for example, a man is killed in the marketplace, and a group departs from the place of the killing and enters upon us informing us of his death — the statement of the first stirs conjecture, the statement of the second and third reinforces it, and its reinforcement continues to increase until it becomes necessary (ḍarūrī), such that we cannot cast doubt upon it in ourselves.

If it were conceivable to pinpoint the very moment at which knowledge is obtained necessarily, and to keep account of the reporters and their number, then pinpointing it would be possible. But grasping that moment is difficult, for the strength of belief increases with an imperceptible gradation — like the increase of the discerning child's intellect until it reaches the threshold of legal obligation (taklīf), and like the increase of the dawn's light until it reaches the limit of perfection. For this reason, this matter remained veiled in obscurity, and its apprehension proved impossible for human power.

As for what some have held — the specification of forty, derived from the Friday [congregation]; others the specification of seventy, derived from His saying — exalted be He: {«And Moses chose seventy men from his people for Our appointed time»} [al-Aʿrāf: 155]; and others the specification of the number of the people of Badr — all of that is corrupt and frigid arbitrariness (taḥakkumāt) that neither suits the purpose nor indicates it. And the mutual contradiction of their statements suffices as proof of their corruption. Since we have no path to enumerating its number, we rather infer by necessary knowledge that the number which is complete in God's sight — exalted be He — has [in fact] concurred upon the report. If it is said: "How do you know that knowledge is obtained by tawātur when you do not know its minimal number?" We say: Just as we know that bread satiates, water quenches, and wine intoxicates, even though we do not know the minimal amount of each; and we know that contextual indicators produce knowledge even though we cannot enumerate their kinds or fix their minimal degrees.

Another question: When the complete number has reported and yet knowledge of their truthfulness is not obtained, then it is incumbent to judge definitively that they have lied. For nothing is required for the attainment of knowledge except two conditions: first, the completeness of the number; second, that they report from certainty and direct observation (mushāhadah). So when the number is complete, the non-attainment of knowledge must be due to the failure of the second condition. We thus know that all of them lied, or that some of them lied in saying "I witnessed that" — rather, he based it on illusion (tawahhum) and conjecture, or deliberately lied. For had they been truthful and their number complete, knowledge would have been obtained necessarily. This too is one of the proofs that four are not the number of tawātur; for the Judge did not obtain knowledge of their truthfulness, and it was permissible for him to adjudicate by preponderant conjecture by consensus. Had their number been complete, the non-attainment of knowledge of their truthfulness would have been a decisive proof of the falsehood of all of them or of one of them — and we would have judged definitively that among them is a liar or one who harbors illusion. And the testimony of four, of whom it is known that one is a liar or harbors illusion, is not accepted.

If it is said: "If knowledge is not obtained by their statement even when they have multiplied to a multitude such that, by customary necessity, their concurrence upon falsehood is impossible, and their falling under a [conspiratorial] control is impossible, and their cooperation in falsehood such that it remains concealed from all of them and not a single one of them divulges it — then upon what basis is their falsehood construed, and how is that conceivable?" We say: That is only possible by their being divided into truthful and lying [groups]. As for the truthful ones, their number falls short of the threshold that independently produces knowledge. As for the liars, it is possible that collusion (tawāṭuʾ) occurs among them because their number falls short of the threshold at which collusion with concealment is impossible for them. For if they are at a number at which collusion with concealment is not impossible, then concealment is not impossible in the present moment until one of them divulges it in the next moment.

And the Shīʿah's transmission of the text (naṣṣ) of the imamate, despite its multitude, did not produce knowledge only because they did not report from direct observation and hearing. Rather, had they heard from their predecessors, they would be truthful. But the predecessors who fabricated this falsehood were of a number deficient of the threshold at which collusion with concealment is impossible for them. And perhaps the successors supposed that their number was complete, such that collusion would be impossible for them — and so they erred in their supposition, and thereby issued definitive judgments. And this is the origin of their error.

chapters.title_en: Concluding Remarks on the Invalid Conditions for the Number of Tawātur (Mass Transmission)
