Among them: What appeared from him and from ʿUthmān — may God be pleased with them both — and the masses of the Companions — may God be pleased with them — of reverting from the position that the obligatory bath (ghusl) is not required from the meeting of the two circumcisions (iltiqāʾ al-khitanayn), upon the report of ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — and her saying: «I did that, I and the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and we bathed.» From that also: What is authentically established from ʿUthmān — may God be pleased with him — that he ruled concerning the dwelling (al-suknā) upon the report of Farīʿah bint Mālik, after he had sent to her and asked her.

Among them: What appeared from ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — of accepting the isolated report and seeking corroboration by oath (al-yamīn), until he said in the famous report: "When I heard a hadith from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — God benefited me with what He willed of it. And when someone other than him narrated to me, I would put him on oath; if he swore, I would affirm him. And Abū Bakr narrated to me — and Abū Bakr spoke truthfully — he said: The Messenger of God — peace be upon him — said: «There is no servant who commits a sin...»" — the rest of the hadith. He would put the narrator on oath not out of suspicion of falsehood, but for prudence in conveying the hadith in its proper form, and to guard against altering its wording by narrating it according to meaning (naqlan bil-maʿnā), and so that one would not proceed to narrate based on conjecture, but only upon verified hearing.

Among them: What is related from Zayd ibn Thābit — may God be pleased with him — that he held that a menstruating woman (al-ḥāʾiḍ) may not depart [from Mecca] until her final act is the circumambulation of the House (ṭawāf al-bayt), and he objected to Ibn ʿAbbās's contrary view. It was said to him: "Ibn ʿAbbās asked such-and-such an Anṣāriyyah woman whether the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — had commanded her to do that, and she informed him." So Zayd ibn Thābit reverted, laughing, and said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "I see that you have spoken the truth," and he reverted to agreeing with him upon the report of the Anṣāriyyah woman.

Among them: What is related from Anas — may God be pleased with him — that he said: "I was serving Abū ʿUbaydah, Abū Ṭalḥah, and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb a drink made from unripe dates (fadīkh tamr), when a visitor came to us and said: 'Indeed, wine (al-khamr) has been prohibited.' So Abū Ṭalḥah said: 'Rise, O Anas, to these jars and break them.' So I went to a stone mortar of ours and struck them with its base until they were broken." Among them: What is widely known of the practice of the people of Qubāʾ in turning towards the new qiblah upon an isolated report — that a visitor came to them and informed them of the abrogation (naskh) of the qiblah, so they turned towards the Kaʿbah upon his report.

Among them: What appeared from Ibn ʿAbbās — may God be pleased with him — when it was said to him that a certain man among the Muslims claimed that Moses, the companion of al-Khiḍr, was not the Moses of the Children of Israel — peace be upon him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The enemy of God has lied. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb informed me, saying: «The Messenger of God — peace be upon him — addressed us, then mentioned Moses and al-Khiḍr with something indicating that Moses, the companion of al-Khiḍr, is the Moses of the Children of Israel.»" So Ibn ʿAbbās went beyond acting upon the isolated report and hastened to declare the claim false in its very foundation, and to assert its falsehood definitively, on account of the report of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Among them also: What is related from Abū al-Dardāʾ that when Muʿāwiyah sold some vessels of gold and silver for more than their weight, Abū al-Dardāʾ said to him: "I heard the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — prohibit that." Muʿāwiyah said to him: "I do not see any harm in it." So Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "Who will excuse me from Muʿāwiyah? I inform him of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and he informs me of his own opinion! I will not dwell with you in the same land ever."

Among them: What is widely known of all of them, in reports too numerous to count, of reverting to ʿĀʾishah, Umm Salamah, Maymūnah, and Ḥafṣah — may God be pleased with them — and to Fāṭimah bint Asad, and to such-and-such and such-and-such women whose number cannot be counted, and to Zayd, Usāmah ibn Zayd, and other Companions — may God be pleased with them — from among men, women, slaves, and freedmen. Upon this was the practice (sunnah) of the Followers after them. Al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — said: "We found ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn — may God be pleased with him — relying upon isolated reports, and likewise Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr, Khārijah ibn Zayd, Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār." Likewise was the case of Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ, and Mujāhid. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib would say: "Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī informed me from the Prophet — peace be upon him — concerning currency exchange (al-ṣarf)," and he would establish his hadith as a Sunnah. And he would say: "Abū Hurayrah narrated to me." And ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr would say: "ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — narrated to me that the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — «ruled that revenue is guaranteed by liability (al-kharāj bil-ḍamān),»" and he would object with that against a ruling of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and ʿUmar would overturn his ruling on account of that. Likewise, Maysarah in Yemen and Makḥūl in Syria. Upon this were the jurists of Basra, such as al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, and the jurists of Kufa and their Followers, such as ʿAlqamah, al-Aswad, al-Shaʿbī, and Masrūq. Upon this continued those after them from among the jurists, and no one objected to them in any era. Had there been any objection, it would have been transmitted, and in the settled course of custom (mustaqarr al-ʿādah) it would have been necessary for it to become widely known, and the motives for transmitting it would have been abundant, just as they were abundant for transmitting the practice of acting upon it. Thus it is established that this was a matter of consensus (mujmaʿ ʿalayh) among the predecessors, and that the disagreement only arose after them.

If it is said: Perhaps they acted upon them with corroborating indications (qarāʾin), or with other reports that accompanied them, or with apparent meanings (ẓawāhir), analogies (maqāyīs), and causes that were associated with them — not merely upon these reports, as you claim. Just as you say regarding their acting upon the general (al-ʿumūm), and the imperative and prohibitive forms (ṣīghat al-amr wa-al-nahy) — that these are not an explicit text (naṣṣ) proving that they acted upon the mere form, but rather upon it along with accompanying indications. We say: Because no wording has been transmitted from them [in those cases] indicating that they acted upon the mere form of command, prohibition, and generality. But here they explicitly said: "Had we not heard this, we would have ruled otherwise." And Ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with them both — explicitly stated their reversion from the practice of al-mukhābarah (sharecropping) upon the report of Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, and their reversion concerning the meeting of the two circumcisions upon the report of ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her. How [can this be compared] when the forms of generality, command, and prohibition are never free from an indication arising from the state of the commanded person, the commanded act, and the commander? As for what a narrator relates from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — what indication could accompany it such that it becomes a proof on account of it? To suppose such indications would be like supposing indications in their acting upon the text of the Book, the mass-transmitted report, and consensus — and that would invalidate all evidences.

In sum: Their adjuration in seeking reports had no motive other than acting upon them. If it is said: They also abandoned acting upon many reports. We say: That was due to their lacking the conditions of acceptance (shurūṭ al-qabūl), as will come later — just as they abandoned acting upon the text of the Qurʾān and upon mass-transmitted reports when they learned of their abrogation (naskh), or when the command had lapsed and those to whom the second address was directed had passed away.

The second proof: What has been mass-transmitted of the Messenger of God's — peace be upon him — dispatch of his governors (umarāʾ), judges (quḍāh), messengers (rusul), and collectors (suʿāh) to the outlying regions, while they were individuals (āḥād). He only sent them to collect the alms (ṣadaqāt), to conclude and confirm treaties (ʿuhūd), and to convey the rulings of the Sacred Law. From that: His appointment of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq over the pilgrimage season (al-mawsim) in year nine, his dispatch of Sūrat Barāʾah with ʿAlī, and his charging him with the dissolution of the treaties and covenants that existed between them and him — peace be upon him. From that: His appointment of ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — over the alms, and his appointment of Muʿādh to collect the alms of Yemen and to judge over its people.

From that: His dispatch — peace be upon him — of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān to the people of Mecca as a bearer of a message and a messenger conveying from him, until it reached him that Quraysh had killed him. He was deeply disturbed by that, and on account of it he took the pledge of allegiance of Riḍwān (bayʿat al-riḍwān) and said: «By God, if they have killed him, I will kindle a fire upon them.» From that: His appointment — peace be upon him — over the alms and the tax collections of Qays ibn ʿĀṣim, Mālik ibn Nuwayrah, al-Zibriqān ibn Badr, Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, Usāmah ibn Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, and others whose mention would be lengthy. It is established by the agreement of the historians (ahl al-siyar) that he — peace be upon him — obliged the people of the outlying regions to accept the word of his messengers, collectors, and judges. Had he needed, for every messenger, to dispatch with him a number reaching the level of tawātur, all his Companions would not have sufficed for that, his emigration city (dār hijratihi) would have been emptied of his Companions and supporters, his enemies from the Jews and others would have gained power over him, and the order and administration would have been corrupted. That is a manifestly false supposition.

If it is said: He — peace be upon him — had already informed them of the details of the alms orally and through mass-transmitted reports, and he only sent them to collect them. We say: Why then was it obligatory to affirm them in their claim of collection while they were individuals? Moreover, his dispatch — peace be upon him — was not only for the alms, but for teaching them the religion, judging between disputants, and defining the functions of the Sacred Law. If it is said: Then it would be obligatory upon them to accept the very foundation of prayer (al-ṣalāh) and alms (al-zakāh) — indeed, the very foundation of the call (al-daʿwah), the message (al-risālah), and the miracle (al-muʿjizah). We say: As for the foundation of prayer and alms, it was obligatory to accept them, because they were dispatched to explain the functions of the Sacred Law after the foundation of the call had already spread. As for the foundation of the message, faith (al-īmān), and the signs of prophethood (aʿlām al-nubuwwah), no — for how could the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — say "I have made it obligatory upon you to affirm me" when they did not yet know of his message? As for after affirming him, it is possible to listen to his messengers, by his making it obligatory to listen to them. If it is said: The isolated report is only to be accepted when a decisive proof indicates the obligation of acting upon it, just as consensus and tawātur indicate it according to you. By what did those people affirm the governors in their saying "It is obligatory upon you to act upon our word"? We say: It had reached them through tawātur, from the biography (sīrah) of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — that he dispatched governors and messengers as individuals, like other great men and leaders. Had they not known that, it would have been permissible for a skeptic to dispute it when doubt occurred to him. But doubt rarely occurs concerning it, given the indications (qarāʾin). For one who enters our lands with a judicial decree (manshūr al-qaḍāʾ) — no doubt assails us concerning his truthfulness, even if it has not reached us through tawātur, but rather through the indications of circumstances, knowledge of the writer's handwriting, and the remoteness of his audacity to lie while exposing himself to danger in such matters.

The third proof: The common person (al-ʿāmmī), by consensus, is commanded to follow the jurisconsult (al-muftī) and affirm him, even though he may be reporting his own opinion (ẓann). So one who reports what he has heard, concerning which there is no doubt, is more deserving of affirmation. Falsehood and error are possible for the jurisconsult just as for the narrator — indeed, error is more remote for the narrator, because every mujtahid, even if he is correct, is only correct when he has not fallen short in completing his deliberation (naẓar). But perhaps he thinks he has not fallen short while he has in fact fallen short.

This [argument] is even more forceful on the doctrine of those who permit the taqlīd of a follower of al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — when he transmits the doctrine (madhhab) of his teacher, because he is narrating the opinion of another. How then would he not narrate the statement of another? If it is said: This is an analogy (qiyās) that yields only conjecture (ẓann), and it is not permissible to establish foundational principles (uṣūl) by conjecture and analogy. Acting upon the isolated report is a foundational principle. Moreover, no aspect of conjecture even arises here, for the mujtahid is compelled to it. And if the individual common people were charged with the degree of ijtihād, that would be impossible — so they are compelled to taqlīd of the jurisconsult. We say: There is no necessity in that. Rather, one should revert to the original presumption of innocence (al-barāʾah al-aṣliyyah), since he has no path to knowledge — just as, according to your claim, the jurisconsult, when an isolated report reaches him, must reject the report and revert to the original presumption of innocence when tawātur is unavailable to him. Then we say: This is not a conjectural analogy, but rather a certain one (maqṭūʿ bihi), because it is in its very meaning [the same]. For if acting upon the isolated report were valid in marriage contracts (al-ankiha), we would be certain of it in sales (al-bayūʿāt), and the matter would not differ with the difference of what is reported. Here, nothing differs except the thing reported about: the jurisconsult reports his own opinion, while the narrator reports the statement of another. This is just as no distinction was made, in the case of two witnesses (al-shāhidayn), between their testifying about themselves or about others when they testify to the probity (ʿadālah) of others, or their testifying about their own opinion of the probity of others.

The fourth proof: The saying of God, the Exalted: {«So why should not a group from every section of them go forth to become learned in religion, and to warn their people when they return to them»} [al-Tawbah: 122]. For the group (al-ṭāʾifah) is a small number, like three, and certainty is not attained through their statement. This [argument] requires examination, because if it is decisive, it is decisive concerning the obligation of warning (al-indhār), not concerning the obligation of acting upon the warning on the part of the one warned, when the warner is a single individual — just as a single witness is obligated to give testimony, not so that it may be acted upon alone, but so that when another joins it, [it may be acted upon].

This objection is also what weakens the appeal to the saying of God, the Exalted: {«Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance»} [al-Baqarah: 159], and His saying — peace be upon him: «May God brighten a man who hears my words, comprehends them, and conveys them as he heard them» — the hadith — and similar examples.

Then know that the opponent in this matter has two specious arguments (shubhatān):

The first specious argument: Their saying: There is no basis for establishing the isolated report except consensus (ijmāʿ). How can that be claimed, when there is no Companion who did not reject an isolated report? From that: The Messenger of God's — peace be upon him — hesitation to accept the report of Dhū al-Yadayn, when he had given the salutation after two rakʿahs, until he asked Abū Bakr and ʿUmar — may God be pleased with them both — and they testified to that and affirmed him. Then he accepted it and performed the prostration of forgetfulness (sajdat al-sahw). From that: The rejection by Abū Bakr — may God be pleased with him — of the report of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah concerning the inheritance of the grandfather (mīrāth al-jadd), until Muḥammad ibn Maslamah informed him along with him. From that: The rejection by Abū Bakr and ʿUmar of the report of ʿUthmān — may God be pleased with them — concerning what he narrated of his asking the Messenger's permission to return al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, and they demanded that someone testify with him to that. From that: What is widely known of ʿUmar's — may God be pleased with him — rejection of the report of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī concerning seeking permission (al-istidhān), until Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī — may God be pleased with him — testified with him. From that: The rejection by ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — of the report of Abū Sinān al-Ashjaʿī in the case of Barwaʿ bint Wāshiq, and it appeared from him that he would put narrators on oath concerning the hadith. From that: The rejection by ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — of the report of Ibn ʿUmar concerning the punishment of the dead person by the weeping of his family over him. And it appeared from ʿUmar his prohibition to Abū Mūsā and Abū Hurayrah against narrating from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and similar examples that are numerous. Most of these reports indicate the doctrine of those who require a number in the narrator, not the doctrine of those who require tawātur — for they did not gather together and wait for tawātur.

But we say in response to what they asked: What we have narrated is decisive concerning their practice. What you have mentioned is a rejection due to incidental causes (asbāb ʿāriḍah) that necessitate rejection, and does not indicate the invalidity of the foundational principle — just as their rejection of some texts of the Qurʾān, their abandonment of some types of analogy (qiyās), and a judge's rejection of some types of testimonies does not indicate the invalidity of the foundational principle. We shall indicate the general kinds of excuses (maʿādhir) in rejecting reports and hesitating concerning them:

As for the Messenger of God's — peace be upon him — hesitation concerning the statement of Dhū al-Yadayn, it admits of three possibilities:

First: That he deemed error (al-wahm) possible for him, due to the large gathering and the remoteness of his being alone in knowing that while all were heedless — for error is closer to him than heedlessness to a large gathering. And when indications of error appear, hesitation becomes obligatory.

Second: That even if he knew him to be truthful, it is possible that the reason for his hesitation was to teach them the obligation of hesitation in similar cases. Had he not hesitated, affirming [such reports] with the silence of the group would have become an established practice (sunnah māḍiyah). So he cut off that path.

Third: That he said something which, had it been known to be true, its effect would have appeared with respect to the group and their consciences would have become engaged — so it was akin to testimony (shahādah), in which the statement of a single individual is not accepted. The strongest [of these possibilities] is what we mentioned before. Indeed, if one who requires a number in testimony were to cling to this, he would be required to require three, and to require that it be in a gathering where the rest remain silent — for that is how it was.

As for Abū Bakr's hesitation concerning the hadith of al-Mughīrah regarding the inheritance of the grandmother (tawrīth al-jaddah), perhaps there was an aspect there that necessitated hesitation, which no one may have perceived. Or it was to consider whether the ruling was settled or abrogated, or to know whether anyone else had what he had, so that the ruling might be more firmly established, or so that a contrary [report] might be repelled. Or he hesitated awaiting corroboration by an additional [narrator], just as a judge, after the testimony of two witnesses, awaits corroboration before rendering a definitive ruling — if the addition does not come, he rules, not intending rejection. Or he displayed hesitation so that people would not proceed too readily to narrate with carelessness. It must be interpreted in one of these ways, since it is definitively established from him that he accepted the isolated report and did not object to those who acted upon it.

As for the rejection of the hadith of ʿUthmān concerning al-Ḥakam ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, it is because it was a report of establishing a right for a specific person, so it is like testimony, which is not established by the statement of a single individual. Or the hesitation was due to ʿUthmān's kinship to al-Ḥakam, as he was known to be solicitous for his relatives — so they hesitated to protect his honor and position from a critic who might say: "He only said that because of his kinship," until it was established by the statement of another. Or perhaps they both hesitated to teach the people hesitation in the case of a close relative who is treated with leniency, so that they might learn from them the need for caution in such cases.

As for the report of Abū Mūsā concerning seeking permission, ʿUmar was in need of it to repel from himself the charge of [harsh] conduct, when Abū Mūsā had turned away from his door after knocking three times, as one who disdains to present himself at his door. He feared that this might become a path for others to narrate the hadith according to their own purposes. The proof of that is that when Abū Mūsā returned with Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and he testified with him, ʿUmar said: "I did not accuse you, but I feared that people would speak falsely about the Messenger of God — peace be upon him." It is permissible for the leader (al-imām) to hesitate, even with the absence of accusation, for such a public interest (maṣlaḥah). How [can this be compared], when such reports are not equal in fame and soundness to our hadiths concerning the transmission of statements from them? As for ʿAlī's rejection of the report of al-Ashjaʿī, he mentioned its cause and said: "How can we accept the statement of a Bedouin who urinates on his heels?" He made clear that he did not know his probity (ʿadālah) and precision (ḍabṭ), and therefore described him with roughness and lack of care in avoiding urine. Likewise, ʿUmar said concerning Fāṭimah bint Qays in the hadith of the dwelling (al-suknā): "We do not abandon the Book of our Lord and the Sunnah of our Prophet for the statement of a woman of whom we do not know whether she spoke truthfully or falsely."

This is the way of discussing what is transmitted of hesitation concerning reports.

The second specious argument: Their appeal to the saying of God, the Exalted: {«And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge»} [al-Isrāʾ: 36], and {«And that you say about God what you do not know»} [al-Baqarah: 169], and His saying, the Exalted: {«And we do not testify except to what we know»} [Yūsuf: 81], and His saying, the Exalted: {«If a sinner comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance»} [al-Ḥujurāt: 6]. And ignorance is present in the statement of the upright person [according to them].

This is false from several aspects:

First: That their denial of acting upon the isolated report is not known by a decisive proof — rather, error is possible in it. So they are ruling without knowledge.

Second: That the obligation of acting upon it is known by a decisive proof from consensus, so there is no ignorance in it.

chapters.title_en: Section 77 — The Second Chapter on the Conditions and Attributes of the Narrator (al-Rāwī)
chapters.arabic_text: ### | [الباب الثاني في شروط  الراوي وصفته]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ر ط (sharṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A condition, sign, or mark that delimits or qualifies something; in legal theory, that without which a thing is invalid but which is not itself part of the essence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A stipulation (sharṭ) in uṣūl al-fiqh denotes an external requisite for the validity of an act or report, distinct from its constitutive pillar (rukn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) for a binding condition; metaphorical (majāz) for a descriptive attribute (ṣifah) when applied to persons, as here.
- Root: و ص ف (waṣafa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To describe, characterize, or qualify; a ṣifah is an attribute or quality that inheres in a subject.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In transmission (riwāyah), ṣifah refers to the moral and intellectual qualities (ʿadālah, ḍabṭ) that render a narrator reliable.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for inherent traits; here used technically for the requisite qualifications of a transmitter.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "wa-ṣifatihi" is a genitive annexation (muḍāf ilayh) coordinated with "shurūṭ," indicating that conditions and attributes are conceptually parallel yet distinct categories in the science of ḥadīth criticism.

chapters.title_en: The Conditions for Accepting the Report of the Single Narrator (Khabar al-Wāḥid) and the Definition of Its Acceptability
chapters.arabic_text:
وإذا ثبت وجوب العمل بخبر الواحد فاعلم أن كل خبر فليس بمقبول وافهم أولا
أنا لسنا نعني بالقول التصديق ولا بالرد التكذيب، بل يجب علينا قبول قول
العدل وربما كان كاذبا أو غالطا، ولا يجوز قبول قول الفاسق وربما كان
صادقا. بل نعني بالمقبول ما يجب العمل به وبالمردود ما لا تكليف علينا في
العمل به والمقبول رواية كل مكلف عدل مسلم ضابط منفردا كان بروايته أو معه
غيره، فهذه خمسة أمور لا بد من النظر فيها.
الأول: أن رواية الواحد تقبل وإن لم تقبل شهادته، خلافا للجبائي وجماعة
حيث شرطوا العدد ولم يقبلوا إلا قول رجلين. ثم لا تثبت رواية كل واحد إلا
من رجلين آخرين وإلى أن ينتهي إلى زماننا يكثر كثرة عظيمة لا يقدر معها على
إثبات حديث أصلا وقال قوم: لا بد من أربعة أخذا من شهادة الزنا.
ودليل بطلان مذهبهم أنا نقول: إذا
ثبت قبول قول الآحاد مع أنه لا يفيد العلم فاشتراط العدد تحكم لا يعرف
إلا بنص أو قياس على منصوص ولا سبيل إلى دعوى النص وما نقل عن الصحابة من
طلب استظهار فهو في واقعتين أو ثلاث لأسباب ذكرناها أما ما قضوا فيه بقول
عائشة وحدها وقول زوجات رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وقول عبد الرحمن
بن عوف وأبي هريرة وغيرهم فهو خارج عن الحصر فقد علمنا قطعا من أحوالهم
قبول خبر الواحد كما علمنا قطعا رد شهادة الواحد، وإن أخذوا من قياس
الشهادة فهو قياس باطل إذ عرف من فعلهم الفرق ولم لا يقاس عليه في شرط
الحرية والذكورة واشترط في أخبار الزنا أربعة وفيما يتعلق برؤية الهلال
وشهادة القابلة واحد؟ والمصير إلى ذلك خرق للإجماع، ولا فرق إن وجب القياس.
الشرط الثاني: وهو الأول تحقيقا، فإن العدد ليس عندنا من الشروط وهو
التكليف، فلا تقبل رواية الصبي لأنه لا يخاف الله تعالى فلا وازع له من
الكذب فلا تحصل الثقة بقوله، وقد اتبعوا في قبول الشهادة سكون  النفس وحصول
الظن، والفاسق أوثق من الصبي، فإنه يخاف الله تعالى وله وازع من دينه وعقله
والصبي لا يخاف الله تعالى أصلا فهو مردود بطريق الأولى.
والتمسك بهذا أولى من التمسك برد إقراره، وإنه إذا لم يقبل قوله فيما
يحكيه عن نفسه فبأن لا يقبل فيما يرويه عن غيره أولى، فإن هذا يبطل بالعبد
فإنه قد لا يقبل إقراره وتقبل روايته. فإن كان سببه أنه يتناول ملك السيد
وملك السيد معصوم عنه فملك الصبي أيضا محفوظ عنه لمصلحته، فما لا يتعلق به
قد يؤثر فيه قوله بل حاله حتى يجوز الاقتداء به اعتمادا على قوله إنه طاهر
وعلى أنه لا يصلي إلا طاهرا، لكنه كما يجوز الاقتداء بالبر والفاجر فكذلك
بالصبي والبالغ، وشهادة الفاسق لا تقبل والصبي أجرأ على الكذب منه.
أما إذا كان طفلا مميزا عند التحمل بالغا عند الرواية فإنه يقبل لأنه لا
خلل في تحمله ولا في أدائه ويدل على قبول سماعه إجماع الصحابة على قبول خبر
ابن عباس وابن الزبير والنعمان بن بشير وغيرهم من أحداث الصحابة من غير فرق
بين ما تحملوه بعد البلوغ أو قبله، وعلى ذلك درج السلف والخلف من إحضار
الصبيان مجالس الرواية ومن قبول شهادتهم فيما تحملوه في الصغر.
فإن قيل فقد قال بعض العلماء تقبل شهادة الصبيان في الجنايات التي تجري
بينهم. قلنا: ذلك منه استدلال بالقرائن إذا كثروا وأخبروا قبل التفرق، أما
إذا تفرقوا فيتطرق إليهم التلقين الباطل ولا وازع لهم، فمن قضى به فإنما
قضى به لكثرة الجنايات بينهم ولمسيس الحاجة إلى معرفته بقرائن الأحوال فلا
يكون ذلك على منهاج الشهادة.
الشرط الثالث: أن يكون ضابطا، فمن كان عند التحمل غير مميز أو كان مغفلا
لا يحسن ضبط ما حفظه ليؤديه على وجهه فلا ثقة بقوله وإن لم يكن فاسقا.
الشرط الرابع: أن يكون مسلما، ولا خلاف في أن رواية الكافر لا تقبل لأنه
متهم في الدين وإن كان تقبل شهادة بعضهم على بعض عند أبي حنيفة. ولا  يخالف
في رد روايته، والاعتماد في ردها على الإجماع المنعقد على سلبه أهلية هذا
المنصب في الدين وإن كان عدلا في دين نفسه وهو أولى من قولنا الفاسق مردود
الشهادة والكفر أعظم أنواع الفسق، وقد قال تعالى.
{إن جاءكم فاسق بنبإ فتبينوا أن تصيبوا} [الحجرات: 6] لأن الفاسق متهم
لجرأته على المعصية، والكافر المترهب قد لا
يتهم لكن التعويل على الإجماع في سلب الكافر هذا المنصب. فإن قيل: هذا
يتجه في اليهود والنصارى ومن لا يؤمن بديننا، إذ لا يليق في السياسة تحكيمه
في دين لا يعتقد تعظيمه، فما قولكم في الكافر المتأول وهو الذي قد قال
ببدعة يجب التكفير بها فهو معظم للدين وممتنع من المعصية وغير عالم بأنه
كافر، فلم لا تقبل روايته وقد قبل الشافعي رواية بعض أهل البدع وإن كان
فاسقا ببدعته لأنه متأول في فسقه؟ قلنا: في رواية المبتدع المتأول كلام
سيأتي، وأما الكافر وإن كان متأولا فلا تقبل روايته لأن كل كافر متأول، فإن
اليهودي أيضا لا يعلم كونه كافرا.
أما الذي ليس بمتأول وهو المعاند بلسانه بعد معرفة الحق بقلبه فذلك مما
يندر، وتورع المتأول عن الكذب كتورع النصراني فلا ينظر إليه، بل هذا المنصب
لا يستفاد إلا بالإسلام، وعرف ذلك بالإجماع لا بالقياس
. الشرط الخامس: العدالة قال الله تعالى {إن جاءكم فاسق بنبإ فتبينوا}
[الحجرات: 6] وهذا زجر عن اعتماد قول الفاسق ودليل على شرط العدالة في
الرواية والشهادة، والعدالة عبارة عن استقامة السيرة والدين ويرجع حاصلها
إلى هيئة راسخة في النفس تحمل على ملازمة التقوى والمروءة جميعا حتى تحصل
ثقة النفوس بصدقه، فلا ثقة بقول من لا يخاف الله تعالى خوفا وازعا عن
الكذب.
ثم لا خلاف في أنه يشترط العصمة من جميع المعاصي. ولا يكفي أيضا اجتناب
الكبائر بل من الصغائر ما يرد به كسرقة بصلة وتطفيف في حبة قصدا. وبالجملة
كل ما يدل على ركاكة دينه إلى حد يستجرئ على الكذب بالأعراض الدنيوية، كيف
وقد شرط في العدالة التوقي عن بعض  المباحات الفادحة في المروءة نحو الأكل
في الطريق والبول في الشارع وصحبة الأراذل وإفراط المزح؟ والضابط في ذلك
فيما جاوز محل الإجماع أن يرد إلى اجتهاد الحاكم، فما دل عنده على جراءته
على الكذب رد الشهادة به وما لا فلا، وهذا يختلف بالإضافة إلى المجتهدين،
وتفصيل ذلك من الفقه لا من الأصول.
ورب شخص يعتاد الغيبة ويعلم الحاكم أن ذلك له طبع لا يصبر عنه، ولو حمل
على شهادة الزور لم يشهد أصلا، فقبوله شهادته بحكم اجتهاده جائز في حقه،
ويختلف ذلك بعادات البلاد واختلاف أحوال الناس في استعظام بعض الصغائر دون
بعض.
ويتفرع عن هذا الشرط مسألتان:
مسألة: قال بعض أهل العراق، العدالة عبارة عن إظهار الإسلام فقط مع
سلامته عن فسق ظاهر فكل مسلم مجهول عنده عدل، وعندنا لا تعرف عدالته إلا
بخبرة باطنة والبحث عن سيرته وسريرته.
ويدل على بطلان ما قالوه أمور:
الأول: أن الفاسق مردود الشهادة والرواية بنص القرآن ولعلمنا بأن دليل
قبول خبر الواحد قبول الصحابة إياه وإجماعهم ولم ينقل ذلك عنهم إلا في
العدل، والفاسق لو قبلت روايته لقبل بدليل الإجماع أو بالقياس على العدل
المجمع عليه، ولا إجماع في الفاسق ولا هو في معنى العدل في حصول الثقة
بقوله، فصار الفسق مانعا من الرواية كالصبا والكفر وكالرق في الشهادة،
ومجهول الحال في هذه الخصال لا يقبل قوله فكذلك مجهول الحال في الفسق لأنه
إن كان فاسقا فهو مردود الرواية وإن كان عدلا فغير مقبول أيضا للجهل به،
كما لو شككنا في صباه ورقه وكفره، ولا فرق.
الثاني: أنه لا تقبل شهادة المجهول وكذلك روايته، وإن منعوا شهادة المال
فقد سلموا شهادة
العقوبات.
ثم المجهول مردود في العقوبات، وطريق الثقة في الرواية والشهادة واحد وإن
اختلفا في بقية الشروط
الثالث: أن المفتي المجهول الذي لا يدرى أنه بلغ رتبة الاجتهاد أم لا، لا
يجوز للعامي قبول قوله، وكذلك إذا لم يدر أنه عالم أم لا، بل سلموا أنه لو
لم تعرف عدالته وفسقه  فلا يقبل، وأي فرق بين حكاية المفتي عن نفسه اجتهاده
وبين حكايته خبرا عن غيره.
الرابع: أن شهادة الفرع لا تسمع ما لم يعين الفرع شاهد الأصل، وهو مجهول
عند القاضي فلم يجب تعيينه وتعريفه إن كان قول المجهول مقبولا.
وهذا رد على من قبل شهادة المجهول، ولا جواب عنه. فإن قيل: يلزمه ذكر
شاهد الأصل، فلعل القاضي يعرفه بفسق فيرد شهادته. قلنا: إذا كان حد العدالة
هو الإسلام من غير ظهور فسق فقد تحقق ذلك فلم يجب التتبع حتى يظهر الفسق.
ثم يبطل ما ذكره بالخبر المرسل، فإنهم لم يوجبوا ذكر الشيخ ولعل المروي له
يعرف فسقه.
الخامس: أن مستندنا في خبر الواحد عمل الصحابة وهم قد ردوا خبر المجهول،
فرد عمر - رضي الله عنه - خبر فاطمة بنت قيس وقال: كيف نقبل قول امرأة لا
ندري صدقت أم كذبت ورد علي خبر الأشجعي في المفوضة وكان يحلف الراوي، وإنما
يحلف من عرف من ظاهره العدالة دون الفسق. ومن رد قول المجهول منهم كان لا
ينكر عليه غيره فكانوا بين راد وساكت، وبمثله ظهر إجماعهم في قبول العدل إذ
كانوا بين قابل وساكت غير منكر ولا معترض.
السادس: ما ظهر من حال رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في طلبه العدالة
والعفاف وصدق التقوى ممن كان ينفذه للأعمال وأداء الرسالة، وإنما طلب الأشد
التقوى لأنه كان قد كلفهم أن لا يقبلوا إلا قول العدل. فهذه أدلة قوية في
محل الاجتهاد قريبة من القطع، والمسألة اجتهادية لا قطعية. شبه الخصوم، وهي
أربع:
الأولى: أنه - صلى الله عليه وسلم - قبل شهادة الأعرابي وحده على رؤية
الهلال ولم يعرف منه إلا الإسلام.
قلنا: وكونه أعرابيا لا يمنع كونه معلوم العدالة عنده إما بالوحي وإما
بالخبرة وإما بتزكية من عرف حاله، فمن يسلم لكم أنه كان مجهولا عنده
الثانية: أن الصحابة قبلوا قول العبيد والنسوان والأعراب لأنهم لم
يعرفوهم بالفسق وعرفوهم بالإسلام. قلنا: إنما قبلوا قول أزواج رسول الله -
صلى الله عليه وسلم - وأزواج  أصحابه وكانت عدالتهن وعدالة مواليهم مشهورة
عندهم وحيث جهلوا ردوا، كرد قول الأشجعي وقول فاطمة بنت قيس.
الثالثة: قولهم لو أسلم كافر وشهد في الحال أو روى، فإن قلتم لا نقبل
شهادته فهو بعيد، وإن قبلتم فلا مستند للقبول إلا إسلامه وعدم معرفة الفسق
منه، فإذا انقضت مدة ولم نعرف منه فسقا لطول مدة إسلامه لم نوجب رده. قلنا:
لا نسلم قبول روايته فقد يسلم الكذوب ويبقى على طبعه، فما لم نطلع على خوف
في قلبه وازع عن الكذب لا نقبل شهادته، والتقوى في القلب وأصله الخوف وإنما
تدل عليه أفعاله في مصادره وموارده فإن سلمنا قبول روايته فذلك لطرق إسلامه
وقرب عهده بالدين، وشتان بين من هو في طراوته وبدايته وبين من قسا قلبه
بطول الإلف.
فإن قيل: إذا رجعت العدالة إلى هيئة باطنة في النفس وأصلها الخوف، وذلك
لا يشاهد بل يستدل عليه بما ليس بقاطع، بل هو مغلب على الظن، فأصل ذلك
الخوف هو الإيمان، فذلك يدل على الخوف دلالة -
ظاهرة فلنكتف به. قلنا: لا يدل عليه، فإن المشاهدة والتجربة دلت على أن
عدد فساق المؤمنين أكثر من عدد عدولهم، فكيف نشكك نفوسنا فيما عرفناه
يقينا؟ ثم هلا اكتفي بذلك في شهادة العقوبات وشهادة الأصل وحال المفتي في
العدالة وسائر ما سلموه
الرابعة: قولهم: يقبل قول المسلم المجهول في كون اللحم لحم ذكي وكون
الماء في الحمام طاهرا وكون الجارية المبيعة رقيقة غير متزوجة ولا معتدة
حتى يحل الوطء بقوله، وقول المجهول في كونه متطهرا للصلاة عن الحدث
والجنابة إذا أم الناس، وكذلك قول من يخبر عن نجاسة الماء وطهارته بناء على
ظاهر الإسلام، وكذلك قول من يخبر الأعمى عن القبلة.
قلنا: أما قول العاقد فمقبول لا لكونه مجهولا لكنه مع ظهور الفسق، وذلك
رخصة لكثرة الفساق ولمسيس حاجتهم إلى المعاملات، وكذلك جواز الاقتداء بالبر
والفاجر فلا يشترط الستر، أما الخبر عن القبلة وعن طهارة الماء فما لم يحصل
سكون النفس بقول المخبر فلا يجب قبوله، والمجهول  لا تسكن النفس إليه بل
سكون النفس إلى قول فاسق جرب باجتناب الكذب أغلب منه إلى قول المجهول وما
يخص العبد بينه وبين الله تعالى فلا يبعد أن يرد إلى سكون نفسه.
فأما الرواية والشهادة فأمرهما أرفع وخطرهما عام، فلا يقاسان على غيرهما،
وهذه صور ظنية اجتهادية، أما رد خبر الفاسق والمجهول فقريب من القطع.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ل (Q-B-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To receive, accept, take; the opposite of rejection (radd); implies a deliberate act of taking something offered.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acceptance (qabūl) in legal-theological terms signifies the obligation to act upon a thing, not the intellectual assent to its truth-content.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of taking hold; metaphorical (majāz) in legal usage where it denotes "deeming valid" (iʿtibār) and "acting upon" (ʿamal).
- Root: ع-د-ل (ʿ-D-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be straight, upright, balanced; justice as the mean between extremes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAdālah is a settled disposition (hayʾah rāsikhah) in the soul that compels one to persist in piety (taqwā) and manly virtue (murūʾah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal straightness of a path; metaphorical for moral probity that engenders trust in one's veracity.
- Root: ض-ب-ط (Ḍ-B-Ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guard, retain firmly, master; the ability to preserve what one has heard until its transmission.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The cognitive faculty of accurate retention and precise conveyance, a prerequisite for reliable testimony.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal seizing firmly; metaphorical for the intellectual mastery of transmitted material.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Condition-Clusters (al-Sharṭ wa al-Mashrūṭ) — The five conditions (taklīf, ʿadālah, islām, ḍabṭ, and the negation of number) are syntactically coordinated as sequential qualifiers of the single narrator (al-mukhbir al-wāḥid), each restricting the scope of the preceding general claim.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now that the obligation to act upon the report of the single narrator (khabar al-wāḥid) has been established, know that not every report is acceptable. First, understand that by "acceptance" (qabūl) we do not mean intellectual assent (taṣdīq), nor by "rejection" (radd) do we mean denial (takdhīb). Rather, we are obligated to accept the statement of the upright person (al-ʿadl), even if he might be lying or mistaken; and it is not permissible to accept the statement of the wicked person (al-fāsiq), even if he might be truthful. Rather, by "acceptable" (maqbūl) we mean that which it is obligatory to act upon, and by "rejected" (mardūd) we mean that regarding which we have no obligation to act. The acceptable report is the narration of every legally responsible (mukallaf), upright (ʿadl), Muslim, precise (ḍābiṭ) narrator, whether he narrates alone or with others. These are five matters that must be examined.

**The First Condition:** That the report of a single person is accepted even if his testimony (shahādah) is not accepted, contrary to al-Jubbāʾī and a group who stipulated a number and accepted only the statement of two men. Then, the narration of each single person would not be established except through two other men, and so on until it reaches our time, multiplying to such a great number that it would be impossible to establish any hadith at all. Some said: four are necessary, derived from the testimony required for [the crime of] fornication (zinā).

The proof of the invalidity of their doctrine is that we say: When the acceptance of single reports is established despite the fact that it does not yield certain knowledge (ʿilm), then stipulating a number is arbitrary (taḥakkum) that is known only through a text (naṣṣ) or through analogy (qiyās) upon a text — and there is no way to claim a text. As for what is transmitted from the Companions regarding seeking corroboration, that occurred in only two or three incidents for reasons we have mentioned. As for their judgments based solely on the statement of ʿĀʾishah, the statements of the wives of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and the statements of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Abū Hurayrah, and others, these are beyond enumeration. We know with certainty from their conduct the acceptance of the single report, just as we know with certainty the rejection of the testimony of a single person. If they derive [their position] from analogy upon testimony, it is a false analogy, since the distinction [between narration and testimony] is known from their practice. Why is it not analogized in the condition of freedom and masculinity, and why was four stipulated for reports concerning fornication, while one suffices for matters related to sighting the crescent moon and the testimony of the midwife? Resorting to that would breach the consensus (ijmāʿ), and there is no difference [in this regard] even if analogy were obligatory.

**The Second Condition:** This is truly the first, for number is not among our conditions — namely, legal responsibility (taklīf). The narration of a child is not accepted because he does not fear God — may He be exalted — and thus has no deterrent (wāziʿ) from lying, so no trust is placed in his statement. In accepting testimony, they have followed the tranquility of the soul (sukūn al-nafs) and the attainment of probable conjecture (ẓann). The wicked person (fāsiq) is more trustworthy than the child, for he fears God and has a deterrent from his religion and his intellect, whereas the child does not fear God at all. Thus [the child's narration] is rejected by the more compelling reason (ṭarīq al-awlā).

Adhering to this is more appropriate than adhering to the rejection of his confession (iqrār), [arguing that] if his statement is not accepted regarding what he reports about himself, then it is even more fitting that it not be accepted regarding what he narrates about others. For this [latter argument] is invalidated by the case of the slave: his confession may not be accepted while his narration is accepted. If the reason [for rejecting the slave's confession] is that it pertains to the property of his master, and the master's property is protected from him, then the child's property is also protected for his own benefit. What does not pertain to [property] may be affected by his statement — indeed, by his very condition — such that it is permissible to pray behind him (iqtidāʾ), relying on his statement that he is pure and that he does not pray except in a state of purity. But just as it is permissible to pray behind the pious and the wicked, so too behind the child and the adult. The testimony of the wicked is not accepted, yet the child is more audacious in lying than he is.

However, if he was a discerning child (mumayyiz) at the time of hearing (taḥammul) and an adult at the time of narrating (adāʾ), then it is accepted, because there is no defect in his hearing nor in his conveyance. Evidence for the acceptance of his hearing is the consensus of the Companions on accepting the reports of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, and other young Companions, without distinction between what they heard after reaching maturity or before it. Upon this the predecessors (salaf) and successors (khalaf) proceeded, by bringing children to narration sessions and accepting their testimony regarding what they had heard in their youth.

If it is said: Some scholars have accepted the testimony of children in injuries (jināyāt) that occur among themselves. We say: That is from them an inference from circumstantial evidence (qarāʾin) when they are numerous and report before dispersing. As for when they disperse, false prompting (talqīn) can reach them and they have no deterrent. Whoever judged by it did so only because of the frequency of injuries among them and the pressing need to know it through circumstantial indicators of the situation — this is not upon the methodology of testimony.

**The Third Condition:** That he be precise (ḍābiṭ). Whoever at the time of hearing was not discerning, or was heedless (mughaffal), not mastering the preservation of what he memorized so as to convey it accurately, then there is no trust in his statement, even if he is not wicked.

**The Fourth Condition:** That he be Muslim. There is no disagreement that the narration of the disbeliever (kāfir) is not accepted, because he is suspect (mutahham) regarding religion, even if the testimony of some of them against others is accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfah. There is no dissent regarding the rejection of his narration. Reliance in rejecting it is upon the consensus (ijmāʿ) established on stripping him of the qualification for this station in religion, even if he is upright in his own religion. This is more appropriate than our saying: the wicked person's testimony is rejected, and disbelief (kufr) is the greatest type of wickedness (fisq). God — may He be exalted — has said: {«إن جاءكم فاسق بنبإ فتبينوا أن تصيبوا»} [al-Ḥujurāt: 6] — "If a wicked person comes to you with a report, investigate, lest you harm a people in ignorance." Because the wicked person is suspect due to his audacity in disobedience, whereas the disbelieving ascetic (mutarahhib) may not be suspect — but reliance is upon consensus in stripping the disbeliever of this station.

If it is said: This applies to the Jews and Christians and those who do not believe in our religion, since it is not fitting in policy (siyāsah) to make him an arbiter over a religion whose veneration he does not believe in. What do you say about the disbeliever who is a misinterpretive innovator (kāfir mutaʾawwil) — one who has adopted a heresy (bidʿah) that necessitates declaring him a disbeliever — for he venerates religion, refrains from disobedience, and does not know that he is a disbeliever? Why is his narration not accepted, given that al-Shāfiʿī accepted the narration of some heretics (ahl al-bidaʿ), even though they were wicked by their heresy, because he was a misinterpretive innovator in his wickedness?

We say: Regarding the narration of the misinterpretive innovator (mubtadiʿ mutaʾawwil), there is discussion to come. As for the disbeliever, even if he is a misinterpretive innovator, his narration is not accepted, because every disbeliever is a misinterpretive innovator — for the Jew also does not know that he is a disbeliever. As for the one who is not a misinterpretive innovator — namely, the obstinate one (muʿānid) who professes with his tongue after knowing the truth with his heart — that is rare. The misinterpretive innovator's abstention from lying is like the Christian's abstention — it is not considered. Rather, this station is not attained except through Islam, and that is known through consensus, not through analogy.

**The Fifth Condition:** Uprightness (ʿadālah). God — may He be exalted — has said: {«إن جاءكم فاسق بنبإ فتبينوا»} [al-Ḥujurāt: 6] — "If a wicked person comes to you with a report, investigate." This is a prohibition against relying on the statement of the wicked and evidence for the condition of uprightness in narration and testimony. Uprightness (ʿadālah) is an expression for the rectitude of conduct and religion (istiqāmat al-sīrah wa al-dīn). Its essence reduces to a settled disposition (hayʾah rāsikhah) in the soul that compels one to adhere persistently to both piety (taqwā) and manly virtue (murūʾah), such that trust in his truthfulness is attained by souls. There is no trust in the statement of one who does not fear God — may He be exalted — with a fear that deters from lying.

Then, there is no disagreement that immunity (ʿiṣmah) from all sins is required. Nor is it sufficient to avoid major sins (kabāʾir) alone; rather, some minor sins (ṣaghāʾir) also disqualify, such as stealing a single onion or giving short measure in a single grain deliberately. In sum, everything that indicates the shoddiness of his religion to the extent that he would be audacious in lying for worldly trifles [disqualifies him]. How [could it be otherwise] when uprightness requires abstaining from some permissible acts (mubāḥāt) that are egregious against manly virtue, such as eating in the street, urinating in the public thoroughfare, associating with the rabble, and excessive jesting? The controlling principle in this, beyond the locus of consensus, is to refer it to the ijtihād of the judge. Whatever indicates to him audacity in lying, testimony is rejected by it; whatever does not, is not. This varies relative to the mujtahids, and the detailing of that belongs to jurisprudence (fiqh), not to the principles (uṣūl).

There may be a person who habitually engages in backbiting (ghībah), and the judge knows that this is a nature he cannot resist — were he pressed to give false testimony, he would not do so at all. Accepting his testimony by the judge's ijtihād is permissible in his case. This varies with the customs of lands and the differing conditions of people in deeming some minor sins grave and others not.

From this condition branch two sub-issues (masʾalah):

**Sub-Issue One:** Some of the people of Iraq said: Uprightness is merely the manifestation of Islam (iẓhār al-islām) along with freedom from apparent wickedness — so every Muslim of unknown status (majhūl) is upright according to them. According to us, his uprightness is not known except through inner acquaintance (khibrah bāṭinah) and investigation of his conduct and his inner conscience (sarīrah).

Evidence for the invalidity of what they said includes several matters:

**First:** The wicked person's testimony and narration are rejected by the text of the Qurʾān, and by our knowledge that the evidence for accepting the single report is the Companions' acceptance of it and their consensus — and it is not transmitted from them except regarding the upright. If the wicked person's narration were accepted, it would be by evidence of consensus or by analogy upon the upright who is agreed upon. There is no consensus regarding the wicked, nor is he in the meaning of the upright in attaining trust in his statement. Thus wickedness becomes a preventive from narration, like childhood, disbelief, and like slavery in testimony. The person of unknown status (majhūl al-ḥāl) in these characteristics — his statement is not accepted. Likewise, the person of unknown status regarding wickedness — because if he is wicked, his narration is rejected, and if he is upright, it is also not accepted due to ignorance of him, just as if we doubted his childhood, slavery, or disbelief. There is no difference.

**Second:** The testimony of the unknown person is not accepted, nor is his narration. Even if they deny [the acceptance of] testimony in property matters, they have conceded testimony in penal matters (ʿuqūbāt). Then the unknown person is rejected in penal matters. The path of trust in narration and testimony is one, even if they differ in the remaining conditions.

**Third:** The unknown muftī (mufī majhūl) — who is not known whether he has reached the rank of ijtihād or not — it is not permissible for the layperson (ʿāmmī) to accept his statement. Likewise, if it is not known whether he is a scholar or not. Rather, they conceded that if his uprightness and wickedness are not known, his statement is not accepted. What difference is there between the muftī's report about himself of his ijtihād and his report of a report from another?

**Fourth:** The testimony of the secondary witness (shahādat al-farʿ) is not heard unless the secondary witness identifies the primary witness (shāhid al-aṣl), who is unknown to the judge. So why is his identification and definition not required if the statement of the unknown person is acceptable? This is a refutation against those who accept the testimony of the unknown, and there is no answer to it. If it is said: He is required to mention the primary witness, perhaps the judge knows him to be wicked and thus rejects his testimony. We say: If the definition of uprightness is Islam without apparent wickedness, then that has been realized, so there is no need to investigate until wickedness appears. Then what he mentioned is invalidated by the mursal report (al-khabar al-mursal), for they did not require mentioning the shaykh — perhaps the one to whom it is reported knows his wickedness.

**Fifth:** Our basis in [accepting] the single report is the practice of the Companions, and they rejected the report of the unknown. ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — rejected the report of Fāṭimah bint Qays and said: "How can we accept the statement of a woman when we do not know whether she spoke truthfully or falsely?" He also rejected the report of al-Ashjaʿī regarding the mufawwaḍah, and he made the narrator swear an oath. He only made him swear because his apparent state indicated uprightness without wickedness. Whoever among them rejected the statement of the unknown, no one else objected to him — so they were between rejecter and silent. By the like of this, their consensus on accepting the upright became apparent, as they were between accepter and silent, without objection or protest.

**Sixth:** What appeared from the condition of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — in his seeking uprightness, chastity (ʿafāf), and truthfulness of piety from those he dispatched for tasks and the conveyance of messages. He only sought the most stringent piety because he had charged them not to accept except the statement of the upright. These are strong evidences in a locus of ijtihād, approaching certainty (qaṭʿ). The issue is one of ijtihād, not of certainty.

**The Opponents' Doubts (shubah), which are four:**

**First Doubt:** That he — peace be upon him — accepted the testimony of the Bedouin (aʿrābī) alone on sighting the crescent moon, without knowing from him anything but Islam.

We say: His being a Bedouin does not prevent him from being known to him as upright — either through revelation (waḥy), or through acquaintance (khibrah), or through the commendation (tazkiyah) of one who knew his condition. Who concedes to you that he was unknown to him?

**Second Doubt:** That the Companions accepted the statements of slaves, women, and Bedouins because they did not know them to be wicked and knew them to be Muslim.

We say: They only accepted the statements of the wives of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and the wives of his Companions, and their uprightness and the uprightness of their clients (mawālī) was well-known among them. Where they were ignorant, they rejected — like the rejection of the statement of al-Ashjaʿī and the statement of Fāṭimah bint Qays.

**Third Doubt:** Their saying: If a disbeliever embraces Islam and testifies or narrates immediately — if you say we do not accept his testimony, that is far-fetched; and if you accept, there is no basis for acceptance except his Islam and the absence of known wickedness from him. So if a period elapses and we do not know wickedness from him due to the length of his Islam, we do not deem his rejection obligatory.

We say: We do not concede the acceptance of his narration — for a liar may embrace Islam and remain upon his nature. As long as we have not discerned in his heart a fear that deters from lying, we do not accept his testimony. Piety (taqwā) is in the heart, and its root is fear (khawf); only his actions in his comings and goings indicate it. If we concede the acceptance of his narration, that is due to the freshness of his Islam and the recency of his covenant with religion. How different is the one in his freshness and beginning from the one whose heart has hardened through long familiarity!

If it is said: If uprightness reduces to an inner disposition in the soul whose root is fear, and that is not observed but rather inferred from what is not decisive but merely preponderant in conjecture (ẓann), then the root of that fear is faith (īmān) — so that indicates fear with an apparent indication, so let us suffice with it.

We say: It does not indicate it. For observation and experience have shown that the number of wicked believers is greater than the number of their upright ones. How can we cast doubt in our souls regarding what we have known with certainty? Then why was it not sufficed with this in penal testimony, primary testimony, the condition of the muftī regarding uprightness, and all the rest that they conceded?

**Fourth Doubt:** Their saying: The statement of the unknown Muslim is accepted regarding meat being from ritually slaughtered (madhkī) animals, water in the bathhouse being pure (ṭāhir), and the purchased slave-girl being a slave (raqīqah) not married nor in waiting-period (ʿiddah) — such that intercourse becomes permissible by his statement. Also the statement of the unknown person regarding his being purified for prayer from ritual impurity (ḥadath) and major impurity (janābah) when he leads people in prayer. Likewise, the statement of one who reports the impurity or purity of water based on the apparent Islam [of the reporter], and the statement of one who informs the blind man about the direction of the qiblah.

We say: As for the statement of the contracting party (al-ʿāqid), it is accepted not because he is unknown but even with apparent wickedness. That is a concession (rukḥṣah) due to the abundance of the wicked and the pressing need for transactions. Likewise, the permissibility of praying behind the pious and the wicked — concealment [of sins] is not stipulated. As for the report about the qiblah and the purity of water, as long as tranquility of the soul (sukūn al-nafs) is not attained by the reporter's statement, its acceptance is not obligatory. The unknown person does not bring tranquility to the soul; rather, tranquility of the soul toward the statement of a wicked person who has been tested as avoiding lying is more preponderant than toward the statement of the unknown. What pertains between the servant and his Lord — may He be exalted — is not far-fetched to be referred to the tranquility of his own soul.

As for narration and testimony, their matter is loftier and their consequence is general (ʿāmm), so they are not analogized to other matters. These are conjectural, ijtihādī cases. As for rejecting the report of the wicked and the unknown, it approaches certainty (qaṭʿ).

chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة الفاسق المتأول]

وهو الذي لا يعرف فسق نفسه اختلفوا في شهادته وقد قال الشافعي أقبل شهادة
الحنفي وأحده إذا شرب النبيذ؛ لأن هذا فسق غير مقطوع به إنما المقطوع به
فسق الخوارج الذين استباحوا الديار وقتلوا الذراري وهم لا يدرون أنهم فسقة.
وقد قال الشافعي تقبل شهادة أهل الأهواء إلا الخطابية من الرافضة لأنهم
يرون الشهادة بالزور لموافقيهم في المذهب. واختار القاضي أنه لا تقبل رواية
المبتدع وشهادته لأنه فاسق بفعله وبجهله بتحريم فعله ففسقه مضاعف، وزعم أن
جهله بفسق نفسه كجهله بكفر نفسه ورق نفسه. ومثار هذا الخلاف أن الفسق يرد
الشهادة لأنه نقصان منصب يسلب الأهلية كالكفر والرق أو هو مردود القول
للتهمة، فإن كان للتهمة فالمبتدع متورع عن الكذب فلا يتهم، وكلام الشافعي
مشير إلى هذا وهو في محل الاجتهاد، فمذهب أبي حنيفة أن الكفر والفسق لا
يسلبان الأهلية بل يوجبان التهمة ولذلك قبل شهادة أهل الذمة بعضهم على بعض،
ومذهب القاضي أن كليهما نقصان منصب يسلب الأهلية، ومذهب الشافعي أن الكفر
نقصان والفسق موجب للرد للتهمة، وهذا هو الأغلب على الظن عندنا.
فإن قيل: هذا مشكل على الشافعي من وجهين أحدهما أنه قضى بأن النكاح لا
ينعقد بشهادة الفاسق وذلك لسلب الأهلية، الثاني: أنه إن كان للتهمة فإذا
غلب على ظن القاضي صدقه فليقبل قلنا: أما الأول فمأخذه قوله - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -: «لا نكاح إلا بولي وشاهدي عدل» وأما الثاني فسببه أن الظنون
تختلف، وهو أمر خفي ناطه الشرع بسبب ظاهر وهو عدد مخصوص ووصف مخصوص وهو
العدالة، فيجب اتباع السبب الظاهر دون المعنى الخفي كما في العقوبات وكما
في رد شهادة الوالد لأحد ولديه على الآخر، فإنه قد يتهم وترد شهادته
لأن الأبوة مظنة للتهمة فلا ينظر إلى الحال، وإنما مظنة التهمة ارتكاب
الفسق مع المعرفة دون من لا يعرف ذلك.
ويدل أيضا على مذهب الشافعي قبول الصحابة قول الخوارج في الأخبار
والشهادة وكانوا فسقة متأولين وعلى قبول ذلك درج التابعون لأنهم متورعون عن
الكذب جاهلون بالفسق. فإن قيل: فهل يمكن دعوى الإجماع في ذلك؟ قلنا: لا،
فإنا نعلم أن عليا والأئمة قبلوا قول قتلة عثمان والخوارج، لكن لا نعلم ذلك
من جميع الصحابة فلعل فيهم من أضمر إنكارا لكن لم يرد على الإمام في محل
الاجتهاد، فكيف ولو قبل جميعهم خبرهم فلا يثبت أن جميعهم اعتقدوا فسقهم؟
وكيف يفرض والخوارج من جملة أهل الإجماع وما اعتقدوا فسق أنفسهم بل فسق
خصومهم وفسق عثمان وطلحة ووافقهم عليه عمار بن ياسر وعدي بن حاتم وابن
الكواء والأشتر النخعي وجماعة من الأمراء وعلي في تقية من الإنكار عليهم
خوف الفتنة؟ فإن قيل لو لم يعتقدوا فسق الخوارج لفسقوا.
قلنا على أنهم اعتقدوا رد خبر الفاسق للتهمة ولم يتهموا المتأول، والله
أعلم.

### | [خاتمة جامعة للرواية والشهادة]

: اعلم أن التكليف والإسلام والعدالة والضبط يشترك فيه الرواية والشهادة،
فهذه أربعة. أما الحرية والذكورة والبصر والقرابة والعدد والعداوة فهذه
الستة تؤثر في الشهادة دون الرواية؛ لأن الرواية حكمها عام لا يختص بشخص
حتى تؤثر فيه الصداقة والقرابة والعداوة، فيروي أولاد رسول الله - صلى الله
عليه وسلم - عنه، ويروي كل ولد عن والده، والضرير الضابط للصوت تقبل روايته
وإن لم تقبل شهادته، إذ كانت الصحابة يروون عن عائشة اعتمادا على صوتها وهم
كالضرير في حقها.
ولا يشترط كون الراوي عالما فقيها سواء خالف ما رواه القياس أو وافق، إذ
رب حامل فقه غير فقيه ورب حامل فقه إلى من هو أفقه منه، فلا يشترط إلا
الحفظ. ولا يشترط مجالسة العلماء وسماع الأحاديث، بل قبلت الصحابة قول
أعرابي لم يرو إلا حديثا واحدا.
نعم إذا عارضه  حديث العالم الممارس ففي الترجيح نظر سيأتي. ولا تقبل
رواية من عرف باللعب والهزل في أمر الحديث أو بالتساهل في أمر الحديث أو
بكثرة السهو فيه، إذ تبطل الثقة بجميع ذلك، أما الهزل والتساهل في حديث
نفسه فقد لا يوجب الرد. ولا يشترط كون الراوي معروف النسب، بل إذا عرف
عدالة شخص بالخبرة قبل حديثه وإن لم يكن له نسب فضلا عن أن يكون لا يعرف
نسبه، ولو روى عن مجهول العين لم نقبله بل من يقبل رواية المجهول صفته لا
يقبل رواية المجهول عينه؛ إذ لو عرف عينه ربما عرفه بالفسق بخلاف من عرف
عينه ولم يعرفه بالفسق، فلو روى عن شخص ذكر اسمه مردد بين مجرح وعدل فلا
يقبل لأجل التردد.

### | [الباب الثالث في الجرح والتعديل وفيه أربعة فصول]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-س-ق (f-s-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Departure from the straight path; emergence from obedience into transgression, whether minor or major.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Moral corruption as a legal descriptor affecting probity (ʿadālah) and epistemic reliability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is deviation from divine command; metaphorical extension applies to one whose error is interpretive (muta’awwil).
- Root: ش-ه-د (sh-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Bearing witness; presence and attestation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Testimony as a legal act requiring moral probity and capacity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal witnessing of events; metaphorical use for legal deposition.
- Root: ر-و-ي (r-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To carry water; to convey narration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Transmission of reports (riwāyah) as a distinct epistemic channel from testimony.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal carrying; metaphorical for transmitting knowledge.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa’l-istithnā’) — Governing the logical structure of “if…then” arguments and exceptions in legal reasoning.
chapters.translation:
I say: Concerning the case of the erring sinner (al-fāsiq al-muta’awwil) — that is, one who does not recognize his own sinfulness — scholars have differed regarding the acceptance of his testimony. Al-Shāfiʿī said: “I accept the testimony of a Ḥanafī, and I deem him upright even if he drinks date-wine (nabīdh), for this is a sin not definitively established; what is definitively established is the sinfulness of the Khawārij who deemed lawful the seizure of abodes and the killing of children, yet they do not realize that they are sinners.” Al-Shāfiʿī also said: “The testimony of the people of heretical inclinations (ahl al-ahwā’) is accepted, except for the Khaṭṭābiyyah among the Rāfiḍah, for they deem it lawful to bear false witness on behalf of those who share their sect.” The Judge (al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī) chose the view that the narration and testimony of an innovator (mubtadiʿ) are not accepted, because he is a sinner by his act and by his ignorance of the prohibition of his act, so his sinfulness is doubled. He claimed that his ignorance of his own sinfulness is like his ignorance of his own unbelief and his own enslavement. The crux of this disagreement is whether sinfulness (fisq) rejects testimony because it is a deficiency of status (nuqṣān manṣib) that strips legal capacity (ahlīyah), like unbelief and enslavement — or whether it is a rejection of one’s statement due to suspicion (tuhmah). If it is due to suspicion, then the innovator is scrupulous (mutawarriʿ) about lying, so he is not suspected. Al-Shāfiʿī’s words point to this latter view, and it lies within the domain of juristic reasoning (ijtihād). The school of Abū Ḥanīfah holds that unbelief and sinfulness do not strip legal capacity but rather necessitate suspicion; for this reason, he accepted the testimony of the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah) against one another. The school of the Judge holds that both are deficiencies of status that strip legal capacity. The school of al-Shāfiʿī holds that unbelief is a deficiency, while sinfulness necessitates rejection due to suspicion — and this is the most preponderant opinion in our view.

If it is said: “This is problematic for al-Shāfiʿī in two respects. First, he ruled that marriage is not contracted with the testimony of a sinner, which indicates stripping of legal capacity. Second, if it is due to suspicion, then when the judge’s predominant opinion is that he is truthful, he should accept it.” We say: As for the first, its basis is his saying — peace be upon him — {«لا نكاح إلا بولي وشاهدي عدل»} (“No marriage except with a guardian and two upright witnesses”). As for the second, its cause is that opinions (ẓunūn) vary, and it is a subtle matter that the Law (al-sharʿ) has tied to an apparent cause — namely, a specific number and a specific attribute, which is uprightness (ʿadālah). Thus, one must follow the apparent cause rather than the hidden meaning, as in the case of penal sanctions (ʿuqūbāt), and as in the rejection of a father’s testimony for one of his two children against the other — for he may be suspected, and his testimony is rejected because fatherhood is a locus of suspicion (maẓinnah), so one does not look to the particular case. Rather, the locus of suspicion is the commission of sin with knowledge, not one who does not know that [he is sinning].

This also supports the school of al-Shāfiʿī: the Companions accepted the statements of the Khawārij in reports and testimony, and they were erring sinners (fussāq muta’awwilīn). Upon this acceptance the Followers (tābiʿūn) proceeded, because they were scrupulous about lying and ignorant of their own sinfulness. If it is said: “Can one claim consensus (ijmāʿ) on this?” We say: No, for we know that ʿAlī and the Imams accepted the statements of the killers of ʿUthmān and the Khawārij, but we do not know this from all the Companions — perhaps among them were those who concealed disapproval, yet did not object to the Imam in a matter of ijtihād. How then, even if all of them accepted their reports, would it be established that all of them believed them to be sinners? And how could this be supposed, given that the Khawārij were among the people of consensus (ahl al-ijmāʿ) and did not believe themselves to be sinners, but rather believed their opponents to be sinners — and ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah, and those who agreed with them, such as ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, Ibn al-Kawwā’, al-Ashtar al-Nakhaʿī, and a group of commanders — while ʿAlī was in a state of dissimulation (taqīyah) from disapproving of them, fearing discord (fitnah)? If it is said: “If they did not believe the Khawārij to be sinners, then they themselves would be sinners.” We say: Rather, they believed that the report of a sinner is rejected due to suspicion, and they did not suspect the erring one. And God knows best.

### | [Concluding Summary on Narration and Testimony]

Know that legal obligation (taklīf), Islam, uprightness (ʿadālah), and precision (ḍabṭ) are shared between narration (riwāyah) and testimony (shahādah) — these are four [conditions]. As for freedom (ḥurriyyah), masculinity (dhukūrah), sight (baṣar), kinship (qarābah), number (ʿadad), and enmity (ʿadāwah) — these six affect testimony but not narration. For the ruling of narration is general, not specific to a person such that friendship, kinship, or enmity would affect it. Thus, the children of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — narrate from him, and every child narrates from his father. A blind person who is precise in [recognizing] voices has his narration accepted, even if his testimony is not accepted, for the Companions used to narrate from ʿĀ’ishah relying on her voice, and they were in her case like the blind.

It is not required that the narrator be a learned jurist (ʿālim faqīh), whether what he narrates contradicts analogical reasoning (qiyās) or agrees with it, for many a carrier of jurisprudence is not himself a jurist, and many a carrier of jurisprudence carries it to one more juristic than himself. Only memory (ḥifẓ) is required. Nor is it required that he sit with scholars and hear hadiths; rather, the Companions accepted the statement of a Bedouin who narrated only a single hadith. However, if the hadith of a learned, practiced scholar conflicts with it, then there is a question of preponderance (tarjīḥ) that will come later. The narration of one known for jesting and frivolity in the matter of hadith, or for carelessness in the matter of hadith, or for frequent error in it, is not accepted, for trust is nullified by all of that. As for jesting and carelessness in his own hadith, that may not necessitate rejection. Nor is it required that the narrator be of known lineage; rather, if a person’s uprightness is known through experience (khibrah), his hadith is accepted even if he has no lineage — let alone if his lineage is unknown. And if he narrates from an unknown person (majhūl al-ʿayn), we do not accept it; rather, even one who accepts the narration of one whose attribute is unknown does not accept the narration of one whose very identity is unknown — for if his identity were known, perhaps he would be known for sinfulness, unlike one whose identity is known but who is not known for sinfulness. So if he narrates from a person whose name is mentioned ambiguously between one who is discredited (majrūḥ) and one who is upright, it is not accepted due to the ambiguity.
