chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل الأول  في مبدإ اللغات]

القطب الثالث في كيفية استثمار الأحكام من مثمرات الأصول
ويشتمل هذا القطب على صدر ومقدمة وثلاثة فنون. صدر القطب الثالث: اعلم أن
هذا القطب هو عمدة علم الأصول.
لأن ميدان سعي المجتهدين في اقتباس الأحكام من أصولها واجتنائها من
أغصانها إذ نفس الأحكام ليست ترتبط باختيار المجتهدين ورفعها ووضعها.
والأصول الأربعة من الكتاب والسنة والإجماع والعقل لا مدخل لاختيار العباد
في تأسيسها وتأصيلها، وإنما مجال اضطراب المجتهد واكتسابه استعمال الفكر في
استنباط الأحكام واقتباسها من مداركها، والمدارك هي الأدلة السمعية ومرجعها
إلى الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، إذ منه يسمع الكتاب أيضا وبه يعرف
الإجماع. والصادر منه من مدارك الأحكام ثلاثة: إما لفظ، وإما فعل، وإما
سكوت وتقرير. ونرى أن نؤخر الكلام في الفعل والسكوت؛ لأن الكلام فيهما أوجز
واللفظ إما أن يدل على الحكم بصيغته ومنظومه، أو بفحواه ومفهومه، أو بمعناه
ومعقوله، وهو الاقتباس الذي يسمى قياسا. فهذه ثلاثة فنون المنظوم والمفهوم
والمعقول.
الفن الأول: في المنظوم وكيفية الاستدلال بالصيغة من حيث اللغة والوضع.
ويشتمل هذا الفن على مقدمة وأربعة أقسام: القسم الأول: في المجمل
والمبين، القسم الثاني: في الظاهر والمؤول، القسم الثالث: في الأمر والنهي،
القسم الرابع: في العام والخاص. فهذا صدر هذا القطب. أما المقدمة: فتشتمل
على سبعة فصول: الفصل الأول: في مبدإ اللغات أنه اصطلاح أم توقيف، الفصل
الثاني: في أن اللغة هل تثبت قياسا الفصل الثالث: في الأسماء العرفية،
الفصل الرابع: في الأسماء الشرعية، الفصل الخامس: في اللفظ المفيد وغير
المفيد، الفصل السادس: في طريق فهم المراد من الخطاب على الجملة، الفصل
السابع: في المجاز والحقيقة.
الفصل الأول: في مبدإ اللغات.
وقد ذهب قوم إلى أنها اصطلاحية، إذ كيف تكون توقيفا ولا يفهم التوقيف إذا
لم يكن لفظ صاحب التوقيف معروفا للمخاطب باصطلاح سابق، وقال قوم: إنها
توقيفية، إذ الاصطلاح لا يتم إلا بخطاب ومناداة ودعوة إلى الوضع، ولا يكون
ذلك إلا بلفظ معروف قبل الاجتماع للاصطلاح وقال قوم: القدر الذي يحصل  به
التنبيه والبعث على الاصطلاح يكون بالتوقيف وما بعده يكون بالاصطلاح.
والمختار أن النظر في هذا إما أن يقع في الجواز أو في الوقوع. أما الجواز
العقلي فشامل للمذاهب الثلاثة والكل في حيز الإمكان. أما التوقيف فبأن يخلق
الأصوات والحروف بحيث يسمعها واحد أو جمع ويخلق لهم العلم بأنها قصدت
للدلالة على المسميات والقدرة الأزلية لا تقصر عن ذلك.
وأما الاصطلاح فبأن يجمع الله دواعي جمع من العقلاء للاشتغال بما هو
مهمهم وحاجتهم من تعريف الأمور الغائبة التي لا يمكن الإنسان أن يصل إليها،
فيبتدئ واحد ويتبعه الآخر حتى يتم الاصطلاح؛ بل العاقل الواحد ربما ينقدح
له وجه الحاجة وإمكان التعريف بتأليف الحروف فيتولى الوضع ثم يعرف الآخرين
بالإشارة والتكرير معها للفظ مرة بعد أخرى، كما يفعل الوالدان بالولد
الصغير وكما يعرف الأخرس ما في ضميره بالإشارة، وإذا أمكن كل واحد من
القسمين أمكن التركيب منهما جميعا.
أما الواقع من هذه الأقسام فلا مطمع في معرفته يقينا إلا ببرهان عقلي أو
بتواتر خبر أو سمع قاطع، ولا مجال لبرهان العقل في هذا ولم ينقل تواتر ولا
فيه سمع قاطع فلا يبقى إلا رجم الظن في أمر لا يرتبط به تعبد عملي ولا ترهق
إلى اعتقاده حاجة، فالخوض فيه إذا فضول لا أصل له. فإن قيل: قال الله
تعالى: {وعلم آدم الأسماء كلها:} [البقرة: 31] وهذا يدل على أنه كان بوحي
وتوقيف، فيدل على الوقوع، وإن لم يدل على استحالة خلافه. قلنا: وليس ذلك
دليلا قاطعا على الوقوع أيضا، إذ يتطرق إليه أربعة احتمالات:
أحدها: أنه ربما ألهمه الله تعالى الحاجة إلى الوضع فوضع بتدبيره وفكره
ونسب ذلك إلى تعليم الله تعالى؛ لأنه الهادي والملهم ومحرك الداعية كما
تنسب جميع أفعالنا إلى الله تعالى
الثاني: أن الأسماء ربما كانت موضوعة باصطلاح من خلق خلقه الله تعالى قبل
آدم من الجن أو فريق من الملائكة فعلمه الله تعالى ما تواضع عليه غيره.
الثالث: أن الأسماء صيغة عموم فلعله أراد به أسماء السماء والأرض  وما في
الجنة والنار دون الأسامي التي حدثت مسمياتها بعد آدم - عليه السلام - من
الحرف والصناعات والآلات، وتخصيص قوله تعالى كلها كتخصيص قوله تعالى:
{وأوتيت من كل شيء} [النمل: 23] وقوله تعالى {تدمر كل شيء بأمر ربها}
[الأحقاف: 25] وهو على كل شيء قدير إذ يخرج عنه ذاته وصفاته.
الرابع أنه بما علمه ثم نسيه أو لم يعلم غيره ثم اصطلح بعده أولاده على
هذه اللغات المعهودة الآن، والغالب أن أكثرها حادثة بعد.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و ض ع (waḍʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To place, put down, establish; al-waḍʿ is the act of positing a thing in a locus; from it derives "linguistic coinage" (waḍʿ al-lughah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, waḍʿ denotes the primordial act of assigning signification—whether by divine decree or human convention—to articulate sounds for meanings; it underlies the entire theory of divine speech (kalām).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage of waḍʿ is physical placement; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the "positing" of a name for a meaning, i.e., coinage.
- Root: و ق ف (tawqīf)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To stop, halt, make stand; tawqīf is the act of causing one to stand still—hence, stopping at a revealed text; technically, it means "divine instruction" that fixes a matter without room for rational derivation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tawqīf in uṣūl al-fiqh refers to knowledge or language that comes solely from revelation (waḥy), not from human reasoning or convention; it is the counterpoint to iṣṭilāḥ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: making someone stand in place; metaphorical: restricting a matter to what is transmitted from the Lawgiver, as if the mind is "stopped" at the revealed boundary.
- Root: ص ل ح (iṣṭilāḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be sound, right, fitting; iṣṭilāḥ is mutual agreement upon a convention, derived from ṣulḥ (reconciliation)—the aligning of parties upon a shared practice.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In technical terms, iṣṭilāḥ is the communal accord of rational beings to assign particular sounds to particular meanings, a purely human act of positing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: reconciliation between parties; metaphorical: the "truce" struck between speakers and hearers that a given utterance shall signify a given meaning.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm ʿalā al-ʿIllah (Attribution of a Ruling to its Cause) — When a ruling is predicated upon a cause (ʿillah), the ruling is confined to that cause; here, the possibility of both tawqīf and iṣṭilāḥ is established by the rational faculty, while actual occurrence (wuqūʿ) is suspended pending decisive evidence, mirroring the grammatical suspension of judgment (taʿlīq) in conditional constructions.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that this pole is the very pillar of the science of legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh). For it is the arena of the strivings of the mujtahids in deriving rulings (aḥkām) from their sources and plucking them from their branches—since the rulings themselves are not tied to the choice of the mujtahids, nor to their elevation or abrogation. The four sources—the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijmāʿ), and reason (ʿaql)—admit no entry for the choice of servants in their establishment and rooting. Rather, the field of the mujtahid's fluctuation and acquisition is the employment of thought in extracting rulings and deriving them from their repositories (madārik). The repositories are the scriptural evidences (adillah samʿiyyah), and their reference is to the Messenger—peace be upon him—for from him the Book is heard, and through him consensus is known. What issues from him as repositories of rulings is threefold: either a verbal utterance (lafẓ), or an act (fiʿl), or a silence and tacit approval (sukūt wa taqrīr). We see fit to defer speech concerning the act and the silence, for speech about them is briefer. As for the utterance, it either indicates the ruling by its very wording and composition (naẓm), or by its implication and understood meaning (mafhūm), or by its significance and rational extension (maʿqūl)—and this latter derivation is what is called analogical reasoning (qiyās). These, then, are the three arts: the composed (al-manẓūm), the understood (al-mafhūm), and the rationalized (al-maʿqūl).

The first art: concerning the composed, and the manner of drawing inference from the wording (ṣīghah) in respect of language and coinage. This art comprises an introduction and four sections: the first section on the ambiguous (mujmal) and the clarified (mubayyan); the second on the apparent (ẓāhir) and the interpreted (muʾawwal); the third on command (amr) and prohibition (nahy); the fourth on the general (ʿāmm) and the specific (khāṣṣ). This, then, is the preamble of this pole. As for the introduction, it comprises seven chapters: the first chapter on the origin of languages—whether it is conventional agreement or divine institution; the second on whether language is established by analogy (qiyās); the third on customary names (asmāʾ ʿurfiyyah); the fourth on religious names (asmāʾ sharʿiyyah); the fifth on the meaningful utterance and the meaningless; the sixth on the way of understanding the intended meaning of discourse in general; the seventh on metaphor (majāz) and literal truth (ḥaqīqah).

The first chapter: on the origin of languages.

Some have held that languages are conventional (iṣṭilāḥiyyah)—for how could they be divinely instituted (tawqīfiyyah) when divine institution cannot be understood unless the word of the institutor is already known to the addressee through a prior convention? Others have held that they are divinely instituted—for convention cannot be completed except through address, calling, and summons to coinage, and that cannot occur except through a word already known prior to the assembly for convention. Yet others have held that the amount by which prompting and impulsion toward convention is achieved occurs through divine institution, and what comes after it occurs through convention.

The chosen position is that inquiry into this matter is either concerning permissibility (jawāz) or concerning actual occurrence (wuqūʿ). As for rational permissibility, it encompasses all three doctrines, and all are within the sphere of possibility. As for divine institution, it is that God creates sounds and letters such that one person or a group hears them, and He creates in them the knowledge that these sounds were intended to signify the named things—and eternal power is not incapable of that. As for convention, it is that God brings together the motives of a group of rational beings to occupy themselves with what is their concern and need—namely, the definition of absent matters which a human being cannot reach—so one begins and another follows him until the convention is completed. Indeed, a single rational person may have the need and the possibility of definition flash upon his mind through the composition of letters, so he undertakes the coinage, then makes it known to others by gesture and by repetition of the utterance along with it, time after time—just as parents do with a small child, and just as a mute person makes known what is in his mind by gesture. And when each of the two divisions is possible, their combination from both together is also possible.

As for which of these divisions actually occurred, there is no hope of knowing it with certainty except through a rational proof (burhān ʿaqlī), or through mass transmission (tawātur) of reports, or through a decisive scriptural text (samʿ qāṭiʿ). There is no room for rational proof in this matter, and no mass transmission has been reported concerning it, nor is there a decisive scriptural text—so nothing remains but the casting of conjecture (rajm al-ẓann) in a matter with which no practical obligation is connected, and to which no need impels us to believe. Thus, delving into it is superfluous talk with no foundation.

If it is said: God—exalted is He—said: {«And He taught Adam all the names»} (al-Baqarah 2:31), and this indicates that it was by revelation and divine institution, and thus indicates actual occurrence—even if it does not indicate the impossibility of its contrary—we say: This too is not a decisive proof of actual occurrence, for four possibilities attach to it:

The first: that perhaps God—exalted is He—inspired him with the need for coinage, so he coined by his own deliberation and thought, and this was attributed to God's teaching because He is the Guide, the Inspirer, and the Mover of the motive—just as all our acts are attributed to God—exalted is He.

The second: that perhaps the names were coined by the convention of a creation whom God—exalted is He—created before Adam, whether of the jinn or a company of the angels, and God taught him what others had mutually agreed upon.

The third: that "the names" is a general expression (ṣīghat ʿumūm), and perhaps He intended thereby the names of the heaven and the earth and what is in Paradise and the Fire—not the names whose referents came into being after Adam—peace be upon him—such as crafts, industries, and instruments. The specification of His saying "all" is like the specification of His saying—exalted is He—{«And she was given of everything»} (al-Naml 27:23), and His saying—exalted is He—{«It destroys everything by the command of its Lord»} (al-Aḥqāf 46:25), and His saying—exalted is He—"He is over everything powerful" (al-Baqarah 2:20)—for His essence and attributes are excluded therefrom.

The fourth: that He taught him, then he forgot it, or He did not teach others, and then his descendants later agreed by convention upon these languages now in use—and the predominant likelihood is that most of them originated afterward.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل الثاني الأسماء اللغوية هل تثبت قياسا]

الفصل الثاني في أن الأسماء اللغوية هل تثبت قياسا الأسماء اللغوية هل
تثبت قياسا.
وقد اختلفوا فيه، فقال بعضهم: سموا الخمر من العنب خمرا؛ لأنها تخمر
العقل، فيسمى النبيذ خمرا لتحقق ذلك المعنى فيه قياسا عليه حتى يدخل في
عموم قوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - «حرمت الخمر لعينها» وسمي الزاني زانيا؛
لأنه مولج فرجه في فرج محرم فيقاس عليه اللائط في إثبات اسم
الزاني حتى يدخل في عموم قوله تعالى: {الزانية والزاني} [النور: 2] وسمي
السارق سارقا؛ لأنه أخذ مال الغير في خفية، وهذه العلة موجودة في النباش
فيثبت له اسم السارق قياسا حتى يدخل تحت عموم قوله تعالى: {والسارق
والسارقة} [المائدة: 38] وهذا غير مرضي عندنا؛ لأن العرب إن عرفتنا
بتوقيفها أنا وضعنا الاسم للمسكر المعتصر من العنب خاصة فوضعه لغيره تقول
عليهم واختراع فلا يكون لغتهم بل يكون وضعا من جهتنا، وإن عرفتنا أنها
وضعته لكل ما يخامر العقل أو يخمره، فكيفما كان فاسم الخمر ثابت للنبيذ
بتوقيفهم لا بقياسنا، كما أنهم عرفونا أن كل مصدر فله فاعل، فإذا سمينا
فاعل الضرب ضاربا كان ذلك عن توقيف لا عن قياس، وإن سكتوا عن الأمرين احتمل
أن يكون الخمر اسم ما يعتصر من العنب خاصة واحتمل غيره فلم نتحكم عليهم
ونقول لغتهم هذا، وقد رأيناهم يضعون الاسم لمعان ويخصصونها بالمحل كما
يسمون الفرس أدهم لسواده وكميتا لحمرته، والثوب المتلون بذلك اللون بل
الآدمي المتلون بالسواد لا يسمونه بذلك الاسم؛ لأنهم ما وضعوا الأدهم
والكميت للأسود والأحمر بل لفرس أسود وأحمر، وكما سموا الزجاج الذي تقر فيه
المائعات قارورة أخذا من القرار ولا يسمون الكوز والحوض قارورة، وإن قر
الماء فيه.
فإذا كل ما ليس على قياس التصريف الذي عرف منهم بالتوقيف فلا سبيل إلى
إثباته ووضعه بالقياس، وقد أطنبنا في شرح هذه المسألة في كتاب أساس القياس
فثبت بهذا أن اللغة وضع كلها وتوقيف ليس فيها قياس أصلا.

### | [الفصل الثالث في الأسماء العرفية]

الأسماء العرفية
اعلم أن الأسماء اللغوية تنقسم إلى وضعية وعرفية، والاسم يسمى عرفيا
باعتبارين
أحدهما: أن يوضع الاسم لمعنى عام ثم يخصص عرف الاستعمال من أهل اللغة ذلك
الاسم ببعض مسمياته، كاختصاص اسم الدابة بذوات الأربع مع أن الوضع لكل ما
يدب، واختصاص اسم المتكلم بالعالم بعلم الكلام مع أن كل قائل ومتلفظ متكلم،
وكاختصاص اسم الفقيه والمتعلم ببعض العلماء وبعض المتعلمين مع أن الوضع عام
قال الله تعالى " وعلم آدم الأسماء كلها " وقال تعالى: {خلق الإنسان}
[الرحمن: 3] {علمه البيان} [الرحمن: 4] وقال عز وجل: {فمال هؤلاء القوم لا
يكادون يفقهون حديثا} [النساء: 78]
الاعتبار الثاني: أن يصير الاسم شائعا في غير ما وضع له أولا بل فيما هو
مجاز فيه، كالغائط المطمئن من الأرض، والعذرة البناء الذي يستتر به وتقضى
الحاجة من ورائه؛ فصار أصل الوضع منسيا، والمجاز معروفا سابقا إلى الفهم
بعرف الاستعمال وذلك بالوضع الأول. فالأسامي اللغوية إما وضعية وإما عرفية،
أما ما انفرد المحترفون وأرباب الصناعات بوضعه لأدواتهم فلا يجوز أن يسمى
عرفيا؛ لأن مبادئ اللغات والوضع الأصلي كلها كانت كذلك فيلزم أن يكون جميع
الأسامي اللغوية عرفية.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-م-ر (khamara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The core meaning is "to cover, conceal, or ferment" — hence khamr (wine) is that which veils the intellect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, khamr denotes any intoxicant that obscures rational discernment, the effective cause (ʿillah) being the covering of the mind.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) application is to pressed grape-wine; metaphorical (majāz) extension to other intoxicants is contested — the dispute turns on whether the name is tied to the substance or the attribute.
- Root: ز-ن-ي (zanā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Illicit sexual intercourse; the agent is zānī, the act zinā.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal-theological sense is penetration of the genitals into a forbidden orifice; the question is whether liwāṭ (sodomy) shares this definitional core.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is restricted to the specific act; analogical extension requires proof that the name was coined for the meaning, not the particular instance.
- Root: س-ر-ق (saraqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taking another's property covertly; sāriq is the thief.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The effective cause is clandestine appropriation; the nabsh (grave-robber) takes shrouds secretly, yet the name's extension is not self-evident.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal vs. metaphorical hinges on whether the Arabs coined the name for the genus (taking covertly) or the species (taking from a living owner's custody).
- Root: د-ب-ب (dabba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To creep or move slowly; dābbah is anything that moves on the earth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The general coinage covers all creeping things; customary restriction (ʿurf) to quadrupeds is a narrowing, not a new coinage.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): This illustrates the first mode of customary names — the original literal scope is general, then usage specializes it.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿillah (Estimation of the Effective Cause) — In analogical extension of names, one must verify whether the Arabs coined the term for the attribute (maʿnā) or the specific substrate (maḥall); if the latter, qiyās is impermissible, for it would be imposing our own linguistic convention upon them.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second chapter concerns whether linguistic names are established by analogy. They have differed on this matter. Some have said: The Arabs named wine from grapes "khamr" because it veils the intellect; thus, date-wine (nabīdh) is called "khamr" because that same meaning is realized in it, by analogy upon it, so that it enters under the generality of his saying — peace be upon him — {«Wine is forbidden for its very essence»}. Likewise, the fornicator is called "zānī" because he inserts his genitals into a forbidden orifice; thus, the sodomite is measured against him in establishing the name "zānī," so that he enters under the generality of His saying — exalted be He: {«The fornicatress and the fornicator»} [al-Nūr: 2]. And the thief is called "sāriq" because he takes another's property covertly; this cause is present in the grave-robber (nabbāsh), so the name "sāriq" is established for him by analogy, so that he enters under the generality of His saying — exalted be He: {«And the thief, male and female»} [al-Māʾidah: 38].

This is not satisfactory in our view. For if the Arabs, by their authoritative instruction (tawqīf), have made known to us that they coined the name specifically for the intoxicant pressed from grapes, then applying it to other things is an imposition upon them and an invention on our part — it would not be their language, but rather a coinage from our own side. And if they have made known to us that they coined it for everything that veils or covers the intellect, then however it may be, the name "khamr" is established for date-wine by their instruction, not by our analogy — just as they have made known to us that every verbal noun (maṣdar) has an active participle (fāʿil); so when we name the agent of striking "ḍārib," that is from their instruction, not from analogy. But if they are silent about both matters, then it is possible that "khamr" is the name of what is pressed from grapes specifically, and possible that it is otherwise; we do not then impose upon them and say, "This is their language."

Indeed, we have observed them coining names for meanings and restricting them to specific substrates. Thus they call a horse "adham" for its blackness and "kumayt" for its redness — yet a garment colored with that color, nay even a human being colored with blackness, they do not call by that name. For they did not coin "adham" and "kumayt" for the black and the red absolutely, but rather for a black horse and a red horse. Likewise, they named the glass vessel in which liquids settle "qārūrah," derived from al-qarār (settling), yet they do not call the earthen jug or the basin "qārūrah," even if water settles therein.

Thus, everything that is not upon the pattern of morphological derivation (qiyās al-taṣrīf) which has been made known from them by authoritative instruction — there is no way to establish it or coin it by analogy. We have already expounded this question at length in the book Asās al-Qiyās. It is thereby established that language is entirely coinage and instruction; there is no analogy in it at all.

### | The Third Chapter: Customary Names

Know that linguistic names are divided into coinage-based (waḍʿiyyah) and customary (ʿurfiyyah). A name is called "customary" in two respects:

The first: That a name is coined for a general meaning, then the custom of usage among the people of the language specializes that name to some of its referents — as the name "dābbah" is specialized to quadrupeds, although the coinage is for everything that creeps; and as the name "mutakallim" is specialized to the scholar of theology (ʿilm al-kalām), although every speaker and utterer is a mutakallim; and as the name "faqīh" and "mutaʿallim" is specialized to some scholars and some learners, although the coinage is general. God — exalted be He — said: {«And He taught Adam the names, all of them»} [al-Baqarah: 31], and said — exalted be He: {«He created man»} [al-Raḥmān: 3], {«He taught him eloquence»} [al-Raḥmān: 4], and said — mighty and majestic: {«What is the matter with these people that they scarcely understand any discourse?»} [al-Nisāʾ: 78].

The second respect: That a name becomes prevalent in something other than what it was first coined for — rather, in what is metaphorical for it — like "ghāʾiṭ" for the low-lying ground, and "ʿadhirah" for the structure behind which one screens oneself and relieves oneself. Thus the original coinage is forgotten, and the metaphorical usage is well-known and foremost in understanding, by the custom of usage — and that is by the first coinage. So linguistic names are either coinage-based or customary. As for what the professionals and craftsmen have exclusively coined for their tools, it is not permissible to call it "customary" — because the origins of languages and the original coinage were all of that sort; thus it would follow that all linguistic names would be customary.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل الرابع في الأسماء الشرعية]

الأسماء الشرعية.
قالت المعتزلة والخوارج وطائفة من الفقهاء: الأسماء لغوية ودينية وشرعية؛
أما اللغوية فظاهرة، وأما الدينية فما نقلته الشريعة إلى أصل الدين كلفظ
الإيمان والكفر والفسق، وأما الشرعية فكالصلاة والصوم والحج والزكاة،
واستدل القاضي على إفساد مذهبهم بمسلكين:
الأول: أن هذه الألفاظ يشتمل عليها القرآن
والقرآن نزل بلغة العرب قال الله تعالى: {إنا جعلناه  قرآنا عربيا}
[الزخرف: 3] و {بلسان عربي مبين} [الشعراء: 195] {وما أرسلنا من رسول إلا
بلسان قومه} [إبراهيم: 4] ولو قال: أطعموا العلماء وأراد الفقراء لم يكن
هذا بلسانهم، وإن كان اللفظ المنقول عربيا، فكذلك إذا نقل اللفظ عن موضوعه
إلى غير موضوعه أو جعل عبارة عن بعض موضوعه أو متناولا لموضوعه وغير موضوعه
فكل ذلك ليس من لسان العرب.
الثاني: أن الشارع لو فعل ذلك للزمه تعريف الأمة بالتوقيف نقل تلك
الأسامي، فإنه إذا خاطبهم بلغتهم لم يفهموا إلا موضوعها، ولو ورد فيه توقيف
لكان متواترا فإن الحجة لا تقوم بالآحاد، احتجوا بقوله تعالى {وما كان الله
ليضيع إيمانكم} [البقرة: 143] وأراد به الصلاة نحو بيت المقدس «وقال - صلى
الله عليه وسلم -: نهيت عن قتل المصلين» وأراد به المؤمنين، وهو خلاف
اللغة. قلنا: أراد بالإيمان التصديق بالصلاة والقبلة وأراد بالمصلين
المصدقين بالصلاة، وسمى التصديق بالصلاة صلاة على سبيل التجوز وعادة العرب
تسمية الشيء بما يتعلق به نوعا من التعلق والتجوز من نفس اللغة. احتجوا
بقوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: «الإيمان بضع وسبعون بابا أعلاها شهادة أن
لا إله إلا الله وأدناها إماطة الأذى عن الطريق» ، وتسمية الإماطة إيمانا
خلاف الوضع.
قلنا: هذا من أخبار الآحاد فلا يثبت به مثل هذه القاعدة، وإن ثبتت فهي
دلالة الإيمان فيتجوز بتسميته إيمانا. احتجوا بأن الشرع وضع عبادات لم تكن
معهودة فافتقرت إلى أسام وكان استعارتها من اللغة أقرب من نقلها من لغة
أخرى أو إبداع أسام لها. قلنا: لا نسلم أنه حدث في الشريعة عبادة لم يكن
لها اسم في اللغة. فإن قيل: فالصلاة في اللغة ليست عبارة عن الركوع والسجود
ولا الحج عبارة عن الطواف والسعي. قلنا عنه جوابان:
الأول: أنه ليس الصلاة في الشرع أيضا عبارة عنه بل الصلاة عبارة عن
الدعاء كما في اللغة، والحج عبارة عن القصد، والصوم عبارة عن الإمساك،
والزكاة عبارة عن النمو؛ لكن الشرع شرط في إجزاء هذه الأمور أمورا أخر تنضم
إليها، فشرط في الاعتداد بالدعاء الواجب انضمام  الركوع والسجود إليه، وفي
قصد البيت أن ينضم إليه الوقوف والطواف، والاسم غير متناول له لكنه شرط
الاعتداد بما ينطلق عليه الاسم، فالشرع تصرف بوضع الشرط لا بتغير الوضع.
الثاني: أنه يمكن أن يقال: سميت جميع الأفعال صلاة لكونها متبعا بها فعل
الإمام، فإن التالي للسابق في الخيل يسمى مصليا لكونه متبعا، هذا كلام
القاضي - رحمه الله - والمختار عندنا أنه لا سبيل إلى إنكار تصرف الشرع في
هذه الأسامي، ولا سبيل إلى دعوى كونها منقولة عن اللغة بالكلية كما ظنه
قوم، ولكن عرف اللغة تصرف في الأسامي من وجهين:
أحدهما: التخصيص ببعض المسميات كما في الدابة فتصرف الشرع في الحج والصوم
والإيمان من هذا الجنس إذ للشرع عرف في الاستعمال كما للعرب
والثاني: في إطلاقهم الاسم على ما يتعلق به الشيء ويتصل به، كتسميتهم
الخمر محرمة والمحرم شربها والأم محرمة والمحرم وطؤها فتصرفه في الصلاة
كذلك؛ لأن الركوع والسجود شرطه الشرع في تمام الصلاة فشمله الاسم بعرف
استعمال الشرع، إذ إنكار كون الركوع والسجود ركن الصلاة ومن نفسها بعيد.
فتسليم هذا القدر من التصرف بتعارف الاستعمال للشرع أهون من
إخراج السجود والركوع من نفس الصلاة، وهو كالمهم المحتاج إليه، إذ ما
يصوره الشرع من العبادات ينبغي أن يكون لها أسام معروفة ولا يوجد ذلك في
اللغة إلا بنوع تصرف فيه. وأما ما استدل به من أن القرآن عربي فهذا لا يخرج
هذه الأسامي عن أن تكون عربية ولا يسلب اسم العربي عن القرآن، فإنه لو
اشتمل على مثل هذه الكلمات بالعجمية لكان لا يخرجه عن كونه عربيا أيضا كما
ذكرناه في القطب الأول من الكتاب.
وأما قوله: إنه كان يجب عليه التوقيف على تصرفه، فهذا أيضا إنما يجب إذا
لم يفهم مقصوده من هذه الألفاظ بالتكرير والقرائن مرة بعد أخرى، فإذا فهم
هذا فقد حصل الغرض، فهذا أقرب عندنا مما ذكره القاضي - رحمه الله -.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-م-و (s-m-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes elevation, naming, and designation; al-ism (name) is that by which a thing is distinguished and elevated into recognition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-ism signifies the divinely instituted designation that carries legal and creedal import, distinguishing the named object’s ruling (ḥukm) in this world and the next.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, ism is a mark of identity; metaphorically (majāzan), it extends to what is attached to the named thing, as in calling the prayer (ṣalāh) by its condition or attendant act.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿdiyah bi-al-Ḥarf (Transitivity via Preposition) — The syntactic shift of a verbal noun’s scope (e.g., ṣalāh from duʿāʾ to the full ritual) is governed by contextual restriction (takhṣīṣ) and customary extension (taʿāruf), not by a change in the root’s grammatical valence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Muʿtazilah, the Khawārij, and a group of jurists have held: Names are of three kinds — linguistic (lughawiyyah), religious (dīniyyah), and religious-legal (sharʿiyyah). As for the linguistic, their meaning is evident. As for the religious, they are what the Sacred Law has transmitted to the very foundation of religion, such as the terms faith (īmān), unbelief (kufr), and wickedness (fisq). As for the religious-legal, they are like the prayer (ṣalāh), the fast (ṣawm), the pilgrimage (ḥajj), and the alms (zakāh).

Al-Qāḍī (Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī — may God have mercy on him) argued for the corruption of their doctrine by two paths:

The first: These very expressions are comprised in the Qurʾān, and the Qurʾān was revealed in the language of the Arabs. God — exalted is He — says: {«Innā jaʿalnāhu qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan»} [al-Zukhruf 43:3], and {«bi-lisānin ʿarabiyyin mubīn»} [al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:195], and {«Wa-mā arsalnā min rasūlin illā bi-lisāni qawmih»} [Ibrāhīm 14:4]. If someone said: “Feed the scholars” while meaning the poor, this would not be in their tongue, even if the transmitted word were Arabic. Likewise, if a word is transferred from its original designation (mawḍūʿ) to something other than it, or made to express part of its original designation, or made to encompass both its original designation and what is other than it — all of this is not from the tongue of the Arabs.

The second: If the Lawgiver had done this, He would have been obliged to apprise the community, by explicit instruction (tawqīf), of the transmission of those names. For when He addresses them in their tongue, they understand nothing but its original designation. And had such an instruction come, it would have had to be transmitted en masse (mutawātir), since the proof cannot be established by isolated reports (āḥād).

They adduced as proof His saying — exalted is He — {«Wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuḍīʿa īmānakum»} [al-Baqarah 2:143], intending thereby the prayer toward the Sacred House of Jerusalem. And he — peace and blessings be upon him — said: “I was forbidden from killing the praying ones (al-muṣallīn),” intending thereby the believers — which is contrary to the language.

We say: By “faith” He meant the affirmation (taṣdīq) of the prayer and the qiblah, and by “the praying ones” He meant those who affirm the prayer. He named the affirmation of the prayer “prayer” by way of metaphorical extension (tajawwuz), and it is the custom of the Arabs to name a thing by what is attached to it with some kind of attachment; and metaphorical extension is itself part of the language.

They adduced as proof his saying — peace and blessings be upon him —: “Faith has seventy-odd branches; the highest of them is the testimony that there is no god but God, and the lowest of them is removing harm from the road.” And naming the removal of harm “faith” is contrary to the original designation.

We say: This is from isolated reports (ākhād), and such a foundational rule cannot be established by it. And even if it were established, it is an indication of faith, and it is permissible to name it “faith” metaphorically.

They adduced as proof that the Sacred Law instituted acts of worship that were not previously known, so they required names; and borrowing them from the language was closer than transmitting them from another language or inventing names for them.

We say: We do not concede that any act of worship arose in the Sacred Law that had no name in the language. If it is said: “But prayer (ṣalāh) in the language is not an expression for bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration (sujūd), nor is pilgrimage (ḥajj) an expression for circumambulation (ṭawāf) and the running (saʿy),” we have two answers to this:

The first: Prayer in the Sacred Law is also not an expression for these acts; rather, prayer is an expression for supplication (duʿāʾ), just as in the language; pilgrimage is an expression for intention (qaṣd); fasting is an expression for abstention (imsāk); and alms is an expression for growth (numuww). But the Sacred Law made other matters conditions for the validity (ijzāʾ) of these things, annexed to them. Thus it made it a condition for the counting of the obligatory supplication that bowing and prostration be annexed to it, and for the intention toward the House that the standing (wuqūf) and circumambulation be annexed to it. The name does not encompass these annexed acts, but they are conditions for the counting of what the name does apply to. So the Sacred Law disposed by way of positing conditions (waḍʿ al-sharṭ), not by way of altering the designation (taghyīr al-waḍʿ).

The second: It may be said that all the acts were named “prayer” because they are performed in following the act of the imam; for the one who follows the leader in horse-racing is called muṣallin (the follower) because he follows. This is the speech of al-Qāḍī — may God have mercy on him.

But the chosen view with us is this: There is no way to deny that the Sacred Law has disposed over these names, nor is there any way to claim that they have been wholly transmitted from the language, as some have supposed. Rather, customary usage (ʿurf) disposes over names in two respects:

One of them: Specification (takhṣīṣ) to some of the named objects, as in the case of “beast” (dābbah). The Sacred Law’s disposal over pilgrimage, fasting, and faith is of this kind, for the Sacred Law has a customary usage in its employment, just as the Arabs have one.

The second: Their applying the name to what is attached to a thing and connected with it, as when they call wine “forbidden” (muḥarramah) while what is forbidden is drinking it, and the mother “forbidden” while what is forbidden is intercourse with her. Its disposal over prayer is likewise; for bowing and prostration are made by the Sacred Law conditions for the completion of the prayer, so the name encompasses them by the customary usage of the Sacred Law’s employment. For denying that bowing and prostration are pillars of the prayer and part of its very self is far-fetched.

Thus conceding this measure of disposal through the customary employment of the Sacred Law is easier than excluding prostration and bowing from the very essence of the prayer. And this is a matter of necessity and need, for the acts of worship that the Sacred Law conceives ought to have known names, and that is not found in the language except through some kind of disposal within it.

As for their argument that the Qurʾān is Arabic — this does not remove these names from being Arabic, nor does it strip the name “Arabic” from the Qurʾān. For even if it contained such words from a foreign tongue, that would not remove it from being Arabic either, as we mentioned in the First Pole (al-Quṭb al-Awwal) of this book.

As for his saying that the Lawgiver was obliged to give explicit instruction (tawqīf) regarding His disposal — this too is only obligatory if His intent from these expressions is not understood through repetition and contextual indicators (qarāʾin) time after time. When this is understood, the purpose is achieved. This, in our view, is closer than what al-Qāḍī — may God have mercy on him — mentioned.

### | [الفصل الخامس في الكلام المفيد]

في الكلام المفيد.
اعلم أن الأمور منقسمة إلى ما يدل على  غيره وإلى ما لا يدل. فأما ما يدل
فينقسم إلى ما يدل بذاته وهو الأدلة العقلية، وقد ذكرنا مجامع أقسامها في
مدارك العقول من مقدمة الكتاب. وإلى ما يدل بالوضع، وهو ينقسم إلى صوت وغير
صوت كالإشارة والرمز. والصوت ينقسم في دلالته إلى مفيد وغير مفيد، والمفيد
كقولك زيد قائم وزيد خرج راكبا، وغير المفيد كقولك زيد لا وعمرو في؛ فإن
هذا لا يحصل منه معنى، وإن كان آحاد كلماته موضوعة للدلالة.
وقد اختلف في تسمية هذا كلاما، فمنهم من قال هو كمقلوب رجل وزيد " لجر "
و " ديز "، فإن هذا لا يسمى كلاما، ومنهم من سماه كلاما لأن آحاده وضعت
للإفادة. واعلم أن المفيد من الكلام ثلاثة أقسام: اسم وفعل وحرف كما في علم
النحو، وهذا لا يكون مفيدا حتى يشتمل على اسمين أسند أحدهما إلى الآخر نحو
زيد أخوك، والله ربك، أو اسم أسند إلى فعل نحو قولك ضرب زيد وقام عمرو.
وأما الاسم والحرف كقولك زيد من وعمرو في، فلا يفيد حتى نقول من مضر وفي
الدار وكذلك قولك ضرب قام لا يفيد إذا لم يتخلله اسم، وكذلك قولك من في قد
على. واعلم أن المركب من الاسم والفعل والحرف تركيبا مفيدا ينقسم إلى مستقل
بالإفادة من كل وجه، وإلى ما لا يستقل بالإفادة إلا بقرينة وإلى ما يستقل
بالإفادة من وجه دون وجه.
مثال الأول قوله تعالى: {ولا تقربوا الزنا} [الإسراء: 32] و {ولا تقتلوا
أنفسكم} [النساء: 29] وذلك يسمى نصا لظهوره، والنص في السير هو الظهور فيه،
ومنه منصة العروس للكرسي الذي تظهر عليه. والنص ضربان ضرب هو نص بلفظه
ومنظومه كما ذكرناه، وضرب هو نص بفحواه ومفهومه نحو قوله تعالى: {فلا تقل
لهما أف} [الإسراء: 23] {ولا تظلمون فتيلا} [النساء: 77] {فمن يعمل مثقال
ذرة خيرا يره} [الزلزلة: 7] {ومنهم من إن تأمنه بدينار لا يؤده إليك} [آل
عمران: 75] فقد اتفق أهل اللغة على أن فهم ما فوق التأفيف من الضرب والشتم
وما وراء الفتيل والذرة من المقدار الكثير أسبق  إلى الفهم منه من نفس الذرة
والفتيل والتأفيف. ومن قال: إن هذا معلوم بالقياس فإن أراد به أن المسكوت
عنه عرف بالمنطوق فهو حق، وإن أراد به أنه يحتاج فيه إلى تأمل أو يتطرق
إليه احتمال فهو غلط.
وأما الذي لا يستقل إلا بقرينة فكقوله تعالى: {أو يعفو الذي بيده عقدة
النكاح} [البقرة: 237] وقوله {ثلاثة قروء} [البقرة: 228] وكل لفظ مشترك
ومبهم، كقوله: رأيت أسدا وحمارا
وثورا إذا أراد شجاعا وبليدا فإنه لا يستقل بالدلالة على مقصوده إلا
بقرينة. وأما الذي يستقل من وجه دون وجه فكقوله تعالى: {وآتوا حقه يوم
حصاده} [الأنعام: 141] وكقوله تعالى: {حتى يعطوا الجزية عن يد وهم صاغرون}
[التوبة: 29] فإن الإيتاء ويوم الحصاد معلوم ومقدار ما يؤتى غير معلوم،
والقتال وأهل الكتاب معلوم وقدر الجزية مجهول. فخرج من هذا أن اللفظ المفيد
بالإضافة إلى مدلوله إما أن لا يتطرق إليه، احتمال فيسمى نصا، أو يتعارض
فيه الاحتمالات من غير ترجيح فيسمى مجملا ومبهما، أو يترجح أحد احتمالاته
على الآخر فيسمى بالإضافة إلى الاحتمال الأرجح ظاهرا وبالإضافة إلى
الاحتمال البعيد مؤولا.
فاللفظ المفيد إذا إما نص أو ظاهر أو مجمل.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ي-د (f-y-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of yielding benefit, utility, or conveying a complete sense; al-Ifādah is the act of rendering something beneficial or informative.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, al-kalām al-mufīd is the utterance that yields a complete, self-contained meaning (maʿnā) sufficient for comprehension, as opposed to mere phonetic articulation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes actual conveyance of meaning; metaphorical (majāz) usage would be applying ifādah to sounds that merely hint without completing a proposition.
- Root: د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Dalālah is the act of guiding or pointing toward something; a dalīl is that which indicates.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Dalālah bi-al-waḍʿ (conventional indication) is contrasted with dalālah bi-al-dhāt (essential indication); the former is the basis of linguistic signification in uṣūl al-fiqh.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal indication is direct; metaphorical would be a sign (ishārah) or gesture (ramz) that indicates only by convention, not by nature.
- Root: ن-ص-ص (n-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Naṣṣ means the elevation or manifestation of something; the nuṣṣah (platform) of a bride is that upon which she is displayed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, naṣṣ is the text whose meaning is fully manifest (ẓāhir) with no room for alternative interpretation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the text itself; metaphorical: the "elevation" of meaning to full clarity, as in the bride's platform.
- Root: ج-م-ل (j-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ijmāl is the gathering or summarizing; mujmal is that which is gathered but not detailed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A mujmal term is one whose meaning is ambiguous (mubham) due to competing possibilities without preponderance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: aggregation; metaphorical: ambiguity arising from unresolved multiplicity of senses.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Isnād (Predication) — A complete informative sentence (kalām mufīd) requires either two nouns with one predicated of the other (e.g., Zayd is your brother) or a noun predicated of a verb (e.g., Zayd struck). Without this syntactic bond, mere juxtaposition of particles and nouns yields no complete meaning.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that matters are divided into that which indicates something other than itself and that which does not indicate. As for that which indicates, it is divided into that which indicates by its very essence — and these are the rational proofs (al-adillah al-ʿaqliyyah), whose comprehensive divisions we have already mentioned in the section on the Perceptions of Intellects (Madārik al-ʿUqūl) from the introduction of this book — and into that which indicates by convention (al-waḍʿ), and this is divided into sound and non-sound, such as gesture (ishārah) and allusion (ramz). Sound, in its indication, is divided into informative (mufīd) and non-informative. The informative is like your saying: "Zayd is standing" and "Zayd went out riding." The non-informative is like your saying: "Zayd not" and "Amr in" — for no meaning is obtained from this, even though each individual word is conventionally placed for indication.

There has been disagreement over naming this [non-informative utterance] "speech" (kalām). Some said it is like the reversed [words] of "rajul" and "Zayd" — "lujar" and "dayz" — for this is not called speech. And some called it speech because its individual parts were placed for the purpose of conveying meaning. Know that the informative [utterance] from speech is of three divisions: noun (ism), verb (fiʿl), and particle (ḥarf), as in the science of grammar (naḥw). And this is not informative until it comprises two nouns, one of which is predicated of the other, such as "Zayd is your brother" and "Allah is your Lord," or a noun predicated of a verb, such as your saying "Zayd struck" and "Amr stood." As for the noun and the particle, like your saying "Zayd from" and "Amr in," it does not inform until we say "from Mudar" and "in the house." Likewise, your saying "struck stood" does not inform if no noun intervenes between them, and likewise your saying "from in upon."

Know that the composite of noun, verb, and particle in an informative composition is divided into: that which is independent in conveying meaning from every aspect; that which is not independent in conveying meaning except with a contextual indicator (qarīnah); and that which is independent in conveying meaning from one aspect but not from another.

An example of the first is the saying of the Exalted: {«And do not approach fornication»} [al-Isrāʾ: 32] and {«And do not kill yourselves»} [al-Nisāʾ: 29]. This is called naṣṣ (explicit text) due to its manifestness (ẓuhūr). And al-naṣṣ in [the root] al-sayr (movement) is manifestness therein; from it [is derived] the nuṣṣah (platform) of the bride, which is the chair upon which she appears. The naṣṣ is of two types: a type that is naṣṣ by its very wording and composition, as we have mentioned; and a type that is naṣṣ by its import (faḥwā) and understood meaning (mafhūm), such as the saying of the Exalted: {«So do not say to them 'uff'»} [al-Isrāʾ: 23], {«And you shall not be wronged even by a thread»} [al-Nisāʾ: 77], {«So whoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it»} [al-Zalzalah: 7], and {«And among them is he who, if you entrust him with a dinar, he will not return it to you»} [Āl ʿImrān: 75]. For the people of language have agreed that understanding what is beyond "uff" — namely beating and insulting — and what is beyond the thread and the atom — namely the greater amount — is more immediate to the understanding than the very atom, the thread, and the "uff" itself. And whoever says that this is known by analogy (qiyās): if he means thereby that the unmentioned [case] is known through the mentioned [case], then this is correct. But if he means that it requires reflection (taʾammul) or that possibility (iḥtimāl) attaches to it, then this is an error.

As for that which is not independent except with a contextual indicator, it is like the saying of the Exalted: {«Or he who holds the knot of marriage in his hand pardons»} [al-Baqarah: 237], and His saying {«three qurūʾ (menstrual periods)»} [al-Baqarah: 228], and every equivocal (mushtarak) and ambiguous (mubham) expression, such as his saying: "I saw a lion, a donkey, and an ox," if he intends thereby a brave man, a dullard, and a stupid one — for it is not independent in indicating his intended meaning except with a contextual indicator. As for that which is independent from one aspect but not from another, it is like the saying of the Exalted: {«And give its due on the day of its harvest»} [al-Anʿām: 141], and like the saying of the Exalted: {«Until they pay the jizyah out of hand while they are humbled»} [al-Tawbah: 29]. For the giving and the day of harvest are known, but the amount of what is given is not known; and the fighting and the People of the Book are known, but the amount of the jizyah is unknown.

It follows from this that the informative utterance, in relation to its signification (madlūl), is either: that to which no possibility (iḥtimāl) attaches — and it is called naṣṣ; or that in which possibilities conflict without preponderance (tarjīḥ) — and it is called mujmal (ambiguous) and mubham (obscure); or that in which one of its possibilities is preponderant over the other — and it is called, in relation to the preponderant possibility, ẓāhir (manifest), and in relation to the remote possibility, muʾawwal (interpreted). Thus the informative utterance is either naṣṣ, ẓāhir, or mujmal.

chapters.title_en: The Sixth Chapter on the Means of Comprehending the Intended Meaning of Discourse
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل السادس في طريق فهم المراد من الخطاب]

طريق فهم المراد من الخطاب.
اعلم أن الكلام إما أن يسمعه نبي أو ملك من الله تعالى، أو يسمعه نبي أو
ولي من ملك، أو تسمعه الأمة من النبي. فإن سمعه ملك أو نبي من الله تعالى
فلا يكون حرفا ولا صوتا ولا لغة موضوعة حتى يعرف معناه بسبب تقدم المعرفة
بالمواضعة، لكن يعرف المراد منه بأن يخلق الله تعالى في السامع علما ضروريا
بثلاثة أمور: بالمتكلم وبأن ما سمعه من كلامه وبمراده من كلامه، فهذه ثلاثة
أمور لا بد وأن تكون معلومة. والقدرة الأزلية ليست قاصرة عن اضطرار الملك
والنبي إلى العلم بذلك، ولا متكلم إلا وهو محتاج إلى نصب علامة لتعريف ما
في ضميره إلا الله تعالى فإنه قادر على اختراع علم ضروري به غير نصب علامة.
وكما  أن كلامه ليس من جنس البشر فسمعه الذي يخلقه لعبده ليس من جنس سمع
الأصوات، ولذلك يعسر علينا تفهم كيفية سماع موسى كلام الله تعالى الذي ليس
بحرف ولا صوت كما يعسر على الأكمه تفهم كيفية إدراك البصير للألوان
والأشكال. أما سماع النبي من الملك فيحتمل أن يكون بحرف وصوت دال على معنى
كلام الله، فيكون المسموع الأصوات الحادثة التي هي فعل الملك دون نفس
الكلام ولا يكون هذا سماعا لكلام الله بغير واسطة، وإن كان يطلق عليه اسم
سماع كلام الله تعالى، كما يقال: فلان سمع شعر المتنبي وكلامه، وإن سمعه من
غيره وسمع صوت غيره، وكما قال تعالى: {وإن أحد من المشركين استجارك فأجره
حتى يسمع كلام الله} [التوبة: 6] وكذلك سماع الأمة من الرسول - صلى الله
عليه وسلم - كسماع الرسول من الملك، ويكون طريق فهم المراد تقدم المعرفة
بوضع اللغة التي بها المخاطبة.
ثم إن كان نصا لا يحتمل كفى معرفة اللغة، وإن تطرق إليه الاحتمال فلا
يعرف المراد منه حقيقة إلا بانضمام قرينة إلى اللفظ، والقرينة إما لفظ
مكشوف كقوله تعالى: {وآتوا حقه يوم حصاده} [الأنعام: 141] والحق هو العشر
وإما إحالة على دليل العقل كقوله تعالى: {والسماوات مطويات بيمينه} [الزمر:
67] وقوله - عليه السلام - «قلب المؤمن بين أصبعين من أصابع الرحمن» . وإما
قرائن أحوال من إشارات ورموز وحركات وسوابق ولواحق لا تدخل تحت الحصر
والتخمين يختص بدركها المشاهد لها فينقلها المشاهدون من الصحابة إلى
التابعين بألفاظ صريحة أو مع قرائن من ذلك الجنس أو من جنس آخر حتى توجب
علما ضروريا بفهم المراد أو توجب ظنا وكل ما ليس له عبارة موضوعة في اللغة
فتتعين فيه القرائن وعند منكري صيغة
العموم والأمر يتعين تعريف الأمر والاستغراق بالقرائن، فإن قوله تعالى:
{فاقتلوا المشركين} [التوبة: 5] ، وإن أكده بقوله كلهم وجميعهم فيحتمل
الخصوص عندهم كقوله تعالى: {تدمر كل شيء بأمر ربها} [الأحقاف: 25] {وأوتيت
من كل شيء} [النمل: 23] فإنه أريد به البعض، وسيأتي تفصيله إن شاء الله
تعالى.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ط-ب (Kha-Ta-Ba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Speech addressed to another; formal discourse (khiṭāb) implying a speaker, a listener, and a directed message.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, khiṭāb is the divine address (al-khiṭāb al-ilāhī) whose comprehension requires either linguistic convention (waḍʿ) or divinely-created necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) khiṭāb is audible speech; metaphorical (majāz) khiṭāb extends to any divine communication, even without letters or sounds.
- Root: س-م-ع (Sīn-Mīm-ʿAyn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Auditory perception; hearing as a physical act involving sound waves.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, samāʿ of God’s speech is not sensory but a created cognition (ʿilm) in the prophet or angel, bypassing physical sound.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal hearing requires sound; metaphorical hearing (e.g., “he heard the poet’s speech” via a transmitter) applies to conveyed divine words.
- Root: ق-ر-ن (Qāf-Rāʾ-Nūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Joining or coupling; a contextual indicator (qarīnah) that accompanies a text to disambiguate meaning.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Qarīnah is the extrinsic evidence (dalīl) that resolves ambiguity (ijmāl) in scriptural commands, whether textual, rational, or situational.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal qarīnah is a physical conjunction; metaphorical qarīnah is any circumstantial clue (ḥāl) that guides interpretation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Maʿnā (Semantic Reconstruction) — When a sentence’s surface form admits multiple readings, the intended meaning is determined by contextual presuppositions (qarāʾin al-ḥāl) and syntactic ellipsis (ḥadhf), as in the verse {«وآتوا حقه يوم حصاده»} where “right” (ḥaqq) is specified by external evidence.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that discourse is either heard by a prophet or an angel directly from God—Exalted is He—or heard by a prophet or a saint (walī) from an angel, or heard by the community (ummah) from the prophet. If an angel or prophet hears it directly from God—Exalted is He—then it is neither a letter (ḥarf) nor a sound (ṣawt) nor a conventional language (lughah mawḍūʿah) whose meaning is known through prior acquaintance with linguistic convention (waḍʿ). Rather, the intended meaning is known by God—Exalted is He—creating in the hearer a necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī) of three matters: of the Speaker, of the fact that what he heard is His speech, and of His intended meaning from that speech. These three matters must necessarily be known. The eternal power (al-qudrah al-azaliyyah) is not incapable of necessitating in the angel and prophet such knowledge. And there is no speaker who is not in need of erecting a sign (ʿalāmah) to indicate what is in his conscience—except God—Exalted is He—for He is able to invent necessary knowledge of Himself without erecting any sign. And just as His speech is not of the genus of human speech, so too the hearing that He creates for His servant is not of the genus of hearing sounds. For this reason, it is difficult for us to comprehend the modality of Moses’ hearing of God’s speech—which is neither letter nor sound—just as it is difficult for the congenitally blind (akmah) to comprehend the modality of the sighted person’s perception of colors and shapes.

As for the prophet’s hearing from the angel, it is possible that it occurs through a letter and sound indicating the meaning of God’s speech. In that case, what is heard is the originated sounds (al-aṣwāt al-ḥādithah) that are the act of the angel, not the speech itself. This would not be hearing God’s speech without mediation (bi-ghayr wāsiṭah), even though the name “hearing God’s speech” is applied to it—just as one says: “So-and-so heard al-Mutanabbī’s poetry and speech,” even if he heard it from someone else and heard another’s voice. And as God—Exalted is He—said: {«وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِّنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّىٰ يَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ»} [Al-Tawbah: 6] (“And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of God”). Likewise, the community’s hearing from the Messenger—peace be upon him—is like the Messenger’s hearing from the angel. And the means of comprehending the intended meaning is prior knowledge of the linguistic convention (waḍʿ) of the language in which the address is made.

Then, if the text is unequivocal (naṣṣ) admitting no possibility (iḥtimāl), knowledge of the language suffices. But if possibility attaches to it, then the intended meaning is not truly known except by the conjunction of a contextual indicator (qarīnah) with the wording. The contextual indicator is either an explicit verbal one (lafẓ makshūf)—as in His saying—Exalted is He: {«وَآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِ»} [Al-Anʿām: 141] (“And give its due on the day of its harvest”), where “the due” (al-ḥaqq) is the tithe (al-ʿushr)—or it is a referral to a rational proof (dalīl al-ʿaql)—as in His saying—Exalted is He: {«وَالسَّمَاوَاتُ مَطْوِيَّاتٌ بِيَمِينِهِ»} [Al-Zumar: 67] (“And the heavens are folded in His right hand”)—and his saying—peace be upon him: «قَلْبُ الْمُؤْمِنِ بَيْنَ أُصْبُعَيْنِ مِنْ أَصَابِعِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ» (“The believer’s heart is between two fingers of the Merciful’s fingers”). Or it is contextual indicators of circumstances (qarāʾin aḥwāl) consisting of gestures (ishārāt), symbols (rumūz), movements (ḥarakāt), and antecedents and consequents (sawābiq wa lawāḥiq) that cannot be exhaustively enumerated. Their perception is exclusive to the eyewitness (mushāhid), who then transmits them from the Companions (ṣaḥābah) to the Followers (tābiʿīn) either in explicit words or with indicators of that kind or another kind, until they necessitate either necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī) of the intended meaning or produce conjecture (ẓann). And everything for which there is no conventional expression (ʿibārah mawḍūʿah) in the language—there the contextual indicators become indispensable.

And for those who deny the universal form (ṣīghat al-ʿumūm) and the command form (ṣīghat al-amr), defining the command and the universal scope (istiḥrāq) is necessarily achieved through contextual indicators. For His saying—Exalted is He: {«فَاقْتُلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ»} [Al-Tawbah: 5] (“Then kill the polytheists”)—even if He emphasized it with “all of them” and “every one of them”—still admits particularization (khuṣūṣ) in their view, like His saying—Exalted is He: {«تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ بِأَمْرِ رَبِّهَا»} [Al-Aḥqāf: 25] (“It destroys everything by the command of its Lord”) and {«وَأُوتِيَتْ مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ»} [Al-Naml: 23] (“And she was given of everything”)—for in these, only a part was intended. And its detailed exposition will follow, God—Exalted is He—willing.

chapters.title_en: The Seventh Chapter on the Literal (Ḥaqīqah) and the Metaphorical (Majāz)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل السابع في الحقيقة  والمجاز]

الحقيقة والمجاز
اعلم أن اسم الحقيقة مشترك، إذ قد يراد به ذات الشيء وحده ويراد به حقيقة
الكلام؛ ولكن إذا استعمل في الألفاظ أريد به ما استعمل في موضوعه. والمجاز
ما استعملته العرب في غير موضوعه وهو ثلاثة أنواع: الأول ما استعير للشيء
بسبب المشابهة في خاصية مشهورة كقولهم للشجاع أسد وللبليد حمار، فلو سمي
الأبخر أسدا لم يجز لأن البخر ليس مشهورا في حق الأسد الثاني: الزيادة،
كقوله تعالى: {ليس كمثله شيء} [الشورى: 11] فإن الكاف وضعت للإفادة، فإذا
استعملت على وجه لا يفيد كان على خلاف الوضع الثالث: النقصان الذي لا يبطل
التفهيم، كقوله عز وجل {واسأل القرية} [يوسف: 82] والمعنى: واسأل أهل
القرية. وهذا النقصان اعتادته العرب فهو توسع وتجوز.
وقد يعرف المجاز بإحدى علامات أربع الأولى: أن الحقيقة جارية على العموم
في نظائره، إذ قولنا عالم لما عني به ذو علم صدق على كل ذي علم وقوله
{واسأل القرية} [يوسف: 82] يصح في بعض الجمادات لإرادة صاحب القرية، ولا
يقال: سل البساط والكوز، وإن كان قد يقال سل الطلل والربع لقربه من المجاز
المستعمل. الثانية: أن يعرف بامتناع الاشتقاق عليه، إذ الأمر إذا استعمل في
حقيقته اشتق منه اسم الآمر وإذا استعمل في الشأن مجازا لم يشتق منه آمر،
والشأن هو المراد بقوله تعالى {وما أمر فرعون برشيد} [هود: 97] وبقوله
تعالى: {إذا جاء أمرنا} [هود: 40] الثالثة: أن تختلف صيغة الجمع على الاسم
فيعلم أنه مجاز في أحدهما، إذ الأمر الحقيقي يجمع على أوامر، وإذا أريد به
الشأن يجمع على أمور. الرابعة: أن الحقيقي إذا كان له تعلق بالغير، فإذا
استعمل فيما لا تعلق له به لم يكن له متعلق كالقدرة إذا أريد بها الصفة كان
لها مقدور، وإن أريد بها المقدور كالنبات الحسن العجيب، إذ يقال: انظر إلى
قدرة الله تعالى أي إلى عجائب مقدوراته، لم يكن له متعلق، إذ النبات لا
مقدور له. واعلم أن كل مجاز فله حقيقة.
وليس من ضرورة كل حقيقة أن يكون لها  مجاز، بل ضربان من الأسماء لا
يدخلهما المجاز، الأول: أسماء الأعلام نحو زيد وعمرو؛ لأنها أسام وضعت
للفرق بين الذوات لا للفرق في الصفات. نعم الموضوع للصفات قد يجعل علما
فيكون مجازا، كالأسود بن الحارث إذ لا يراد به الدلالة على الصفة مع أنه
وضع له فهو مجاز.
أما إذا قال: قرأت المزني وسيبويه وهو يريد كتابيهما فليس ذلك إلا كقوله
تعالى: {واسأل القرية} [يوسف: 82] فهو على طريق حذف اسم الكتاب، معناه:
قرأت كتاب المزني، فيكون في الكلام مجاز بالمعنى الثالث المذكور للمجاز
الثاني: الأسماء التي لا أعم منها ولا أبعد، كالمعلوم والمجهول والمدلول
والمذكور، إذ لا شيء إلا وهو حقيقة فيه فكيف يكون مجازا عن شيء؟ هذا تمام
المقدمة.

### | [القسم الأول من الفن الأول من مقاصد القطب الثالث في المجمل والمبين]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "being established, certain, and due"; the essence of a thing as it truly is.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥaqīqah denotes the fixed reality of a thing; in uṣūl, it is the utterance used in its original lexical placement (waḍʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) is the primary, settled application; metaphorical (majāz) is a licensed departure from that placement.
- Root: ج-و-ز (j-w-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Passing through, crossing over; permissibility of traversal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Majāz is the crossing of an expression from its original locus to another due to a relation (ʿalāqah) with a preventing factor (qarīnah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz is a "trope" — a permissible crossing, not a corruption of speech, but an expansion (tawassuʿ).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis Restoration) — When an omission (ḥadhf) occurs, the grammatical regimen (ʿamal) is restored by estimating the deleted element, as in "ask the village" where the true object is "the people of the village."
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the name "literal" (ḥaqīqah) is equivocal (mushtarak), for it may denote the essence of a thing by itself, or it may denote the literalness of speech. But when applied to utterances, it means that which is used in its original lexical placement (mawḍūʿ). The metaphorical (majāz) is what the Arabs used outside its original placement, and it is of three types:

The first: what is borrowed for a thing due to resemblance in a well-known characteristic, as when they say of the courageous man "lion" and of the dull man "donkey." If one called a foul-breathed man a "lion," it would not be permissible, because foul breath is not a well-known trait of the lion.

The second: augmentation (ziyādah), as His saying, the Exalted: {«Laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ»} [al-Shūrā: 11] — "There is nothing like unto Him." For the particle kāf was placed for comparison (tafʿīl), so when it is used in a manner that does not yield comparison, it is contrary to the original placement.

The third: omission (nuqṣān) that does not nullify comprehension, as His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: {«Wa-isʾali al-qaryah»} [Yūsuf: 82] — "And ask the village," the meaning being: "ask the people of the village." This omission is customary among the Arabs, so it is an expansion (tawassuʿ) and a metaphorical license (tajawwuz).

The metaphorical may be recognized by one of four signs:

The first: that the literal runs universally across its analogues. For when we say "knower" (ʿālim) meaning "one who possesses knowledge," it holds true of every knower. But His saying {«Wa-isʾali al-qaryah»} [Yūsuf: 82] is valid only for some inanimate objects, intending "the owner of the village." One does not say "ask the carpet and the jug," although one may say "ask the ruined abode (ṭalal) and the dwelling (rabʿ)" due to its proximity to the established metaphorical usage.

The second: that it is known by the impossibility of derivation (ishtiqāq) upon it. For when "command" (amr) is used in its literal sense, the name "commander" (āmir) is derived from it; but when it is used metaphorically for "affair" (shaʾn), no "commander" is derived from it. And "affair" is what is meant by His saying, the Exalted: {«Wa-mā amru Firʿawna bi-rashīd»} [Hūd: 97] — "And the affair of Pharaoh was not right-minded," and by His saying, the Exalted: {«Idhā jāʾa amrunā»} [Hūd: 40] — "When Our command came."

The third: that the plural form of the noun differs, so one knows it is metaphorical in one of the two. For the literal "command" (amr) is pluralized as awāmir, but when it means "affair," it is pluralized as umūr.

The fourth: that the literal, when it has a relation to another, if used for what has no relation to it, then it has no object of relation. Like "power" (qudrah): if it means the attribute, it has a "powered object" (maqdūr); but if it means the "powered object" itself — like the beautiful, wondrous plant, for one says "look at the power of God, the Exalted," meaning "at the wonders of His powered objects" — then it has no object of relation, for the plant has no "powered object" of its own.

Know that every metaphor has a literal basis. But it is not necessary that every literal have a metaphor. Rather, there are two kinds of names that metaphor does not enter:

The first: proper names (aʿlām) like Zayd and ʿAmr, because they are names placed to distinguish between essences (dhawāt), not to distinguish between attributes. Yes, that which is placed for an attribute may be made a proper name, and then it is metaphorical — like al-Aswad ibn al-Ḥārith, for it does not intend to indicate the attribute (blackness), even though it was placed for it; thus it is metaphorical.

As for one who says: "I read al-Muzanī and Sībawayh," meaning their books — that is nothing other than like His saying, the Exalted: {«Wa-isʾali al-qaryah»} [Yūsuf: 82]. It is on the path of omitting the noun "book," the meaning being: "I read the book of al-Muzanī." So in the speech there is metaphor of the third type mentioned above.

The second: names for which there is nothing more general and nothing more remote — like "the known" (maʿlūm), "the unknown" (majhūl), "the indicated" (madlūl), and "the mentioned" (madhkūr). For there is nothing except that it is literal in them, so how could it be metaphorical of something else? This completes the introduction.

### | [The First Division of the First Art of the Third Pole's Objectives: On the Ambiguous (Mujmal) and the Clarified (Mubayyan)]

chapters.title_en: The Clarified (Mubayyan) and the Ambiguous (Mujmal) — On the Verse {Forbidden to you are your mothers}
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة قوله تعالى حرمت عليكم أمهاتكم]

القسم الأول من الفن الأول من مقاصد القطب الثالث في المجمل والمبين.
ولنشتغل بالمقاصد وهي كيفية اقتباس الأحكام من الصيغ والألفاظ المنطوق بها
وهي أربعة أقسام.
القسم الأول من الفن الأول من مقاصد القطب الثالث: في المجمل والمبين.
اعلم أن اللفظ إما أن يتعين معناه بحيث لا يحتمل غيره فيسمى مبينا ونصا،
وإما أن يتردد بين معنيين فصاعدا من غير ترجيح فيسمى مجملا، وإما أن يظهر
في أحدهما ولا يظهر في الثاني فيسمى ظاهرا. والمجمل هو اللفظ الصالح لأحد
معنيين الذي لا يتعين معناه لا بوضع اللغة ولا بعرف الاستعمال، وينكشف ذلك
بمسائل.
مسألة: قوله تعالى: {حرمت عليكم أمهاتكم} [النساء: 23] و {حرمت عليكم
الميتة} [المائدة: 3] ليس بمجمل
وقال قوم من القدرية: هو مجمل؛ لأن الأعيان لا تتصف بالتحريم، وإنما يحرم
فعل ما يتعلق بالعين وليس يدرى ما ذلك الفعل فيحرم من الميتة مسها أو أكلها
أو النظر إليها أو بيعها أو الانتفاع بها فهو مجمل.
والأم يحرم منها النظر أو المضاجعة أو الوطء فلا يدرى أيه، ولا بد من
تقدير فعل، وتلك الأفعال كثيرة وليس بعضها أولى من بعض. وهذا فاسد، إذ  عرف
الاستعمال كالوضع، ولذلك قسمنا الأسماء إلى عرفية ووضعية وقدمنا بيانها،
ومن أنس بتعارف أهل اللغة واطلع على عرفهم علم أنهم لا يستريبون في أن من
قال: حرمت عليك الطعام والشراب أنه يريد الأكل دون النظر والمس، وإذا قال:
حرمت عليك هذا الثوب أنه يريد اللبس، وإذا قال: حرمت عليك النساء أنه يريد
الوقاع، وهذا صريح عندهم مقطوع به، فكيف يكون مجملا؟ والصريح تارة يكون
بعرف الاستعمال وتارة بالوضع وكل ذلك واحد في نفي الإجمال؟ وقال قوم: هو من
قبيل المحذوف، كقوله تعالى: {واسأل القرية} [يوسف: 82] أي: أهل القرية،
وكذلك قوله تعالى: {أحلت لكم بهيمة الأنعام} [المائدة: 1] أي: أكل البهيمة،
و {أحل لكم صيد البحر} [المائدة: 96] وهذا إن أراد به إلحاقه بالمجمل فهو
خطأ، وإن أراد به حصول الفهم به مع كونه محذوفا فهو صحيح، وإن أراد به
إلحاقه بالمجاز فيلزمه تسمية الأسماء العرفية مجازا.

### | [مسألة قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم رفع عن أمتي الخطأ والنسيان]

» يقتضي بالوضع نفي نفس الخطإ والنسيان، وليس كذلك. وكلامه - صلى الله
عليه وسلم - يجل عن الخلف، فالمراد به رفع حكمه لا على الإطلاق بل الحكم
الذي عرف بعرف الاستعمال قبل ورود الشرع إرادته بهذا اللفظ فقد كان يفهم
قبل الشرع من قول القائل لغيره رفعت عنك الخطأ والنسيان إذ يفهم منه رفع
حكمه لا على الإطلاق وهو المؤاخذة بالذم والعقوبة فكذلك قول رسول الله -
صلى الله عليه وسلم - نص صريح فيه وليس بعام في جميع أحكامه من الضمان
ولزوم القضاء وغيره، ولا هو مجمل بين المؤاخذة التي ترجع إلى الذم ناجزا أو
إلى العقاب آجلا وبين الغرم والقضاء؛ لأنه لا صيغة لعمومه حتى يجعل عاما في
كل حكم كما لم يجعل قوله تعالى: {حرمت عليكم أمهاتكم} [النساء: 23] عاما في
كل فعل مع أنه لا بد من إضمار فعل، فالحكم ههنا لا بد من إضماره لإضافة
الرفع إليه كالفعل، ثم ينزل على ما يقتضيه عرف الاستعمال وهو الذم والعقاب
ههنا والوطء ثم.
فإن قيل: فالضمان  أيضا عقاب فليرتفع. قلنا: الضمان قد يجب امتحانا ليثاب
عليه لا للانتقام، ولذلك يجب على الصبي والمجنون وعلى العاقلة بسبب الغير
ويجب حيث يجب الإتلاف كالمضطر في
المخمصة وقد يجب عقابا كما يجب على المتعمد لقتل الصيد ليذوق وبال أمره،
وإن وجب على المخطئ بالقتل امتحانا فغاية ما يلزم أن يقال: ينتفي به كل
ضمان هو بطريق العقاب؛ لأنه مؤاخذة وانتقام بخلاف ما هو بطريق الجبران
والامتحان. والمقصود أن من ظن أن هذا اللفظ خاص أو عام لجميع أحكام الخطأ
ومجمل متردد فقد غلط فيه. فإن قيل: فلو ورد في موضع لا عرف فيه يدرك به
خصوص معناه فهل يجعل نفيا لأثره بالكلية حتى يقوم مقام العموم أو يجعل
مجملا؟ قلنا: هو مجمل يحتمل نفي الأثر مطلقا ونفي آحاد الآثار ويصلح أن
يراد به الجميع ولا يترجح أحد الاحتمالات.
وهذا عند من لا يقول بصيغة العموم ظاهر، أما من يقول بها فيتبع فيه
الصيغة ولا صيغة للمضمرات، وهذا قد أضمر فيه الأثر فعلى ماذا يعول في
التعميم؟ فإن قيل: هو نفي فيقتضي وضعه نفي الأثر والمؤثر جميعا، فإن تعذر
نفي المؤثر بقرينة الحس فالتعذر مقصور عليه فيبقى الأثر منفيا. قلنا: ليس
قوله:: " لا صيام ولا عمل ولا خطأ ولا نسيان " أو «رفع الخطأ والنسيان»
عاما في نفي المؤثر والأثر حتى إذا تعذر في المؤثر بقي في الأثر، بل هو
لنفي المؤثر فقط. والأثر ينتفي ضرورة بانتفاء المؤثر لا بحكم عموم اللفظ
وشموله له، فإذا تعذر حمله على المؤثر صار مجازا إما عن جميع الآثار أو عن
بعض الآثار، ولا تترجح الجملة على البعض ولا أحد الأبعاض على غيره.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-م-ل (j-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of gathering, summarizing, or combining parts into a whole; hence "total" (jumla) and "ambiguous" (mujmal) as that whose parts are not distinguished.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, al-mujmal is that which lacks sufficient bayān (clarification) to determine a single referent; its theological import ties to the necessity of divine clarification (tabyīn) for obligation (taklīf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes a gathered aggregate; metaphorical (majāz) usage applies to speech whose intended meaning is concealed until external evidence (qarīnah) resolves it.
- Root: ب-ي-ن (b-y-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation and clarity; something "clear" (mubīn) is severed from ambiguity, manifest in itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Bayān is the divine act of making the law evident; al-mubayyan is the term whose referent is fixed by linguistic convention (waḍʿ) or customary usage (ʿurf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal clarity vs. metaphorical concealment — a term is mubayyan when no alternative meaning competes; mujmal when two or more meanings are equipoised.
- Root: ظ-ه-ر (ẓ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Becoming apparent, overt, dominant.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-ẓāhir is the term whose apparent meaning is preponderant (rājiḥ) over alternatives without full certainty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): In rhetoric, ẓāhir is the literal sense that prevails by usage, distinct from naṣṣ (explicit text) which admits no other reading.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis/Supposition) — When a sentence requires an omitted element (muḍmar) for grammatical completion, the omitted element is determined by the governing context (ʿāmil) and customary usage, not by arbitrary choice; the ḥadhf (deletion) does not render the utterance mujmal if the intended referent is fixed by convention.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first division of the first art of the aims of the third pole concerns the ambiguous (mujmal) and the clarified (mubayyan). Let us occupy ourselves with the aims, namely, the manner of deriving legal rulings (aḥkām) from the uttered formulas and expressions. These are four divisions.

The first division of the first art of the aims of the third pole: on the ambiguous (mujmal) and the clarified (mubayyan).

Know that an expression (lafẓ) is either such that its meaning is determined such that it admits no other — this is termed "clarified" (mubayyan) and "explicit text" (naṣṣ); or it wavers between two or more meanings without any preponderance — this is termed "ambiguous" (mujmal); or it is apparent in one of them but not in the second — this is termed "apparent" (ẓāhir). The ambiguous (mujmal) is the expression suitable for one of two meanings, whose meaning is not determined neither by linguistic convention (waḍʿ al-lughah) nor by customary usage (ʿurf al-istimāl), and this is disclosed through specific questions.

Question: The saying of God Most High: {Forbidden to you are your mothers} [al-Nisāʾ 4:23] and {Forbidden to you is carrion} [al-Māʾidah 5:3] is not ambiguous (mujmal).

A group of the Qadariyyah said: It is ambiguous; because physical entities (aʿyān) are not qualified by prohibition (taḥrīm); rather, what is prohibited is the act pertaining to the entity, and it is not known what that act is — whether from carrion it is touching it, eating it, looking at it, selling it, or benefiting from it — so it is ambiguous. Likewise, from the mother, what is prohibited is looking, lying beside, or intercourse — so it is not known which one, and an act must be estimated (taqdīr), and those acts are many, and none of them is more fitting than another.

This is corrupt, for customary usage (ʿurf al-istimāl) is like linguistic convention (waḍʿ); and for this reason we divided nouns into customary (ʿurfiyyah) and conventional (waḍʿiyyah), and we have already presented their explanation. Whoever is familiar with the customs of the people of language and is acquainted with their usage knows that they do not doubt that when one says: "I have forbidden you food and drink," he means eating, not looking or touching; and when he says: "I have forbidden you this garment," he means wearing; and when he says: "I have forbidden you women," he means intercourse. This is explicit (ṣarīḥ) among them, decisively affirmed — so how could it be ambiguous? The explicit (ṣarīḥ) is sometimes by customary usage and sometimes by linguistic convention, and all of that is one in negating ambiguity (ijmāl).

And a group said: It is of the category of the deleted (maḥdhūf), like His saying: {And ask the village} [Yūsuf 12:82], i.e., the people of the village; and likewise His saying: {Made lawful to you is the beast of cattle} [al-Māʾidah 5:1], i.e., eating the beast; and {Made lawful to you is the game of the sea} [al-Māʾidah 5:96]. If by this he intends to annex it to the ambiguous (mujmal), it is an error; if he intends thereby that understanding is attained despite its being deleted, it is correct; and if he intends to annex it to the metaphorical (majāz), then he is obliged to call customary nouns metaphorical.

Question: The saying of the Prophet — peace be upon him — "Lifted from my community are error and forgetfulness" by linguistic convention entails the negation of error and forgetfulness themselves, but it is not so. And his speech — peace be upon him — is exalted above falsehood (khulf); so what is meant is the lifting of their ruling (ḥukm), not absolutely, but the ruling which was known by customary usage before the advent of the Law (sharʿ) as intended by this expression. For before the Law, it was understood from one's saying to another: "I have lifted from you error and forgetfulness," that what is understood is the lifting of their ruling, not absolutely — namely, accountability (muʾākhadhah) by blame and punishment. Thus likewise, the saying of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — is an explicit text (naṣṣ ṣarīḥ) therein, and it is not general (ʿāmm) over all its rulings — such as liability (ḍamān), obligation of recompense (luzūm al-qaḍāʾ), and others — nor is it ambiguous (mujmal) between the accountability that reverts to immediate blame or to future punishment, and between indemnity (ghurm) and recompense (qaḍāʾ); because there is no formula for its generality such that it would be made general over every ruling — just as His saying: {Forbidden to you are your mothers} [al-Nisāʾ 4:23] was not made general over every act, even though an act must be implied (iḍmār). So here, the ruling must be implied (iḍmār) because of the annexation of the lifting to it, just like the act; then it is interpreted according to what customary usage requires — namely, blame and punishment here, and intercourse there.

If it is said: But liability (ḍamān) is also a punishment, so let it be lifted. We say: Liability may be obligatory as a trial (imtiḥān) so that one is rewarded for it, not for vengeance; and for this reason it is obligatory upon the child and the insane, and upon the ʿāqilah (kinsmen paying blood-money) due to another, and it is obligatory where destruction (itlāf) occurs, as with the one compelled by dire hunger (muḍṭarr fī al-makhmaṣah). And it may be obligatory as a punishment, as it is obligatory upon the deliberate killer of game (in iḥrām) so that he tastes the evil consequence of his affair. And if it is obligatory upon the one who errs in killing as a trial, then the utmost that follows is that one says: every liability that is by way of punishment is negated by it, because it is accountability and vengeance, unlike that which is by way of compensation (jubrān) and trial (imtiḥān). And the point is that whoever supposes that this expression is specific (khāṣṣ) or general (ʿāmm) over all rulings of error, or ambiguous (mujmal) and wavering, has erred therein.

If it is said: If it occurred in a context where there is no custom (ʿurf) by which its specific meaning could be grasped, is it then made a negation of its effect (athar) entirely, such that it stands in the place of generality (ʿumūm), or is it made ambiguous (mujmal)? We say: It is ambiguous (mujmal), admitting the negation of the effect absolutely and the negation of individual effects, and it is suitable that all be intended by it, and none of the probabilities is preponderant.

This is evident for one who does not affirm a formula for generality (ṣīghat al-ʿumūm). As for one who affirms it, he follows the formula therein — but there is no formula for the implied elements (muḍmarāt). And here the effect has been implied (uḍmir), so upon what does he rely for generalization (taʿmīm)?

If it is said: It is a negation (nafy), so its linguistic convention entails the negation of the effect and the cause (muʾaththir) together; and if the negation of the cause is precluded by the evidence of the senses (qarīnat al-ḥiss), then the preclusion is confined to it, and the effect remains negated. We say: His saying — "No fasting, no deed, no error, no forgetfulness" — or "Lifted are error and forgetfulness" is not general over the negation of the cause and the effect, such that when it is precluded regarding the cause, it remains regarding the effect. Rather, it is for the negation of the cause only. And the effect is negated necessarily by the negation of the cause, not by virtue of the generality of the expression and its inclusion of it. So when it is precluded from being carried upon the cause, it becomes metaphorical (majāz), either over all effects or over some effects; and the totality is not preponderant over the part, nor is one part preponderant over another.
