chapters.title_en: On Whether a General Term, When Particularized, Becomes Metaphorical in Its Remaining Application
chapters.arabic_text: ### | [القول في العموم إذا خص هل يصير مجازا في الباقي]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of encompassing, covering all parts without exception; the opposite of particularization (takhṣīṣ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ʿumūm denotes the logical extension of a term over all its referents by virtue of its linguistic form (ṣīghah), not by contextual inference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage applies the term to all individuals; metaphorical (majāz) usage would involve a transfer of meaning due to a constraint, which is the crux of the debate here.
- Root: خ-ص-ص (kh-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To single out, to distinguish, to set apart from the whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Takhṣīṣ is the restriction of a general term’s scope by a separate evidence (dalīl), without altering the term’s core lexical meaning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The question is whether such restriction forces a reclassification of the term from ḥaqīqah to majāz in the remaining instances, or whether the term remains literal in the residue.
- Root: م-ج-ز (m-j-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Passing through, crossing over; a word used in a non-original sense due to a relation (ʿalāqah) with a contextual indicator (qarīnah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Majāz in uṣūl is a term whose application to some referents is not by original linguistic convention but by extension, requiring a transfer of meaning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The debate hinges on whether the remaining referents after takhṣīṣ are still covered by the original ḥaqīqah or whether the term has become majāz in them, since the original comprehensive intent is broken.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAmal fī al-Bāqī (Operation on the Remainder) — When a general noun (ism ʿāmm) is restricted, the syntactic operation (ʿamal) of the term on the remaining individuals is assessed by whether the restriction is a mere external constraint (takhṣīṣ bi-al-dalīl) or an internal modification of the term’s meaning. If the former, the term remains ḥaqīqah in the residue; if the latter, it becomes majāz.
chapters.translation: I say: The discussion on whether a general term, when particularized, becomes metaphorical in its remaining application is a foundational inquiry in the science of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh). Know that the scholars have differed on this matter, and the correct position is that the general term, after particularization, remains literal (ḥaqīqah) in its remaining referents, not metaphorical (majāz). The proof of this is that the general term, in its original linguistic convention, was placed to encompass all individuals falling under its scope. When particularization occurs, it does not negate the term’s applicability to the remaining individuals; rather, it merely excludes those individuals that are not intended by the Lawgiver’s address. The exclusion is an external operation, not an alteration of the term’s core meaning. For if particularization rendered the term metaphorical in the residue, then every general term in the Qur’an and Sunnah that has been particularized would be deemed metaphorical, and this would lead to an unwarranted expansion of metaphorical usage, contradicting the principle that the default in language is literalness (aṣl al-ḥaqīqah). Furthermore, the remaining individuals are still covered by the term’s original meaning, for the term was not placed for the totality as a single indivisible meaning, but for each individual according to its commonality. Thus, the particularization is akin to the exclusion of a part from a whole, leaving the whole’s applicability to the rest intact. This is the view of the majority of the jurists and theologians, and it is the soundest in accordance with the principles of language and legal reasoning.

chapters.title_en: On the General (al-ʿĀmm) When It Is Particularized — Whether It Becomes Metaphorical (Majāz) in the Remainder, and Whether It Remains a Proof (Ḥujjah)
chapters.arabic_text:
القول في العموم إذا خص القول في العموم إذا خص هل يصير مجازا في الباقي،
وهل يبقى حجة؟ ، وهما نظران:
أما صيرورته مجازا فقد اختلفوا فيه على أربعة مذاهب: فقال قوم: يبقى
حقيقة لأنه كان متناولا لما بقي حقيقة فخروج غيره عنه لا يؤثر وقال قوم:
يصير مجازا لأنه وضع للعموم، فإذا أريد به غير ما وضع له بالقرينة  كان
مجازا، وإن لم يكن هذا مجازا فلا يبقى للمجاز معنى، ولا يكفي تناوله مع
غيره لأنه لا خلاف أنه لو رد إلى ما دون أقل الجمع صار مجازا فإذا قال: لا
تكلم الناس، ثم قال: أردت زيدا خاصة كان مجازا، وإن كان هو داخلا فيه وقال
قوم: هو حقيقة في تناوله مجاز في الاقتصار عليه.
وهذا ضعيف، فإنه لو رد إلى الواحد كان مجازا مطلقا لأنه تغير عن وضعه في
الدلالة فالسارق مهما صار عبارة عن سارق النصاب خاصة فقد تغير الوضع
واستعمل لا على الوجه الذي وضعته العرب وقد اختار القاضي في التفريع على
مذهب أرباب العموم أنه صار مجازا، لكن قال إنما يصير مجازا إذا أخرج منه
البعض بدليل منفصل من عقل أو نقل، أما ما خرج بلفظ متصل كالاستثناء فلا
يجعله مجازا بل يصير الكلام بسبب الزيادة المتصلة به كلاما آخر موضوعا لشيء
آخر، فإنا نزيد الواو، والنون في قولنا مسلم " فنقول " مسلمون " فيدل على
أمر زائد، ولا نجعله مجازا، ونزيد الألف، واللام على قولنا رجل " فنقول
الرجل " فيزيد فائدة أخرى، وهي التعريف؛ لأن هذه صارت صيغة أخرى بهذه
الزيادة فجاز أن يدل على معنى آخر، ولا فرق بين أن نزيد حرفا أو كلمة، فإذا
قال: يقطع السارق إلا من سرق دون النصاب كان مجموع هذا الكلام موضوعا
للدلالة على ما دل عليه، فقوله: تعالى: {فلبث فيهم ألف سنة إلا خمسين عاما}
[العنكبوت: 14] دل على تسعمائة، وخمسين لا على سبيل المجاز بل
الوضع كذلك وضع وكأن العرب وضعت عن تسعمائة، وخمسين عبارتين إحداهما ألف
سنة إلا خمسين، والأخرى تسعمائة، وخمسون، ويمكن أن يقال: ما صار عبارة
بالوضع عن هذا القدر بل بقي الألف للألف، والخمسون للخمسين، وإلا للرفع بعد
الإثبات، ونحن بعلم الحساب عرفنا أن هذا تسعمائة، وخمسون، فإنا إذا وضعنا
ألفا، ورفعنا خمسين علمنا مقدار الباقي بعلم الحساب فلا نقول المجموع صار
عبارة موضوعة عن هذا العدد، وهذا أدق، وأحق لا كزيادة الألف، واللام،
والياء،  والنون على المسلم فإن تلك الزيادة لا معنى لها بغير اللفظ الأول.
فإن قيل لو قال الله تعالى: {فاقتلوا المشركين} [التوبة: 5] فقال الرسول
متصلا به: " إلا زيدا " فهل يكون هذا كالمتصل الذي لا يجعل لفظ المشركين
مجازا في الباقي؟ قلنا: اختلفوا فيه، والظاهر أن هذا من غير المتكلم يجري
مجرى الدليل المنفصل من قياس العقل، والنقل، ولهذا لو قال زيد وقال غيره
قام، لا يصير خبرا حتى يصدر من الأول قوله: " قام " لأن نظم الكلام إنما
يكون من متكلم واحد، وذلك يجعله خبرا فإن قيل: فلو أخرج بالاستثناء عن لفظ
المشركين الجميع إلا زيدا فهل يصير لفظ المشركين مجازا؟ قلنا: نعم، لأنه
للجمع بالاتفاق، والخلاف في أنه مستغرق أو غير مستغرق فهو عند أرباب العموم
عند الاستثناء لجمع غير مستغرق دون الاستثناء لجمع مستغرق.
وأما النظر الثاني في كونه حجة في الباقي فقد قال قوم من القائلين
بالعموم: إنه لا يبقى حجة بل صار مجملا، وإليه ذهبت القدرية لأنه إذا لم
يترك على الوضع فلا يبقى للفهم معتمد سوى القرينة وتلك القرينة غير معينة
فلا يهتدى إليها، ومن هؤلاء من قال: أقل الجمع يبقى لأنه مستيقن واحتج
القائلون بكونه مجملا بأن السارق إذا خرج منه سارق ما دون النصاب، والسارق
من غير الحرز، ومن يستحق النفقة، وغير ذلك، فبم يفهم المراد منه على سبيل
الحصر وقد خرج الوضع من أيدينا، ولا قرينة تفصل، وتحصر فيبقى مجملا؟ ،
والصحيح أنه يبقى حجة إلا إذا استثنى منه مجهولا، كما لو قال " اقتلوا
المشركين إلا رجلا أما إذا استخرج منه معلوم فإنه يبقى دليلا في الباقي؛
ولأجله تمسك الصحابة بالعمومات.
وما من عموم إلا وقد تطرق إليه التخصيص، وهذا لأن لفظ السارق يتناول كل
سارق بالوضع لولا دليل مخصوص، والدليل المخصوص صرف دلالته عن البعض، ولا
مسقط لدلالته في الباقي نعم لا يدل اللفظ على إخراج ما خرج فافتقر إلى دليل
مخرج وقصوره عنه لا يدل على قصوره عن تناول الباقي، فمن قال: أعتق  رقبة ثم
قال لا تعتق معيبة، ولا كافرة، لم يخرج به كلامه الأول عن كونه مفهوما،
والرجوع في هذا إلى عادة اللسان، وأهل اللغة، وعادات الصحابة إذ لم يطرحوا
جميع عمومات الكتاب، والسنة لتطرق التخصيص إليها، وعلى الجملة كلام
الواقفية في العموم المخصص أظهر لا محالة.
فإن قيل: قد سلمتم أنه صار مجازا فيفتقر العمل به إلى دليل إذ المجاز لا
يعمل به إلا بدليل قلنا: هو حقيقة في وضعه، والدليل المخصص هو الذي جعله
مجازا، أما سقوط دلالة المجاز فلا وجه له لا سيما المجاز المعروف، فإنا
نتمسك به بغير دليل زائد، كقوله تعالى: {أو جاء أحد منكم من الغائط}
[المائدة: 6] فإنه، وإن كان مجازا فهو معروف وكذلك التفهيم بالعمومات
المخصصة معروف في اللسان، ولا يمكن اطراحه.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Encompassing, covering all parts; al-ʿāmm is that which comprehends its individuals without restriction.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl, al-ʿāmm denotes a lexical form whose import extends to every individual falling under its scope, with the theological nuance of exhaustive inclusion (istighrāq).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) when unrestricted; when particularized, the question arises whether the remaining application is literal or metaphorical — a shift from the original lexical convention (waḍʿ).
- Root: خ-ص-ص (kh-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Singling out, distinguishing a part from the whole; takhṣīṣ is the exclusion of certain individuals from the general term.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The specification of a general command by an indicator (dalīl), whether connected (muttaṣil) or separate (munfaṣil), narrowing its scope.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in its original coverage; metaphorical only if the intended meaning diverges from the waḍʿ via a qarīnah.
- Root: م-ج-ز (m-j-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Passing through, traversing; majāz is the permissible crossing of a word from its settled meaning to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A term used for other than its original referent due to a relation (ʿalāqah) and an indicator (qarīnah), with a theological caution against equivocation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz is the metaphorical extension; its validity depends on the qarīnah, distinguishing it from ḥaqīqah.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm bi-al-Ṣīghah (Attribution of Ruling to the Form) — The syntactic form (ṣīghah) determines the ruling; an appended exception (istithnāʾ) or additional particle (ḥarf) modifies the construction as a new whole, not as a metaphorical shift of the original term.
chapters.translation:
I say: The discourse on the general (al-ʿāmm) when it is particularized — does it become metaphorical (majāz) in the remainder, and does it remain a proof (ḥujjah)? These are two inquiries.

As for its becoming metaphorical, they have differed over it into four schools. A group said: It remains literal (ḥaqīqah), because it was, by its very nature, encompassing what remains as literal, so the exclusion of others from it has no effect. Another group said: It becomes metaphorical, because it was coined (wuḍiʿa) for generality; so when something other than its coinage is intended by it, via an indicator (qarīnah), it is metaphorical. If this were not metaphorical, then no meaning would remain for metaphor at all. Nor is it sufficient that it encompasses [the remainder] along with others, for there is no dispute that if it were reduced to below the least plural (aqall al-jamʿ), it would become metaphorical. Thus, if one says, "Do not speak to the people," then says, "I meant Zayd specifically," it is metaphorical, even though Zayd was included in it. Another group said: It is literal in its encompassing, metaphorical in restricting itself to [the remainder]. This is weak, for if it were reduced to the singular, it would be absolutely metaphorical, because it has changed from its coinage in indication. Thus, "the thief" (al-sāriq), whenever it becomes an expression for the thief of the nisāb (minimum amount) specifically, has changed its coinage and is used not in the manner the Arabs coined it.

Al-Qāḍī (Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī) chose, in his branching upon the school of the proponents of generality, that it becomes metaphorical. But he said: It only becomes metaphorical when some of it is excluded by a separate indicator (dalīl munfaṣil), whether rational or transmitted. As for what is excluded by a connected expression (lafẓ muttaṣil), like exception (istithnāʾ), that does not make it metaphorical. Rather, the speech, due to the connected addition, becomes another speech coined for another thing. For we add the wāw and nūn to our saying "muslim" and say "muslimūn" (Muslims), and it indicates an additional matter, yet we do not deem it metaphorical. We add the alif and lām to our saying "rajul" (a man) and say "al-rajul" (the man), and it adds another benefit, namely definition (taʿrīf). This is because, by this addition, it has become another form (ṣīghah), so it is permissible that it indicate another meaning. There is no difference between adding a letter or a word. So if one says, "Cut off [the hand of] the thief, except the one who steals less than the nisāb," the totality of this speech is coined to indicate what it indicates. Thus His saying, Exalted: {فلبث فيهم ألف سنة إلا خمسين عاما} [al-ʿAnkabūt: 14] — "And he remained among them a thousand years, except fifty years" — indicates nine hundred and fifty, not by way of metaphor, but rather the coinage is thus. It is as though the Arabs coined for nine hundred and fifty two expressions: one is "a thousand years except fifty," and the other is "nine hundred and fifty." Yet it may be said: It did not become an expression by coinage for this amount; rather, the thousand remains for the thousand, the fifty for the fifty, and "except" (illā) for the subtraction after affirmation. We, by the science of arithmetic, know that this is nine hundred and fifty. For when we posit a thousand and subtract fifty, we know the remainder by arithmetic. So we do not say the totality became a coined expression for this number. This is more precise and more correct — unlike the addition of the alif, lām, yāʾ, and nūn upon "muslim," for that addition has no meaning without the first word.

If it is said: If God, Exalted, says: {فاقتلوا المشركين} [al-Tawbah: 5] — "Kill the polytheists" — and the Messenger, peace be upon him, says connected to it: "Except Zayd," would this be like the connected [exception] that does not make the word "polytheists" metaphorical in the remainder? We say: They have differed over it. The apparent view is that this, coming from other than the speaker, runs the course of a separate indicator (dalīl munfaṣil), like rational analogy (qiyās al-ʿaql) and transmission (naql). For this reason, if Zayd said [something] and another said, "He stood," it does not become a report (khabar) until the first issues the statement "He stood," because the composition of speech (naẓm al-kalām) is only from a single speaker, and that makes it a report.

If it is said: If he excluded by exception from the word "polytheists" all except Zayd, would the word "polytheists" become metaphorical? We say: Yes, because it is, by agreement, for the plural (jamʿ). The dispute is whether it is exhaustive (mustaghriq) or non-exhaustive. Thus, in the view of the proponents of generality, with exception it is for a non-exhaustive plural; without exception, for an exhaustive plural.

As for the second inquiry — whether it remains a proof (ḥujjah) in the remainder — a group of those who affirm generality said: It does not remain a proof; rather, it becomes ambiguous (mujmal). This is the view of the Qadariyyah, because when it is not left upon its coinage, nothing remains for understanding to rely upon except the indicator (qarīnah), and that indicator is unspecified, so it cannot be guided to. Among these, some said: The least plural (aqall al-jamʿ) remains, because it is certain (mustayqan). Those who argued for its being ambiguous adduced that when the thief who steals less than the nisāb, the thief from a non-secured place, the one entitled to maintenance, and others are excluded from "the thief," how can the intended meaning be understood from it in an exhaustive manner? The coinage has left our hands, and there is no indicator that distinguishes and delimits, so it remains ambiguous.

The correct view is that it remains a proof, except when an unknown (majhūl) is excepted from it — as if one says, "Kill the polytheists, except a man." But when a known (maʿlūm) is extracted from it, it remains a proof in the remainder. For this reason, the Companions (al-ṣaḥābah) adhered to the general expressions (al-ʿumūmāt). And there is no general expression but that specification (takhṣīṣ) has reached it. This is because the word "thief" encompasses every thief by coinage, were it not for a specific indicator. The specific indicator diverted its indication from some [individuals], but there is nothing that nullifies its indication in the remainder. Indeed, the word does not indicate the exclusion of what was excluded, so it needed an excluding indicator. Its falling short of that does not indicate its falling short of encompassing the remainder. Thus, if one says, "Free a slave," then says, "Do not free a defective one, nor an unbelieving one," he has not thereby removed his first speech from being understood. The reference in this is to the custom of the tongue (ʿādat al-lisān), the people of language, and the customs of the Companions, since they did not discard all the general expressions of the Book and the Sunnah because specification reached them. In sum, the speech of the Wāqifiyyah (those who suspend judgment) regarding the particularized general is more manifest, without doubt.

If it is said: You have conceded that it became metaphorical, so acting upon it requires an indicator, since metaphor is not acted upon except with an indicator. We say: It is literal in its coinage, and the specifying indicator is what made it metaphorical. As for the fall of the indication of metaphor, there is no basis for it — especially the well-known metaphor (al-majāz al-maʿrūf). For we adhere to it without an additional indicator, like His saying, Exalted: {أو جاء أحد منكم من الغائط} [al-Māʾidah: 6] — "Or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself" — for although it is metaphorical, it is well-known. Likewise, the comprehension of particularized general expressions is well-known in the tongue, and it cannot be discarded.

chapters.title_en: The Second Chapter on Distinguishing What Can Be Claimed as General (ʿUmūm) from What Cannot — The Case of General Claim in What the Lawgiver Mentioned by Way of Initiation
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الباب الثاني في تمييز ما يمكن دعوى العموم فيه عما لا يمكن وفيه مسائل]

### | [مسألة دعوى العموم فيما ذكره الشارع على سبيل الابتداء]

الباب الثاني في تمييز ما يمكن دعوى العموم فيه عما لا يمكن تمييز ما
يمكن دعوى العموم فيه عما لا يمكن، وفيه مسائل:
مسألة: إنما يمكن دعوى العموم فيما ذكره الشارع على سبيل الابتداء؛
أما ما ذكره في جواب السائل فإنه ينظر فإن أتى بلفظ مستقل لو ابتدأ به
كان عاما، كما سئل عن بئر بضاعة فقال: «خلق الله الماء طهورا لا ينجسه شيء
إلا ما غير طعمه أو لونه أو ريحه» وكما سئل عن ماء البحر فقال: «هو الطهور
ماؤه الحل ميتته» .
وأما إذا لم يكن مستقلا نظر، فإن لم يكن لفظ السائل عاما فلا يثبت العموم
للجواب، كما لو قال السائل: توضأت بماء البحر فقال: يجزيك، أو قال: وطئت في
نهار رمضان، فقال: أعتق رقبة؛ فهذا لا عموم له لأنه خطاب مع شخص واحد،
وإنما يثبت الحكم في حق غيره بدليل مستأنف من قياس إذا ورد التعبد بالقياس
أو تعلق بقوله: - عليه السلام - «حكمي على الواحد حكمي على الجماعة» وذلك
بشرط أن يكون حال غيره مثل حاله  في كل وصف مؤثر في الحكم حتى لا يفترقا إلا
في الشخص، والأحوال التي لا مدخل لها في التفرقة من الطول، واللون،
وأمثاله، والذكورة، والأنوثة كالطول، واللون في بعض الأحكام كالعتق؛ ولذلك
قلنا حكمه في العبد بالسراية حكم في الأمة، وفي باب ولاية النكاح ليس كذلك،
إذ عرف من الشرع ترك الالتفات إلى الذكورة، والأنوثة في العتق، والرق، ولم
يعرف في النكاح، ولذلك نقول: روي في الصحيح أن «أبا بكر - رضي الله عنه -
أم بالناس في مرض النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - فخرج - عليه السلام - وهو
في أثناء الصلاة فهم بأن يتخلف فأشار عليه بالمنع، ووقف بجانبه واقتدى أبو
بكر بالنبي» - عليه السلام - واستمر الناس على الاقتداء بأبي بكر - رضي
الله عنه - وصلى الناس بصلاة أبي بكر وصلى أبو بكر بصلاة النبي - عليه
السلام -.
، وفيه اقتداء الإمام بغيره واقتداء الناس بالمقتدي بغيره، وليس يظهر لنا
أن غير رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في معنى النبي - عليه السلام -،
فإن التقدم عليه مع حضوره مستبعد فيما يرجع إلى الإمامة وللنبوة فيها
تأثير، وهذا فعل خاص لا عموم له، ودعوى الإلحاق تحكم مع ظهور الفرق، ولا
عموم يتعلق به، بل قوله: لعبد الرحمن بن عوف: «البس الحرير» ولأبي بردة بن
نيار في الأضحية «بجذعة من الضأن: تجزيك» ، وإذنه للعرنيين بشرب أبوال
الإبل وقوله: لعمر «مره فليراجعها» لا عموم لشيء منه فيفتقر تعميمه إلى
دليل مستأنف من قياس أو غيره أما ما نقل من اقتداء الناس بأبي بكر مع
اقتدائه بالنبي - عليه السلام - فيحتمل أن مقتدى الكل كان بالنبي وكان أبو
بكر سفيرا برفع الصوت بالتكبيرات.
أما إذا كان لفظ السائل عاما نزل منزلة عموم لفظ الشارع كما لو سأله سائل
عمن أفطر في نهار رمضان فقال: أعتق رقبة، كان كما لو قال: من أفطر في نهار
رمضان أعتق رقبة لأنه يجيب عن السؤال فلا يكون الجواب إلا مطابقا للسؤال أو
أعم منه فأما أخص منه فلا. أما لو قال السائل: أفطر زيد  في نهار رمضان
فقال: عليه عتق رقبة أو قال طلق ابن عمر زوجته، فقال: «مره فليراجعها» فهذا
لا عموم له، فلعله عرف من حاله ما يوجب العتق، والمراجعة عليه خاصة، ولا
نعرف ما تلك الحال، ومن الذي يساويه فيها، ولا يدرى أنه أفطر عمدا، وسهوا
أو بأكل أو جماع فإن قيل ترك الاستفصال مع تعارض الأحوال يدل على عموم
الحكم، وهذا من كلام الشافعي قلنا: من أين تحقق
ذلك؟ ولعله - عليه السلام - عرف خصوص الحال فأجاب بناء على معرفته، ولم
يستفصل، فهذا تقرير عموم بالوهم المجرد.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehensiveness, encompassing all members of a category without exception; the opposite of particularity (khuṣūṣ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ʿumūm denotes the extension of a legislative ruling (ḥukm) to every individual falling under the linguistic scope of the term, as established by the Lawgiver's usage.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) when the term's generality is intrinsic to its lexical form (e.g., al-nās, kull); metaphorical (majāz) when generality is inferred from context or supplementary evidence.
- Root: ج-و-ب (j-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Returning a response; answering a question or address.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, the answer (jawāb) is semantically constrained by the question (suʾāl); its scope cannot exceed or contradict the interrogative's presuppositions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal correspondence between question and answer; if the answer is more specific (akhaṣṣ) than the question, it is a departure from the norm requiring external justification.
- Root: ب-د-أ (b-d-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beginning, initiating; that which is said without prior prompting or context.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Initiation (ibtidāʾ) in legislative speech establishes the default authority of the Lawgiver's own wording, free from the constraints of an interlocutor's framing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal when the Lawgiver's statement stands alone as a primary ruling; metaphorical when it is contingent upon a prior question, shifting the interpretive burden.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taṭābuq al-jawāb li-l-suʾāl (Correspondence of the answer to the question) — The syntactic and semantic structure of a response must align with the scope of the interrogative; a general answer to a specific question is permissible, but a specific answer to a general question is anomalous unless the questioner's intent is particularized.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second chapter concerns distinguishing what can be claimed as general (ʿumūm) from what cannot, and it contains several issues (masāʾil).

**Issue**: Generality (ʿumūm) can only be claimed for what the Lawgiver mentioned by way of initiation (ibtidāʾ). As for what He mentioned in response to a questioner, then we examine it: if He came with an independent expression (lafẓ mustaqill) that, had it been initiated, would have been general — such as when He was asked about the well of Biḍāʿah and said: «God created water as purifying; nothing defiles it except that which changes its taste, color, or odor» — and likewise when He was asked about seawater and said: «Its water is purifying, its carrion is lawful» — then generality is established.

But if the response was not independent, we examine further: if the questioner's wording was not general, then generality is not established for the answer. For example, if the questioner said: "I performed ablution with seawater," and he replied: "It suffices you," or said: "I had intercourse during the day of Ramadan," and he replied: "Free a slave" — this has no generality, because it is a discourse addressed to a single person. The ruling is only established for others through a fresh proof (dalīl mustaʾnaf) from analogy (qiyās), if one is bound to act by analogy, or by attachment to his saying — peace be upon him — «My ruling upon the one is my ruling upon the congregation» — provided that the state of the other person is like his state in every attribute affecting the ruling, so that they differ only in personhood, and in circumstances that have no bearing on differentiation, such as height, color, and the like, and masculinity and femininity — like height and color in certain rulings such as manumission. For this reason, we say: his ruling regarding the male slave regarding the inclusion (sarāyah) of manumission is a ruling regarding the female slave, but in the chapter of marriage guardianship (wilāyat al-nikāḥ) it is not so, because it is known from the Law that attention is not paid to masculinity and femininity in manumission and slavery, but this is not known in marriage.

For this reason, we say: it is related in the Ṣaḥīḥ that «Abū Bakr — may God be pleased with him — led the people in prayer during the illness of the Prophet — peace be upon him — and he — peace be upon him — came out while he was in the midst of the prayer, and he intended to step back, but Abū Bakr gestured to him to desist, and he stood by his side, and Abū Bakr followed the Prophet — peace be upon him — and the people continued to follow Abū Bakr — may God be pleased with him — and the people prayed with the prayer of Abū Bakr, and Abū Bakr prayed with the prayer of the Prophet — peace be upon him.»

In this there is the following of an imam by someone other than himself, and the following of the people by one who follows another. But it is not apparent to us that anyone other than the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — is in the same meaning (maʿnā) as the Prophet — peace be upon him — for advancing before him in his presence is inconceivable with respect to the imamate, and prophethood has an effect therein. This is a specific act (fiʿl khāṣṣ) with no generality, and claiming its extension (ilḥāq) is arbitrary (taḥakkum) given the apparent difference, and there is no generality to which one may attach. Rather, his saying to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf: «Wear silk,» and to Abū Burdah ibn Niyār regarding the sacrifice: «A young sheep (jadhʿah) of the flock suffices you,» and his permission to the ʿUraynīs to drink camel urine, and his saying to ʿUmar: «Order him to take her back» — none of these has generality, so extending them requires a fresh proof from analogy or otherwise.

As for what is transmitted of the people's following Abū Bakr while he followed the Prophet — peace be upon him — it is possible that the object of everyone's following was the Prophet, and Abū Bakr was merely a transmitter (safīr) raising his voice with the takbīrs.

But if the questioner's wording was general, it takes the rank of the generality of the Lawgiver's wording. For example, if someone asked him about one who breaks his fast during the day of Ramadan, and he said: "Free a slave," it is as if he said: "Whoever breaks his fast during the day of Ramadan, let him free a slave" — because he answers the question, and the answer cannot be anything but conforming to the question or more general than it; it cannot be more specific than it. But if the questioner said: "Zayd broke his fast during the day of Ramadan," and he said: "Upon him is the freeing of a slave," or said: "Ibn ʿUmar divorced his wife," and he said: «Order him to take her back» — this has no generality, for perhaps he knew from his state something that necessitated the manumission and the return (murājaʿah) specifically for him. We do not know what that state was, nor who equals him in it, nor is it known whether he broke his fast intentionally or forgetfully, or by eating or by intercourse.

If it is said: "The omission of further inquiry (istifṣāl) despite conflicting states indicates the generality of the ruling — and this is from the speech of al-Shāfiʿī" — we say: whence is that established? Perhaps he — peace be upon him — knew the particularity of the state and answered based on his knowledge, without inquiring further. Thus, this would be an establishment of generality by mere conjecture (wahm mujarrad).

chapters.title_en: The General Word (ʿĀmm) Occurring Upon a Specific Cause Does Not Negate Its Claim to Generality
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة ورود العام على سبب خاص لا يسقط دعوى العموم]

ورود العام على سبب خاص لا يسقط دعوى العموم،
كقوله: - صلى الله عليه وسلم - حيث مر بشاة ميمونة «أيما إهاب دبغ فقد
طهر» وقال قوم: يسقط عمومه، وهو خطأ، نعم يصير احتمال التخصيص أقرب، ويقنع
فيه بدليل أخف، وأضعف، وقد يعرف بقرينة اختصاصه بالواقعة كما إذا قيل كلم
فلانا في واقعة، فقال: والله لا أكلمه أبدا فإنه يفهم بالقرينة أنه يريد
ترك الكلام في تلك الواقعة لا على الإطلاق.
والدليل على بقاء العموم أن الحجة في لفظ الشارع لا في السؤال، والسبب
ولذلك يجوز أن يكون الجواب معدولا عن سنن السؤال حتى لو قال السائل: أيحل
شرب الماء، وأكل الطعام والاصطياد؟ فيقول: الأكل واجب، والشرب مندوب،
والصيد حرام فيجب اتباع هذه الأحكام، وإن كان فيه حظر، ووجوب، والسؤال وقع
عن الإباحة فقط؛ وكيف ينكر هذا، وأكثر أصول الشرع خرجت على أسباب كقوله
تعالى: {، والسارق والسارقة} [المائدة: 38] في سرقة المجن أو رداء صفوان،
ونزلت آية الظهار في سلمة بن صخر، وآية اللعان في هلال بن أمية وكل ذلك على
العموم. وشبه المخالفين ثلاث: الأولى: أنه لو لم يكن للسبب تأثير، والنظر
إلى اللفظ خاصة فينبغي أن يجوز إخراج السبب بحكم التخصيص عن عموم المسميات
كما لو لم يرد على سبب قلنا: لا خلاف في أن كلامه بيان للواقعة، لكن الكلام
في أنه بيان له خاصة  أو له ولغيره، واللفظ يعمه، ويعم غيره، وتناوله له
مقطوع به، وتناوله لغيره ظاهر، فلا يجوز أن يسأل عن شيء فيجيب عن غيره نعم
يجوز أن يجيب عنه، وعن غيره، ويجوز أيضا أن يجيب عن غيره بما ينبه على محل
السؤال، كما «قال لعمر: أرأيت لو تمضمضت» وقد سأله عن القبلة وقال
للخثعمية: «أرأيت لو كان على أبيك دين فقضيتيه» .
الشبهة الثانية: أنه لو لم يكن للسبب مدخل لما نقله الراوي، إذ لا فائدة
فيه. قلنا: فائدته معرفة أسباب التنزيل، والسير، والقصص، واتساع علم
الشريعة، وأيضا امتناع إخراج السبب بحكم التخصيص بالاجتهاد؛ ولذلك غلط أبو
حنيفة - رحمه الله - في إخراج الأمة المستفرشة من قوله: «الولد للفراش»
والخبر إنما ورد في وليدة زمعة إذ قال عبد بن زمعة هو أخي، وابن وليدة أبي
ولد على فراشه، فقال - عليه السلام -: «الولد للفراش وللعاهر الحجر» فأثبت
للأمة فراشا،، وأبو حنيفة لم يبلغه السبب فأخرج الأمة من العموم.
الشبهة الثالثة: أنه لولا أن المراد بيان السبب لما أخر البيان إلى وقوع
الواقعة، فإن الغرض إذا كان تمهيد قاعدة عامة فلم أخرها إلى وقوع واقعة؟
قلنا: ولم قلتم لا فائدة في تأخيره، والله تعالى أعلم بفائدته؟ ولم طلبتم
لأفعال الله فائدة؟ بل لله تعالى أن ينشئ التكليف في أي وقت شاء، ولا يسأل
عما يفعل. ثم نقول: لعله علم أن تأخيره إلى الواقعة لطف، ومصلحة للعباد
داعية إلى الانقياد، ولا يحصل ذلك بالتقديم، والتأخير. ثم نقول: يلزم لهذه
العلة اختصاص الرجم بماعز، والظهار، واللعان وقطع السرقة بالأشخاص الذين
ورد فيهم؛ لأن الله تعالى أخر البيان إلى وقوع وقائعهم، وذلك خلاف الإجماع.

### | [مسألة المقتضى لا عموم له]

المقتضى لا عموم له، وإنما العموم للألفاظ لا للمعاني
فتضمنها من ضرورة الألفاظ. بيانه أن قوله: «لا صيام لمن لم يبيت الصيام»
ظاهره ينفي صورة الصوم حسا لكن وجب رده إلى الحكم، وهو نفي الإجزاء أو
الكمال وقد قيل إنه: متردد بينهما فهو مجمل وقيل: إنه عام لنفي الإجزاء،
والكمال، وهو غلط نعم لو قال: لا حكم لصوم بغير تبييت لكان الحكم لفظا عاما
في الإجزاء، والكمال، أما إذا قال لا صيام، فالحكم غير منطوق به، وإنما
أثبت ذلك من طريق الضرورة.
وكذلك قوله: - عليه السلام -: «رفع عن أمتي الخطأ، والنسيان» معناه حكم
الخطإ، والنسيان، ولا عموم له، ولو قال لا حكم للخطإ لأمكن حمله على نفي
الإثم، والغرم، وغير ذلك لا على العموم في الإجزاء، والكمال؛ لأن الإجزاء،
والصحة إذا انتفيا كان انتفاء الكمال ضرورة، وإنما العموم ما يشتمل على
معنيين يمكن انتفاء كل واحد منهما دون الآخر
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of encompassing, covering, and including all members of a category without exception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ʿumūm denotes the linguistic scope of a term that extends to every individual (afrād) falling under its semantic domain, unless a specifier (mukhaṣṣiṣ) intervenes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of ʿumūm is comprehensive inclusion; its metaphorical (majāz) application would be claiming generality where the context restricts it to a particular incident.
- Root: س-ب-ب (s-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A cause, occasion, or connecting link; that which leads to something else.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sabab is the incidental occasion for revelation or utterance, distinct from the intended legislative import (maʿnā).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally a rope or cord that ties; metaphorically, the occasioning circumstance that does not delimit the universal predicate.
- Root: خ-ص-ص (kh-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To single out, particularize, or distinguish a part from the whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Takhṣīṣ is the restriction of a general term to a subset of its individuals by evidence (dalīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal is setting apart; the metaphorical is the juristic operation of narrowing ʿumūm.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Maḥdhūf (Ellipsis Restoration) — When a general noun (e.g., "no fasting") is uttered, the predicate must be reconstructed by necessity (ḍarūrah) to refer to the legal ruling (ḥukm), not the physical act, since the literal sense is impossible.
chapters.translation:
### | [Issue: The General Word Occurring Upon a Specific Cause Does Not Negate Its Claim to Generality]

The occurrence of a general word upon a specific cause does not negate its claim to generality. For example, his saying — peace be upon him — when he passed by a sheep belonging to Maymūnah: «Any hide that is tanned has been purified» (ayyumā ihāb dubigha fa-qad ṭahura). But some people said: its generality is negated — and this is an error. Yes, the probability of specification (takhṣīṣ) becomes more likely, and a lighter and weaker piece of evidence suffices for it. And it may be known by a contextual indicator (qarīnah) that it is specific to the incident, as when one says: "Speak to so-and-so regarding such-and-such an incident," and he replies: "By God, I will never speak to him ever." For it is understood by the context that he intends to abandon speaking about that particular incident, not absolutely.

The proof that generality remains is that the authoritative evidence (ḥujjah) lies in the wording of the Lawgiver, not in the question or the cause. For this reason, it is permissible that the answer deviate from the course of the question — such that if the questioner asks: "Is drinking water, eating food, and hunting permissible?" and he replies: "Eating is obligatory, drinking is recommended, and hunting is forbidden" — then these rulings must be followed, even though they contain prohibition and obligation, while the question was only about permissibility. And how can this be denied, when most of the principles of the Sacred Law were issued upon specific causes, as His saying — exalted be He: {And the male thief and the female thief} [al-Māʾidah: 38] — was revealed regarding the theft of the shield (mijan) or the cloak of Ṣafwān; and the verse of ẓihār was revealed concerning Salamah ibn Ṣakhr; and the verse of liʿān concerning Hilāl ibn Umayyah — and all of that is upon generality.

The opponents' doubts are three:

**The First Doubt:** If the cause had no effect, and consideration is given to the wording alone, then it should be permissible to exclude the cause itself by way of specification from the generality of the named individuals, just as if it had not occurred upon a cause. We say: There is no disagreement that his speech is an explanation (bayān) of the incident — but the dispute is whether it is an explanation of it alone, or of it and others. The wording encompasses it and encompasses others; its inclusion of it is certain (maqṭūʿ bih), while its inclusion of others is apparent (ẓāhir). Thus it is not permissible that he be asked about something and answer about something else. Yes, it is permissible that he answer about it and about others; and it is also permissible that he answer about others in a manner that alerts to the locus of the question — as he said to ʿUmar: "What do you think if you had rinsed your mouth?" — when ʿUmar had asked him about kissing (while fasting); and he said to the Khathʿamiyyah woman: "What do you think if your father had a debt and you paid it?"

**The Second Doubt:** If the cause had no bearing, then the narrator would not have transmitted it, since there would be no benefit in it. We say: Its benefit is the knowledge of the occasions of revelation (asbāb al-tanzīl), the biographies (siyar), the narratives (qaṣaṣ), and the expansion of the knowledge of the Sacred Law. Also, it prevents the exclusion of the cause by way of specification through personal reasoning (ijtihād). For this reason, Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — erred in excluding the enslaved concubine (al-ummah al-mustafrashah) from his saying: «The child belongs to the bed» (al-walad lil-firāsh). For the report was only issued regarding the slave-girl of Zamʿah, when ʿAbd ibn Zamʿah said: "He is my brother, and he is the son of my father's slave-girl, born on his bed." So he — peace be upon him — said: «The child belongs to the bed, and for the fornicator is the stone» (al-walad lil-firāsh wa lil-ʿāhir al-ḥajar). Thus he established a bed for the slave-girl. But Abū Ḥanīfah did not learn of the cause, so he excluded the slave-girl from the generality.

**The Third Doubt:** Were the intent not the explanation of the cause, the explanation would not have been delayed until the occurrence of the incident — for if the purpose were to lay down a general rule, why was it delayed until an incident occurred? We say: Why do you claim there is no benefit in its delay — and God — exalted be He — knows best its benefit? And why do you seek a benefit for God's acts? Rather, God — exalted be He — may originate obligation (taklīf) at whatever time He wills, and He is not asked about what He does. Then we say: Perhaps He knew that delaying it until the incident was a kindness (luṭf) and a benefit (maṣlaḥah) for the servants, impelling them to submission — and that would not be achieved by advancing or delaying. Then we say: By this very reasoning, one would be compelled to restrict stoning (rajm) to Māʿiz, and ẓihār, and liʿān, and the amputation for theft to the specific persons regarding whom they were revealed — because God delayed the explanation until their incidents occurred — and that is contrary to consensus (ijmāʿ).

### | [Issue: The Implied Predicate (al-Muqtaḍā) Has No Generality]

The implied predicate (al-muqtaḍā) has no generality; rather, generality belongs to words, not to meanings — for the implied meaning is entailed by the necessity of the words. Its clarification: His saying — peace be upon him: «No fasting for one who does not intend (yubayyit) the fast at night» — its apparent sense negates the physical form of fasting (ṣūrat al-ṣawm) sensorily, but it was necessary to redirect it to the ruling (ḥukm), namely the negation of validity (ijzāʾ) or perfection (kamāl). And it has been said that it is ambiguous (mujmal) between the two; and it has been said that it is general in negating both validity and perfection — and this is an error. Yes, had he said: "No ruling for a fast without night-intention," then "ruling" would be a word general over validity and perfection. But when he said "no fasting," the ruling is not uttered; rather, it is established only by way of necessity (ḍarūrah).

Likewise, his saying — peace be upon him: «Lifted from my community are error and forgetfulness» (rufiʿa ʿan ummatī al-khaṭaʾ wa al-nisyān) — its meaning is the ruling of error and forgetfulness, and it has no generality. Had he said "no ruling for error," it would be possible to construe it as negating sin (ithm), indemnity (ghurm), and other things — not as general over validity and perfection; because when validity and soundness are negated, the negation of perfection follows by necessity. Rather, generality is that which encompasses two meanings, each of which can be negated independently of the other.

chapters.title_en: The Transitive Verb and Its Objects: On Generality (ʿUmūm) and the Acts of the Prophet (ʿAlayhi al-Salām)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة الفعل المتعدي إلى مفعول]

اختلفوا في أنه بالإضافة إلى مفعولاته هل يجري مجرى العموم الفعل المتعدي
إلى مفعول اختلفوا في أنه بالإضافة إلى مفعولاته هل يجري مجرى العموم؟
فقال أصحاب أبي حنيفة: لا عموم له حتى لو قال: والله لا آكل، ونوى طعاما
بعينه، أو قال: إن أكلت فأنت طالق، ونوى طعاما بعينه لم يقبل، وكذلك إذا
نوى بالضرب آلة بعينها. واستدل أصحاب أبي حنيفة بأن هذا من قبيل المقتضى
فلا عموم له، لأن الأكل يستدعي مأكولا بالضرورة لا أن اللفظ تعرض له، فما
ليس منطوقا لا عموم له فالمكان للخروج، والطعام للأكل، والآلة للضرب كالوقت
للفعل، والحال للفاعل، ولو قال: " أنت طالق " ثم قال: " أردت به إن دخلت
الدار " أو " أردت به يوم الجمعة " لم يقبل. وكذلك قالوا: لو نوى بقوله: "
أنت طالق " عددا لم يجزه وجوز أصحاب الشافعي ذلك، والإنصاف أن هذا ليس من
قبيل المقتضى، ولا هو من قبيل الوقت، والحال، فإن اللفظ المتعدي إلى
المفعول يدل على المفعول بصيغته، ووضعه، فأما الحال، والوقت فمن ضرورة وجود
الأشياء لكن لا تعلق له بالألفاظ، والمقتضى هو ضرورة صدق الكلام كقوله: لا
صيام، أو ضرورة وجود المذكور كقوله: أعتق عني فإنه على حصول الملك قبله لا
من حيث اللفظ لكن من حيث كون الملك شرطا لتصور العتق شرعا، أما الأكل فيدل
على المأكول، والضرب على الآلة، والخروج على  المكان، وتتشابه نسبته إلى
الجميع فهو بالعموم أشبه.
فإن قيل لا خلاف في أنه لو أمر بالأكل، والضرب، والخروج كان ممتثلا بكل
طعام، وبكل آلة وكل مكان، ولو علق العتق حصل بالجميع، فهذا يدل على العموم.
قلنا: ليس ذلك لأجل العموم، ولكن لأجل أن ما علق عليه وجدوا الآلة،
والمكان، والمأكول غير متعرض له أصلا، حتى لو تصور هذه الأفعال دون الطعام،
والآلة، والمكان، والمأكول يحصل الامتثال، وهو كالوقت، والحال فإنه إن أكل،
وهو داخل في الدار أو خارج وراكب أو راجل حنث وكان ممتثلا لا لعموم اللفظ
لكن لحصول الملفوظ في الأحوال كلها، وإنما تظهر فائدة العموم في إرادة بعض
هذه الأمور.، والأظهر عندنا جواز نية البعض، وأنه جار مجرى العموم، ومفارق
للمقتضى كما ذكرنا

### | [مسألة دعوى العموم في الفعل]

مسألة لا يمكن دعوى العموم في الفعل
دعوى العموم في الفعل
لأن الفعل لا يقع إلا على وجه معين، فلا يجوز أن يحمل على كل وجه يمكن أن
يقع عليه لأن سائر الوجوه متساوية بالنسبة إلى
محتملاته، والعموم ما يتساوى بالنسبة إلى دلالة اللفظ عليه، بل الفعل
كاللفظ المجمل المتردد بين معان متساوية في صلاح اللفظ.
ومثاله ما روي عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - «أنه صلى بعد غيبوبة
الشفق» فقال قائل: الشفق شفقان الحمرة، والبياض، وأنا أحمله على وقوع صلاة
رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - بعدهما جميعا وكذلك صلى رسول الله - صلى
الله عليه وسلم - في الكعبة فليس لقائل أن يستدل به على جواز الفرض في
البيت مصيرا إلى أن الصلاة تعم النفل، والفرض لأنه إنما يعم لفظ الصلاة لا
فعل الصلاة، أما الفعل فإما أن يكون فرضا فلا يكون نفلا أو يكون نفلا فلا
يكون فرضا.

### | [مسألة فعل النبي]

- عليه السلام - كما لا عموم له بالإضافة إلى أحوال الفعل فلا عموم له
بالإضافة إلى غيره
بل يكون خاصا في حقه إلا أن يقول: أريد بالفعل بيان حكم الشرع في حقكم
كما قال «صلوا كما رأيتموني أصلي»  بل نزيد، ونقول: قوله تعالى: {يا أيها
النبي اتق الله} [الأحزاب: 1] وقوله: {لئن أشركت ليحبطن عملك} [الزمر: 65]
يختص به بحكم اللفظ، وإنما يشاركه غيره بدليل لا بموجب هذا اللفظ، كقوله:
{يا أيها الرسول بلغ ما أنزل إليك من ربك} [المائدة: 67] وقوله تعالى:
{فاصدع بما تؤمر} [الحجر: 94] وقال قوم ما ثبت في حقه فهو ثابت في حق غيره
إلا ما دل الدليل على أنه خاص به، وهذا فاسد لأن الأحكام إذ قسمت إلى خاص،
وعام فالأصل اتباع موجب الخطاب فما ثبت بمثل قوله تعالى: {يا أيها الذين
آمنوا} [البقرة: 104] ، و {يا أيها الناس} [البقرة: 21] ، و {يا عبادي}
[الزمر: 53] ، ويا {أيه المؤمنون} [النور: 31] فيتناول النبي إلا ما استثني
بدليل، وما ثبت للنبي كقوله: {يا أيها النبي} [الأنفال: 64] فيختص به إلا
ما دل الدليل على الإلحاق.
وقوله تعالى: {يا أيها النبي إذا طلقتم النساء} [الطلاق: 1] عام لأن ذكر
النبي جرى في صدر الكلام تشريفا، وإلا فقوله: {طلقتم} [الطلاق: 1] عام في
صيغته. وكذلك قول النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - لأبي هريرة " افعل " ولابن
عمر " راجعها " خاص إنما يشمل الحكم غيره بدليل آخر مثل قوله: «حكمي على
الواحد حكمي على الجماعة» أو ما جرى مجراه.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To encompass, include, or cover all particulars; generality as opposed to particularity (khuṣūṣ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ʿumūm denotes the linguistic form's comprehensive extension over all its referents by virtue of its wording (lafẓ), not by extrinsic inference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah: the literal scope of a general term over all instances; Majāz: when generality is claimed for what is merely implied (muqtaḍā) or circumstantial, it is metaphorical and rejected.
- Root: ق-ض-ي (q-ḍ-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To necessitate, require, or demand; the muqtaḍā is that which the truth or existence of a statement logically entails.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The necessary implication of speech (muqtaḍā al-kalām) — e.g., "I freed (a slave) for you" necessitates prior ownership, not by wording but by legal condition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: what the wording itself signifies; Metaphorical: what is entailed by the very existence of the act (e.g., time and state of the agent), which has no bearing on the wording.
- Root: ف-ع-ل (f-ʿ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To do, perform, or act; the verb (fiʿl) as an event occurring in a specific manner.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act (fiʿl) of the Prophet is a revealed datum (bayān) but carries no generality over its modes or objects unless explicitly stated.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the act occurs in one determinate mode; Metaphorical: claiming it covers all possible modes is an unwarranted extension.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿaddī al-Fiʿl (Transitivity) — A transitive verb (fiʿl mutaʿaddin) governs its object (mafʿūl) by its own syntactic form (ṣīghah) and lexical disposition (waḍʿ), unlike circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl, ẓarf) which are governed by the verb's occurrence in time and place, not by the wording's intention.
chapters.translation:
### | [Issue: The Transitive Verb and Its Object]

They differed concerning whether a transitive verb, in relation to its objects, runs the course of generality (ʿumūm). The companions of Abū Ḥanīfah said: It has no generality. Thus, if one swore, "By Allah, I will not eat," intending a specific food, or said, "If I eat, you are divorced," intending a specific food, it is not accepted (from him in his intention). Likewise, if he intended by "striking" a specific instrument. The companions of Abū Ḥanīfah argued that this falls under the category of the implied requisite (muqtaḍā), which has no generality, because eating necessarily requires an edible thing — not that the wording addresses it. Whatever is not uttered (manṭūq) has no generality. Thus, the place for "going out," the food for "eating," and the instrument for "striking" are like the time for the act and the state (ḥāl) for the agent. If one said, "You are divorced," then claimed, "I meant by it 'if you enter the house'" or "I meant by it 'on Friday,'" it would not be accepted. Likewise, they said: If he intended by his statement "You are divorced" a specific number, it is not permissible. The companions of al-Shāfiʿī permitted that. The fair assessment is that this is neither of the category of the implied requisite (muqtaḍā), nor of the category of time and state. For the transitive verb indicates its object by its very form (ṣīghah) and lexical disposition (waḍʿ). As for the state and time, they are necessities of the existence of things, but they have no attachment to the wording. The muqtaḍā is the necessity of the truthfulness of speech — like his saying "no fasting" — or the necessity of the existence of the mentioned thing — like his saying "manumit on my behalf," which requires prior ownership, not by virtue of the wording, but by virtue of ownership being a condition for the legal validity of manumission. As for eating, it indicates the edible; striking indicates the instrument; going out indicates the place. Its relation to all of these is uniform, so it is more akin to generality.

If it is said: There is no dispute that if one were commanded to eat, strike, and go out, he would be compliant with any food, any instrument, and any place; and if divorce were suspended on it, it would occur with all of these — this indicates generality. We say: That is not due to generality, but because what the act is suspended upon is realized, while the instrument, place, and edible are not attended to at all. Even if these acts could be conceived without food, instrument, place, and edible, compliance would still be achieved. It is like time and state: if one eats while inside the house or outside, riding or walking, he breaks his oath and is compliant — not due to the generality of the wording, but due to the occurrence of the uttered act in all states. The benefit of generality only appears in intending some of these matters. The more apparent (al-aẓhar) position with us is the permissibility of intending some [of them], and that it runs the course of generality, differing from the muqtaḍā as we have mentioned.

### | [Issue: The Claim of Generality in the Act]

Issue: Generality cannot be claimed for the act. Because the act only occurs in a specific mode (wajh muʿayyan), it cannot be carried upon every mode in which it could occur, since the remaining modes are equal in relation to its possibilities, whereas generality is what is equal in relation to the wording's indication of it. Rather, the act is like an ambiguous word (mujmal) oscillating between meanings equal in their suitability for the wording.

Its example is what is narrated from the Prophet — peace be upon him — «that he prayed after the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq)». Someone said: The twilight is of two kinds — the redness and the whiteness — and I carry it upon the occurrence of the Messenger of Allah's — peace be upon him — prayer after both of them. Likewise, the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — prayed inside the Kaʿbah. It is not for anyone to use this as evidence for the permissibility of the obligatory prayer inside the House, by recourse to the claim that prayer (ṣalāh) encompasses the supererogatory and the obligatory. For it is the word "prayer" that is general, not the act of praying. As for the act, either it is obligatory and thus not supererogatory, or it is supererogatory and thus not obligatory.

### | [Issue: The Act of the Prophet]

— peace be upon him — just as it has no generality in relation to the modes of the act, so too it has no generality in relation to others. Rather, it is specific to him, unless he says: "I intend by the act to explain the legal ruling (ḥukm al-sharʿ) regarding you," as he said: «Pray as you have seen me praying». Rather, we add and say: His statement — exalted be He — {O Prophet, fear Allah} [al-Aḥzāb: 1] and His statement {If you associate [with Allah], your work would surely become worthless} [al-Zumar: 65] are specific to him by virtue of the wording. Others only share in it by evidence (dalīl), not by the requirement of this wording — like His statement {O Messenger, convey that which has been sent down to you from your Lord} [al-Māʾidah: 67] and His statement — exalted be He — {So proclaim that which you are commanded} [al-Ḥijr: 94]. Some said: Whatever is established regarding him is established regarding others, except what evidence indicates is specific to him. This is corrupt, because since rulings are divided into specific and general, the principle is to follow the requirement of the address (muqtaḍā al-khiṭāb). Thus, what is established by His statement — exalted be He — {O you who have believed} [al-Baqarah: 104], {O mankind} [al-Baqarah: 21], {O My servants} [al-Zumar: 53], and {O you believing women} [al-Nūr: 31] includes the Prophet, except what is excluded by evidence. And what is established for the Prophet — like His statement {O Prophet} [al-Anfāl: 64] — is specific to him, except what evidence indicates should be extended to others.

His statement — exalted be He — {O Prophet, when you divorce women} [al-Ṭalāq: 1] is general, because the mention of the Prophet occurs at the head of the speech as an honor (tashrīf). Otherwise, His statement {you divorce} [al-Ṭalāq: 1] is general in its form. Likewise, the Prophet's — peace be upon him — statement to Abū Hurayrah "Do [it]" and to Ibn ʿUmar "Take her back" is specific; it only extends the ruling to others by another evidence — like his saying: «My ruling upon the one is my ruling upon the group» — or what runs its course.

chapters.title_en: The Statement of a Companion: "The Prophet (peace be upon him) Prohibited Such-and-Such" — On the Absence of Generality (ʿUmūm) in Reported Prohibitions and Judgments
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مسألة قول الصحابي نهى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن كذا]

مسألة قول الصحابي: " نهى النبي - عليه السلام - عن كذا " كبيع الغرر،
ونكاح الشغار، وغيره لا عموم له لأن الحجة في المحكي لا في قول الحاكي،
ولفظه، وما رواه الصحابي من حكى النهي يحتمل أن يكون فعلا لا عموم له نهى
عنه النبي - عليه السلام -، ويحتمل أن يكون لفظا خاصا، ويحتمل أن يكون لفظا
عاما فإذا تعارضت الاحتمالات لم يكن إثبات العموم بالتوهم؛ فإذا قال
الصحابي: " نهي عن بيع الرطب بالتمر " فيحتمل أن يكون قد رأى شخصا باع رطبا
بتمر فنهاه فقال الراوي ما قال، ويحتمل أن يكون قد سمع الرسول - عليه
السلام - ينهى عنه، ويقول: " أنهاكم عن بيع الرطب بالتمر "، ويحتمل أن يكون
قد سئل عن واقعة معينة فنهى  عنها فالتمسك بعموم هذا تمسك بتوهم العموم لا
بلفظ عرف عمومه بالقطع، وهذا على مذهب من يرى هذا حجة في أصل النهي.
وقد قال قوم: لا بد أن يحكي الصحابي قول الرسول، ولفظه، وإلا فربما سمع
ما يعتقده نهيا باجتهاده، ولا يكون نهيا، فإن قوله: " لا تفعل " فيه خلاف
أنه للنهي أم لا وكذلك في ألفاظ أخر. وكذلك إذا قال " نسخ "
فلا يحتج به ما لم يقل " سمعت النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يقول نسخت
آية كذا " لأنه ربما يرى ما ليس بنسخ نسخا، وهذا قد ذكرناه في باب الإخبار،
وهو أصل السنة في القطب الثاني

### | [مسألة قول الصحابي قضى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالشفعة للجار وبالشاهد واليمين]

» كقوله: " نهى " في أنه لا عموم له لأنه حكاية، والحجة في المحكي، ولعله
حكم في عين أو بخطاب خاص مع شخص فكيف يتمسك بعمومه فيقال مثلا يقضى
بالشاهد، واليمين في البضع أو في الدم؛ لأن الراوي أطلق مع أن للراوي أن
يطلق. هذا إذا رآه قد قضى في مال أو في بضع بل لو قال الصحابي: " سمعته
يقول: قضيت بالشفعة للجار " فهذا يحتمل الحكاية عن قضاء لجار معروف، ويكون
الألف، واللام للتعريف وقوله: " قضيت " حكاية فعل ماض. فأما لو قال " قضيت
بأن الشفعة للجار " فهذا أظهر في الدلالة على التعريف للحكم دون الحكاية،
ولو قال الراوي: " قضى النبي - عليه السلام - بأن الشفعة للجار " اختلفوا
فيه؛ فمنهم من جعله عاما، ومنهم من قال يجوز أن يكون قد قضى في واقعة بأن
الشفعة للجار؛ فدعوى العموم فيه حكم بالتوهم.

### | [مسألة دعوى العموم في واقعة لشخص معين قضى فيها النبي]

مسألة لا يمكن دعوى العموم في واقعة لشخص معين قضى فيها النبي - عليه
السلام - بحكم، وذكر علة حكمه
أيضا إذا أمكن اختصاص العلة بصاحب الواقعة، مثاله: حكمه في أعرابي محرم
وقصت به ناقته: «لا تخمروا رأسه، ولا تقربوه طيبا فإنه يحشر يوم القيامة
ملبيا» فإنه يحتمل أن يقال: إما لأنه وقصت به ناقته محرما  لا بمجرد إحرامه
أو لأنه علم من نيته أنه كان مخلصا في عبادته، وأنه مات مسلما، وغيره لا
يعلم موته على الإسلام فضلا عن الإخلاص، وكذلك قال - عليه السلام - في قتلى
أحد «زملوهم بكلومهم، ودمائهم فإنهم يحشرون، وأوداجهم تشخب دما» يجوز أن
يكون لقتلى أحد خاصة لعلو درجتهم أو لعلمه أنهم أخلصوا لله فهم شهداء حقا،
ولو صرح بأن ذلك خاصيتهم قبل ذلك، فاللفظ خاص، والتعميم وهم، والشافعي -
رحمه الله - تعالى عم هذا الحكم نظرا إلى العلة، وأن ذلك كان بسبب الجهاد،
والإحرام، وأن العلة حشرهم على هذه الصفات، وعلة حشرهم الجهاد أو الإحرام
وقد وقعت الشركة في العلة.
وهذا أسبق إلى الفهم، لكن خلافه - وهو الذي اختاره القاضي - ممكن
والاحتمال متعارض، والحكم بأحد الاحتمالين لأنه أسبق إلى الفهم فيه نظر،
فإن الحكم بالعموم إنما أخذ من العادة، ومن وضع اللسان، ولم يثبت ههنا في
مثل هذه الصورة لا وضع، ولا عادة فلا يكون في معنى العموم.

### | [مسألة من يقول بالمفهوم قد يظن للمفهوم عموما]

، ويتمسك به،
، وفيه نظر لأن العموم لفظ تتشابه دلالته بالإضافة إلى المسميات،
والمتمسك بالمفهوم، والفحوى ليس متمسكا بلفظ بل بسكوت، فإذا قال - عليه
السلام -: «في سائمة الغنم زكاة» فنفي الزكاة في المعلوفة ليس بلفظ حتى يعم
اللفظ أو يخص، وقوله تعالى: {فلا تقل لهما أف} [الإسراء: 23] دل على تحريم
الضرب لا بلفظه المنطوق به حتى يتمسك بعمومه، وقد ذكرنا أن العموم للألفاظ
لا للمعاني، ولا للأفعال.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ه-ي (N-H-Y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Prohibition (nahy) as a directive of abstention; its core sense is "to restrain" or "to forbid" an action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, nahy denotes a divine or prophetic command of abstention, but its scope (ʿumūm) is not presumed unless the uttered wording (lafẓ) itself is general.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) prohibition is a spoken command; metaphorical (majāz) usage would be reporting an act of forbidding without the precise utterance — thus ambiguity arises.
- Root: ح-ك-ي (Ḥ-K-Y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To narrate or report (ḥakā) an event; the narrator (ḥākī) conveys, but the authority lies in the narrated content (maḥkī).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The report (ḥikāyah) is a conveyance of another's speech or act; its probative force depends on the authenticity of what is reported, not the reporter's phrasing.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinguishes the literal report of a general utterance from a loose narration that may summarize a specific incident.
- Root: ع-م-م (ʿ-M-M)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Generality (ʿumūm) as encompassing all individuals of a class.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿUmūm is a property of explicit linguistic forms (alfāẓ), not of inferred meanings or actions; it requires a wording whose indication is uniform across all referents.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal generality is established by the tongue's convention (waḍʿ al-lisān); mere conjecture (tawahhum) cannot affirm it.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ambiguity Resolution (Taʿāruḍ al-Iḥtimālāt) — When multiple grammatical and semantic probabilities compete in a reported utterance, the strongest syntactic form (e.g., "qadaytu bi-anna" vs. "qadaytu") determines whether the report indicates a general rule or a specific case; without a decisive form, generality cannot be posited.
chapters.translation:
I say: The statement of a Companion — "The Prophet (peace be upon him) prohibited such-and-such," like the sale of gharar (uncertainty), the marriage of shighār, and other cases — carries no generality (ʿumūm), because the probative authority lies in the narrated content (al-maḥkī), not in the narrator's wording (qawl al-ḥākī). What the Companion narrated — that he reported a prohibition — admits of several possibilities: it may have been an act (fiʿl) that the Prophet (peace be upon him) prohibited, which has no generality; it may have been a specific utterance (lafẓ khāṣṣ); or it may have been a general utterance (lafẓ ʿāmm). When these probabilities conflict, affirming generality through mere conjecture (tawahhum) is impermissible. Thus, if a Companion says: "He prohibited the sale of fresh dates for dried dates," it is possible that he saw a person selling fresh dates for dried dates, and the Prophet forbade him, so the narrator reported what he said; or it is possible that he heard the Messenger (peace be upon him) prohibiting it, saying: "I forbid you from selling fresh dates for dried dates"; or it is possible that he was asked about a specific incident and prohibited it. Therefore, clinging to the generality of such a report is clinging to a conjectured generality, not to a wording whose generality is known with certainty. This is on the doctrine of those who deem such a report probative regarding the very existence of the prohibition (aṣl al-nahy). Some scholars have said: The Companion must narrate the very words of the Messenger, for otherwise he may have heard something he deemed a prohibition by his own reasoning (ijtihād), which is not actually a prohibition. For his saying "Do not do such-and-such" (lā tafʿal) is itself subject to dispute as to whether it indicates prohibition or not, and likewise for other expressions. Similarly, if he says "abrogated" (naskh), it is not accepted as proof unless he says: "I heard the Prophet (peace be upon him) say: 'Such-and-such verse is abrogated,'" because he may deem something abrogation that is not. We have already mentioned this in the chapter on reports (bāb al-ikhbār), and it is a foundational principle of the Sunnah in the Second Pole.

As for the Companion's statement: "The Prophet (peace be upon him) adjudicated by the right of preemption (shufʿah) for the neighbor, and by the testimony of one witness with an oath," it is like his saying "he prohibited" in that it carries no generality, because it is a narration (ḥikāyah), and the authority lies in the narrated content. Perhaps he adjudicated in a specific case (ʿayn) or by a specific address to a particular person — so how can one cling to its generality, saying, for example: "Judgment is rendered by one witness and an oath in cases of honor (buḍʿ) or blood (dam)"? For the narrator spoke in absolute terms, and the narrator is permitted to speak absolutely. This applies when he saw him adjudicate concerning property or honor. But even if the Companion said: "I heard him say: 'I adjudicated by the right of preemption for the neighbor,'" this admits of being a narration about a judgment for a known neighbor, where the definite article (al-) is for specific reference (taʿrīf), and his saying "I adjudicated" (qadaytu) is a narration of a past act. However, if he said: "I adjudicated that the right of preemption belongs to the neighbor" (qadaytu bi-anna al-shufʿah lil-jār), this is more manifest in indicating the definition of the ruling (taʿrīf al-ḥukm) rather than a mere narration. And if the narrator said: "The Prophet (peace be upon him) adjudicated that the right of preemption belongs to the neighbor," scholars differ: some deem it general, while others say it is possible he adjudicated in a specific incident that the right of preemption belongs to the neighbor; thus claiming generality therein is a judgment based on conjecture.

I say: Generality cannot be claimed for an incident involving a specific person in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) adjudicated a ruling and mentioned the rationale (ʿillah) of his ruling, if it is possible that the rationale is specific to the person of that incident. An example is his ruling concerning a Bedouin in a state of iḥrām whose she-camel broke his neck: {«Do not cover his head, nor bring him near perfume, for he will be resurrected on the Day of Judgment in a state of talbiyah»}. It is possible to say: This was either because his she-camel broke his neck while he was in iḥrām — not merely because of his iḥrām — or because he (the Prophet) knew from his intention that he was sincere in his worship and died a Muslim, whereas others are not known to have died upon Islam, let alone upon sincerity. Likewise, he (peace be upon him) said concerning the martyrs of Uḥud: {«Shroud them with their wounds and blood, for they will be resurrected with their jugular veins gushing blood»}. It is permissible that this applies specifically to the martyrs of Uḥud due to their high rank, or because he knew they were sincere for God and were true martyrs. Even if he had explicitly stated that this was their particular characteristic, the wording would be specific, and generalizing it would be conjecture. Al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) generalized this ruling by considering the rationale — that it was due to jihad and iḥrām, and that the rationale for their resurrection in this state is jihad or iḥrām — and the sharing in the rationale (al-shirkah fī al-ʿillah) has occurred. This is more readily grasped by the understanding, but the contrary view — which al-Qāḍī chose — is possible, and the probabilities conflict. Judging one of the two probabilities merely because it is more readily grasped is subject to scrutiny, for the judgment of generality is derived from custom (al-ʿādah) and from the convention of the tongue (waḍʿ al-lisān), and in such a case neither convention nor custom is established; hence it does not fall under the meaning of generality.

As for one who adheres to the implied meaning (al-mafhūm), he may suppose that the implied meaning has generality and cling to it. But this is subject to scrutiny, because generality is a wording whose indication is uniform with respect to its referents (musammayāt). The one who clings to the implied meaning (mafhūm) and the precedence of discourse (faḥwā) is not clinging to a wording but to an omission (sukūt). Thus, when he (peace be upon him) said: {«On grazing sheep (sāʾimah) there is alms (zakāh)»}, the negation of zakāh for fodder-fed sheep (maʿlūfah) is not a wording such that it could be general or specific. And His saying, the Exalted: {«Do not say to them 'uff'»} [al-Isrāʾ 17:23] indicates the prohibition of striking, but not by its uttered wording (manṭūq) such that one could cling to its generality. We have already stated that generality pertains to wordings (alfāẓ), not to meanings (maʿānī) nor to acts (afʿāl).
