What is known by his statement that he performed it as an exposition (bayān) of an obligation — such as his saying, peace be upon him: «Pray as you have seen me praying» and «Take from me your rites of pilgrimage» — or what is known by contextual indication (qarīnat al-ḥāl) that it was an execution of a revealed ruling, such as cutting the hand of the thief from the wrist — this is a proof (dalīl) and an exposition. What is known to be his particularity (khāṣṣiyyah) is not a proof regarding others. As for what is not accompanied by any exposition, neither negating nor affirming, the correct view with us is that it has no indication — rather, it is equivocal between permissibility (ibāḥah), recommendation (nadb), obligation (wujūb), between being specific to him, and between others sharing him in it. None of these categories is determined except by an additional proof. Rather, it also admits the possibility of prohibition (ḥaẓr) for those who permit minor sins for them. Some said: It indicates prohibition. Some said: It indicates permissibility. Some said: It indicates recommendation. Some said: It indicates obligation if in acts of worship, and if in customs (ʿādāt), then recommendation, and it is commendable to emulate him (taʾassī) therein. These are arbitrary assertions (taḥakkumāt), because the action has no linguistic form (ṣīghah), and these possibilities are mutually conflicting. We shall single out each one for refutation.

**As for refuting the attribution to prohibition:** This is the fancy of one who holds that acts before the advent of the Law are on prohibition. He says: This act has no ruling revealed concerning it, and it is not determined by itself for permissibility or obligation, so it remains on what it was. He is truthful in preserving the ruling on what it was, but erroneous in his claim that rulings before the Law are on prohibition — and we have already refuted that. It is countered by the view of one who says they are on permissibility, which is closer than prohibition. Then a contradiction follows from it: that he performs two contradictory acts at two times, leading to the prohibition of a thing and its opposite — which is the imposition of the impossible (taklīf al-muḥāl).

**As for refuting permissibility:** If he means that he has made such an act permissible for us, this is arbitrary, indicated by neither reason nor revelation. If he means that the original principle concerning acts is the negation of hardship (nafy al-ḥaraj), so it remains on what it was before the Law — this is true, and it was so before his act; thus his act has no indication.

**As for refuting the attribution to recommendation:** It is arbitrary if not attributed to obligation, for the possibility of its being recommended does not preclude the possibility of its being obligatory, nor the possibility of its being permissible.

They clung to two dubious arguments (shubhatayn):

**The first:** His act admits the possibility of obligation and recommendation, and recommendation is the lesser of its degrees, so it is attributed to it. We say: What they mentioned would only be valid if recommendation were included within obligation — obligation being recommendation plus an addition. It is not so, for the permissibility of abandonment enters into the definition of recommendation but not into the definition of obligation. The closest of what has been said is the attribution to recommendation, especially in acts of worship. As for customs, the least is to attribute them to permissibility — not by the mere act, but we know that the Companions believed of every act of his that it was permissible and used it as evidence for permissibility. This indicates the negation of minor sins from him, and they sought blessing (tabarruk) by following him in customs. But this too is not decisive, for it is possible that their inference was accompanied by contextual indications that eliminated the remaining possibilities. Our discourse concerns mere acts without contextual indication. There is no doubt that Ibn ʿUmar, when he saw him facing the Sacred House (Bayt al-Maqdis) while relieving himself, inferred from it its permissibility when in a building — because he was in a building — and he did not believe that one should emulate him in it, because he secluded himself and did not intend to display it; thus it is known by contextual indication that he did not intend to call to emulation.

It is thus clarified that they believed what he did was permissible, and this indicates that they did not permit minor sins for him, and that they did not believe in emulation in every act — rather, only in what is accompanied by a contextual indication showing his intention of exposition by the act.

**The second:** Their clinging to His saying: {«Indeed, in the Messenger of God you have a good example (uswah ḥasanah).»} [Al-Aḥzāb: 21]. He informed us that we have emulation (taʾassī), and did not say "upon you is emulation" — so it is attributed to recommendation, not obligation. We say: The verse is an argument against you, for emulation of him consists in performing the act he performed in the manner he performed it. What he performed as obligatory or permissible — if we perform it in the manner of recommendation, we have not emulated him. Likewise, if he intended recommendation and we performed it as obligatory, we have contravened emulation. There is no way to emulate him before knowing his intention, and his intention is known only by his statement or by contextual indication. Then we say: If his actions are divided into obligatory and recommended, then neither the one who attributes all to obligation nor the one who makes all recommended is emulating him. Rather, the Prophet — peace be upon him — used to do what is not known; so whoever does what is not known, in what manner he did it, has not emulated him.

**As for refuting the attribution to obligation:** This is not known by rational necessity, nor by reflection (naẓar), nor by a decisive proof — it is arbitrary. For his act is equivocal between obligation and recommendation, and for those who do not affirm his infallibility from minor sins, it also admits prohibition. Thus it is not arbitrary to attribute it to obligation.

**Their first dubious argument:** They say: His act must be described as true (ḥaqq), correct (ṣawāb), and beneficial (maṣlaḥah) — for were it not so, he would not have undertaken it, nor would he have been obligated to perform it. We say: All of that is conceded regarding him specifically, to exclude it from being prohibited for him. The discourse concerns us. It does not follow that what was true, correct, and beneficial for him is likewise for us — perhaps it is beneficial relative to the attribute of prophethood or an attribute specific to him. For this reason, we differ from him in a number of permissible, obligatory, and prohibited matters. Indeed, the resident and the traveler, the menstruating woman and the pure woman differ in prayers — so the difference between the Prophet and the community is not impossible.

**The second:** He is a prophet, and venerating the prophet is obligatory, and emulating him is veneration. We say: Venerating the king consists in submitting to him in what he commands and forbids — not in sitting cross-legged when he sits cross-legged, nor in sitting on the throne when he sits on it. If the Messenger vowed things, his veneration would not consist in our vowing what he vowed. If he divorced, sold, or bought, his veneration would not consist in imitating him in that.

**The third:** If he were not followed in his actions, it would be permissible not to follow him in his statements — and that diminishes his stature and repels hearts from him. We say: This is nonsense (hadhayān). For opposition in statement is disobedience to him, and he was sent to convey so that he is obeyed in his statements — because his statement extends to others, while his action is confined to himself. As for repelling hearts, we have already shown that no attention is paid to it. If refraining from imitating him were a diminishment, then our refraining from continuous fasting (wiṣāl), our refraining from marrying nine women, indeed our refraining from claiming prophethood would be a diminishment. Thus it is clear that these are fancies, and that the truth is that the action is equivocal — just as the equivocal word (al-lafẓ al-mushtarak) like "qarʾ" is equivocal — and it is not permissible to attribute it to any one of its aspects except by an additional proof.

**The fourth:** Their clinging to verses of the Book, such as His saying: {«And follow him»} [Al-Aʿrāf: 158], which they claim is general over statements and actions; and His saying: {«So let those who oppose his command beware»} [Al-Nūr: 63]; and His saying: {«And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it»} [Al-Ḥashr: 7], and similar verses. All of that reverts to accepting his statements, and at most it is general over statements and actions — and the specification of the general (takhṣīṣ al-ʿumūm) is possible. For this reason, the menstruating woman and the sick person are not obligated to match him, even though they are commanded to follow and obey.

**The fifth — and it is the most apparent:** Their clinging to the action of the Companions — that they fasted continuously when he fasted continuously, removed their sandals in prayer when he removed his, and in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyyah he commanded them to exit the state of iḥrām by shaving, but they hesitated. He complained to Umm Salamah, who said: Go out to them, slaughter, and shave. He did so, and they slaughtered and shaved hastily. And that he removed his ring, so they removed theirs. And that ʿUmar used to kiss the Black Stone, saying: "I know you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits, and were it not that I saw the Prophet — peace be upon him — kissing you, I would not kiss you." And that he said in response to one who asked Umm Salamah about kissing while fasting: «Did you not tell him that I kiss while fasting?» Likewise, the Companions — may God be pleased with them — all differed concerning the major ablution (ghusl) from the meeting of the two circumcisions, and ʿĀʾishah — may God be pleased with her — said: "I did it, I and the Messenger of God, and we bathed" — so they reverted to that.

**The answer is from several aspects:**

**The first:** These are solitary reports (akhbār āḥād), and just as analogical reasoning (qiyās) and the solitary report are not established except by a decisive proof, so likewise this — because it is a root among the roots (aṣl min al-uṣūl).

**The second:** They did not follow him in all his actions and acts of worship — so how did their following him in some become a proof, while their opposition to him in some did not become a proof of the permissibility of opposition?

**The third — and it is the verification:** Most of these reports pertain to prayer, pilgrimage, fasting, and ablution — and it had already been made clear to them that his law and their law therein were the same. He said: «Pray as you have seen me praying» and «Take from me your rites of pilgrimage» — and he taught them ablution, saying: «This is my ablution and the ablution of the prophets before me.» As for continuous fasting, they assumed — since he commanded them to fast and occupied himself with them in it — that he intended by his act to fulfill the obligation and expound it. He rejected their assumption and disapproved of their concurrence. Likewise, regarding kissing while fasting, perhaps he had already made clear to them the equality of the ruling concerning things that break the fast, and that his law is their law. Likewise, regarding the ritual impurities (aḥdāth), he had made known to them the equality of the ruling therein — so they understood not by the mere narration of the act. How could it be so, when it is transmitted that he said, peace be upon him: «When the two circumcisions meet, the major ablution has become obligatory»? As for the removal of the ring, it is permissible — so when he removed it, they loved to concur with him, not because they believed it obligatory upon them, nor did they imagine that since he equated them in the sunnah of wearing the ring, he equated them in the sunnah of removing it.

If it is said: The principle is that what is established regarding him is general except what is excepted. We say: No — rather, the principle is that what is established regarding him is specific (khāṣṣ) except what he made general.

If it is said: The general is more frequent, so let it be attributed to it. We say: Attribution to the more frequent is not obligatory. If a sister is confused with ten foreign women, the more frequent is lawful — yet it is not permissible to act upon it? How so, when permissible things are more frequent than recommended ones — so let them be attributed to them? And recommended things are more frequent than obligatory ones — so let them be attributed to them? Indeed, one might say: Prohibited things are more frequent than obligatory ones — so let them be attributed to them?

chapters.title_en: Section 176 — Chapter Two on Scattered Doubts Concerning the Rulings of Acts
chapters.arabic_text: ### | [الفصل الثاني في شبهات متفرقة في أحكام الأفعال]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ب ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, ambiguity, confusion between two similar things; a "doubt" (shubhah) arises when an issue bears partial similarity to multiple rulings.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, shubhah denotes an epistemic uncertainty that prevents definitive attribution of a ruling (ḥukm) to an act, often due to conflicting indicators (adillah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is visual resemblance; metaphorical extension to rational equivocation where the mind cannot decisively distinguish between two juridical categories.
- Root: ف ص ل (f-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, division, decisive distinction; "chapter" (faṣl) as a demarcated segment of discourse.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In scholarly composition, faṣl marks a structural partition of subject matter, here specifically for "scattered" (mutafarriqāt) subsidiary issues.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal cutting apart; metaphorically, the logical separation of one topic from another for analytical clarity.
- Root: ح ك م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Judgment, governance, decisive command; in fiqh, the legal qualification of an act (obligation, prohibition, permission, etc.).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥukm as divine address (khiṭāb) concerning the acts of the legally responsible (mukallaf), whether requiring, prohibiting, or permitting.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal arbitration between two parties; metaphorical application to God's legislative determination of human actions.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "aḥkām al-afʿāl" (rulings of acts) uses the construct state to specify the domain of rulings, while "shubuhāt mutafarriqah" employs an indefinite adjective postposed to an indefinite noun, indicating a non-exhaustive, open-ended set of doubts.
chapters.translation: I say: This is the second chapter, concerning scattered doubts pertaining to the rulings of acts (aḥkām al-afʿāl).

chapters.title_en: The Prophet's Action as Clarification (Bayān): Obligations of the Mujtahid and Evidences of Clarificatory Status
chapters.arabic_text:
الأولى: قال قائل: إذا نقل إلينا فعله - عليه السلام - فما الذي يجب على
المجتهد أن يبحث عنه، وما الذي يستحب؟ قلنا: لا يجب إلا أمر واحد، وهو
البحث عنه هل ورد بيانا لخطاب عام أو تنفيذا لحكم
لازم عام، فيجب علينا اتباعه، أو ليس كذلك، فيكون قاصرا عليه، فإن لم يقم
دليل على كونه بيانا لحكم عام فالبحث عن كونه ندبا في حقه أو واجبا أو
مباحا أو محظورا أو قضاء أو أداء موسعا أو مضيقا، لا يجب بل هو زيادة درجة،
وفضل في العلم يستحب.
للعالم أن يعرفه.
فإن قيل: كم أصناف ما يحتاج إلى البيان سوى الفعل؟ قلنا: ما يتطرق إليه
احتمال، كالمجمل، والمجاز، والمنقول عن وضعه، والمنقول بتصرف الشرع، والعام
المحتمل للخصوص، والظاهر المحتمل للتأويل، ونسخ الحكم بعد استقراره، ومعنى
قول افعل أنه للندب أو الوجوب أو أنه على الفور أو التراخي أو أنه للتكرار
أو المرة الواحدة، والجمل المعطوفة إذا أعقبت باستثناء، وما يجري مجراه مما
يتعارض فيه الاحتمال، والفعل من جملة ذلك. فإن قيل: فإن بين لنا بفعله ندبا
فهل يكون فعله واجبا قلنا: نعم هو من حيث إنه بيان واجب؛ لأنه تبليغ للشرع،
ومن حيث إنه فعل ندب، وذهب بعض القدرية إلى أن بيان الواجب واجب، وبيان
الندب ندب، وبيان المباح مباح، ويلزم على ذلك أن يكون بيان المحظور محظورا،
فإذا كان بيان المحظور واجبا فلم لا يكون بيان الندب واجبا؟ وكذلك بيان
المباح، وهي أحكام الله تعالى على عباده، والرسول مأمور بالتبليغ
وبيانه بالقول أو الفعل، وهو مخير بينهما، فإذا أتى بالفعل فقد أتى بإحدى
خصلتي الواجب، فيكون فعله واقعا عن الواجب. فإن قيل:، وبم يعرف كون فعله
بيانا؟ قلنا: إما بصريح قوله، وهو ظاهر أو بقرائن، وهي كثيرة
إحداها: أن يرد خطاب مجمل، ولم يبينه بقوله إلى وقت الحاجة ثم فعل عند
الحاجة، والتنفيذ للحكم فعلا صالحا للبيان فيعلم أنه بيان، إذ لو لم يكن
لكان مؤخرا للبيان عن وقت الحاجة، وذلك  محال عقلا عند قوم، وسمعا عند
آخرين، وكونه غير واقع متفق عليه، لكن كون الفعل متعينا للبيان يظهر
للصحابة إذ قد علموا عدم البيان بالقول، أما نحن، فيجوز أن يكون قد بين
بالقول، ولم يبلغنا، فيكون الظاهر عندنا أن الفعل بيان؛ فقطع يد السارق من
الكوع، وتيممه إلى المرفقين بيان لقوله عز وجل: {فاقطعوا أيديهما}
[المائدة: 38] ولقوله تعالى: {فامسحوا بوجوهكم، وأيديكم} [المائدة: 6] .
الثانية: أن ينقل فعل غير مفصل كمسحه رأسه، وأذنيه من غير تعرض لكونهما
مسحا بماء واحد أو بماء جديد ثم ينقل أنه أخذ لأذنيه ماء جديدا، فهذا في
الظاهر يزيل الاحتمال عن الأول، ولكن يحتمل أن الواجب ماء واحد، وأن
المستحب ماء جديد، فيكون أحد الفعلين على الأقل، والثاني على الأكمل.
الثالثة: أن يترك ما لزمه، فيكون بيانا لكونه منسوخا في حقه أما في حق
غيره فلا يثبت النسخ إلا ببيان الاشتراك في الحكم، نعم لو ترك غيره بين
يديه فلم ينكر مع معرفته، فيدل على النسخ في حق الغير.
الرابعة: أنه إذا أتي بسارق ثمر أو ما دون النصاب فلم يقطع، فيدل على
تخصيص الآية؛ لكن هذا بشرط أن يعلم انتقاء شبهة أخرى تدرأ القطع؛ لأنه لو
أتي بسارق سيف فلم يقطعه فلا يتبين لنا سقوط القطع في السيف، ولا في الحديد
لكن يبحث عن سببه، فكذلك الثمر، وما دون النصاب، وكذلك تركه القنوت،
والتسمية، والتشهد الأول مرة واحدة لا يدل على النسخ إذ يحمل على نسيان أو
على بيان جواز ترك السنة، وإن ترك مرات دل على عدم الوجوب، وكذلك لو ترك
الفخذ مكشوفا دل على أنه ليس من العورة.
الخامسة: إذا فعل في الصلاة ما لو لم يكن واجبا لأفسد الصلاة دل على
الوجوب، كزيادة ركوع في الخسوف، وكحمل أمامة في الصلاة يدل على أن الفعل
القليل لا يبطل، وأنه فعل قليل، هذا مع قوله: «صلوا كما رأيتموني أصلي»
يكون بيانا في حقنا.
السادسة: إذا أمر الله تعالى بالصلاة، وأخذ الجزية، والزكاة مجملا ثم
أنشأ  الصلاة، وابتدأ بأخذ الجزية، فيظهر كونه بيانا، وتنفيذا، لكن إن لم
تكن الحاجة متنجزة بحيث يجوز تأخير البيان فلا يتعين لكونه بيانا بل يحتمل
أن يكون فعلا أمر به خاصة في ذلك الوقت، فإذا لا يصير بيانا للحكم العام
إلا بقرينة أخرى.
السابعة أخذه مالا ممن فعل فعلا أو إيقاعه ضربا أو نوع عقوبة فإنه له
خاصة ما لم ينبه على أن من فعل ذلك الفعل فعليه مثل ذلك المال فإنه لا
يمتنع؛ لأنه، وإن تقدم ذلك
الفعل فلا يتعين لكونه موجب أخذ المال، وأنه لا يمتنع وجود سبب آخر هو
المقتضي للمال وللعقوبة. أما قضاؤه على من فعل فعلا بعقوبة أو مال، كقضائه
على الأعرابي بإعتاق رقبة، فإنه يدل على أنه موجب ذلك الفعل؛ لأن الراوي لا
يقول قضي على فلان بكذا لما فعل كذا إلا بعد معرفته بالقرينة. فإن قيل:
فإذا فعل فعلا، وكان بيانا، ووقع في زمان، ومكان، وعلى هيئة، فهل يتبع
الزمان، والمكان، والهيئة؟ فيقال: أما الهيئة، والكيفية فنعم، وأما الزمان،
والمكان فهو كتغيم السماء وصحوها، ولا مدخل له في الأحكام، إلا أن يكون
الزمان، والمكان لائقا به بدليل دل عليه، كاختصاص الحج بعرفات، والبيت،
واختصاص الصلوات بأوقات؛ لأنه لو اتبع المكان للزم مراعاة تلك الرواية
بعينها، ووجب مراعاة ذلك الوقت، وقد انقضى، ولا يمكن إعادته، وما بعده من
الأوقات ليس مثلا، فيجب إعادة الفعل في الزمان الماضي، وهو محال، وقد قال
قوم: إن تكرر فعله في مكان واحد، وزمان واحد دل على الاختصاص، وإلا فلا،
وهو فاسد لما سبق ذكره. فإن قيل: إن كان فعله بيانا فتقريره على الفعل،
وسكوته عليه، وتركه الإنكار، واستبشاره بالفعل أو مدحه له، هل يدل على
الجواز، وهل يكون بيانا؟ قلنا: نعم، سكوته مع المعرفة، وتركه الإنكار دليل
على الجواز، إذ لا يجوز له ترك الإنكار لو كان حراما، ولا يجوز له
الاستبشار بالباطل، فيكون دليلا على الجواز كما نقل في قاعدة القيافة،
وإنما تسقط دلالته عند من يحمل ذلك  على المعصية، ويجوز عليه الصغيرة، ونحن
نعلم اتفاق الصحابة على إنكار ذلك، وإحالته. فإن قيل: لعله منع من الإنكار
مانع كعلمه بأنه لم يبلغه التحريم فلذلك فعله، أو بلغه الإنكار مرة فلم
ينجع فيه فلم يعاوده. قلنا: ليس هذا مانعا؛ لأن من لم يبلغه التحريم،
فيلزمه تبليغه، ونهيه حتى لا يعود، ومن بلغه، ولم ينجع فيه، فيلزمه إعادته،
وتكراره كي لا يتوهم نسخ التحريم. فإن قيل: فلم لم يجب عليه أن يطوف صبيحة
كل سبت، وأحد على اليهود، والنصارى إذا اجتمعوا في كنائسهم، وبيعهم؟ قلنا:؛
لأنه علم أنهم مصرون مع تبليغه، وعلم الخلق أنه مصر على تكفيرهم دائما، فلم
يكن ذلك مما يوهم النسخ، بخلاف فعل يجري بين يديه مرة واحدة أو مرات فإن
السكوت عنه يوهم النسخ
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ي-ن (B-Y-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation and manifestation; the core sense is the emergence of something from obscurity into clarity, whether by speech or by act.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, bayān is the divine disclosure of an ambiguous (mujmal) or general (ʿāmm) command through a specifying or explicating indicator (dalīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes actual separation and clarification; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to any act or statement that removes doubt from a legal obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (fa-in qīla... qulnā) and exceptions (illā an...), requiring precise tracking of protasis and apodosis to preserve the dialectical structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: The First [Question]: A questioner said: "When the action of the Prophet — peace be upon him — is transmitted to us, what is obligatory upon the mujtahid to investigate, and what is commendable?" We reply: Nothing is obligatory except one single matter, namely: investigating whether it [the action] came as a clarification (bayān) of a general address (khiṭāb ʿāmm) or as an execution (tanfīdh) of a universally binding ruling — in which case following it is obligatory upon us — or whether it is not so, in which case it is restricted to him alone. If no evidence establishes that it is a clarification of a general ruling, then investigating whether it was a commendation (nadb) in his regard, or an obligation (wujūb), or permissible (ibāḥah), or prohibited (ḥaẓr), or a make-up (qaḍāʾ) or a performance in time (adāʾ), or expansive (mūsāʿ) or restricted (muḍayyaq) — this is not obligatory; rather, it is an additional degree and a merit in knowledge, and it is commendable for the scholar to know it.

If it is said: "How many categories are there of what requires clarification besides the action?" We reply: Everything to which probability (iḥtimāl) attaches — such as the ambiguous (mujmal), the metaphorical (majāz), what is transferred from its original lexical sense, what is transferred by the disposition of the Sacred Law (taṣarruf al-sharʿ), the general term admitting specification (al-ʿāmm al-muḥtamil li-l-khuṣūṣ), the apparent term admitting interpretation (al-ẓāhir al-muḥtamil li-l-taʾwīl), the abrogation (naskh) of a ruling after its establishment, the meaning of the command "do" — whether it indicates commendation or obligation, whether it indicates immediacy (fawr) or delay (tarākhī), whether it indicates repetition (takrār) or a single instance (marrah wāḥidah), and coordinate clauses (al-jumal al-maʿṭūfah) when followed by an exception (istithnāʾ) — and whatever runs in their course where probability conflicts. The action is among this category.

If it is said: "If he clarified for us by his action that something is commendable (nadb), is his action then obligatory?" We reply: Yes — inasmuch as it is a clarification, it is obligatory; because it is a conveyance (tablīgh) of the Sacred Law. And inasmuch as it is an action, it is commendable. Some of the Muʿtazilah (Qadariyyah) held that the clarification of the obligatory is obligatory, the clarification of the commendable is commendable, and the clarification of the permissible is permissible. But this entails that the clarification of the prohibited would be prohibited — yet if the clarification of the prohibited is obligatory, why should the clarification of the commendable not be obligatory? Likewise the clarification of the permissible. These are rulings of God — exalted be He — upon His servants, and the Messenger is commanded to convey (tablīgh) and to clarify by speech or by action, and he is given the choice between the two. So when he performs the action, he has performed one of the two aspects of the obligatory, and thus his action falls as fulfillment of the obligatory.

If it is said: "By what means is it known that his action is a clarification?" We reply: Either by his explicit statement — which is apparent (ẓāhir) — or by contextual indicators (qarāʾin), which are numerous:

The First: That a general address (khiṭāb) comes as ambiguous (mujmal), and he does not clarify it by speech until the time of need, then he acts at the time of need — and the execution of the ruling by an action suitable for clarification — so it is known that it is a clarification. For were it not so, it would be a deferral of clarification beyond the time of need, which is impossible rationally (ʿaqlan) according to some, and by revelation (samʿan) according to others; and that it did not occur is agreed upon. But that the action is specifically determined as the clarification is apparent to the Companions, since they knew there was no clarification by speech. As for us, it is possible that he clarified by speech and it did not reach us — yet the apparent [ruling] for us is that the action is the clarification. Thus, cutting the thief's hand from the wrist, and the dry ablution (tayammum) up to the elbows, are clarifications of His saying — exalted be He: {«Fa-qṭaʿū aydiyahumā»} [al-Māʾidah 5:38] — and of His saying — exalted be He: {«Fa-msaḥū bi-wujūhikum wa-aydīkum»} [al-Māʾidah 5:6].

The Second: That an undetailed action is transmitted — such as his wiping his head and ears without specifying whether they were wiped with a single water or with fresh water — then it is transmitted that he took fresh water for his ears. This, in appearance, removes the probability from the first [narration]. But it remains possible that the obligatory is a single water, and the commendable is fresh water — so one of the two actions is at minimum [fulfillment], and the second is at perfection.

The Third: That he abandons what was incumbent upon him — this is a clarification that it is abrogated (mansūkh) in his regard. As for others, abrogation is not established except by evidence of shared participation in the ruling. Yes — if he saw another person [doing it] before him and did not disapprove, despite his knowledge, this indicates abrogation in regard to that other person.

The Fourth: That when a thief of fruit or of less than the niṣāb [threshold] was brought to him and he did not cut [the hand], this indicates specification (takhṣīṣ) of the verse. But this is conditional upon knowing the absence of another ambiguity (shubhah) that would repel the cutting. For if a thief of a sword was brought to him and he did not cut, it would not become clear to us that the cutting is dropped for the sword, nor for iron — rather, one investigates its cause. Likewise for fruit and less than the niṣāb. Similarly, his abandoning the qunūt, the basmalah, and the first tashahhud once does not indicate abrogation, for it is attributed to forgetfulness or to a clarification of the permissibility of abandoning the sunnah. But if he abandoned them repeatedly, it indicates the absence of obligation. Likewise, if he left his thigh uncovered, it indicates that it is not part of the ʿawrah.

The Fifth: If he did something in prayer which, had it not been obligatory, would have invalidated the prayer, this indicates obligation — such as the additional bowing (rukūʿ) in the eclipse prayer, and such as carrying a child in prayer, which indicates that a small action does not invalidate [the prayer] and that it is a small action. This, together with his saying: «Ṣallū kamā raʾaytumūnī uṣallī» ("Pray as you have seen me praying"), constitutes a clarification in our regard.

The Sixth: When God — exalted be He — commanded prayer, the jizyah, and the zakāh in an ambiguous manner, then he initiated the prayer and commenced the collection of jizyah — this makes apparent that it is a clarification and execution. But if the need was not yet imminent such that deferral of clarification would be impermissible, then it is not specifically determined as a clarification; rather, it is possible that it was an action commanded to him specifically at that time. Thus it does not become a clarification of the general ruling except with another contextual indicator.

The Seventh: His taking wealth from someone who committed an act, or his inflicting a beating or a type of punishment — this is specific to him unless he indicated that whoever commits that act owes the like of that wealth; for this is not precluded. For even if that act preceded, it is not specifically determined as the cause obligating the taking of wealth, and it is not impossible that another cause exists which necessitates the wealth and the punishment. As for his adjudicating against someone who committed an act with a punishment or wealth — such as his adjudication against the Bedouin to free a slave — this indicates that it is the cause obligating that act; because the narrator does not say "he adjudicated against so-and-so with such-and-such because he did such-and-such" except after his knowledge of the contextual indicator.

If it is said: "When he performed an action and it was a clarification, and it occurred at a time, in a place, and in a particular manner — is the time, place, and manner to be followed?" It is said: As for the manner and modality — yes. As for the time and place — it is like the clouding of the sky and its clearing; they have no entry into the rulings. Except if the time and place are appropriate to it by an evidence indicating so — such as the exclusivity of the Ḥajj to ʿArafāt and the House, and the exclusivity of the prayers to their times. For if the place were followed, it would necessitate observing that very narration, and it would be obligatory to observe that time — yet it has passed, and it cannot be repeated, and the times after it are not its like. Thus it would necessitate repeating the action in the past time, which is impossible. Some have said: If his action was repeated in a single place and a single time, it indicates exclusivity; otherwise not. This is corrupt for what was previously mentioned.

If it is said: "If his action was a clarification, then his confirming (taqrīr) someone upon an action, his silence upon it, his refraining from disapproval, his rejoicing at the action, or his praising it — does this indicate permissibility, and is it a clarification?" We reply: Yes. His silence with knowledge, and his refraining from disapproval, is evidence of permissibility; for it is not permissible for him to refrain from disapproval were it forbidden, and it is not permissible for him to rejoice at falsehood. Thus it is evidence of permissibility, as transmitted in the principle of physiognomy (qiyāfah). Its evidentiary force is only dropped for those who attribute that to sin and deem minor sins (ṣaghāʾir) possible for him — but we know the Companions' consensus on disapproving that and deeming it impossible.

If it is said: "Perhaps some obstacle prevented him from disapproving — such as his knowledge that the prohibition had not reached that person, so he did it; or that disapproval had reached him once and did not avail, so he did not repeat it." We reply: This is not an obstacle; for one to whom the prohibition has not reached — it is incumbent upon him to convey it and forbid him so that he does not return. And one to whom it reached and did not avail — it is incumbent upon him to repeat and reiterate it, lest the abrogation of the prohibition be imagined.

If it is said: "Then why was it not obligatory upon him to circumambulate every Saturday and Sunday morning over the Jews and Christians when they gathered in their churches and synagogues?" We reply: Because he knew that they were persistent despite his conveyance, and the creation knew that he was persistent in declaring them disbelievers perpetually — so that was not something that would suggest abrogation. This is unlike an action performed before him once or several times, for silence upon it suggests abrogation.

chapters.title_en: Section 178 — On the Conflict of Two Acts (Taʿāruḍ al-Fiʿlayn)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | [الفصل الثالث في تعارض الفعلين]

فنقول: معنى التعارض التناقض، فإن وقع في الخبر أوجب كون واحد منهما
كذبا، ولذلك لا يجوز التعارض في الأخبار من الله تعالى، ورسوله، وإن وقع في
الأمر، والنهي، والأحكام، فيتناقض، فيرفع الأخير الأول، ويكون نسخا، وهذا
متصور، وإذا عرفت أن التعارض هو التناقض فلا يتصور التعارض في الفعل؛ لأنه
لا بد من فرض الفعلين في زمانين أو في شخصين، فيمكن الجمع بين وجوب أحدهما،
وتحريم الآخر، فلا تعارض.
فإن قيل: فالقول أيضا لا يتناقض، إذ يوجد القولان في حالتين، وإنما
يتناقض حكمهما فكذلك يتناقض حكم الفعلين. قلنا: إنما يتناقض حكم القولين؛
لأن القول الأول اقتضى حكما دائما، فيقطع القول الثاني دوامه، والفعل لا
يدل أصلا على حكم، ولا على دوام حكم، نعم لو أشعرنا الشارع بأنه يريد
بمباشرة فعل بيان دوام وجوبه، ثم ترك ذلك الفعل بعده كان ذلك نسخا، وقطعا
لدوام حكم ظهر بالفعل مع تقدم الإشعار، فهذا القدر ممكن.
وأما التعارض بين القول، والفعل
فممكن بأن يقول قولا يوجب على أمته فعلا دائما، وأشعرهم بأن حكمه فيه
حكمهم ابتداء، ونسخا ثم فعل خلافه أو سكت على خلافه كان الأخير نسخا، وإن
أشكل التاريخ وجب طلبه،  وإلا فهو متعارض، كما روي أنه قال في السارق: «وإن
سرق خامسة فاقتلوه» ثم «أتي بمن سرق خامسة فلم يقتله» ، فهذا إن تأخر فهو
نسخ القول بالفعل، وإن تأخر القول فهو نسخ ما دل عليه الفعل، وقد قال قوم:
إذا تعارضا، وأشكل التاريخ يقدم القول؛ لأن القول بيان بنفسه بخلاف الفعل،
فإن الفعل يتصور أن يخصه، والقول يتعدى إلى غيره؛ ولأن القول يتأكد
بالتكرار بخلاف الفعل.
فنقول: أما قولكم إن الفعل ليس بيانا بنفسه فمسلم ولكن كلامنا في فعل صار
بيانا لغيره وبعد أن صار بيانا لغيره، فلا يتأخر عما كان بيانا بنفسه، وأما
خصوص الفعل فمسلم أيضا، ولكن كلامنا في فعل لا يمكن حمله على خاصيته، وأما
تأكيد القول بالتكرار، إن عني به أنه إذا تواتر أفاد العلم، فهذا مسلم إذا
تواتر من أشخاص، فليس ذلك تكرارا، وتكراره من شخص واحد لا أثر له كتكرار
الفعل.
هذا تمام الكلام في الأفعال الملحقة بالأقوال، وبيان ما فيها من البيان،
والإجمال، ولنشتغل بعدها بالفن الثالث من القطب، وهو المرسوم لبيان كيفية
دلالة الألفاظ على المدلولات بمعقولها، ومعناها، وهو الذي يسمى قياسا،
فلنخض في شرح كتاب القياس مستعينين بالله عز وجل.

### | [الفن الثالث في كيفية استثمار الأحكام من الألفاظ والاقتباس من معقول الألفاظ بطريق القياس]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ر ض (ʿ-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To appear, to present oneself; taʿāruḍ denotes mutual opposition or confrontation of two things.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl, taʿāruḍ is the logical contradiction (tanāquḍ) between two evidences, entailing that one must be false or abrogated.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical encounter; metaphorical usage extends to conflict of rulings or statements.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-Sharṭ wa-l-Istithnāʾ) — The argument hinges on distinguishing the temporal and personal conditions (zarf al-zamān wa-l-shakhṣ) under which two acts occur, requiring precise parsing of the protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The meaning of conflict (taʿāruḍ) is contradiction (tanāquḍ). If it occurs in a report (khabar), it necessitates that one of the two [reports] be false; for this reason, conflict is not permissible in reports from God Most High or His Messenger. If it occurs in a command, a prohibition, or a ruling, then they contradict, and the latter [of the two] abrogates the former, constituting abrogation (naskh). This is conceivable. And once you know that conflict is contradiction, then conflict is not conceivable in [the case of] an act; for one must posit the two acts either in two times or in two persons, and thus it is possible to combine the obligatoriness of one with the prohibition of the other — so there is no conflict.

If it is said: "Speech too does not contradict, since the two statements exist in two states; rather, their ruling contradicts — so likewise the ruling of the two acts contradicts." We say: The ruling of the two statements contradicts only because the first statement entailed a perpetual ruling (ḥukm dāʾim), and the second statement cuts off its perpetuity. But an act does not indicate at all a ruling, nor the perpetuity of a ruling. Yes — if the Lawgiver (al-shāriʿ) had apprised us (ashʿaranā) that by performing an act He intends to clarify the perpetuity of its obligatoriness, and then He abandoned that act afterward, that would be abrogation and a cutting off of the perpetuity of a ruling manifested by the act, with the prior apprisal (ishʿār) — this much is possible.

As for conflict between a statement and an act, it is possible: namely, that he [the Prophet] utters a statement imposing upon his community an act perpetually, and apprises them that his ruling therein is their ruling, ab initio and by way of abrogation; then he performs contrary to it, or remains silent upon what is contrary to it — then the latter [act or silence] is abrogation. If the chronology (tārīkh) is ambiguous, it must be sought; otherwise, it is [genuinely] conflicting. This is as it was narrated that he said concerning the thief: {«And if he steals a fifth time, then kill him»} — then {«a man who had stolen a fifth time was brought to him, and he did not kill him»}. So if the act is later, it is an abrogation of the statement by the act; and if the statement is later, it is an abrogation of what the act indicated. Some have said: When they conflict and the chronology is ambiguous, the statement is given precedence, because the statement is a clarification (bayān) by itself, unlike the act — for the act may be conceived as specific to him [the Prophet], whereas the statement extends to others; and because the statement is strengthened by repetition, unlike the act.

We say: As for your claim that the act is not a clarification by itself — this is conceded. But our discussion concerns an act that has become a clarification for something else; and once it has become a clarification for something else, it is not inferior to that which is a clarification by itself. As for the specificity of the act — this too is conceded. But our discussion concerns an act that cannot be construed upon its specificity. As for the strengthening of the statement by repetition — if what is meant is that when it is transmitted recurrently (tawātur) it yields certain knowledge, this is conceded when it is recurrently transmitted from multiple persons; that is not repetition [in the relevant sense]. Its repetition from a single person has no effect, just like the repetition of an act.

This completes the discussion of acts annexed to statements, and the clarification of what they contain of clarification (bayān) and ambiguity (ijmāl). Let us now occupy ourselves after this with the third art (al-fann al-thālith) of the pole [of jurisprudence], which is designated for clarifying how words indicate their referents by their intelligible import (maʿqūl) and their meaning — that which is called analogical reasoning (qiyās). Let us plunge into the exposition of the Book of Qiyās, seeking aid from God, Exalted and Glorious.

### | [The Third Art: On How Rulings Are Derived from Words and How the Intelligible Import of Words Is Quarried by Way of Analogical Reasoning]

chapters.arabic_text:
### | [مقدمة في حد القياس]

الفن الثالث: في كيفية استثمار الأحكام من الألفاظ والاقتباس من معقول
الألفاظ بطريق القياس.
ويشتمل على مقدمتين، وأربعة أبواب الأول: في إثبات أصل القياس على
منكريه. الثاني: في طريق إثبات العلة. الثالث: في قياس الشبه. الرابع: في
أركان القياس، وهي أربعة: الأصل، والفرع، والعلة، والحكم، وبيان شروط كل
ركن من هذه الأركان. مقدمة: في حد القياس.، وحده أنه حمل معلوم على معلوم
في إثبات حكم لهما أو نفيه عنهما بأمر جامع بينهما من إثبات حكم أو صفة أو
نفيهما عنهما. ثم إن كان الجامع موجبا للاجتماع على الحكم كان قياسا صحيحا،
وإلا كان فاسدا، واسم القياس يشتمل على الصحيح، والفاسد في اللغة، ولا  بد
في كل قياس من فرع، وأصل، وعلة، وحكم، وليس من شرط الفرع، والأصل كونهما
موجودين بل ربما يستدل بالنفي على النفي؛ فلذلك لم نقل حمل شيء على شيء؛
لأن المعدوم ليس بشيء عندنا، وأبدلنا لفظ الشيء بالمعلوم، ولم نقل حمل فرع
على أصل؛ لأنه ربما ينبو هذا اللفظ عن المعدوم، وإن كان لا يبعد إطلاق هذا
الاسم عليه بتأويل ما، والحكم يجوز أن يكون نفيا، ويجوز أن يكون إثباتا،
والنفي كانتفاء الضمان، والتكليف، والانتفاء أيضا يجوز أن يكون علة فلذلك
أدرجنا الجميع في الحد، ودليل صحة هذا الحد اطراده، وانعكاسه. أما قول من
قال في حد القياس: " إنه الدليل الموصل إلى الحق، أو العلم الواقع بالمعلوم
عن نظر أو رد غائب إلى شاهد "، فبعض هذا أعم من القياس، وبعضه أخص، ولا
حاجة إلى الإطناب في إبطاله، وأبعد منه إطلاق الفلاسفة
اسمه على تركيب مقدمتين يحصل منهما نتيجة، كقول القائل: كل مسكر حرام،
وكل نبيذ مسكر، فيلزم منه أن كل نبيذ حرام فإن لزوم هذه النتيجة من
المقدمتين لا ننكره؛ لكن القياس يستدعي أمرين يضاف أحدهما إلى الآخر بنوع
من المساواة، إذ تقول العرب: لا يقاس فلان إلى فلان في عقله، ونسبه،، وفلان
يقاس إلى فلان، فهو عبارة عن معنى إضافي بين شيئين، وقال بعض الفقهاء:
القياس هو الاجتهاد.
، وهو خطأ؛ لأن الاجتهاد أعم من القياس؛ لأنه قد يكون بالنظر في
العمومات، ودقائق الألفاظ، وسائر طرق الأدلة سوى القياس، ثم إنه لا ينبئ في
عرف العلماء إلا عن بذل المجتهد وسعه في طلب الحكم، ولا يطلق إلا على من
يجهد نفسه، ويستفرغ الوسع، فمن حمل خردلة لا يقال اجتهد، ولا ينبئ هذا عن
خصوص معنى القياس، بل عن الجهد الذي هو حال القياس فقط.

### | [حصر مجاري الاجتهاد في العلل]
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ي-س (q-y-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "measuring" or "estimating" — measuring one thing against another to determine equivalence or proportion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudential theology, qiyās denotes the transference of a ruling (ḥukm) from an established case (aṣl) to a novel case (farʿ) based on a shared effective cause (ʿillah), grounded in the principle of divine law's coherence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, "measuring" (qiyās al-thawb) is ḥaqīqah; applying it to legal analogy is a well-established metaphorical extension (majāz) in scholarly convention, yet it retains the core notion of proportional equivalence.
- Root: ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To carry, bear, or convey; also to impose or attribute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Carrying the ruling of one case onto another — a technical sense of "attribution" in legal reasoning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal carrying of a physical load; metaphorical in legal context as "imposing" a rule.
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repeat, to follow in succession; also to be ill — hence a "cause" (ʿillah) as that which repeatedly brings about an effect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The effective cause in law — the attribute (waṣf) that is the ratio legis for a ruling.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "illness" or "recurrence"; in legal usage, the operative cause that justifies a ruling.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Conditional Dependency) — The definition must be co-extensive (muṭṭarid) and co-exclusive (munʿakis) with the definiendum; any term in the definition must apply universally and exclusively to the defined concept.
chapters.translation:
### | [Introduction on the Definition of Qiyās]

The third art: concerning the method of extracting rulings from expressions and deriving from the intelligible content of expressions by way of analogical reasoning (qiyās).

It comprises two introductory premises and four chapters. The first: on establishing the validity of qiyās against those who deny it. The second: on the method of establishing the effective cause (ʿillah). The third: on analogy of resemblance (qiyās al-shabah). The fourth: on the pillars (arkān) of qiyās, which are four: the original case (aṣl), the branch case (farʿ), the effective cause (ʿillah), and the ruling (ḥukm), with an exposition of the conditions of each of these pillars.

**Introductory Premise: On the Definition of Qiyās.**

Its definition is: the carrying of a known thing (maʿlūm) onto a known thing in affirming a ruling for both or negating it from both, by virtue of a uniting factor (jāmiʿ) between them — whether that factor be the affirmation of a ruling, an attribute, or the negation of either from both.

Then, if the uniting factor necessitates the shared ruling, it is sound qiyās (qiyās ṣaḥīḥ); otherwise, it is corrupt (fāsid). The name "qiyās" encompasses both the sound and the corrupt in the language. In every qiyās, there must be a branch (farʿ), an original (aṣl), a cause (ʿillah), and a ruling (ḥukm). It is not a condition of the branch and the original that they both exist [in actuality]; rather, one may sometimes infer from negation to negation. For this reason, we did not say "the carrying of a thing onto a thing," because the non-existent (maʿdūm) is not a "thing" (shayʾ) in our view. We substituted the word "thing" with "known thing" (maʿlūm). Nor did we say "carrying a branch onto an original," because this expression may fail to apply to the non-existent, although it is not far-fetched to apply this name to it with some interpretation.

The ruling may be a negation (nafy) or an affirmation (ithbāt). Negation is like the absence of liability (ḍamān) or obligation (taklīf). Negation itself may also serve as a cause (ʿillah). Therefore, we included all of these in the definition. The proof of the soundness of this definition is its universal applicability (iṭṭirād) and its exclusive applicability (inʿikās).

As for the statement of one who defines qiyās as "the proof (dalīl) that leads to truth" or "the knowledge that occurs regarding the known thing through reflection (naẓar)" or "the returning of the absent (ghāʾib) to the witnessed (shāhid)" — some of these are more general than qiyās, and some are more specific. There is no need to elaborate on refuting them.

Even more remote [from the correct definition] is the philosophers' application of this name to the composition of two premises from which a conclusion necessarily follows — as when one says: "Every intoxicant is unlawful, and every nabīdh (date-wine) is intoxicating," which entails that "every nabīdh is unlawful." For we do not deny the entailment of this conclusion from the two premises. However, qiyās requires two things, one of which is related to the other by a type of equivalence (musāwāh). For the Arabs say: "So-and-so is not measured (lā yuqās) to so-and-so in his intellect or lineage," and "So-and-so is measured to so-and-so." Thus, it is an expression denoting a relative meaning (maʿnā iḍāfī) between two things.

Some jurists said: "Qiyās is ijtihād (independent reasoning)." This is an error, because ijtihād is more general than qiyās; for it may occur through examining general statements (ʿumūmāt), the subtleties of expressions, and all other methods of evidence besides qiyās. Moreover, in scholarly convention, the term "ijtihād" only signifies the mujtahid's expending of his effort (badhl al-wusʿ) in seeking the ruling, and it is only applied to one who exerts himself and exhausts his capacity. One who carries a mustard seed is not said to have "exerted himself" (ijtahada). Nor does this term signify the specific meaning of qiyās; rather, it signifies the effort (juhd) which is merely the condition of qiyās, not its essence.

### | [Restricting the Channels of Ijtihād to the Effective Causes]
