- Root: ن-س-ب (n-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of connection, relation, affinity, and proportionality between two things.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, it denotes the attribute (waṣf) that is proportionate to the ruling (ḥukm) in terms of realizing a maṣlaḥah (human welfare) intended by the Lawgiver.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for genealogical relation; metaphorically (majāz) for a rational connection between a cause and its effect in legal reasoning.
- Root: أ-ث-ر (ʾ-th-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Trace, mark, or impression left by something; transmission of a report.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for a cause (ʿillah) whose efficacy in the ruling is attested by explicit text (naṣṣ) or consensus (ijmāʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical trace; metaphorical for the proven causal efficacy of a legal attribute.
- Root: ل-ء-م (l-ʾ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be fitting, suitable, harmonious, or congruent with something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A cause whose specific efficacy is unproven, but whose genus (jins) is attested as a ground for similar rulings in the Sharīʿah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical compatibility; metaphorical for the harmony of a legal cause with the general pattern of divine legislation.
- Root: غ-ر-ب (gh-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be remote, distant, unfamiliar, or strange.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A cause that is proportionate to the ruling but has neither proven specific efficacy nor proven congruence with the genus of legal rulings.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial remoteness; metaphorical for a legal attribute that is alien to the established methods of the Lawgiver.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Conditional Suspension) and Taqābūl (Contrastive Pairing) — The sentence structure frequently employs conditional clauses (sharṭ) and contrastive oppositions (muqābalah) to delineate the boundaries between the three categories of munāsib, requiring the translator to preserve the logical force of each protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sufficiency of mere appropriateness (al-munāsabah) in establishing a ruling is a matter of disagreement. From this arises the question of what is meant by "appropriate" (al-munāsib): it is that which follows the pattern of human interests (maṣāliḥ), such that when the ruling is attached to it, the matter is properly ordered. Our example is our saying: "Wine is prohibited because it removes the intellect, which is the very locus of legal obligation (manāṭ al-taklīf)" — this is appropriate. It is not like our saying: "It is prohibited because it casts up foam," or "because it is preserved in a cask" — for that is not appropriate.

We have already mentioned the reality of the appropriate meaning, its divisions, and its ranks at the end of the second pole (al-quṭb al-thānī) in the chapter on juristic preference (al-istiḥsān) and public welfare (al-istiṣlāḥ), so we shall not repeat it. Rather, we say: The appropriate meaning (al-munāsib) divides into the effective (muʾaththir), the congruent (mulāʾim), and the strange (gharīb).

An example of the effective (al-muʾaththir): the causal explanation of guardianship (al-wilāyah) by minority (al-ṣighar). The meaning of its being "effective" is that its efficacy in the ruling has become manifest through consensus (ijmāʿ) or explicit text (naṣṣ). When its efficacy is manifest, there is no need for appropriateness. Rather, his saying — peace be upon him — «Whoever touches his penis, let him perform ablution» (man massa dhakarahu fa-l-yatawaḍḍaʾ), since it indicated the efficacy of touching, we analogize to it the touching of another's penis.

As for the congruent (al-mulāʾim), it is an expression for that whose specific efficacy in that specific ruling has not become manifest — as in the case of minority — but the efficacy of its genus (jins) in the genus of that ruling has become manifest. Its example is his saying — peace be upon him — that the menstruating woman is not obligated to make up the prayer (al-ṣalāh) but is obligated to make up the fast (al-ṣawm), due to the hardship (al-ḥaraj) in making up the prayer because of its frequency. Now, the efficacy of its genus has become manifest, for the genus of hardship has an efficacy in bringing about leniency (al-takhfīf). But as for this specific hardship itself — namely, the hardship of repetition — its efficacy has not become manifest in another place. Indeed, had the text (al-naṣṣ) come down regarding the non-obligation of making up prayer for free menstruating women, and we analogized slave women to them, that would have been a causal explanation by that whose specific efficacy in the specific ruling had become manifest — but in a particular locus — and we would have transferred it to another locus.

Another example of it is our saying: The small amount of nabīdh (date-wine), even if it does not intoxicate, is prohibited by analogy to the small amount of wine (khamr). Our causal explanation of the small amount of wine is that it invites to its large amount. This is an appropriate meaning whose specific efficacy has not become manifest, but the efficacy of its genus has become manifest — for when seclusion (al-khalwah) was an invitation to fornication (al-zinā), the Law prohibited it just as it prohibited fornication. Thus this was congruent with the genus of the Law's actions, even if its specific efficacy in the ruling did not become manifest.

As for the strange (al-gharīb) — that whose efficacy has not become manifest, nor its congruence with the genus of the Law's actions — its example is our saying: Wine was only prohibited because it is intoxicating (muskir), and in its meaning is everything intoxicating. Yet the effect of intoxication has not become manifest in another place, but it is appropriate. This is an example of the strange, were it not for the indication (al-tanbīh) in His saying — exalted be He: {«Indeed, Satan only desires to cast between you enmity and hatred through wine»} [al-Māʾidah: 91].

Another example of it is our saying: The woman divorced three times during the death-illness (marad al-mawt) inherits, because the husband intended to flee from her inheritance, so he is countered by the opposite of his intention (nuqīḍ qaṣdihi), by analogy to the killer (al-qātil), who does not inherit because he hastened the inheritance, so he was countered by the opposite of his intention. For the causal explanation of the killer's deprivation (al-ḥirmān) by this is an explanation by an appropriate meaning that is not congruent with the genus of the Law's actions; for we do not see the Law in another place having paid attention to its genus. Thus it remains a bare, strange appropriateness.

But if the deprivation were explained by his being an aggressor (mutʿaddī) through the killing, and this were made a recompense for the aggression, it would be an explanation by a congruent appropriate meaning, not an effective one — because the specific injury (al-jināyah), even if its efficacy has become manifest in punishments (al-ʿuqūbāt), has not become manifest in deprivation from inheritance. Thus it did not effect the specific ruling; it only effected another genus of rulings. So it belongs to the genus of the congruent, not the genus of the effective, nor the genus of the strange.

Now that you have recognized the examples of these three divisions, know that the effective (al-muʾaththir) is accepted by agreement of those who affirm analogy (al-qiyās). Abū Zayd al-Dabūsī restricted analogy to it, saying: "Only the effective is accepted." However, he adduced examples of the effective by which it is known that he accepted the congruent — but he also called it "effective." We have mentioned the detailed examples of this and the objections against them in our book Shifāʾ al-Ghalīl.

There is no way to restrict [analogy] to the effective alone, because what is sought is preponderant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann). Whoever surveys the analogies of the Companions — may God be pleased with them — and their juristic exertions (ijtihādāt) knows that they did not stipulate in every analogy that the cause be known by text (naṣṣ) and consensus (ijmāʿ).

As for the strange appropriate meaning (al-munāsib al-gharīb), this is a locus of ijtihād. It is not far in my view that it may produce preponderant conjecture for some mujtahids, and no decisive proof (dalīl qāṭiʿ) indicates the invalidity of his ijtihād.

If it is said: "What indicates its invalidity is that he is being arbitrary (mutahakkim) in his causal explanation without any evidence testifying to the attachment of the ruling to its cause," we say: The establishment of the ruling in accordance with it (ʿalā wa-fqihi) testifies to the Law's consideration of it and produces preponderant conjecture.

If it is said: "Your statement — 'the establishment of the ruling in accordance with it' — is obfuscation (talbīs), for its meaning is that the ruling demanded the ruling through appropriateness, and the Lawgiver was impelled to the ruling, so He answered its impulsion and the ruling arose in accordance with His impulsion. This is arbitrariness (taḥakkum), because it is possible that the Law's ruling prohibiting wine was a pure devotional ordinance (taʿabbud) and an arbitrary determination (taḥakkum), like the prohibition of pork, carrion, blood, domesticated donkeys, every beast of prey with fangs, and every bird with talons — while the hyena and fox are deemed lawful in some schools — these being arbitrary determinations. But the meaning of intoxication happened to coincide in wine, so it was thought that it was for the sake of intoxication, while no such thing coincided in carrion and pork, so it was said that it is arbitrary."

This is on the supposition of the absence of the indication (al-tanbīh) in the Qurʾān mentioning enmity and hatred. And it is possible that there is another appropriate meaning that has not become manifest to us, and it is possible that it is for intoxication. These are three possibilities. To rule by one of these three is arbitrariness without evidence. Otherwise, by what does this possibility become preponderant? This does not apply to the effective (al-muʾaththir), for it is known to be a cause by the attachment of the ruling to it through text or consensus — like minority, and the precedence of the brother over the father and mother [in inheritance].

The answer: We preponderate this possibility over the possibility of arbitrariness by what we used to refute the school of the deniers of analogy (munkirū al-qiyās) — just as in the case of the effective. For when the ruling is attached to a cause in one locus, it is possible that it is specific to that locus, just as the efficacy of fornication (al-zinā) is specific to the married person (al-muḥṣan) and the efficacy of theft (al-sariqah) is specific to the nisāb (minimum threshold). Thus it is not far that minority effects guardianship over property but not guardianship over marriage (al-buḍʿ), and that the mixing of brotherhood effects precedence in inheritance but not in guardianship. It is by this that the deniers of analogy clung. It was said to them: "It is known from the Companions — may God be pleased with them — that they followed causes (al-ʿilal) and discarded the application of the Law to arbitrariness as much as possible." So likewise here, and there is no difference.

As for their saying: "Perhaps there is in it another appropriate meaning that is the impeller of the Lawgiver, but it has not become manifest to us; our souls merely inclined to the meaning that became manifest due to the non-manifestation of the other, not due to any evidence indicating it" — this is pure illusion (wahm). We say: Preponderant conjecture in every place is based on such an illusion and relies on the non-manifestation of another meaning — for were it to become manifest, the preponderant conjecture would be invalidated. If this door were opened, no analogy would stand. For the cause that unites the branch (al-farʿ) and the root (al-aṣl), even if it is effective, only produces preponderant conjecture due to the absence of a manifest difference (al-farq). Perhaps there is in it a meaning which, were it to become manifest, would remove the preponderant conjecture from it. And due to the absence of a conflicting cause (ʿillah muʿāriḍah) to that cause. For were another root to become manifest testifying for the branch with another cause contradicting the first cause, the preponderant conjecture would be repelled. Rather, conjecture arises from the forms of generality (ṣiyagh al-ʿumūm) and apparent meanings (al-ẓawāhir) on the condition of the absence of a specifying indicator (qarīnah mukhaṣṣiṣah) — were it to become manifest, the conjecture would cease. But when it does not become manifest, reliance upon it is permissible. This is because nothing has become manifest to us from the consensus of the Companions — may God be pleased with them — on ijtihād except the following of the preponderant opinion (al-raʾy al-aghlab). Otherwise, they did not delimit the genera of preponderant conjecture, nor did they distinguish one genus from another. If you concede that conjecture arises from mere appropriateness, then following it becomes obligatory.

If it is said: "We do not concede that this is conjecture (ẓann); rather, it is pure illusion (wahm). For arbitrariness is possible, and another appropriate meaning not manifest to us is possible, and this meaning that became manifest is possible. The human illusion (wahm) is inclined to seek a cause and reason for every ruling; then it races to what became manifest to it and judges that nothing exists except what became manifest to it. Thus his soul judges that there must be a cause, and there is no cause except this — so it is the cause." His statement "there must be a cause" — even if we concede it and do not apply it to arbitrariness, and we say "without cause and without reason" — his statement "there is no cause except this" is an arbitrariness whose basis is that he only knew this one, so he made his ignorance of another cause a knowledge of the non-existence of another cause — and this is an error.

By this very method you invalidated the doctrine of the implied meaning (al-mafhūm). For the basis of its proponent is that there must be an impeller for the specification (al-takhṣīṣ), and no impeller became manifest to us except the specificity of the ruling — so it is the impeller. For you said: "How do you know that there is no impeller other than it? Perhaps an impeller for the specification impelled Him that has not become manifest to you?" This speech falls within the possibility of causal explanation by an appropriate meaning that neither effects nor is congruent.

The answer: This is drawing from the source of the deniers of analogy, and it applies equally to the effective and the congruent. For the conjecture arising from them is also confronted by the possibility of arbitrariness, the possibility of a difference (farq) that may suggest itself, and the possibility of a conflicting cause to this cause in the branch. There is no difference between these possibilities. Were it not for them, the annexation (al-ilḥāq) would not be conjectural but rather certain — like annexing the slave woman (al-ummah) to the slave (al-ʿabd), and understanding beating (al-ḍarb) from [the word] "uff" (al-taʾfīf) [in the verse «Do not say to them 'uff'»].

The statement of the objector — "This is illusion (wahm), not conjecture (ẓann)" — is not so. For illusion (al-wahm) is an expression for the inclination of the soul without a preponderating cause (sabab murajjīḥ), while conjecture (al-ẓann) is an expression for inclination with a cause. Whoever bases his affairs in worldly transactions on illusion is deficient in his intellect; whoever bases them on conjecture is excused. Thus, if one disposes of a child's property based on illusion, he is liable (ḍamina); if he disposes based on conjecture, he is not liable. Whoever sees the mount of the chief (al-raʾīs) at the gate of the sultan's house and believes that the chief is not in his house but in the sultan's house, and builds his interest upon that, is not deemed deluded (mutawahhim) — even though it is possible that the chief lent his mount, or that the groom rode it on some errand. Whoever sees the chief order his servant to beat a man, and he knew that the man had been insulting the chief, and he interpreted the beating as [a punishment for] his insulting him, he is excused. Whoever sees a goat (māʿiz) confess to fornication, then sees the Prophet — peace be upon him — order its stoning, and believes that he ordered its stoning for its fornication, and narrates that, he is excused as one conjecturing (ẓānn), not deluded. Whoever knows a person to be a spy (jāsūs), then sees the sultan order his execution, and interprets it accordingly, is not deluded.

If it is said: "No, rather he is deluded. For if he knew of the chief's habit of repaying evil with good, and that he does not beat those who insult him, and he knew of the commander's habit of overlooking the spy — either out of disdain or out of winning him over — then he saw him execute a spy and judged that he executed him for his espionage, he is deluded and arbitrary. But if he knew of his habit [of punishing], then his consistent habit is a sign testifying to his conjectural judgment. Its analogue in our question is the congruent (al-mulāʾim) to whose like the Law has paid attention, and from whose habit the consideration of its specific instance or its genus is known. But our discussion is about the strange (al-gharīb) that is neither congruent nor effective."

The answer: Here there are three ranks. The first: that it be known that the chief's habit is to do good to the wrongdoer, and the commander's habit is to overlook the spy — this prevents the causal explanation of the beating and execution by insult and espionage. Its analogue is to explain a ruling by an appropriate meaning from which the Law has turned away and by which it ruled the opposite of its implication (naqīḍ mūjibihi). This is not to be relied upon, for just as the Law has paid attention to interests (maṣāliḥ), it has also turned away from interests; what it has turned away from is not to be used as a cause.

The second: that it be known that the habit of the chief and the commander is to beat the insulter and execute the spy. Its analogue is the congruent (al-mulāʾim), and this is accepted by agreement of the proponents of analogy (al-qāʾisūn). The consideration is only in a third rank: one of whom no habit is known at all regarding the insulter and the spy. We know that he beat and executed — the conjectures of rational people preponderate toward attributing it to him and that he followed the path of requital (al-mukāfaʾah), because the crime is proportionate to the punishment.

If it is said: "Because the predominant habit of kings is that, and the predominant [fact] is that their natures are similar," we say: There is nothing in this except taking the predominant (al-akthar). Likewise, the predominant habit of the Law in non-devotional matters (ghayr al-ʿibādāt) is the following of appropriateness and interests, not rigid arbitrariness. Thus, applying its ruling to that is more preponderant in conjecture.

It remains to be said: "Perhaps He ruled by another appropriate meaning not manifest to us." We say: What we have investigated to the best of our effort and have not found is, for us, non-existent. The mujtahid is not obligated to anything beyond that. Upon this the analogies of the Companions indicate, and the adherence to the effective and the congruent. For the saying of the Prophet — peace be upon him — «What do you think, if you had rinsed your mouth?» (araʾayta law tamammaḍta?) means: "Why did you not understand that the kiss (al-qublah) is the prelude to intercourse (al-wiqāʿ), and rinsing the mouth is the prelude to drinking?" For if ʿUmar had said: "Perhaps you pardoned the rinsing due to a specific property in rinsing, or an appropriate meaning not manifest to me, and that is not realized in the kiss," that would not have been accepted from him, and it would have been deemed contentious disputation (mujādalah). Likewise his saying: «What do you think, if your father had a debt and you paid it?» And likewise every analogy transmitted from the Companions.

In sum: When the door of analogy is opened, precise delimitation (al-ḍabṭ) thereafter is impossible. Rather, conjecture is followed, and conjecture has ranks. The strongest of them is the effective (al-muʾaththir), for nothing opposes it except the possibility of causal explanation by the specification of the locus (takhṣīṣ al-maḥall). Below it is the congruent (al-mulāʾim). Below it is the appropriate meaning that is not congruent — and this too has degrees, even if it is weak. It varies according to the strength of the appropriateness, and it may produce conjecture for some mujtahids in some places, so its invalidity is not to be decisively asserted.

It is impossible to delimit the degrees of appropriateness at all; rather, each case has its own taste (dhawq) that the mujtahid must consider.

As for the implied meaning (al-mafhūm), it is not far either that it may produce preponderant conjecture for some mujtahids in some places. At that point, it becomes difficult to ascertain whether that conjecture arose from mere specification alone or from it together with an indicator (qarīnah). Thus it is not far to say: It is a locus of ijtihād, not a matter of certainty. For it has become manifest to us that the form of generality (ṣīghat al-ʿumūm) by itself, when stripped of indicators, yields generality. But this is not understood from the mere wording of specification (lafẓ al-takhṣīṣ), even if it may suggest itself to the mind in some places. Let that also be a locus of ijtihād.

From this it follows that the meaning, considered in terms of congruence (al-mulāʾamah) and the testimony of a specific root (shahādat al-aṣl al-muʿayyan), is of four divisions:

1. A congruent meaning (mulāʾim) testified to by a specific root — this is accepted definitively by the proponents of analogy.
2. An appropriate meaning that is not congruent and is not testified to by a specific root — this is not accepted definitively by the proponents of analogy, for it is juristic preference (istiḥsān) and the imposition of law by opinion (waḍʿ lil-sharʿ bi-al-raʾy). Its example is the deprivation of the killer [from inheritance] were no text to have come down regarding it, by countering him with the opposite of his intention — this is imposing law by opinion.
3. An appropriate meaning testified to by a specific root but not congruent — this is a locus of ijtihād.
4. A congruent meaning not testified to by a specific root — this is the unrestricted inference (al-istidlāl al-mursal), and it too is a locus of ijtihād. We have mentioned it in the chapter on public welfare (al-istiṣlāḥ) at the end of the second pole, and we have explained its ranks.

### | [القول في المسالك الفاسدة في إثبات علة الأصل]

وهي ثلاثة
الأول: أن نقول: الدليل على صحة علة الأصل سلامتها عن علة تعارضها تقتضي
نقيض حكمها، وسلامتها عن المعارضة دليل صحتها.
وهذا فاسد؛ لأنه إن سلم عنه فإنما سلم عن مفسد واحد فربما لا يسلم عن
مفسد آخر، وإن سلم عن كل مفسد أيضا لم يدل على صحته، كما لم نسلم شهادة
المجهول عن علة قادحة لا يدل على كونه حجة ما لم تقم بينة معدلة مزكية،
فكذلك لا يكفي للصحة انتفاء المفسد بل لا بد من قيام الدليل على الصحة. فإن
قيل: دليل صحتها انتفاء المفسد. قلنا: لا بل دليل فساده انتفاء المصحح،
فهذا منقلب ولا فرق بين الكلامين
المسلك الثاني: الاستدلال على صحتها باطرادها وجريانها في حكمها وهذا لا
معنى له إلا سلامتها عن مفسد واحد. وهو النقض فهو كقول القائل زيد عالم؛
لأنه دليل يفسد دعوى العلم، ويعارضه أنه جاهل؛ لأنه لا دليل يفسد دعوى
الجهل.
والحق أنه لا يعلم كونه عالما بانتفاء دليل الجهل ولا كونه جاهلا  بانتفاء
دليل العلم بل يتوقف فيه إلى ظهور الدليل، فكذلك الصحة والفساد. فإن قيل
ثبوت حكمها معها واقترانه بها دليل على كونها علة.
قلنا: غلطتم في قولكم ثبوت حكمها؛ لأن هذه إضافة للحكم لا تثبت إلا بعد
قيام الدليل على كونها علة، فإذا لم يثبت لم يكن حكمها بل بحال غلبة الظن
عليه كان حكم علته، واقترن بها، والاقتران لا يدل على الإضافة، فقد يلزم
الخمر لون وطعم يقترن به التحريم ويطرد وينعكس والعلة الشدة واقترانه بما
ليس بعلة كاقتران الأحكام بطلوع كوكب وهبوب ريح، وبالجملة فنصب العلة مذهب
يفتقر إلى دليل كوضع الحكم ولا يكفي في إثبات الحكم أنه لا نقض عليه ولا
مفسد له بل لا بد من دليل فكذلك العلة.
المسلك الثالث الطرد والعكس وقد قال قوم: الوصف إذا ثبت الحكم معه، وزال
مع زواله يدل على أنه علة.
وهو فاسد؛ لأن الرائحة المخصوصة مقرونة بالشدة في الخمر، ويزول التحريم
عند زوالها ويتجدد عند تجددها وليس بعلة بل هو مقترن بالعلة، وهذا؛ لأن
الوجود عند الوجود طرد محض فزيادة العكس لا تؤثر؛ لأن العكس ليس بشرط في
العلل الشرعية فلا أثر لوجوده وعدمه؛ ولأن زواله عند زواله يحتمل أن يكون
لملازمته للعلة كالرائحة أو لكونه جزءا من أجزاء العلة وشرطا من شروطها
والحكم ينفي بعض شروط العلة وبعض أجزائها فإذا تعارضت الاحتمالات فلا معنى
للتحكم، وعلى الجملة فنسلم أن ما ثبت الحكم بثبوته فهو علة، فكيف إذا انضم
إليه أنه زال بزواله؟ أما ما ثبت مع ثبوته وزال مع زواله فلا يلزم كونه
علة، كالرائحة المخصوصة مع الشدة.
أما إذا انضم إليه سبر وتقسيم كان ذلك حجة كما لو قال: هذا الحكم لا بد
له من علة؛ لأنه حدث بحدوث حادث ولا حادث يمكن أن يعلل به إلا كذا، وكذا
وقد بطل الكل إلا هذا فهو العلة، ومثل هذا السبر حجة في الطرد المحض وإن لم
ينضم إليه العكس. ولا يرد على هذا إلا أنه ربما شذ  عنه وصف آخر هو العلة،
ولا يجب على المجتهد إلا سبر بحسب وسعه، ولا يجب على الناظر غير ذلك وعلى
من يدعي وصفا آخر إبرازه حتى ينظر فيه.
فإن قيل: فما معنى إبطالكم التمسك بالطرد والعكس وقد رأيتم تصويب
المجتهدين، وقد غلب هذا على ظن قوم؟ فإن قلتم لا يجوز لهم الحكم به فمحال
إذ ليس على المجتهد إلا الحكم بالظن، وإن قلتم لم يغلب على ظنهم فمحال؛ لأن
هذا قد غلب على ظن قوم لولاه لما حكموا به.
قلنا: أجاب القاضي - رحمه الله - عن هذا بأن قال: نعني بإبطاله أنه باطل
في حقنا؛ لأنه لم يصح عندنا ولم يغلب على ظننا، أما من غلب على ظنه فهو
صحيح في حقه.
وهذا فيه نظر عندي؛ لأن المجتهد مصيب إذا استوفى النظر وأتمه، وأما إذا
قضى بسابق الرأي وبادئ الوهم فهو مخطئ، فإن سبر وقسم فقد أتم النظر وأصاب.
أما حكمه قبل السبر والتقسيم بأن ما اقترن بشيء ينبغي أن يكون علة فيه
تحكم ووهم، إذ تمام دليله أن ما اقترن بشيء فهو علته وهذا قد اقترن به فهو
إذا علته، والمقدمة الأولى منقوضة بالطم والرم فإذا كأنه لم ينظر ولم يتمم
النظر ولم يعثر على مناسبة العلة ولم يتوصل إليه بالسبر والتقسيم.
ومن كشف هذا لم يبق له غلبة ظن بالطرد المجرد إلا أن يكون جاهلا ناقص
الرتبة عن درجة المجتهدين، ومن اجتهد وليس أهلا له فهو مخطئ، وليس كذلك
عندي المناسب الغريب واستدلال المرسل فإن ذلك مما يوجب الظن لبعض المجتهدين
وليس يقوم فيه دليل قاطع، من عرفه محق ظنه بخلاف الطرد المجرد الذي ليس معه
سبر وتقسيم.
هذا تمام القول في قياس العلة، ولنشرع في قياس الشبه.

chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ل-م (salima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freedom from defect; soundness; safety from harm or corruption
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, denotes the absence of countervailing evidence against a legal indicator, not positive establishment of validity
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical safety; here used metaphorically (majāz) for epistemic immunity from objection
- Root: ط-ر-د (ṭarada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Continuous succession; uninterrupted flow; regularity of occurrence
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for the constant concomitance of a descriptive attribute with a legal ruling across all cases
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: chasing away; metaphorical: the uniform application of a legal attribute without exception
- Root: ع-ك-س (ʿakasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Reversal; inversion; turning back
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic method, the converse relation — the ruling's absence when the attribute is absent
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: to reflect (as a mirror); metaphorical: the reciprocal entailment between attribute and ruling
- Root: س-ب-ر (sabra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Probing; testing; examining a wound with a probe
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The jurist's exhaustive survey of all possible attributes to isolate the sole valid ratio legis
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: medical probing; metaphorical: systematic elimination of candidate causes in juristic investigation
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ḥukm ʿalā al-waṣf (Conditional suspension of judgment on an attribute) — The syntactic structure "if X then Y" (sharṭ wa jazāʾ) governs the logical relation between attribute and ruling, requiring positive proof of causation, not mere concomitance.
chapters.translation:
### | [Discourse on the Corrupt Methods of Establishing the Validity of the Root's Ratio Legis]

These are three.

**The First:** That we say: The evidence for the validity of the root's ratio legis (ʿillah) is its freedom from any countervailing ratio legis that would necessitate the negation of its ruling, and its freedom from opposition is evidence of its validity.

This is corrupt; because if it is free from one particular corrupting factor, perhaps it is not free from another corrupting factor. And even if it were free from every corrupting factor, that would not indicate its validity — just as we do not accept the testimony of an unknown person (majhūl) merely because no impeaching defect (qādiḥah) is established against him; that does not prove he is an authoritative witness (ḥujjah) unless a justificatory, purifying evidence (bayyinah muʿaddilah muzakkiyah) is established. Likewise, for validity, the mere absence of a corrupting factor is insufficient; rather, positive evidence for validity must be established. If it is said: "The evidence of its validity is the absence of the corrupting factor," we say: No — rather, the evidence of its corruption is the absence of the validating factor. This is inverted, and there is no difference between the two statements.

**The Second Method:** Arguing for its validity by its constant application (iṭṭirād) and its running uniformly in its ruling. This has no meaning other than its freedom from one single corrupting factor, namely the objection of counter-example (naqḍ). It is like one who says: "Zayd is knowledgeable, because there is no evidence that corrupts the claim of knowledge," and it is countered that he is ignorant, "because there is no evidence that corrupts the claim of ignorance." The truth is that one does not know he is knowledgeable by the absence of evidence for ignorance, nor that he is ignorant by the absence of evidence for knowledge; rather, one suspends judgment until evidence appears. So likewise with validity and corruption. If it is said: "The establishment of its ruling along with it, and its conjunction with it, is evidence that it is the ratio legis," we say: You have erred in your statement "the establishment of its ruling"; for this is an attribution (iḍāfah) of the ruling that is not established except after evidence arises that it is the ratio legis. When that is not established, it is not its ruling; rather, by way of predominant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann) it is the ruling of its ratio legis, and it is conjoined with it. But conjunction does not indicate attribution. For wine has a color and taste that are conjoined with its prohibition, and this runs uniformly and conversely, while the ratio legis is the intoxicating potency (shiddah). And the conjunction of a ruling with what is not its ratio legis is like the conjunction of rulings with the rising of a star or the blowing of a wind. In sum, the installation of a ratio legis (naṣb al-ʿillah) is a doctrine that requires evidence, just as the establishment of a ruling does. It is not sufficient for establishing a ruling that there is no counter-example against it and no corrupting factor; rather, evidence is indispensable. So likewise for the ratio legis.

**The Third Method:** Constant application and converse (al-ṭard wa al-ʿaks). Some have said: When a descriptive attribute is such that the ruling is established with it and ceases with its cessation, this indicates that it is the ratio legis.

This is corrupt; because the specific odor is conjoined with the intoxicating potency in wine, and the prohibition ceases with its cessation and is renewed with its renewal — yet it is not the ratio legis but merely conjoined with the ratio legis. This is because existence alongside existence is pure constant application (ṭard maḥḍ); the addition of the converse has no effect, because the converse is not a condition in legal ratios legis, so neither its existence nor its absence has any effect. And because its cessation upon its cessation may be due to its inseparability from the ratio legis — like the odor — or because it is a part of the parts of the ratio legis or a condition of its conditions, and the ruling is negated by the negation of some conditions of the ratio legis and some of its parts. When the probabilities conflict, there is no meaning to arbitrary assertion (taḥakkum). In sum, we concede that whatever is established by the establishment of the ruling is a ratio legis — how then when it is added that it ceases with its cessation? As for that which is established with its establishment and ceases with its cessation, it does not necessarily follow that it is the ratio legis — like the specific odor with the intoxicating potency.

However, when there is added to it a comprehensive survey and division (sabr wa taqsīm), it becomes a proof (ḥujjah). For example, if one says: "This ruling must have a ratio legis, because it originated with the origination of some event (ḥādith), and there is no event by which it can be causally explained except such-and-such; and all have been invalidated except this one — so it is the ratio legis." Such a survey is a proof in pure constant application, even if the converse is not added to it. Nothing can be objected to this except that perhaps another attribute has escaped him which is the true ratio legis. But the mujtahid is only obligated to survey according to his capacity, and the investigator is not obligated beyond that. And whoever claims another attribute must produce it so that it may be examined.

If it is said: "What is the meaning of your invalidating adherence to constant application and converse, when you have affirmed the correctness (taṣwīb) of the mujtahids, and this has prevailed as predominant conjecture for some people? If you say they are not permitted to judge by it, that is impossible — for the mujtahid is only obligated to judge by conjecture. And if you say it did not prevail as their predominant conjecture, that too is impossible — for this has prevailed as predominant conjecture for some people; otherwise they would not have judged by it."

We say: The Judge (al-Qāḍī) — may God have mercy on him — answered this by saying: "We mean by its invalidation that it is invalid with respect to us; because it has not been established as sound for us, nor has it prevailed as our predominant conjecture. As for the one for whom it has prevailed as predominant conjecture, it is valid with respect to him."

But this is subject to scrutiny in my view; because the mujtahid is correct (muṣīb) when he exhausts his investigation and completes it. But when he judges by prior opinion (sābiq al-raʾy) and initial conjecture (bādiʾ al-wahm), he is mistaken (mukhṭiʾ). For if he surveys and divides, he has completed the investigation and hit the mark. As for his judgment before survey and division — that whatever is conjoined with something ought to be its ratio legis — this is arbitrary assertion and conjecture; for the completion of his proof is: "Whatever is conjoined with something is its ratio legis; and this is conjoined with it; therefore it is its ratio legis." But the first premise is refuted by the cases of saliva (al-ṭam) and ashes (al-ram). Thus it is as if he did not investigate, did not complete the investigation, did not stumble upon the suitability (munāsabah) of the ratio legis, and did not arrive at it through survey and division.

And whoever uncovers this will have no remaining predominant conjecture in favor of bare constant application — unless he is an ignorant person deficient in rank below the degree of the mujtahids. And whoever engages in ijtihād without being qualified for it is mistaken. But this is not the case, in my view, with the suitable-but-strange (al-munāsib al-gharīb) and the argument of the mursal (al-istidlāl al-mursal); for that necessitates conjecture for some mujtahids, and no decisive proof stands against it. Whoever recognizes it has a justified conjecture — unlike bare constant application that has no survey and division with it.

This completes the discourse on the analogy of the ratio legis (qiyās al-ʿillah). Let us now commence on the analogy of resemblance (qiyās al-shabah).
